### Phare
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/phare-e849) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Red3lue/Phare-protocol) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://phare-protocol-orbital-orchestrator.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/McyekAYVnkc) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-5-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> What satellites can't see, citizens can

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![claude](https://img.shields.io/badge/claude-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenClaw](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenClaw-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Phare is a bonded, citizen-powered registry for sightings of sanctioned oil tankers, ships that move sanctioned cargo by disabling their AIS transponders and going dark. Anyone with a phone can photograph a suspicious vessel, upload the photo to Swarm, and submit a bonded on-chain report from their wallet. The protocol holds the bond in escrow, opens a UMA OOv3 optimistic assertion, and runs a challenge window. Verifier agents running the OpenClaw skill race to dispute fakes; reports that survive settlement are recorded permanently.

- For reporters: an ordinary citizen in Cyprus or a sailor in the Laconian Gulf can document a vessel that has no official record anywhere. No account, no KYC, no permission. The PWA handles photo capture, Swarm upload, wallet approval, and auto-settlement in one flow.

For journalists, NGOs, and enforcement bodies: every sanctioned vessel that survives adjudication acquires a permanent ENS identity that any browser can resolve. The records include the satellite orbital corroboration from SpaceComputer, signed on-chain by the KMS key. The full dossier lives on Swarm, pointer in the ENS contenthash.

For verifier operators: anyone can run the phare/verifier OpenClaw skill, self-register an ENS subname, and earn 50% of slashed bonds when they successfully dispute fake reports. The agent writes its reasoning JSON to Swarm and updates its own ENS verifier.lastDecision record after every dispute, a live, public accountability trail.

**Challenges we ran into**

1. USDC was the bond currency until it wasn't.
The original spec pinned USDC as the bond currency for ReportRegistry. After probing UMA OOv3's Sepolia AddressWhitelist and calling getMinimumBond, we discovered the UMA minimum bond for that USDC token on Sepolia is 400 USDC, completely impractical for a $5-equivalent demo bond. We switched to WETH, which has a minimum bond of 0.002 WETH (a few dollars), and rebuilt the escrow and faucet instructions around it. Mainnet deployment can revisit USDC.

2. NameStone was replaced by an on-chain contract mid-design.
The original spec used NameStone's off-chain CCIP-Read resolver for all ENS minting; no gas per mint, but a centralized write key held by the project. As the ENS integration deepened, we realised that CCIP-Read off-chain resolvers don't support on-chain writes initiated by smart contracts: ReportRegistry cannot call a NameStone API from inside a Solidity callback. The entire minter service and the off-chain NameStone path were replaced with Lighthouse.sol; an 80-line on-chain contract that calls NameWrapper directly and is the sole write authority for both vessel and verifier subnames. This was a significant mid-flight redesign but resulted in a cleaner and more prize-competitive integration.

3. spaceTEE doesn't exist yet.
The SpaceComputer architecture documents a spaceTEE inference layer that would let a satellite-hosted TEE predict vessel destinations from imagery. We designed the full integration (plugin methods, inference JSON schema, on-chain attestation) then discovered spaceTEE is on the SpaceComputer roadmap but not yet shipped. Rather than drop the integration, we built the call site honestly: the phare-imager Orbitport plugin exposes the full four-method JSON-RPC interface, but underneath it returns fixture imagery and a rule-based destination prediction that always carries "mocked": true. The KMS signing and on-chain attest() are real; the inference is mock-now-real-later. The plugin is the contribution SpaceComputer can wire to real hardware.

**Future Society**

Phare is built for the Future Society track in the most direct sense: it is civic infrastructure for ecological accountability, owned by no one, built bottom-up.

The shadow fleet causes sanctions failure, war financing, and uninsured ecological disasters. When these ships spill or sink there is no liable party, no insurance, no clean-up. Outside expensive government surveillance budgets, almost no one can see them.

Phare replaces institutional surveillance with a citizen-funded, privacy-respecting sighting network. Anyone with a phone opens the PWA, photographs a vessel, and submits a bonded report; no account, no KYC, no permission. The bond is the background check. Autonomous verifier agents dispute fakes; reports that survive become permanent ENS identities that journalists, NGOs, and enforcement bodies can query forever, with no project-controlled API in the resolution path.

Orbital corroboration from SpaceComputer adds a second layer of evidence: after settlement, the phare-imager plugin tasks satellite imagery over the reported coordinates, the SpaceComputer KMS signs the attestation digest, and ReportRegistry.attest() writes the corroboration on-chain signed by space, verifiable by anyone.

Reporter privacy is explicit: anonymous EOA, rotatable per report, no off-chain authentication at any layer that touches a citizen.

This is the solarpunk thesis applied to maritime accountability: bonds replace permission lists, decentralised storage replaces proprietary databases, citizen observation plus orbital corroboration replaces satellite monopolies.

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

Phare integrates SpaceComputer across three real surfaces, with two mocked layers that are explicitly labelled and have a clear path to becoming real once SpaceComputer ships the underlying hardware capability.

What is real and ships today:

- phare-imager is a new Orbitport Application Plugin: the first photo-tasking plugin published to the Orbitport ecosystem. It conforms to JSON-RPC 2.0 over the Orbitport gateway with Client ID + Secret authentication and exposes four methods: imagery request, imagery-ready callback, inference request, and inference-ready callback. No imaging plugin existed in the Orbitport ecosystem before this. The plugin defines the shape of the integration that SpaceComputer can wire to real celestial-layer cameras later.

- ReportRegistry.attest(reportId, imageSwarm, imageHash, teePrediction, signature) is a real, immutable on-chain function. It verifies an EIP-191 signature via ecrecover against orbitalAttestor: a SpaceComputer KMS-derived Ethereum address hardcoded at deploy time. The KMS ETHEREUM key scheme produces secp256k1 signatures that are natively verifiable on any EVM chain without a custom precompile. Every orbital corroboration in Phare is signed by the live KMS endpoint and verified on-chain. This is not mocked.

What is mocked and why:

- Satellite imagery is fixture-keyed by coordinate: pre-curated Sentinel-2 ESA scenes for the demo locations. spaceTEE inference is a rule-based stub (imo % ports.length) that always returns "mocked": true in the inference JSON. SpaceComputer's own architecture documentation confirms spaceTEE is on the roadmap but not yet shipped, there is no production endpoint to call. The mock is honest, labelled, and separated cleanly from the real KMS signing so judges can see exactly what is real.

The cross-track combination: Orbitport Application Plugin (new ecosystem contribution) + KMS ETHEREUM signing wired into an immutable smart contract. SpaceComputer's bounty criteria reward cross-track builds explicitly, this hits both the Application layer and the Security API layer in one integration.

**Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway**

Phare uses Swarm as the storage layer for every artefact that matters to the protocol: reporter photos, metadata JSON, vessel dossiers, verifier policy and soul documents, reasoning JSONs pinned at dispute time, and orbital imagery. Every one of these is content-addressed, the reference baked into the on-chain report is a commitment to specific bytes, not a location.

The PWA uploads photo and metadata via bee-js, receiving BMT root references that are passed directly to ReportRegistry.submit(). The on-chain photoHash is independently computed as keccak256(photoBytes), giving consumers two cryptographic anchors per report: the BMT root (what Swarm committed to) and the keccak256 (what the reporter photographed). Both must match the fetched bytes.

The orbital orchestrator fetches imagery via the orbitalImager-sdk and pins the result to Swarm before calling attest(). The orbitalImageHash stored on-chain by ReportRegistry.attest() is the independent hash of the orbital image bytes so on-chain verification doesn't require trusting the Swarm gateway at all.

The swarm/ module defines the shared Verified Fetch interface used across the minter, verifier skill, and orbital orchestrator: verifyImmutable(reference, bytes) throws on BMT mismatch; readFeedLatest(owner, identity) SOC-verifies the chunk signature before returning any mutable vessel state. Neither function ever returns bytes without verifying them. A tampered gateway is caught locally, every time.

**A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm**

Phare implements mutable, verifiable key-value state on Swarm using Single Owner Chunks and Swarm Feeds for two registries that need to be updated over time.

Vessel state feed — after each settled sighting, the minter writes a SOC-backed feed entry per vessel:

- Key: (owner = minter EOA, topic = keccak256("phare:vessel:<imo>")) -> deterministic feed address per IMO
- Value: latest dossier bzz:// reference, last-seen position, sighting count

Any consumer looks up a vessel by IMO using this deterministic derivation and gets the current state without querying any project API.

Verifier activity feed — each verifier agent maintains its own feed:

- Key: (owner = verifier EOA, topic = keccak256("phare:verifier:<handle>")) -> deterministic per-agent
- Value: latest activity log bzz:// reference, updated after every settled assertion the agent touched

Both feeds follow the same SOC verification recipe: fetch the chunk at the deterministic address, recover the signer from the chunk's signature over keccak256(identity || payload), confirm it matches the expected owner before acting on the value. The swarm/ helper module exposes readFeedLatest(owner, identity) and writeFeedNext(owner, identity, payload) for all consumers.

The result is a decentralised, cryptographically verified, mutable KV registry (vessel state and agent reputation) with no database, no API, and no trusted write authority beyond the owner key that signed each chunk.

**Best ENS Integration for AI Agents**

Phare's verifier agents are autonomous OpenClaw agents that dispute fraudulent vessel sightings via UMA OOv3. Each one acquires a real, on-chain ENS identity not minted by the project team, but self-registered by the agent's own wallet during onboarding by calling Lighthouse.enrollVerifier(handle, policyURI, soulURI) directly.

Lighthouse calls NameWrapper's setSubnodeRecord with the agent as token owner and PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL burned. From that point, not even the project team can overwrite the agent's records, the agent is sovereign. The agent then writes verifier.policy, verifier.soul, and verifier.runtime directly to PublicResolver from its own key.

What makes the integration deep is verifier.lastDecision. After every dispute, the verifier pins a reasoning JSON to Swarm, the evidence it cited, the policy rule that fired, the IMO it challenged and writes the bzz:// reference to its own ENS subname from its own wallet. Resolve agent-3a4b5c.verifier.phare.eth in any ENS browser, click verifier.lastDecision, and you get the agent's live reasoning trail. No project API. No centralized indexer. No CCIP-Read resolver — real on-chain NameWrapper ENS.

The skill library (skill/) ships with all the primitives to make this work: enrollVerifier, setVerifierLastDecision, setVerifierPolicy, setVerifierSoul, and readVerifier, all via viem calling NameWrapper and PublicResolver directly. The agent's ENS subname is not a static profile. It is a live, agent-curated public log written by the agent itself after every decision it makes.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

ENS is designed for humans and organisations with wallets. Phare uses it for something it was never designed for: physical objects that have no wallet, no public registry, and actively try not to be seen.

Every sanctioned vessel that survives a UMA challenge acquires a permanent ENS subname. The owner of that wrapped ERC-1155 NameWrapper token is Lighthouse.sol, an immutable on-chain contract. Three fuses are burned at mint: PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL, CANNOT_TRANSFER, and CANNOT_UNWRAP. The vessel subname is sealed to the contract permanently, it cannot be sold, moved, revoked, or transferred. The only entity that can update its records is ReportRegistry, calling through Lighthouse, upon a new settled sighting.

This means a shadow-fleet tanker that disabled its AIS transponder to be invisible acquires a permanent, tamper-evident on-chain identity the moment a citizen sighting survives adjudication. The identity deepens over time: vessel.swarm.log and contenthash point to the full Swarm dossier, updated per sighting; vessel.orbital.image, vessel.orbital.imageHash, and vessel.orbital.tee.prediction are written when SpaceComputer corroboration arrives.

The two namespaces also interlink: the vessel's Swarm dossier references the verifier agents that ruled on its disputes; each verifier's own ENS subname references the IMOs it challenged. The full accountability graph is browsable through ENS alone, with no project API in the resolution path.

ENS as a permanent public registry for a class of physical objects that has no public registry, and that funds its own evasion, is the creative use.

Team **eStorm** -- Nicolò Vanzo, Ruben Soro, [Lorenzo Gilardi](https://github.com/Red3lue)

**The problem it solves**

# Argus

> Trust infrastructure for agent-managed capital.

Two ENS-named agents managing a USDC position on Base. The **manager** parks funds in Aave v3 and exits on signed alerts. The **watcher** scrapes social, news, and prediction markets via Apify, scores threats, and signs alerts that the manager verifies via live ENS lookup. Every action is on-chain or signed-and-stored on Swarm.

## Bounties targeted

### 1. ENS — agent identity + agent-to-agent discovery (primary)

**What we built:**
- Three ENS subnames under user-owned `divljo.eth`, issued onchain via NameWrapper:
  - `argus.divljo.eth` — namespace root
  - `manager.argus.divljo.eth` — manager EOA + ENSIP-26 records
  - `watcher.argus.divljo.eth` — watcher EOA + ENSIP-26 records
- ENSIP-26 text records on each agent: `agent-endpoint[a2a]`, `agent-context`, `description`, plus a custom `bounty` record on the watcher publishing its reward terms.
- Live A2A discovery — the watcher resolves the manager's HTTP endpoint on **every** alert via `getEnsAddress` + `getEnsText("agent-endpoint[a2a]")`. No hardcoded URLs anywhere.
- Manager verifies watcher signatures by recovering the EIP-712 signer and comparing it to the **live ENS-resolved address** of `watcher.argus.divljo.eth`, refreshed every 60s. Renaming or rotating an agent updates the trust path with zero code changes.

**Where in the code:**
- [`packages/shared/src/ens.ts`](packages/shared/src/ens.ts) — CCIP-Read aware `resolveAgent()` helper used by all three runtimes
- [`agents/watcher/src/index.ts:35-47`](agents/watcher/src/index.ts#L35-L47) — `resolveManagerEndpoint()` runs before every POST
- [`agents/manager/src/index.ts:28-34, 72-76`](agents/manager/src/index.ts#L28-L34) — periodic ENS refresh + signature verification against ENS-resolved address

**What we built:**
- Four Apify actors integrated, three signal types in parallel:
  - **`fatihtahta/polymarket-scraper-ppe`** (PPE) — prediction-market implied probabilities, **the x402-eligible actor**
  - `apidojo/tweet-scraper` (PPR) — Twitter/X

- Polymarket items are special-cased in the classifier — implied probability is the threat probability directly, no LLM in the loop.

**Why the split matters:** Apify's experimental x402 endpoint only settles against Pay-Per-Event actors. We ship one PPE actor wired through x402 and three PPR actors on token auth — clearly documented in code and in the env (`USE_X402` flag), so the bounty path is real, not decorative.

**Network Economy**

## Network Economy fit

- **Identity, user-controlled.** Both agents are ENSIP-26 named with on-chain records. The watcher publishes its bounty terms (`50 bps of saved capital, paid in USDC on Base`) as a signed-by-mainnet text record — a public economic commitment.
- **Real on-chain economy.** Every Polymarket scrape pays Apify on Base via Coinbase x402: 1 USDC settled per call, verifiable on Basescan. Manager exits trigger `bounty-paid` receipts attributing 50 bps to the watcher's EOA.
- **Privacy by content-addressing.** Every action emits a vault tx + signed JSON on Swarm via `bzz.limo`. We additionally ship `@argus/swarm-kv`, a reusable encrypted-by-default KV library on Swarm (AES-256-GCM, HMAC-derived topics, keys from your wallet) — `localStorage` for dApps that follows the wallet across devices.
- **No central failure points.** Vault contract lets the manager move funds vault↔Aave only — leaked manager key cannot drain. Owner can always exit. Trust path is a pure function of ENS state.

**Best Agentic Venture**

**The thesis:** capital management agents are coming. The hard part isn't running the strategy — it's giving humans verifiable trust that an autonomous agent can't drain you, won't hide its actions, and earns its keep only when it actually saves you money. Argus is a small, end-to-end demonstration of that trust stack.

**A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm**

### 3. Swarm — verifiable evidence trail + a reusable KV library (secondary)

We ship two distinct Swarm contributions:

#### 3a. Live receipt trail (used by the agents)

- All receipts (deposits, withdraws, threat alerts, evidence bundles) are uploaded to Swarm via `@ethersphere/bee-js` v12.
- Uses the **bzz.limo** hosted gateway with `NULL_STAMP` — no postage batch setup required, the gateway rewrites it. Verified live: upload returns a 64-char ref, retrieval at `bzz.limo/bytes/<ref>` returns the exact JSON.
- Receipts are linked from the frontend audit log — every row has a `swarm ↗` link the audience can click to see the actual signed payload.
- Graceful fallback: on network failure, refs become `stub:<unixMs>` so the SQLite audit log stays canonical and downstream UI doesn't break.

**Where in the code:**
- [`agents/manager/src/swarm.ts`](agents/manager/src/swarm.ts), [`agents/watcher/src/swarm.ts`](agents/watcher/src/swarm.ts) — `Bee('https://bzz.limo')` + `NULL_STAMP`
- [`frontend/components/ThreatPanel.tsx`](frontend/components/ThreatPanel.tsx) — Evidence and Exits sections render `bzz.limo/bytes/<ref>` deep-links

#### 3b. `@argus/swarm-kv` — a reusable developer library

A standalone TypeScript package that wraps Swarm's low-level primitives (Feeds, Single Owner Chunks, postage batches) into a `get` / `put` / `list` / `delete` API with end-to-end encryption derived from the user's Ethereum private key. Most app code shouldn't have to know about feeds or topics — `swarm-kv` makes Swarm feel like an encrypted, decentralized `localStorage`.

```ts
import { openKv } from "@argus/swarm-kv";

const kv = await openKv({ bee, privateKey, namespace: "myapp.v1", postage: { auto: true } });
await kv.put("user.profile", { age: 30, theme: "dark" });
await kv.getJson("user.profile");   // → { age: 30, theme: "dark" }
await kv.list();                    // → ["user.profile", ...]
```

What it gives you:
- **End-to-end encryption** — values encrypted with AES-256-GCM, key derived via HKDF-SHA256 from your private key. Key names hidden as HMAC-derived topics.
- **String / JSON / binary** support with automatic type detection on read.
- **Listable** — an encrypted index feed tracks all keys, no manifest plumbing needed.
- **Auto-postage** — buys a batch on first write if you don't have one, or uses any usable batch on the node.
- **No bee-js leakage** — your app code never touches feeds, topics, SOCs, or stamps directly.

Use cases beyond Argus: dApp user profiles, app settings sync, chat history, bookmarks — anything you'd put in `localStorage` but want to follow a wallet across devices.

**Where in the code:** [`packages/swarm-kv/`](packages/swarm-kv/) — see its [README](packages/swarm-kv/README.md) for the full API and privacy model.

x402 is powerful. It's also painful to integrate.

The protocol is promising but getting it production ready means handling cryptographic verification, on-chain transaction validation, real-time price checks, and middleware wiring yourself. Most developers give up and fall back to Stripe  which means account approvals, webhook management, subscription tiers, and billing dashboards that AI agents fundamentally cannot use.
Neither option was built for the agentic web. NexusPay is.

**- Monetize Any API in 3 Lines of Code**

No Stripe account. No x402 boilerplate. No infrastructure overhead. Drop in the paygateNext middleware, set a price, set a wallet  and you're live. Any AI agent that hits your endpoint gets a 402, pays in USDC on Base, and retries with proof. The whole handshake is handled for you.
You ship. You earn. That's it.

The right worker for every job. Every time.

**Challenges we ran into**

****1.  x402 Payment Retry Race Condition****

When an agent got a `402` and retried with payment, the middleware was checking the transaction too fast  before the blockchain had actually confirmed it. So valid payments were being rejected and agents kept retrying forever.

Fixed it by waiting for **2 block confirmations** before accepting any payment as valid.

**2. **USDC Approval Silently Killing Transactions****
 

USDC needs a one-time `approve` before any contract can spend it. What we didn't realize is that allowance gets used up over time — so mid-workflow, agent payments started silently failing with a vague error and no clear reason why.

Fixed it by checking the remaining allowance before every payment and topping it up automatically when it runs low.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![MetaMask](https://img.shields.io/badge/MetaMask-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Most Web3 projects fail because they make users deal with the hard parts upfront: buying crypto, setting up wallets, understanding gas fees. People leave before they even see what the product does. LapLogic flips that. You connect your wallet, you get GameCoin instantly, and you're playing. No friction, no prior crypto knowledge needed.
The game itself is built around the 2026 Formula 1 season. You act as a team principal : picking 3 drivers and 1 constructor under a 60 million GameCoin cost cap. Since driver prices reflect real-world performance, you can't just pick the obvious names. You have to think smart, spot undervalued picks, and back your F1 knowledge. Before each race, an AI integration generates fresh prediction challenges based on real conditions like weather, track history, and championship standings , so every weekend feels different.
The core mechanic that makes it unique is what you do with your remaining budget. Whatever GameCoin is left after building your team, you can invest into the race pool. Your return depends on how well your strategy performs against other players. Better knowledge, better picks, better return. (Skill is directly tied to reward)
Everything runs on a smart contract on Polygon, so payouts are automatic, transparent, and go straight to your wallet. Your earnings are yours : no platform holding them, no approval process, no delays. F1 is booming globally and Web3 adoption is accelerating. LapLogic sits right at that intersection, at exactly the right time.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest part was Solidity. Writing smart contracts is one thing but getting deployment right on Polygon, making sure the contract logic actually synced with the backend, and debugging on-chain errors without straightforward error messages took way more time than expected. Web3 development has a very unforgiving feedback loop compared to normal backend work.
Working in the Web3 space also meant we could not test with real money at any stage. Everything had to run on testnet, which adds a layer of uncertainty because you are never fully sure how things behave until there is actual value on the line.
On the AI side, the prediction generation currently runs on a local 8 billion parameter Llama model. It works, but the quality and depth of the predictions is something we know can be much better. It is one of the clearest things we want to improve going forward.

**The problem it solves**

#  Problem It Solves

Modern campuses generate a significant amount of waste daily, yet there is **no effective system to track, incentivize, or reward responsible disposal behavior**. Students often lack motivation to segregate or properly dispose of waste because:

*  No immediate benefit or feedback
*  No accountability for individual contribution
*  Existing systems rely on manual effort (QR scans, reporting, etc.)
*  Sustainability efforts feel invisible and unrewarding

---

#  How BIN2COIN Solves This

BIN2COIN transforms waste management into a **smart, automated, and rewarding system** using IoT and Blockchain.

##  Key Improvements

###  1. Eliminates Manual Effort

* No need for QR scans or manual input
* Students simply:

  * Tap RFID card
  * Drop waste
* System automatically:

  * Identifies user
  * Measures weight
  * Logs data

---

###  2. Creates Accountability & Transparency

* Every waste deposit is:

  * Tracked per user
  * Stored in database
* Enables:

  * Individual contribution tracking
  * Fair measurement of impact

---

###  3. Introduces Gamification

* Converts waste into **points and tokens**
* Encourages:

  * Healthy competition
  * Consistent participation
* Makes sustainability **engaging and fun**

---

###  4. Real Reward System (Token Economy)

* Points are converted into **GC tokens**
* Tokens can be:

  * Redeemed for food/items
  * Used in campus ecosystem
* Adds **real value to sustainable behavior**

---

###  5. Secure & Trustless System (Blockchain)

* Rewards are:

  * Transparent
  * Tamper-proof
* Ensures:

  * No fake entries
  * Fair distribution

---

#  Impact

BIN2COIN turns passive sustainability into an **active, measurable, and rewarding experience**.
 Students are no longer just “throwing waste”
 They are **contributing, earning, and competing**

---

#  Final Outcome

> **“From Trash to Tokens — making sustainability visible, measurable, and rewarding.”**

**Challenges we ran into**

# Challenges I Ran Into

Building BIN2COIN involved integrating **hardware (IoT), backend systems, and blockchain**, which introduced several real-world challenges.

---

##  1. Arduino Upload & Hardware Issues

**Problem:**
While setting up the Arduino Nano, I faced repeated errors like:

* `not in sync`
* `unable to open port`

**Cause:**

* Wrong processor selection (ATmega168 vs ATmega328P)
* Faulty USB cable / port conflicts

**Solution:**

* Identified the correct processor (**ATmega168**)
* Reinstalled Arduino IDE and drivers
* Used proper reset timing during upload

---

##  2. Load Cell (HX711) Calibration & Inconsistent Readings

**Problem:**
The weight readings were inconsistent or not showing correctly.

**Cause:**

* Raw values from HX711 without calibration
* Wiring issues

**Solution:**

* Verified wiring connections carefully
* Switched to `read_average()` for stable readings
* Treated raw values for hackathon demo instead of full calibration

---

##  3. Arduino → Backend Communication

**Problem:**
Arduino cannot directly send HTTP requests using Arduino Nano.

**Cause:**

* No WiFi module on Arduino Nano

**Solution:**

* Built a **Serial → Node.js bridge**
* Used `serialport` in Node.js to read Arduino output
* Sent data to backend API using Axios

---

##  4. Managing Real-Time IoT Logic

**Problem:**
Continuous RFID scanning caused multiple triggers and duplicate entries.

**Cause:**

* No session control logic

**Solution:**

* Implemented a **state machine system**:

  * RFID Scan → Timer → Weight → Send → Reset
* Added cooldown period to prevent repeated scans

---

##  5. Backend Data Consistency

**Problem:**
Handling cases where:

* User exists vs does not exist
* Dustbin capacity overflow

**Solution:**

* Added validation logic:

  * Check user by UID
  * Allow waste logging even if user not found
  * Prevent deposits if dustbin is full

---

##  6. Blockchain Integration Complexity

**Problem:**
Understanding how to:

* Convert points → tokens
* Send tokens via smart contract

**Solution:**

* Simplified logic:

  * **1 Point = 1 Token**
* Used `ethers.js` to interact with contract
* Created a backend function to call `rewardStudent()`

---

## 7. Token Transfer vs Approval Confusion

**Problem:**
Initially confused between:

* `transfer`
* `transferFrom`
* `approve`

**Solution:**

* For hackathon simplicity:

  * Used direct `transfer` approach
  * Avoided complex approval flow

---

#  Key Learning

> Integrating hardware + backend + blockchain is not just about coding —
> it requires **debugging real-world systems, handling edge cases, and simplifying complex flows**.

---

#  Final Takeaway

Despite multiple challenges, each issue helped improve the system’s reliability and design.
The result is a **fully working end-to-end solution combining IoT, backend, and blockchain**.

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Supabase](https://img.shields.io/badge/Supabase-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

In peer-to-peer (P2P) online marketplaces and shipping contracting, **trust is the biggest bottleneck.**
- **Buyers** are afraid of paying upfront and never receiving the promised goods or services.
- **Sellers** hesitate to ship products or deliver work without guaranteed payment.
- Traditional escrow services charge exorbitant fees (often 5-10%), hold funds for agonizingly long periods (3-5 business days), and rely on opaque, centralized dispute resolution processes that are prone to human bias and error.

Additionally, international transactions are plagued by high currency conversion fees and slow wire transfer speeds.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building decentralized legal frameworks involves overcoming systemic barriers:

### 1. Smart Contracts are not Recognized Legally Everywhere
* **Challenge:** Code is not always recognized as "law" in traditional jurisdictions. If an on-chain arbitration occurs, one party might attempt to sue off-chain in a local court, creating legal friction.
* **Mitigation:** TradeVault requires users to sign an explicit "Terms of Use" that designates the smart contract and subsequent arbitration results as legally binding arbitration under the New York Convention (or local equivalents). We bridge the gap by combining cryptographic signatures with formatted, printable PDF legal agreements generated upon deal creation.

### 2. Lack of Awareness / Web3 Friction
* **Challenge:** Non-crypto-native users are intimidated by wallets, gas fees, and token names.
* **Mitigation:** We utilize Account Abstraction and user-friendly wallets (like Lute Wallet via email login). The UI abstracts away "MicroAlgos" and "Teal" and simply shows terms in familiar USD equivalents. Our onboarding focuses entirely on the P2P safety benefits rather than the underlying blockchain tech.

### 3. Oracles bridging "Real-World" Delivery Status
* **Challenge:** Blockchains cannot intrinsically know if a physical item was delivered.
* **Mitigation:** We utilize trusted backend oracles bridging carrier APIs (UPS, FedEx, DHL) to write tracking verification hashes to the blockchain. We also support "Instant Handover" cryptography involving QR-code scanning for in-person local deals.

### 4. AVM Foreign Asset & Account Access
* **Challenge:** The Algorand Virtual Machine requires all foreign assets (e.g. USDC ASA ID) and foreign accounts (e.g. seller's wallet) to be explicitly declared in the outer transaction before inner transactions can reference them.
* **Mitigation:** All contract calls include `foreignAssets: [USDC_ASSET_ID]` and `accounts: [sellerWallet]` in the transaction payload, ensuring the AVM has full context for every inner transfer it needs to execute.

**Web3**

**Trustless custody.** No company holds the money — a smart contract does.

**Permissionless access.** No bank account, no KYC, no institution required to participate.

**Immutable agreements.** Contract terms written on Algorand cannot be altered by either party after signing.

**Cryptographic acceptance.** Karim's wallet signature is mathematically verifiable proof of agreement — stronger than any wet signature.

**On-chain proof of shipment.** Tracking hash stored permanently on Algorand — nobody can claim delivery was never submitted.

**Automatic trustless settlement.** Payment releases by code, not by a human decision.

**Permanent reputation.** Trade history lives on-chain forever — unfakeable, undeletable, publicly verifiable.

**Algorand**

Algorand fits TradeVault for five reasons that are not interchangeable with any other chain.

USDC is native. Circle issues USDC directly on Algorand — no wrapping, no bridging, no additional risk layer. The contract holds and releases real USDC.

Fees are flat and near-zero. Every transaction costs $0.002 regardless of trade size. On Ethereum the same escrow flow costs $15–60 in gas — economically impossible for sub-$5,000 trades. Algorand makes the target market viable.

Atomic transactions are a protocol feature. Karim's acceptance signature and USDC transfer are grouped atomically — both succeed or neither does. This is not application logic. It is guaranteed at the protocol level.
Finality is 4 seconds. No confirmation waiting periods, no chain reorganisation risk. Funds lock or release instantly in user-visible time.

The AVM is constrained by design. The contract is 120 lines, 7 methods. Algorand's execution environment limits complexity, eliminates reentrancy by default, and makes the class of exploits that caused the DAO hack structurally impossible here.

### VAULTLESS
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/vaultless-dea4) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/chhhee10/VAULTLESS) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://vaultless-sys.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/ImOWwMM8VRI) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Hack--Nocturne%202.O-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hack-nocturne-2.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-5-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Your password is how you move.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![MetaMask](https://img.shields.io/badge/MetaMask-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Passwords, OTPs, and 2FA codes can be stolen, phished, or coerced out of people, yet most authentication systems have no way to detect or respond to these scenarios.
VAULTLESS solves this by replacing static credentials with a behavioural biometric profile built from how you naturally type and move. It captures **keystroke rhythm, mouse dynamics, touch patterns, and device motion, signals unique to you that can't be lifted from a database or handed over under pressure.**
It specifically addresses three gaps existing systems ignore:

**Stolen credentials:** no password means nothing to steal or phish
**Coercion:** if someone forces you to log in, VAULTLESS detects the stress in your typing pattern and silently redirects the attacker to a decoy session while alerting your security contact
**Audit gaps:** every authentication event (success, failure, or duress) is permanently logged on an Ethereum smart contract, giving you a tamper-proof record

No specialist hardware. No shared secrets. Works on **PC, Android, and iOS**- using touch and motion sensors on mobile for an even richer behavioural signal.
Built for anyone who needs **security that protects people, not just accounts.**

**Challenges we ran into**

*Scoring consistency:* Early on, the same user would get different scores across attempts due to minor typing variations. Fixed it by averaging three enrollment samples and weighting hold times 3× so the dominant signal carried more influence.
*Tuning the duress zone:* Deciding where "stressed but plausible" should sit took a lot of trial and error. Too tight and real users got flagged. We added a second condition, rhythm variance must exceed 2.5× the enrollment baseline, so both signals had to fire together.
*Mobile sensor fallbacks:* Different browsers expose different APIs, and iOS requires a permission prompt most users dismiss. Built the engine to fuse whatever signals are available so it never fails hard, keystrokes carry the full weight when motion data is absent.

**Ethereum Track**

VAULTLESS is built on **Ethereum Sepolia** as its trust layer - not as an afterthought, but because the **core security guarantee of the system depends on it.**
Every enrollment, authentication, duress event, and failed attempt is permanently logged on-chain via **VaultlessCore.sol**, a **custom Solidity contract** deployed on **Sepolia**. The contract stores a **keccak256** commitment hash of the user's biometric vector - meaning the actual behavioural data never leaves the browser, but a cryptographic proof of it *lives on Ethereum forever*. This makes authentication records honest, tamper-evident, and user-owned rather than controlled by any server.
We used **Remix IDE** to write and deploy the contract, **MetaMask** as the injected wallet provider, **Ethers.js** **v6** to interact with the contract from the frontend, and **Sepolia Etherscan** to verify and monitor transactions in real time.
The contract also implements **nullifier-based** replay protection - each successful authentication burns a unique **keccak256(vectorHash + walletAddress + timestamp) nullifier on-chain**, so a captured transaction can never be reused to impersonate a user.
The duress protocol goes further: when coercion is detected, a *DuressActivated event is emitted on-chain before silently loading a decoy session*. This creates a permanent, timestamped, public record of the coercion attempt that no attacker can erase - something no traditional auth system can offer.
***Ethereum is the core of our trust model***. Without it, authentication records are just logs on a server someone controls. With it, every enrollment, every login, every duress event is a permanent, user-owned, **cryptographically verifiable** fact that no company, no admin, and no attacker can alter or delete.

**The problem it solves**

## The Broken Ad Economy

Traditional online advertising is fundamentally broken:

- **Publishers** get pennies while platforms take 70%+ of ad revenue
- **Viewers** see thousands of ads yearly and earn exactly $0
- **Advertisers** pay middlemen, not the people actually seeing their ads
- **Privacy** is sacrificed — every click, scroll, and view is tracked and sold

### Web3Ads Fixes This

**Fair Revenue Distribution:**
| Stakeholder | Traditional Ads | Web3Ads |
|-------------|-----------------|---------|
| Publishers | ~30% | **50%** |
| Viewers | 0% | **20%** |
| Platform | ~70% | 30% |

- Earn ETH automatically every time you see an ad
- Withdraw anytime with **$0 gas fees** — we pay the gas
- Your data stays private via zkProof identity (Semaphore)

### Unique Innovations

1. **AI Agent Payments (x402 Protocol):** Users can spend their ad earnings through AI agents. Your Claude can pay for APIs using funds you earned viewing ads — completely gasless.

2. **Privacy-Preserving Tracking:** Semaphore zkProofs prove "this viewer saw this ad" without revealing WHO they are. No cookies, no fingerprinting, no surveillance.

3. **True Gasless UX:** Viewers never need ETH to withdraw. Backend signs EIP-712 messages and pays all gas fees. Web3 without the friction.

4. **MCP Server for AI Integration:** AI agents can create campaigns, check balances, and make payments programmatically via Model Context Protocol.

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges I Ran Into

**1. Semaphore WASM in Chrome Extensions**
Service workers block WebAssembly blob URLs. Solved by generating Semaphore identity in the client web app and sending it to the extension via postMessage — extension becomes lightweight storage only.

**2. CSP Blocking Extension Detection**
Inline script injection fails on strict CSP sites. Switched to DOM attributes which content scripts can set regardless of CSP policy.

**3. Gasless Withdrawals Without Full Account Abstraction**
Full ERC-4337 paymasters are complex. Implemented simplified EIP-712 signature flow where backend signs authorization and pays gas directly when calling the withdraw function.

**4. USDC Faucet Reliability**
Base Sepolia USDC faucets were unreliable. Migrated to V2 contract using native ETH, requiring updates across smart contracts, frontend hooks, and all payment flows.

**5. Ad Earnings as x402 Payment Source**
Standard x402 requires direct transfers. Built custom "web3ads-balance" payment method that deducts from user's pending earnings — enabling AI agents to pay for APIs without any wallet interaction.

**Privacy**

**How it fits:** Viewers generate Semaphore identities (zkProof) to prove ad views without revealing identity. Nullifiers prevent double-counting while maintaining anonymity.

**Code Implementation:**
- Viewer.tsx — Semaphore identity generation
- index.ts — Nullifier generation per ad view
- index.ts — Proof relay between SDK and extension
- ads.ts — Server-side nullifier verification

**The problem it solves**

Managing crypto trading and on-chain transactions requires constant monitoring, technical knowledge, and manual execution. OctoHive simplifies this by letting users deploy autonomous AI agents that analyze markets, find optimal routes and exchange rates, and execute transactions automatically — all monitorable from a unified wallet dashboard. Every agent is assigned its own ENS subdomain, giving it a verifiable on-chain identity complete with personality, avatar, and strategy stored as ENS profile records. The platform also features an** Agent Arena, where agents from different users compete head-to-head based on trading performance**, adding a gamified, competitive layer to automated DeFi.

**Challenges we ran into**

Integrating multiple systems like BitGo wallets, AI agents, market analysis tools, and on-chain transaction automation was complex — we solved this by orchestrating the workflow using the Hey Elsa automation layer.
Another challenge was enabling secure autonomous transactions — we addressed this by using Elsa’s x402 framework to safely authorize and execute on-chain actions.

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem

Every DeFi frontend today has a dirty secret: **it's centralized**.

The smart contracts are on-chain. The tokens are yours. But the website
you use to interact with them? It runs on AWS, Vercel, or Cloudflare
servers controlled by a company that can be hacked, subpoenaed, or simply
decide to pull the plug.

This has already caused real damage:
- **Curve Finance, Uniswap, Balancer** frontends hijacked via DNS attacks
  to drain user wallets
- **Tornado Cash** OFAC pressured the frontend offline within hours
- **Compound, dYdX** geo-blocked entire regions via their hosting provider
- **Hundreds of smaller protocols** taken offline the moment their Vercel
  free tier expired or their domain registrar received a complaint

The smart contract is trustless. The frontend is not. **That gap kills people.**

---

## What Deploy.eth Solves

Deploy.eth makes your entire stack trustless — not just the contracts.

### 🌐 For DeFi Protocol Teams

**Ship a frontend that cannot be taken down.**
```bash
web3deploy push
# ✓ Site live on IPFS (content-addressed, immutable)
# ✓ myprotocol.eth now resolves to your new build
# ✓ No Vercel. No AWS. No domain registrar. No kill switch.
```

Your site lives on IPFS a global peer-to-peer network where files are
addressed by their content hash, not a server location. Nobody can redirect
it, modify it silently, or take it offline. Even if your entire team
disappears, the frontend keeps serving users.

**Store your protocol config on-chain, not in a dashboard.**

Every deploy writes your configuration to ENS text records publicly
auditable, immutable history, readable by your smart contracts:
```
swap.slippage      → 0.5
fee.recipient      → 0x...
fee.bps            → 30
access.policy      → public
monitor.riskLevel  → medium
```

Users can verify exactly what your frontend is configured to do before
they connect their wallet. No more "trust us."

**Require multi-sig approval before any frontend update goes live.**

Malicious frontend updates are one of DeFi's biggest attack vectors.
Deploy.eth lets you require 3-of-5 team signatures before the ENS
contenthash changes making a frontend attack as hard as a smart
contract exploit.

**A live, intelligent frontend powered by Elsa x402 with no backend.**

Because there's no server, there are no API keys to steal, no database
to breach, and no company to subpoena for your transaction history.

Your ENS domain becomes your **personal DeFi config** — store your risk

**Your site watches your portfolio even when you're not looking.**

ENS monitor records tell the site what to watch for:

When conditions are met, your ungoverned frontend surfaces the action.

### 🔒 For DAOs and Governance-Heavy Protocols

**Make frontend deployments a governance action.**

Right now, a DAO can vote on treasury decisions, parameter changes, and
contract upgrades — but a single developer can push a malicious frontend
unilaterally. Deploy.eth closes that gap.

Every frontend update is a proposal. Signers review the CID diff. The
ENS contenthash only changes when the threshold is met. The full deploy
history — who proposed what, when, with which CID — lives on-chain forever.

**Environment routing without a backend.**
```
myprotocol.eth          → production (CID: bafybeig3...)

Each subname is independently owned. Staging can move fast. Production

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges I Ran Into

### 1. ENS `contenthash` encoding is not what you think it is

The first wall I hit. ENS doesn't store a raw IPFS CID string in the
`contenthash` field — it stores a binary-encoded value following a
specific multicodec spec. Passing a raw CIDv1 string to the resolver
contract just reverts silently.

The CID has to be encoded as:
```
0xe3010170 + varint(cid-length) + cid-bytes
```

The `0xe3010170` prefix encodes the namespace (IPFS), the version, and
the codec. Miss any byte and the ENS gateway refuses to resolve it —
with no error message, just a blank page.

**Fix:** Used `@ensdomains/content-hash` library which handles the
encoding correctly. But it took hours to diagnose because the ENS
resolver accepts the malformed transaction — it only fails silently
at resolution time, not at write time.
```typescript
import { encode } from '@ensdomains/content-hash';
const encoded = encode('ipfs', cid); // '0xe301017012...'
```

---

### 2. IPFS CIDs change every build even when nothing changes

The second major hurdle. Vite's build output includes chunk hashes in
filenames — `index-BvXk3a91.js` — so every build produces a different
`dist/` tree even if the source hasn't changed. Every different tree
produces a different root CID. This meant every `git push`, even a
README typo fix, produced a new CID, a new ENS transaction, and ~$5-15
in gas fees on mainnet.

**Fix 1:** Switched to deterministic chunk naming in `vite.config.ts`:
```typescript
build: {
  rollupOptions: {
    output: {
      entryFileNames: 'assets/[name].js',
      chunkFileNames: 'assets/[name].js',
      assetFileNames: 'assets/[name].[ext]',
    }
  }
}
```

**Fix 2:** Added a CID comparison step in the deploy script — reads the
current ENS `contenthash`, decodes it, compares with the new CID, and
skips the ENS transaction entirely if they match:
```typescript
const currentCid = await getCurrentEnsCid(domain);
if (currentCid === newCid) {
  console.log('CID unchanged, skipping ENS update');
  process.exit(0);
}
```

Gas saved. Sanity restored.

---

### 3. Elsa x402 payment tokens expire mid-pipeline

The x402 payment flow generates a short-lived JWT-style payment token
before each API call. In a multi-step pipeline —
`get_portfolio` → `get_yield_suggestions` → `execute_swap_dry_run` —
if any step takes longer than expected (slow IPFS pin, RPC congestion),
the token for the next step has already expired by the time you use it.

This caused the swap dry-run to fail silently, returning a `402 Payment
Required` response that I initially mistook for a broken endpoint.

**Fix:** Generate payment tokens lazily — immediately before each
individual API call rather than upfront for the whole pipeline:
```typescript
// ❌ Wrong — tokens generated upfront, may expire
const tokens = await generateTokens(['portfolio', 'yield', 'swap']);
await getPortfolio(tokens[0]);
await sleep(3000); // tokens[1] may already be stale
await getYield(tokens[1]);

// ✅ Correct — token generated fresh per call
await getPortfolio(await generateToken('portfolio'));
await getYield(await generateToken('yield'));
await executeDryRun(await generateToken('swap'));
```

---

### 4. ENS text record updates require a separate resolver transaction

I assumed updating the `contenthash` and updating text records could
be batched into one transaction. They can't — at least not on the
standard public resolver. Each `setText` call is a separate transaction,
and with 8 text records to update per deploy (CID, timestamp, framework,
env, tx hash, version, build command, node version), the deploy script
was firing 9 transactions sequentially.

At ~15 seconds per transaction confirmation and gas for each, a full
deploy was taking 3+ minutes and costing more in gas than the hosting
was worth.

**Fix:** Used ENS's `multicall` on the resolver contract, which batches
multiple `setText` and `setContenthash` calls into a single transaction:
```typescript
const resolver = await provider.getResolver(domain);
await resolver.multicall([
  resolver.interface.encodeFunctionData('setContenthash', [node, encoded]),
  resolver.interface.encodeFunctionData('setText', [node, 'deploy.cid', cid]),
  resolver.interface.encodeFunctionData('setText', [node, 'deploy.timestamp', ts]),
  // ... all 8 records
]);
```

One transaction. One gas fee. Deploy time dropped from 3 minutes to
under 30 seconds.

---

### 5. IPFS gateway resolution lag breaks the "instant deploy" experience

After updating the ENS contenthash to a new CID, there's a propagation
delay before IPFS gateways (ipfs.io, cloudflare-ipfs.com, eth.limo)
actually serve the new content. The CID is correct in ENS immediately,
but visiting `myapp.eth.limo` still shows the old version for anywhere
from 30 seconds to 5 minutes.

Users opening the site right after a deploy would see the old version
with no indication that a new one exists — confusing and undermining
trust in the platform.

**Best creative use of ENS**

Our project treats ENS as a programmable deployment and coordination layer for Web3 apps, not just a wallet alias.

What we built

We let builders deploy directly from a GitHub repo to IPFS, then bind that deployment to an ENS-linked subname.
Every new deploy updates onchain metadata so the ENS name becomes a live pointer to the latest decentralized frontend.
This turns ENS names into versioned, human-readable app endpoints instead of static identity labels.

Why this is a creative ENS use

ENS as decentralized hosting: We use ENS-linked content addressing so the name resolves to a decentralized website, not a centralized server.
ENS as programmable app registry: Subnames act like app namespaces for teams, environments, and products.
ENS as trust surface: Users can interact with DeFi interfaces through memorable names, reducing copy-paste risk from raw addresses and random URLs.
ENS as composable state: Deployment metadata can be attached and resolved through ENS-compatible records, enabling wallets, explorers, and dapps to consume the same canonical app identity.

> Autonomous Expert Agents, Collective Knowledge

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Hedera agent kit](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hedera%20agent%20kit-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTS](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTS-333333?style=flat-square) ![HCS](https://img.shields.io/badge/HCS-333333?style=flat-square) ![UCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/UCP-333333?style=flat-square) ![HIP911](https://img.shields.io/badge/HIP911-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Improving AI Efficiency

Recall - Instead of starting over with every instance, Hive increases it's knowledge base with interactions making every agent connection a multiplier.

Generic answers – Instead of one broad model, tasks go to a domain specialist, improving precision and depth.

Cost inefficiency – You don’t pay a large model to handle everything; lightweight expert agents reduce compute cost.

Trust and reliability – Specialized agents are easier to benchmark, validate, and compare by performance.

System Level Memory Growth - Connecting to the Hive Protocol prevents agents from performing the same work over and over. Working with expert agents already trained there is no system level memory loss.

**Challenges we ran into**

Agent-to-agent communication with OpenClaw.  We resolved this by having OpenClaw subscribed to an HCS inbound topic with hip991 to demonstrate the economy of the protocol.

Triggering an iOT from on-chain. We resolved this with self invoking timed functions on the hedera contract that alert the OpenClaw agent with HCS10 message format.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

HIVE Protocol uses multiple specialized AI agents that coordinate through an on-chain workflow to research, verify, and monetize knowledge on Hedera.

**AI Agents in the System:**

**1) MCP (Master Control Program) — Orchestration Layer**

- Receives user research questions (via OpenClaw).
- Reads all relevant Hedera HCS topics (fee-exempt).
- Decides whether existing knowledge answers the question or new execution is required.
- Routes tasks to the appropriate Executor agents.
- Aggregates validated topic data for final response generation.

AI Role: Decision-making and routing using LLM reasoning.

**2) Executor Agents — Research & Task Execution**

- Specialized domain agents (e.g., sensor, data, analysis).
- Use LLM-driven tool-calling to determine how to fulfill a request.
- Execute off-chain logic or data retrieval.

Publish results to their own HIP-991 Executor topics on Hedera.

AI Role: Generate new knowledge through structured reasoning + execution.

**3) Validator Agent — Verification & Attestation**

Purchases responses from Executor topics.

- Uses LLM-guided validation logic to assess correctness.
- Attests verified answers on-chain.
- Creates paid HIP-991 Knowledge Topics containing validated results.

AI Role: Trust enforcement and economic settlement.

**How They Work Together**

- User submits a research question.
- MCP uses LLM reasoning to determine relevant topics or Executors.
- If new research is required, MCP triggers Validator.
- Validator purchases Executor output.
- Executor publishes results.
- Validator verifies and writes attested knowledge to a paid topic.
- MCP returns attested topic data to the client.
- Client LLM synthesizes the final user response.

This creates a fully autonomous propose → execute → validate cycle with no human intervention

**Futurllama**

Hive Protocol is a coordination layer for machine intelligence transforming isolated AI agents into a unified, collaborative intelligence network.

Today, agents operate alone - relearning what others already know and recomputing the same work across thousands of systems. Hive Protocol replaces isolation with coordination. When an agent encounters a complex or expensive task, it publishes a request to the network and recruits specialized experts to contribute.

Expertise is dynamically allocated. Lightweight domain specialists replace heavy generic models. Complex problems are decomposed into layered workflows where agents can recruit, refine, validate, and optimize in parallel.

Every solved task strengthens the collective. Knowledge is not lost between agents - it compounds. New agents plug into an accumulated intelligence layer instead of starting from zero, eliminating redundant computation across the system.

The result is faster convergence, lower cost, higher reliability, and network-level resilience. No single model defines the system. Intelligence is composable, distributed, and adaptive.

Hive Protocol doesn’t just connect AI agents.
It turns them into a coordinated, compounding intelligence economy.

> Find love on chain.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![ngrok](https://img.shields.io/badge/ngrok-333333?style=flat-square) ![Supabase](https://img.shields.io/badge/Supabase-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Current dating apps revolve around the same style of users advocating for themselves, but we believe getting the audience involved is best way to find a match. We know that people enjoy watching reality tv shows and love getting obsessed in relationships so we’ve tapped into the same instinct to allow people a front row seat, with actual influence over the outcomes. 

Chained Together is the first decentralized dating ecosystem where your community is your wingman. When users aren’t Tending to their own messages, they can spend time thoughtfully voting on matches for others, making the quest for love actually fun. To further reduce bias, we implemented an AI model that proposes initial pairings that the community will later vote on. The collective intuition of the "Matchmaker DAO"  combines social consensus with blockchain-backed accountability. Essentially, We are turning the search for love into a transparent, community-driven experience.

**Challenges we ran into**

One specific hurdle we ran into while building the project was integrating Snapshot, which powers the DAO governance layer. The backend initially would not connect correctly because Snapshot requires a properly configured ENS domain. We resolved this by registering and configuring an ENS domain and updating our Snapshot space settings, which allowed proposals and voting to function correctly.

Another major challenge involved JSON parsing from LLM responses. The model frequently returned malformed JSON, often wrapped in markdown blocks or containing unbalanced braces, which caused failures in our backend pipeline. To overcome this, we implemented a robust extraction and recovery system that strips markdown formatting, repairs JSON structure, and automatically retries generation using a correction prompt when parsing fails.

Finally, we could not use a traditional DAO as it would force users to send ETH in order to vote. So we adopted Snapshot’s gasless EIP-712 voting infrastructure so users can participate in DAO governance without paying transaction fees. These solutions allowed us to stabilize ChainedTogether, resulting in a resilient three-layer architecture combining AI inference on 0G Compute, DAO governance through on-chain and Snapshot voting, and Supabase as the application state machine, with fallback mechanisms ensuring the app continues working even when individual services fail.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

AI is used in profile intake and bio generation. The user’s onboarding answers are fed to the Qwen 2.5 7B model running on 0G Compute, which generates a 2-3 sentence bio summary.
 
AI is also used for compatibility scoring (matchmaking). We send two users’ bios to the same Qwen 0G model, which returns a JSON score 0-100 and compatibility reasons. A background process continuously generates scored match pairs and feeds them into a queue.

On the server side we use the 0g serving broker SDK for authenticated requests.

**Prosperia**

Chained Together focuses on community led governance and collective action as it relates to matchmaking in the dating scene.

**Best Use of AI Inference or Fine Tuning (0G Compute)**

Our project fits the 0G Compute track because AI inference directly powers core application features, including onboarding bio generation and compatibility scoring using the Qwen 2.5 7B model running on 0G Compute. User responses are transformed into bios, and pairs of bios are analyzed to produce structured compatibility scores and reasoning, with authenticated requests handled through the 0G Serving Broker SDK and results continuously processed in a matchmaking queue.

**The problem it solves**

Institutions wanting to tokenize real-world assets (bonds, invoices, real estate) face three barriers: their portfolio strategies are exposed on public blockchains, coupon/yield payments depend on fragile off-chain servers, and risk analysis is manual and disconnected from on-chain data. Outward solves all three in a single platform — asset managers tokenize RWA with manual KYC whitelisting and role based access control, negotiate privately through confidential vaults where each party only sees what they're authorized to see, automate coupon payments deterministically on-chain with no centralized infrastructure, and get AI-powered risk analysis with stress testing and actionable recommendations that always require human approval before execution.

**Challenges we ran into**

Our InstitutionRegistry contract hit Ethereum's 24KB deploy limit (EIP-170), so we extracted an InstitutionDeployer to handle the heavy logic externally. The backend had an ESM compatibility issue where ABI file loading broke because __dirname doesn't exist in ES modules. Hedera's Schedule Service precompile had limited documentation, so we relied on iterative testing on testnet. And Daml was new to the whole team — Canton's party-scoped visibility model took time to get right.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

Outward integrates an AI-powered risk analysis assistant built on 0G Compute for decentralized inference. When a user clicks "Analyze" on a vault, the backend sends the vault's composition (asset types, ratings, allocations, maturities) to 0G Compute, which returns a structured risk report — a composite score from 1 to 100, per-position analysis, stress test simulations (rate hikes, issuer defaults), and actionable rebalancing recommendations. The output is validated against strict schemas (Zod) to ensure consistency. Critically, the AI never executes transactions on its own — every recommendation is surfaced in the dashboard with explicit approve/reject buttons, enforcing a human-in-the-loop workflow. A mock inference mode is available as fallback when 0G is not configured.

**New France Village**

Metaphor sits at the intersection of TradFi and DeFi by bringing institutional-grade asset management on-chain. It lets financial institutions tokenize real-world assets like bonds and invoices, manage them in confidential vaults with granular access control, automate coupon payments without off-chain infrastructure, and analyze portfolio risk with AI — all within a single compliant, white-label platform designed for institutional adoption.

**Best DeFAI Application**

Metaphor is a confidential RWA (Real World Assets) hub for institutional finance that embeds AI directly into critical DeFi workflows — vault allocation, risk assessment, and coupon scheduling — rather than treating it as a chatbot layer. Powered by 0G Compute, our AI engine analyzes on-chain portfolio data and market conditions to produce structured, explainable recommendations: which RWA tokens to allocate into a vault, how to rebalance positions based on maturity and yield curves, and whether a proposed trade meets institutional risk thresholds (slippage limits, concentration caps, counterparty allowlists). Every AI-generated plan surfaces a clear rationale ("why") alongside risk scores and simulated outcomes before any transaction is submitted, ensuring full transparency. Crucially, no action executes without explicit user approval — institutional operators review, override, or confirm each recommendation through a human-in-the-loop approval flow, maintaining the guardrails that regulated finance demands. The result is a DeFi product with real working flows (vault creation, deposit, yield distribution, bond coupon payments) where AI materially improves decision quality and operational efficiency while users stay firmly in control.

**Best Use of AI Inference or Fine Tuning (0G Compute)**

Metaphor integrates 0G Compute as the inference backbone of its AI-powered risk engine for institutional RWA (Real World Asset) vaults. When a portfolio manager triggers an analysis, the system formats on-chain vault data — asset allocations, ISIN identifiers, coupon rates, maturities, and historical yield snapshots — into structured prompts sent to a model discovered and served through the 0G Compute network. The AI performs two distinct tasks well-suited to LLM reasoning: risk scoring (classifying each asset on a 1–100 scale based on credit quality, concentration, and duration) and stress testing (simulating adverse macroeconomic scenarios like rate hikes, issuer defaults, and liquidity crises to estimate portfolio impact). Critically, the AI output is not decorative — it drives a full human-in-the-loop approval workflow: recommendations such as REBALANCE, EXIT_POSITION, or ADD_COLLATERAL are surfaced in the UI with priority levels and expected impact, and an authorized user (Admin or Issuer) must explicitly approve each action before an unsigned on-chain transaction is prepared for wallet signing. All LLM responses are validated against strict Zod schemas with automatic retry on malformed output, ensuring reliability in a financial context where structured, parseable results are non-negotiable. The system runs in dual mode — live 0G Compute inference on testnet or deterministic mock — and includes reproducible setup with a single environment variable toggle, integration tests against real 0G providers, and full documentation of model selection and provider discovery.

**On-Chain Automation with Hedera Schedule Service**

Metaphor uses the Hedera Schedule Service System Contract (precompile 0x16b) to automate bond coupon payments entirely from smart contract logic, with zero reliance on off-chain keepers or cron jobs. The CouponScheduler contract allows an issuer to register a bond with its face value, annual rate, and payment frequency (monthly, quarterly, semi-annual, or annual), then automatically computes all future payment dates and coupon amounts. When scheduleCoupon() is called, the contract encodes a self-callback to executeCoupon() and passes it to the Hedera precompile via IHRC1215.scheduleCall(), creating a native Schedule entity that Hedera itself will trigger at the specified date — no external infrastructure required. At execution time, the contract enforces all-or-nothing semantics: if sufficient liquidity exists, the coupon is transferred to the issuer and marked Executed; if not, it is marked Failed with no partial transfer, and an admin can later call recoverPayment() to reset it to Pending for re-scheduling once funds are restored. The full payment lifecycle — Pending, Scheduled, Executed, Failed, Suspended — is tracked on-chain with events at every transition, and the frontend surfaces this as a visual schedule timeline with transaction links. A companion YieldDistributor contract handles snapshot-based pro-rata yield distribution to bond token holders, completing the DeFi automation loop for tokenized securities. Both contracts are deployed and verified on Hedera Testnet, with Foundry tests covering edge cases (insufficient liquidity, payment recovery, bond deactivation) and TypeScript integration scripts for end-to-end demonstration.

**Best Privacy-Focused dApp Using Daml**

Metaphor is a privacy-first institutional RWA hub built natively in Daml and deployed on Canton L1 Devnet, where every contract enforces visibility at the protocol level — not through application-logic access control lists. The core ConfidentialVault template uses Canton's signatory/observer model to give the vault owner full control while selectively granting counterparties observation rights through a mutual-consent invitation pattern (VaultInvitation → VaultAccessRight), ensuring no party ever sees a contract they were not explicitly authorized to observe. Trade negotiation is handled by the PrivateTrade module, where bilateral TradeProposal contracts are visible only to the two negotiating parties — not to other counterparties on the same vault — and support multi-round offer/counter-offer chains with automatic role reversal until a TradeAgreement is reached with both parties as signatories. The privacy model's most distinctive feature is its audit separation: rather than granting auditors visibility into the vault itself, Metaphor creates a separate AuditRight contract containing only compliance-relevant data (asset count, total value, asset type categories, maturity range) while deliberately excluding individual asset details, trade terms, counterparty identities, and strategy descriptions. The frontend demonstrates this with a three-panel side-by-side view showing what each role (owner, counterparty, auditor) can and cannot see simultaneously, with lock icons marking restricted fields — making Canton's privacy guarantees visually tangible. The project includes 29 Daml Script test scenarios covering the full lifecycle (vault creation, deposits, freezing, trade negotiation, audit invitations, revocation, and edge cases), a backend REST API mapping all Daml operations through the Canton JSON API, and is packaged as a reproducible monorepo with clear setup instructions.

**Open Project Submission**

Metaphor is a deployed, institutional-grade RWA tokenization hub running on ADI Chain, where all five core contracts are live and verified. The platform enables institutions to tokenize real-world assets — bonds, invoices, mortgages, equity — as ERC-20 tokens enriched with financial metadata (ISIN, coupon rate, maturity date, issuer) through a RWATokenFactory that also supports fractionalization of existing tokens into independently tradeable sub-units. Every token transfer enforces KYC compliance at the ERC-20 _update() level: non-whitelisted addresses cannot receive RWA tokens regardless of approvals, ensuring regulatory conformity by construction rather than convention. Vault management is handled by a VaultManager contract that tracks deposits, withdrawals, and strategy allocations per token per depositor, preventing withdrawal of funds already allocated to yield or lending strategies. Access is governed by a four-role RBAC system (InstiVaultAccessControl: Admin, Issuer, Investor, Auditor) with batch whitelisting for onboarding, and the entire platform is white-label ready through an InstitutionRegistry that deploys fully isolated contract sets (AccessControl + TokenFactory + VaultManager) per institution via an external InstitutionDeployer, ensuring no cross-tenant data leakage. Institution onboarding follows a 2-of-N multisig proposal flow where at least two platform admins must approve before contracts are deployed, preventing unilateral registration. The system is backed by 111+ Foundry test cases covering role enforcement, whitelist transfers, vault lifecycle, allocation mechanics, fractionalization, burn-at-maturity, and multi-tenant isolation, and integrates with an Express backend that enforces RBAC both at the JWT level and through on-chain role verification fallback.
