### Proof of Reality
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/proof-of-reality-6a31) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Afiyetolsun/proof_of_reality) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://www.realityproof.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/4skD_FlXGpU) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Cryptographic proof that physical things exist

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Swift](https://img.shields.io/badge/Swift-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Swarm](https://img.shields.io/badge/Swarm-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Ethereum](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ethereum-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

AI can fake any photo in five seconds. That broke something basic: looking at a picture used to mean the thing was real. Now it doesn't.

  A lot of things depend on that:

  - **Used-car and used-goods sites** are full of fake photos. People fly across countries to inspect cars that turn out to be nothing like the ad.
  - **Insurance claims** rely on before/after pictures. Anyone with a laptop can make those.
  - **Tokens that represent a real-world asset** ("this NFT is a watch in a vault") have no way to prove the watch is still there.
  - **Smart contracts that care about the real world** (parametric insurance, supply-chain triggers, DePIN sensors) have to trust one central data source.
  - **Provenance for art, wine, watches** is paperwork. Paper can be forged.

  ## What we built

  A 30-second scan from an iPhone or an industrial camera, tied to a random number that came from a satellite seconds before, signed by a chip inside the device, and minted as an NFT on Base. Five separate signatures get checked on every scan. To fake one, you'd have to fake all five at once, and one of them comes from space.

  ## What people can use it for

  **Online marketplaces.** A listing with a Reality NFT was scanned right before posting, on real hardware, with a satellite timestamp on it. Listings without one start to look suspicious by default.
  
  **Rentals and insurance.** Scan the car when you hand over the keys. Scan it when you get them back. Both scans are on-chain. There's nothing to argue about.

  **Tokenized real-world assets.** A watch in a vault gets re-scanned every week by a camera with a hardware signer. The token now points at a real watch, not a PDF promising a watch.

  **Provenance for valuables.** Every time a painting changes hands, a fresh scan goes on-chain. The history is cryptographic, not a folder of certificates.

  **Smart contracts that care about physical things.** Any contract can ask "is this thing actually there, right now?" and get back a real proof.

  **Theft and warranty.** A bicycle, a power tool, a server in a data center all get a hardware identity. Stolen things stay traceable. Warranty fights have an answer.

  ## Why it matters

  Today, the proof that a physical thing exists is a photograph. Photographs broke. We're building a replacement that uses cryptography instead.

**Challenges we ran into**

While integrating with **SpaceComputer**'s gotee_starter, one line in scripts/armory-link.sh silently hung on Linux but worked fine on my Mac: ping -c 2 -W 2000 "$GATEWAY".

No output, no error, no timeout. We assumed it was something else: a routing issue, the **SpaceComputer** Armory not booted yet, a set -e interaction, the case "$OS" block picking the wrong branch. Then we lined up the man pages. On **macOS (BSD ping)**, -W is in **milliseconds**, so 2000 = 2 seconds. On **Linux (iputils ping)**, -W is in **seconds**, so 2000 ≈ 33 minutes. The script wasn't frozen, it was waiting half an hour for a host that hadn't finished booting.

**Fix:** set PING_W per OS inside the case "$OS" branch (2000 on macOS, 2 on Linux), then use $PING_W in the shared ping call.

**Lesson:** when a shared command behaves differently across OSes, the answer is usually in the man pages, not the script. Always diff flags with units before assuming they mean the same thing.

PR to **SpaceComputer**: https://github.com/spacecomputer-io/gotee_starter/pull/5

**Network Economy**

Proof of Reality is itself a small network economy with three roles, each with a clear incentive.

**Capture operators** (organizations running B2B OAK4 stations or fleets of B2C iPhones) register their devices in a permissionless on-chain **DeviceRegistry.sol**. Registration is a public stake of reputation: every scan a device produces is signed by it, and every signature is traceable on-chain back to the registering org. There is no gatekeeper. A used-car dealership, a logistics company, an insurance adjuster, or a citizen-science collective registers under the same contract on the same terms.

**Verifiers** (marketplaces, RWA protocols, DePIN orchestrators, KYC officers) consume scans for free, but their economic question is no longer "do I trust the listing photo." It becomes "is the bundle hash committed on-chain, do the five signatures verify, is the signing device registered to an org I'm willing to credit." That moves the trust decision from human judgment about a stock photo to a deterministic check against public infrastructure.

**Asset holders** (the people who scanned the thing) get a transferable on-chain artifact, the Reality NFT, that travels with the object across marketplaces, custody changes, and protocol boundaries. The proof is durable independent of any single operator: bundle on Swarm, name on ENS, contract on Base, source on Sourcify.

The economic primitive we are adding is "proof of physical existence at a moment in time." Today's RWA and DePIN networks assume this primitive and outsource it to a single trusted operator. We make it a public good, secured by hardware and a satellite, and route incentives so capture operators are rewarded for honest scans and slashable (via on-chain registry revocation) for fraudulent ones. The backend is a thin economic proxy that collects gas, postage, and Orbitport quota, not value.

The result is the missing settlement layer for any network whose economic claims depend on something physical existing. That is the Network Economy contribution.

**Future Society**

A Solarpunk future needs cryptographic ground truth about the physical world. Which solar array exists. Which battery actually holds the capacity it claims. Which carbon-credit forest is a forest, and not a satellite-image overlay. Most of today's RWA, DePIN, and impact-finance protocols collapse onto a single trusted operator who promises the physical thing is real.

We replace that operator with a structural alternative: three independent hardware-rooted witnesses (satellite cTRNG, KMS co-sig, on-device key) plus a permissionless on-chain device registry where any organization can publicly stake reputation by registering its capture devices. No central authority issues the truth. The truth is a recomputable hash, signed by parties with public keys, anchored to a moment in time the operator did not get to choose.

The infrastructure stack carries the same values down to the bottom layer. Storage is Swarm (self-hosted Bee), not S3. Randomness is Orbitport, not a centralized RNG. Device identity is hardware, not a SaaS API. Contract source is verified on Sourcify, not a single-operator dashboard. A Reality NFT is durable in the strict sense: if we disappear tomorrow, the bundle is still on Swarm, the ENS name still resolves, the contract is still on Base, and the proof is still verifiable from a laptop.

The Solarpunk theme isn't a metaphor we borrowed for the pitch. It is the literal scope of the system.

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

SpaceComputer is the spine of this project, not a logo on a slide. Every Reality NFT we mint embeds two independent SpaceComputer-rooted signatures, both verifiable client-side against pinned pubkeys.

The first is **satSig**. The iPhone (or the OAK4 station) pulls a cTRNG nonce from Orbitport before capture, the satellite signs it, and the device paints the value into the scene as a QR plus audio overlay. The signature pins the scan to a moment in time the attacker cannot precompute or roll back.

The second is **cosmoSig**. Every bundle hash gets co-signed by Space Fabric KMS in TEE. The order of operations is fixed in **apps/api/src/routes/upload.routes.ts**: verify the device signature, KMS co-sign the **deviceSigningHash**, embed the **spaceFabric** block, recompute the final **bundleHash**. The KMS pubkey is pinned in the viewer (**docs/trust-model.md**), so verification runs without trusting our backend at all.

Both signatures are committed on-chain via **RealityProof.mint(...)** on Base Sepolia, so they cannot be retroactively swapped. If our backend is fully compromised, the attacker can drain Orbitport quota, Swarm postage, and gas. They cannot forge a scan, because they hold neither the satellite's key nor the KMS's key.

We use Orbitport as the temporal anchor and Space Fabric as the integrity anchor, exactly as they were designed: cryptographic ground truth for an oracle that bridges the physical world onto Ethereum.

**Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway**

We shipped **@proof-of-reality/verified-swarm-fetch**, a **fetch()**-shaped library that downloads from any Bee gateway and recomputes the chunk address client-side before returning the bytes. The IPFS world has **helia-verified-fetch**. Swarm needed its own. We wrote it.

```ts
const { data, verified, scope } = await verifiedFetch(reference, {
  gateway: "https://api.gateway.ethswarm.org",
});
if (!verified) throw new Error("gateway tampered");
```

It runs in browser and Node, no Bee node required, no private keys, no Buffer dependency. Single-chunk CAC (**keccak256(span || payload)**) is fully verified today. Multi-chunk BMT and SOC feed verification are scoped next.

The library is load-bearing for the rest of the project. Every scan is uploaded to Swarm through our self-hosted Bee node (**infra/swarm/**), with postage stamps purchased on Gnosis. The viewer's first verification check uses **verified-swarm-fetch** to refetch the bundle and confirm the gateway returned exactly what was addressed. If the gateway lies, the library catches it and the scan fails verification.

It is published to npm under MIT so anyone else building on Swarm can drop it in. That was the point of the bounty as we read it: trust no gateway, and make it easy for the next team not to trust their gateway either.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

Each Reality NFT publishes its own ENS subname on Sepolia: **vin-<bundleHash[2:14]>.realityproof.eth**. The handle is not decoration. It is how the proof is shared.

Records on each subname carry the full commitment:

- **addr** resolves to the attestor wallet
- **contenthash** is an ENSIP-7 Swarm reference to the canonical bundle JSON
- text records hold **bundleHash**, **satSig**, **cosmoSig**, **capturedAt**, **tokenId**, **mode**, **url**, **avatar**

A verifier holding only the ENS handle can fetch the bundle (Brave, MetaMask, eth.link all resolve ENSIP-7 contenthash natively), recompute the canonical hash, and check the five signatures. They do not need our contract address, our backend, or our app to be online.

That is the creative use: ENS is not a vanity wrapper around an NFT URL. It is the canonical, wallet-native, infrastructure-agnostic sharing surface for an off-chain proof. The contract is a commit log. The bundle lives on Swarm. The ENS name is the human-readable handle that ties them together. If our company disappears tomorrow, the proof remains resolvable.

A demo script (**apps/api/scripts/verify-ens.ts**) walks any judge through resolving a live mint to its records, end to end, in one terminal command.

Team **Proof of Reality** -- [Oleksandr Yuriichuk](https://github.com/Bombonchik), Maryia Charadnichenka, Alex Popov, [Nikita Sokovnin](https://github.com/sokovninn)

### JimmyAgent
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/simbaagent-a916) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/bubon-ik/ETHPrague-2026-Hack) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/GlPcin1WQ4s) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> AI powered satellite wallet

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/Go-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![ENS](https://img.shields.io/badge/ENS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Web3 financial actions are still unsafe and hard to understand for normal users, and the risk becomes even higher when AI agents are allowed to prepare transactions.

Today, users often sign opaque wallet prompts without understanding the real calldata, token approvals, recipients, or contract risks. Browser wallets can be phished, hosted frontends can be compromised, and server-side signing creates dangerous hot-key custody risk. At the same time, AI agents are becoming useful for financial workflows, but giving an agent direct control over private keys is not safe.

Jimmy solves this by separating intent, reasoning, memory, and signing into different trust layers. The user creates intent locally, the AI agent explains and prepares the action, Swarm stores encrypted decentralized memory, ENS provides human-readable identity and agent discovery, and final transaction signing is handled by a satellite-backed SpaceComputer signing layer instead of a normal browser wallet or centralized hot server.

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenge 1 — Reliable tool-calling for real transactions
Our supervisor uses LLM function calls for ENS checks and Sepolia market actions. The model often put fields like amount, recipient, or to next to the tool call instead of inside payload, which broke our market agent’s expectations. We fixed this in code by merging top-level fields into a single payload before dispatch, and we tightened the system prompt so the model follows a consistent quote → confirm → execute flow. That made swaps, sends, and ENS registration repeatable enough for a live demo.

**Network Economy**

Jimmy fits the Network Economy track because it builds a safer, user-controlled model for on-chain financial actions. The project combines satellite-backed transaction signing, AI-assisted wallet operations, ENS identity, and decentralized Swarm memory to reduce reliance on centralized backend custody and opaque browser signing.

Instead of giving an AI agent direct custody of funds, Jimmy separates intent, reasoning, memory, and signing into different trust layers. Users can perform swaps, sends, ENS-related actions, and agent-assisted financial workflows while keeping final transaction authorization in an isolated signing layer.

This directly supports the Network Economy theme by improving user control, wallet security, and decentralized identity for real on-chain economic activity.

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

TL;DR: Private key and signing operations are on SpaceComputer satellite.

Jimmy fits the SpaceComputer track because the core wallet signing flow is built around the idea that financial actions should not be signed by a normal browser wallet or a hot backend server.
In our architecture, the local wallet UI and AI agent create transaction intent, but the signing authority is moved into a KMS Space Computer / satellite-backed signing environment. This means the agent can reason about actions, prepare swaps, sends, or ENS-related operations, but it does not directly custody the private key.
The SpaceComputer layer acts as the isolated trust boundary for transaction signing:
the interface creates intent, but does not own the key
the backend routes and builds transactions, but is not the custodian
the AI agent explains and prepares actions, but cannot directly steal funds
the SpaceComputer-backed signer is responsible for final transaction authorization
This fits the bounty because Jimmy demonstrates a real wallet use case for SpaceComputer: secure signing for autonomous Web3 agents or the users themselves. The project shows how satellite-backed compute can become a safer signing layer for AI-powered financial workflows.

**A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm**

Our project uses Swarm as a decentralized key-value memory layer for the Jimmy AI wallet agent.

Jimmy stores encrypted session history, transaction context, and agent decision logs in Swarm instead of keeping this data only in a centralized backend or local browser state. This gives the agent persistent decentralized memory: it can preserve previous wallet interactions, security context, and audit history across sessions.

In our architecture, Swarm is not just file storage. It acts as a simple decentralized KV store for agent memory:

key: wallet / agent session identifier
value: encrypted session history and transaction context
This fits the track because we use Swarm KV as a practical storage primitive for a real application: a satellite-backed AI wallet where the agent needs persistent, encrypted, decentralized memory.

**Best ENS Integration for AI Agents**

Our project integrates ENS as an identity and discovery layer for AI agents inside Jimmy, our satellite-backed AI wallet.

Jimmy uses ENS in three ways:

ENS agent discovery
We implemented ENSIP-26-style metadata lookup for AI agents. The system can read ENS text records such as agent-context and agent-endpoint[http] to discover whether an ENS name represents an AI agent and where its agent metadata or endpoint lives.

ENS name checks and registration flow
The ENS Agent can check .eth name availability using ENS normalization, Blockscout BENS data, and on-chain Base Registrar reads. Availability checks use Ethereum mainnet sources; registration and sends resolve ENS on Sepolia for the demo. If a name is available, Jimmy can prepare a Sepolia ENS registration flow through the Market Agent.

ENS as human-readable recipients
For wallet actions, users can provide ENS names instead of raw 0x addresses. Jimmy resolves ENS names on Sepolia for actions like native ETH sends or swap output recipients.

This fits the track because ENS is not just displayed as a username. We use ENS as a practical coordination layer for AI agents: agent discovery, human-readable wallet actions, and domain-based identity for autonomous Web3 workflows. In our architecture, ENS helps users and agents understand who they are interacting with before any financial action is prepared or signed.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

Jimmy uses ENS creatively as more than a human-readable wallet name. We use ENS as an identity and discovery layer for AI agents inside a satellite-backed autonomous wallet.

The project integrates ENS in three ways:

AI agent discovery: Jimmy can inspect ENS records for agent metadata, including ENSIP-26-style text records like agent-context and agent-endpoint[http].
Human-readable financial actions: users can send ETH or route swap outputs to ENS names instead of raw 0x addresses.
ENS domain automation: the agent can check .eth availability and prepare a Sepolia ENS registration flow when the user wants to claim a name.
The creative part is that ENS becomes part of the agent workflow: it helps the wallet understand who an agent is, where its metadata lives, and where assets should be sent. In Jimmy, ENS is not just a name label; it is a coordination layer for AI agents and wallet actions.

### Kowalski Market
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/kowalski-market-cb4b) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/milancu/ETH-Prague-2026) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://app.kowalski-market.com/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Predict with Kowalski

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![SQLite](https://img.shields.io/badge/SQLite-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Kowalski Market is an on-chain prediction market where the live trading price of every event is its real-time probability. Three distinct features set it apart: (1) permissionless market creation — anyone can deploy a market with custom rules by posting a bond, with a curator  validating before it goes live; (2) Kowalski, a voice- and text-controlled AI layer that lets users trade, place limit orders, navigate, and discuss markets in natural language while every transaction is signed by the user's own wallet; and (3) Central-Europe-first coverage of events legacy bookmakers and global prediction markets ignore — CE politics, weather, energy prices, regional sport, and culture.

Together these features unlock things today's prediction markets can't:

1. Niche markets get real liquidity. A user asks "Will US tariffs on European steel exceed 15% by Q3 2026?"  - user get a prediction on the probability of an event of his/hers interest

2. Standard prediction markets and their interfaces aren't intuitive — most users don't understand order books or CLOB mechanics. Through Kowalski's agentic interface, beginners interact by simply talking, and the agent explains whatever they need along the way.

3. Research happens in the same flow. "Why did this move 8% in the last hour?" — the agent surfaces the news behind the move. Voice works hands-free.

4. CE coverage that didn't exist finally does — politics, weather, energy, regional sport, and culture, in the region's own language and context.

**Challenges we ran into**

The interesting part was designing the prediction market around the end user — improving on what existing prediction markets get wrong and rethinking how the trading surface should feel for someone who isn't already a crypto-native trader. 

On the technical side, ENS resolution was returning stale or near-match records, so Kowalski would confidently answer about a different market than the user named — solved by exact-match first, fuzzy only as a confirmation prompt, plus a sanity check that the resolved market's question matches user intent before any action. The other big opportunity was making a CLOB and an AMM coexist so liquid markets get tight order-book spreads while freshly created ones aren't dead on arrival; we routed every quote through a single pricing layer that aggregates both sources, with the AMM as implicit counterparty when the book is thin — fillable prices on day one, tighter book-driven prices once real makers arrive.

**Network Economy**

Kowalski Market puts the user — not the platform, not the agent — in control of every economic action. Three ways we address the track:

1. Non-custodial even with an AI in the loop. Most "AI agent" products quietly take custody to make UX work. Kowalski inverts this: the agent interprets intent, drafts orders, and chains multi-step trades, but the wallet stays with the user and every transaction is signed locally. No session tokens that can move funds, no bypass of the signing prompt — conversational UX without giving up self-custody.

2. No central point of failure. Markets are created on chain via bond, prices come from CLOB + AMM, resolution is protocol-enforced. No bookmaker can rewrite odds. Identity is wallet-native.

3. Real economic activity, privacy-respecting by default. Settlement is on-chain; positions and fills are auditable without exposing personal data. With no central account system, there's no honeypot linking trades to real identities — and agents acting on a user's behalf inherit that same boundary, so AI participation doesn't leak data into a centralized ledger.

Net effect: users keep their keys, their identity, and their data, while still getting AI-native UX and real on-chain economic activity — the "user control first" stack the track asks for.

**Future Society**

Kowalski Market addresses this by removing three concrete barriers that keep on-chain tools out of ordinary people's hands:

1. Onboarding is a conversation, not a learning curve. Most people never interact with Ethereum because the interface assumes you already understand wallets, gas, slippage, and order books. Kowalski's voice- and text-controlled agent translates all of that into plain language — "buy €5 of YES if it drops below 30¢" — while the user signs every transaction themselves. The agent never holds keys, so non-custodial self-sovereignty stays intact; the wall in front of it just disappears.

2. Anyone can price an event, not just the legacy bookmakers. Forecasting outcomes — elections, energy prices, regional weather — has historically been gatekept by centralized markets that ignore anything outside their commercial top tier. Open, bond-backed market creation means a community can mint a market on a question that matters to them (a Czech referendum, a Polish energy cap, a regional drought) and the crowd prices it transparently on-chain. Information that would otherwise live in opaque polls or paywalled reports becomes a public, verifiable signal.

3. AI-native participation expands who counts as a trader. When agents can trade on a user's behalf within the limits the user sets, liquidity stops being a function of how many humans happen to click through an order book. Niche, civically important markets that used to die from thin volume now get priced by agent participation, which means better forecasts on the long-tail questions communities actually care about — without sacrificing user custody, transparency, or on-chain auditability.

Together: a non-custodial, AI-native, community-creatable prediction layer that turns Ethereum into infrastructure for collective forecasting — open to anyone who can speak, not just anyone who can read a CLOB.

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

We use SpaceComputer's cosmic-radiation true RNG (cTRNG) as the supplier of entropy for our project. There are two main uses of entropy in our project:
1/ Some actors’ utility function is maximized by betting on randomness. We have a prediction market where they can bet on verifiable randomness - the market is resolved based on a  modulo of randomness in a predefined (defined before the market is created) block in SpaceComputer. An optimistic oracle (UMA style) provides the data on-chain.
2/ For matching the orders, we use a 0x-like off-chain order book protocol. The holder of the off-chain order book can always abuse the situation and front-run their own put or call options. SpaceComputer provides randomness for the decision of which order should be executed first.


Demo: https://www.loom.com/share/9cbeabbc145f49299a8cb3c941ab0f9c

**Best Agentic Venture**

We have built an agent-agnostic backend protocol for a prediction market MCP server, featuring an x402 paywall for premium tools. Any AI agent—whether it is Claude Code, a Custom GPT, an autonomous Python bot, or any entity with httpx and a wallet—can fully interact with these markets.
While agents can operate independently, users can also utilize our agentic frontend when preferred. Our execution stack consists of three cleanly integrated layers:
* End-user agents place trades on behalf of humans.
* Our backend operations agent manages overhead, such as paying Apify for real-time scraping.
* Our public intelligence API monetizes data by selling up-to-date world news to other agents.

Potential Revenue Streams
Global betting is an approximately $500B annual category—encompassing sports betting, casinos, and lotteries. Online betting alone accounts for over $90B, with prediction markets being the fastest-growing segment (notably, Polymarket cleared multi-billion dollar notional volume in 2024).
Our potential revenue streams include:
1. Bond Slashing: Penalties for bad-faith or unethical market routes are captured as protocol revenue and distributed as curator rewards.
2. Trading Fees: A fee toggle can be activated per market once liquidity is sufficient. Implementation timing may be determined by a UMIA decision market.
3. Intelligence API: Earns $0.50–$0.75 per call via the x402 protocol.
4. Asset Yield: On-chain interest generated from liquidity locked within betting markets represents a significant secondary revenue source.

UMIA Integration
Integrating UMIA is optimal for our DAO token distribution and is essential for securing the financing needed to scale the project.
Furthermore, it strengthens company governance through decision markets. Our DAO is built on the core belief that markets are the ultimate predictors; therefore, implementing them into our own decision-making mechanisms is both a logical and strategic move.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

Each prediction market gets a <slug>.kowalski.eth subname that AI agents discover, pay for, and consume — without API keys, accounts, or off-chain config.

 - Self-describing API contract on-chain. Text records api / api-input / price tell the agent where to call, what body to send, and how much to pay in USDC.
 - Cross-chain live state mirror. Indexer streams MarketCreated / Resolved events from Base Sepolia → ENS text records on Ethereum Sepolia (status, outcome, expiresAt) update within seconds. ENS is not just a snapshot — it's a real-time on-chain projection of market state.
 - Agent flow in 3 RPC calls. Resolve subname → POST endpoint → 402 challenge → sign USDC → retry → signed intelligence. No SDK, no docs, no allowlist. Wallet = identity, payment = auth.
 - Beyond name → address. ENS becomes the addressing layer for x402-paywalled data oracles. The pattern generalizes to any priced resource — ENS as the universal directory for the agent payment economy.
 - Live & functional. 9 markets registered on Eth Sepolia via custom MarketSubnameRegistrar + MarketResolver contracts. Verifiable end-to-end: cast call returns the URL → curl returns 402 → demo script ships with the repo.

**Apify Bounty**

AI agents reasoning about prediction markets need real-time web data — tweets, news, Reddit, sentiment — but lack native payment rails for paid APIs, forcing manual API key provisioning, accounts, and invoices. We wrap Apify actors behind an x402 paywall: autonomous agents hit our /v1/intelligence/* endpoints, the server returns HTTP 402 with payment requirements, the agent signs a USDC transferWithAuthorization on Base Sepolia, retries, and receives fresh scraped data within seconds ($0.50 USDC per call, $0.75 for premium tools, settled via the public x402.org facilitator). The novel piece: we chain two x402 hops in a single user flow — the agent pays us on Base Sepolia, then we pay Apify on Base mainnet, both via x402, producing two visible 402sign200 across both layers. 
Effect: agents become first-class data consumers without manual API key provisioning, accounts, or invoices.

### Nexora
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/nexora-57a5) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Hackathon-Escrow-Fiit) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Freelance Platform entirely on DeFi  DAO  AI

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenZeppelin](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenZeppelin-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Hardhat](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hardhat-333333?style=flat-square) ![Wagmi](https://img.shields.io/badge/Wagmi-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Nexora solves the trust gap at the heart of every online freelance transaction. When a client and a freelancer who have never met agree to work together, there is no neutral, transparent system guaranteeing fairness for both sides. Centralised platforms like Upwork or Fiverr act as judge, jury, and fee collector simultaneously — charging up to 20% in fees while making opaque, unappealable decisions about disputes behind closed doors. Freelancers face delayed payments and subjective rulings. Clients struggle with vague deliverables and limited recourse when work falls short.
Nexora replaces the middleman with a verifiable, trustless stack.
For Clients

AI-assisted task creation — instead of writing a vague brief and hoping for the best, Nexora's AI co-pilot structures your task into a precise specification with measurable acceptance criteria, milestone breakdowns, and deliverable formats. Both sides know exactly what "done" means before work begins.
Funds locked in smart contract escrow — your payment is secured on-chain from day one. No platform can freeze it, redirect it, or charge hidden fees. It releases only when work is verified — automatically, transparently, and on your terms.
Verified freelancer ratings — every freelancer's skill level is represented by an AI-evaluated Elo rating, not self-reported experience. You see a verified track record, not a curated portfolio.

For Freelancers

Guaranteed payment — once you complete work that meets the agreed spec, the escrow releases automatically. No chasing invoices, no waiting on client goodwill, no platform deciding to hold your funds.
Fair dispute resolution — if a client disputes your work unfairly, a decentralised jury of qualified community members reviews the evidence and decides — not a customer support agent with no accountability.
Portable reputation — your Elo rating and work history live in your ENS identity, not inside Nexora's database. Take your reputation with you to any platform that reads it.

For the Ecosystem

DAO-governed disputes — contested work is resolved by a community jury using a blind voting system that prevents groupthink. Jurors stake tokens on their verdicts and are rewarded for honest participation, creating a self-sustaining court system with real skin in the game.
Newcomer discovery incentives — clients who hire new freelancers earn token rewards, solving the cold-start problem that locks talented newcomers out of traditional platforms.
Zero platform lock-in — no company controls your account, your reputation, or your funds. Nexora is a protocol, not a gatekeeper.

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges We Ran Into
Making the AI evaluator trustless
Our first approach called the OpenAI API from the frontend and passed results directly to the contract — anyone could fake an evaluation. The fix was giving the evaluator its own Ethereum wallet that signs every Completion Report. The escrow contract only accepts results signed by the registered evaluator address. A security constraint turned into the core design feature that made the agent real.

Preventing jurors from influencing each other
We built the dispute screen showing a live vote tally — standard DAO behaviour. Testing immediately revealed the problem: late voters just copy early voters. We fixed this at two levels simultaneously: commit-reveal voting in the contract makes it cryptographically impossible to see others' choices early, and the UI deliberately hides all juror reasoning until after you've committed your own vote. The frontend information sequencing mirrors the on-chain cryptographic guarantee.

ENS reputation update costs
Writing every Elo change directly to ENS text records on L1 cost more in gas than most task values. Solution: reputation changes live in our ReputationStore contract on L2 (cheap per update), with ENS records updated in batches via a CCIP-Read offchain resolver. Reputation stays portable and readable from ENS — just not updated on every single action.

**Network Economy**

At its core Nexora is on-chain economic infrastructure. The smart escrow system handles programmable milestone payments between pseudonymous parties without any intermediary holding funds. The DWK token creates a self-sustaining incentive loop — jurors stake to participate, earn for honest verdicts, and lose for bad ones. Freelancer Elo ratings are AI-evaluated and stored on-chain, creating verifiable economic identities that travel across platforms. Every economic interaction on Nexora — hiring, paying, disputing, voting — is transparent, auditable, and user-controlled.

**Future Society**

Nexora is a direct answer to the coordination failures in the global freelance economy. We replace a centralised, opaque gatekeeper with a transparent protocol where funds are governed by smart contracts, disputes are resolved by the community, and reputation is owned by the individual. The platform empowers freelancers who have historically had no recourse against unfair rulings, and gives clients verifiable guarantees that no traditional platform can offer. Governance, fairness, and economic autonomy are not features we added — they are the architecture.

**Best Agentic Venture**

Nexora is built to function as an agentic venture from day one. The AI evaluator operates as a fully autonomous on-chain agent — it has its own wallet, stakes DWK tokens on its assessments, pays for IPFS storage from its own treasury, and loses stake when the DAO overrides its judgment. It improves its model based on override feedback, creating a self-correcting loop with no human in the middle. The platform generates real revenue through a 1-3% fee on every escrow release, flowing directly to the DAO treasury governed by DWK token holders through Umia's decision markets. The DWK token has five concrete utilities — dispute staking, juror rewards, governance voting, reputation boosting, and fee discounts — making it a functional token, not a speculative one. Post-hackathon, Nexora will apply for a Tailored Auction on Umia, giving early community members (freelancers and clients who used the platform at launch) priority access via zkTLS proofs of their on-chain activity.

**Best ENS Integration for AI Agents**

The Nexora AI evaluator is not a backend service — it is an on-chain agent with its own wallet and ENS identity at evaluator.nexora.eth. Its capabilities, model version, accuracy rate, total evaluations, and specialisations are stored in ENS text records and publicly readable by anyone. When the escrow contract needs a completion assessment, it resolves evaluator.nexora.eth to find the agent's wallet, routes the evaluation request to it, and the agent signs its Completion Report with that wallet before submitting the IPFS hash on-chain. Removing ENS from this flow breaks it entirely — the contract has no other way to discover, authenticate, or trust the evaluator. Multiple specialised agents (code-eval.nexora.eth, design-eval.nexora.eth) can be registered as subnames with different capability records, enabling domain-specific evaluation routing.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

Nexora uses ENS in three ways that go well beyond name-to-address resolution. First, juror access tokens — when a dispute jury is assembled, each selected juror receives a temporary ENS subname (juror-3.dispute-42.nexora.eth). Only wallets resolving to a valid juror subname can decrypt the encrypted dispute evidence on IPFS. When the dispute closes, subnames are revoked. ENS becomes a time-limited, role-based cryptographic access credential. Second, portable reputation — every freelancer's Elo rating, task history, and DAO reputation score live in their ENS text records at alice.nexora.eth. Any external platform can read this data by resolving the name — no API, no permission, no lock-in. Third, multichain payment routing — clients pay alice.nexora.eth regardless of which chain she prefers. ENSIP-9 coin types in her text records route the payment to the right address on the right chain automatically.

### Krtek Wallet + 2FA
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/krtek-wallet-fa-6655) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/JustAnotherDevv/Krtek-Wallet) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Easy to use wallet with 2FA that feels like web2

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![ENS](https://img.shields.io/badge/ENS-333333?style=flat-square) ![sourcify](https://img.shields.io/badge/sourcify-333333?style=flat-square) ![Apify](https://img.shields.io/badge/Apify-333333?style=flat-square) ![Space-computer](https://img.shields.io/badge/Space--computer-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Demo Video: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1sm5W6mXupJr4u48jPRc-gyBWgD5eg

A self-custodial EVM wallet for non-crypto-natives.
**No seed phrase, ever.** Signing in with ENS and password derives your owner key in the browser
(Argon2id), funds live in an ERC-4337 smart account, and a custom paymaster
sponsors gas so users never need ETH to make their first move.

## What's built

### 1. Password-only login → on-chain smart account
Argon2id over `(password, sha256("krtek.wallet.v1.password-key:" + handle))`
deterministically derives a secp256k1 owner key in the browser. The owner key
lives only in tab memory; nothing secret touches localStorage. The same
password+handle on any device yields the same wallet — a real ERC-4337 v0.7
SCA at a CREATE2 address. See `web/src/lib/password-key.ts`,
`PASSWORD_LOGIN.md`.

### 2. Custom verifying paymaster (gasless onboarding)
A Bun service signs `paymasterAndData` for every UserOp; the on-chain
`KrtekPaymaster` verifies the signature in `validatePaymasterUserOp`. Works
on any chain you give it addresses for — anvil, Sepolia, real L2s. Users
never need ETH to make their first move. See `paymaster-server/`.

### 3. M-of-N social recovery
The SCA carries a `setGuardians(address[], threshold)` slot. Recovery is a
single `recoverOwner(newOwner, deadline, signatures[])` call that verifies M
unique guardian sigs against a per-account replay nonce. Lose your password,
collect signatures from your friends, rotate to a fresh owner key — same SCA
address. See `contracts/src/KrtekSCA.sol`,
[`web/src/routes/Recover.tsx`](./web/src/routes/Recover.tsx).

### 4. Phone 2FA via WebSocket relay
The SCA's `validateUserOp` accepts a 130-byte signature: `ownerSig`
(EIP-191) `||` `phoneSig` (raw secp over the userOpHash). With
`lockToPhone=true`, every UserOp must be co-signed by a paired phone.
Pairing flow lives in Settings → Phone 2FA; the existing `mobile/`
companion handles the user-side approval UX. See
`web/src/lib/relay/`, `mobile/`.

### 5. Sourcify APIv2 deep integration
Built specifically for the Sourcify bounty:
- **Provenance Card** — animated visualization of the source-files →
  metadata.json → IPFS CID → CBOR auxdata → on-chain bytecode chain
- **Transformations diff** — renders the `transformations[]` array as
  bullets *and* annotated hex showing constructor args / libraries /
  immutables / cborAuxdata regions in the deployed bytecode
- **Multi-chain trust strip** — `/v2/contract/all-chains/{address}`
  showing where else the same code is verified
- **In-browser re-verification** — applies `transformations[]` to
  `recompiledBytecode` locally, decodes the CBOR auxdata, attempts to
  reproduce the IPFS CID — proves the verification mathematically without
  trusting the public Sourcify server
- **Source files drawer** — every source file with a Solidity highlighter,
  the file containing the called function highlighted

Uses APIv2 (the legacy `/files/...` endpoints went into brownouts in May
2026), the new `exact_match` / `match` vocabulary, and `proxyResolution`
to follow proxies natively. See `web/src/lib/sourcify.ts`,
`web/src/lib/sourcify-verify.ts`,
`web/src/components/wallet/{ProvenanceCard,TransformationsView,SourceFilesDrawer,MultiChainStrip}.tsx`.

### 6. Multi-profile + auto-resume
Multiple wallets per device under different handles. Pairing state and SCA
caches persist per profile; logging in re-attaches the relay session
transparently. See `web/src/lib/profiles.ts`.

### 7. USB Armory MK II — hardware-attested 2FA
Same SCA cosigner slot as the phone, different transport: an i.MX6ULL
Trusted Applet (Rust, no_std, ARM TrustZone Secure World) holds a
secp256k1 key derived from the chip's DCP hardware-attestation primitive
(`sk = sha256("krtek-signer-v1" || RPC.Attest)`). The applet only
exposes `GetPubkey`, `GetAddress`, `Approve(digest)` and `Health` — it
has no `ExportSecret` method, so the key never crosses the syscall
boundary back to Normal World. Pulling the SD card and cloning storage
doesn't yield the key; the DCP secret is silicon-locked.

End-to-end: web app → `armory-bridge/` (Bun + Hono on `:4141`) →
`nc 10.0.0.1:4000` (USB-CDC-ECM bridge) → applet → 65-byte recoverable
ECDSA signature → web concatenates `ownerSig || armorySig` into the
same 130-byte UserOp signature shape the phone path produces. The SCA
verifies with one `ECDSA.recover` call per signature; it doesn't care
whether the cosigner is a phone or an Armory.

`web/src/lib/send.ts` runs `decideCosigner(sender)`: if the Armory's
deterministic address matches the on-chain `phoneSigner`, sign via the
Armory; else if the relay-paired phone matches, sign via the phone; else
owner-only (which the contract refuses if `lockToPhone=true`). The
applet itself lives in the gitignored `gotee_starter/` SDK fork; the
host-side wiring is `armory-bridge/`,
`web/src/lib/armory/`, `web/src/components/wallet/ArmoryTfaCard.tsx`.

### 8. Cosmic Backup — cTRNG-seeded self-recovery phrase
A 24-word BIP-39 phrase

**Challenges we ran into**

We had some issues setting up armory hardware device from space computer but we were able to make it work on one of the laptops.

**Ethereum Core**

- First ever implementation of noncustodial decentralized 2FA for onchain transactions protecting users even if their main device is compromised.

- Web2 UX: Users can access the same smart wallet account just like they would log in from any device to their web2 account thanks to sign-in with ENS + password that derives access key to the smart account wallet.

**Future Society**

If we want to onboard non crypto native users to blockchain we need to have web2-like UX.

We've created new wallet that can connect to any defi applications through WalletConnect and can:

- Be accessed from any device without seedphrase using sign-in with ENS + password that derives access key to smart account
- First ever self custody decentralized 2FA implementation for onchain transactions, each time user wants to sign tx from web app they have to also provide OTP code that is generated using SpaceComputer RNG.

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

We have used SpaceComputer armory hardware to create backend for 2FA verification and to host decentralized AI agent that verifies and does analysis of transactions that are about to be signed by the user.

**Sourcify Bounty**

Each time raw unsigned tx is about to be signed our AI agent receives context about it, contract, its verified source code which then used by agent to explain what the transaction does in human readable way, check for potential security issues and allows user to ask follow-up questions about the smart contract e.g. user is about to sign swap transaction, so they ask agent with access to sourcify data to fetch pool balance information from this contract.

**Best ENS Integration for AI Agents**

Each time user registers they choose their ENS subdomain which later allows them to login through sign in with ENS. Once they start using app they can also choose ENS subdomain for each agent deployed in TEE, ENS can then be used to communicate and interact with agent.

**Apify Bounty**

Each agent defi serices like transaction analysis, scanning for vulnerabilities, reading from contracts etc are exposed through x402 services endpoints and can be purchased by other agents.

### SignGuard
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/signguard-c190) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/KovalenkoDima236961/EthPrague_Hackathon) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/AkaAHgDmnFg) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Know What You Sign

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenZeppelin](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenZeppelin-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Swarm](https://img.shields.io/badge/Swarm-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![AI](https://img.shields.io/badge/AI-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem It Solves

One of the biggest problems in Ethereum today is that users are regularly asked to sign transactions they do not fully understand. Wallets often show raw calldata, contract addresses, token approvals, hex signatures, or vague method names, but this does not clearly explain what will actually happen after signing.

Many existing transaction security tools focus mainly on whether something is “safe” or “unsafe.” While this is useful, it often leaves users without enough context. A green checkmark does not explain what permissions are being granted, which assets may move, who the user is interacting with, or whether the transaction matches the user’s real intent.

This problem affects not only beginners, but also developers. Complex Web3 transactions can involve proxy contracts, batched calls, internal contract calls, delegate execution, account abstraction flows, ERC-4337 UserOperations, paymasters, session keys, plugins, and multiple protocol layers. Even experienced developers often need to jump between explorers, contract addresses, calldata decoders, traces, ABIs, and documentation just to understand what a single transaction is doing.

SignGuard solves this by adding a transaction understanding layer before signing. Instead of only showing a generic risk label, SignGuard analyzes and explains what the transaction actually does using transaction simulation, calldata decoding, contract inspection, approval analysis, ENS verification, Sourcify source verification, phishing detection, protocol identification, and suspicious permission checks.

People can use SignGuard to:

* understand what they are signing before confirming a wallet transaction;
* detect dangerous approvals, suspicious spenders, fake contracts, and drainer-style interactions;
* verify whether the target contract is known, verified, or suspicious;
* understand ENS-related actions such as record updates, name transfers, resolver changes, or Name Wrapper approvals;
* inspect complex developer flows such as proxy interactions, batched calls, ERC-4337 UserOperations, paymasters, session keys, and internal execution paths;
* ask AI follow-up questions about the transaction using the full analyzed context;
* debug complex transaction flows through traces, execution graphs, decoded calldata, simulation results, and contract interaction data;
* integrate transaction safety checks into wallets, dApps, browser extensions, SDKs, or backend tools.

SignGuard adapts the explanation to the user’s knowledge level. Beginners receive simple, human-readable explanations focused on what will happen and what to watch out for. Regular users receive more context about risks, permissions, assets, and protocol behavior. Developers can inspect advanced evidence such as decoded calldata, simulation traces, ENS validation results, contract interaction graphs, source verification data, internal calls, and low-level execution details.

The AI assistant makes the workflow interactive. Instead of being limited to a static report, users and developers can ask questions such as “What exactly happens if I sign this?”, “Why is this approval risky?”, “Which internal call changed?”, “Why did this UserOperation call a different contract?”, or “Is this ENS identity legitimate?” The assistant answers using the structured analysis results, not just raw calldata.

Overall, SignGuard makes Ethereum signing easier, safer, and more understandable. For users, it turns confusing wallet confirmations into clear transaction explanations. For developers, it reduces the time needed to inspect, debug, and understand complex transaction flows before anything is signed or executed on-chain.

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges We Ran Into

One of the biggest challenges was making the analysis reliable without treating AI as the source of truth. It was tempting to let the LLM directly explain the transaction, but that could create incorrect or unsafe answers. We solved this by building a deterministic analysis pipeline first: decode calldata, simulate execution, collect Sourcify metadata, detect effects, score risks, and only then use AI as an optional explanation layer based on those facts.

Another challenge was handling transactions when contract source or ABI data was missing. In those cases, raw calldata is hard for users to understand. We added fallback behavior so the analyzer still returns useful information from simulation, traces, selector lookup, risk rules, and conservative explanations instead of failing.

ENS support also required extra care. An ENS name can help users recognize an address, but it should not automatically make a transaction safe. We handled this by using reverse lookup with forward confirmation, showing warnings for mismatches, and treating ENS as identity context rather than proof of trust.

Finally, integrating the analyzer into wallet UX was difficult because browser extensions, MetaMask Snaps, backend services, and SDK packages all have different security boundaries. We separated the project into a core engine, browser SDK, backend SDK, Snap, and extension so that sensitive API keys stay on the backend while wallets and dApps can still use the analysis safely.

**Ethereum Core**

SignGuard fits the Ethereum Core track by addressing one of the biggest UX and security problems in Ethereum today: users regularly sign transactions without actually understanding what those transactions do.

Today, many existing transaction security tools focus primarily on answering a single question: “Is this transaction safe or unsafe?” In many cases, if the transaction is considered safe, the tool simply shows a green checkmark or a short confirmation without explaining anything else. For users, this creates another problem — they still do not truly understand what they are approving, we often heard from both newcomers and even experienced crypto users that they regularly sign transactions without fully understanding what those transactions actually do. Because of this uncertainty, many users feel uncomfortable or even afraid of signing transactions, worrying that they might accidentally approve something malicious or lose their funds.

This problem becomes even more important because different users have completely different levels of blockchain knowledge. A beginner, a regular crypto user, and a developer require very different types of explanations. However, most existing tools provide explanations in one generic format, which is often either too technical for newcomers or too simplified for advanced users.

SignGuard solves this problem by introducing an adaptive transaction understanding layer for Ethereum.

We built SignGuard as a reusable SDK that can be integrated into wallets, dApps, browser extensions, and other Ethereum applications. To demonstrate the flexibility and reusability of our approach, we built two separate integrations on top of the SDK:

- a MetaMask Snap plugin that brings transaction analysis and explanations directly into the MetaMask ecosystem;
- and a standalone browser extension that enhances the transaction signing flow before the wallet confirmation step.

In the browser extension flow, before MetaMask opens for signing, SignGuard intercepts the transaction and displays an explanation interface where the user can fully understand what the transaction is about before approving it. The system analyzes the transaction, simulates its execution, detects potential risks, and explains the expected outcome in human-readable language.

The explanation adapts to the user’s experience level:

- Beginner mode focuses on simple and intuitive explanations that reduce fear and uncertainty.
- Regular user mode provides additional context about assets, approvals, swaps, and protocol interactions.
- Developer mode exposes advanced technical information such as calldata interpretation, contract interactions, and simulation details.

To achieve this, SignGuard combines multiple modern transaction analysis and simulation approaches, including transaction simulation, calldata decoding, ENS resolution, contract inspection, approval analysis, phishing and spoofing detection, and validation of suspicious transaction patterns. These techniques are used not only to evaluate transaction security, but also to improve the user experience by transforming low-level blockchain data into understandable explanations.

Additionally, SignGuard includes an AI-powered assistant that already knows the full transaction context, including simulation results, decoded calldata, detected risks, and protocol analysis. Users can ask follow-up questions in natural language and receive contextual answers before making a signing decision.

Only after the user fully understands the transaction can they choose to continue to MetaMask and sign it, or reject the transaction entirely.

For developers, SignGuard also provides advanced debugging and transaction inspection capabilities. In developer mode, the platform can visualize calldata traces, transaction execution flows, contract interaction graphs, and other low-level execution details that help developers better understand, inspect, and debug complex smart contract interactions.

As a result, SignGuard solves multiple problems simultaneously:

1. Security: helping users understand whether a transaction is potentially dangerous or suspicious.
2. User Experience: clearly explaining what the transaction actually does before signing.
3. Personalization: adapting explanations to the user’s technical knowledge level.
4. Interactive Understanding: allowing users to ask follow-up questions if they still do not understand part of the transaction.

**Sourcify Bounty**

## Bounty Fit Explanation

Users often sign Web3 transactions without fully understanding what they authorize. Wallet prompts usually expose low-level data such as contract addresses, token approvals, calldata, or generic permission messages, but they rarely explain whether the transaction matches the user’s intent or whether the target contract behavior is trustworthy.

We built a transaction analysis and simulation tool that explains what a transaction will actually do before the user signs it. The system combines transaction simulation, contract intelligence, ENS identity checks, source verification, permission analysis, and UX-focused explanation generation. The final output is adapted for different knowledge levels: beginner, regular user, and developer.

Sourcify is a core part of our analysis pipeline. We use Sourcify as a trusted source of verified contract evidence, including ABI, Solidity source files, compiler metadata, contract metadata, and verification status. This matters because raw calldata, frontend labels, and wallet-provided descriptions are not enough to reliably explain a transaction. Without verified source and ABI data, the analyzer can only infer behavior from traces or bytecode-level effects. With Sourcify, we can connect a transaction to the actual verified contract interface and source context.

In our workflow, when the analyzer receives a transaction target, it queries Sourcify using the chain ID and contract address. If verified metadata is available, the ABI is used to decode the calldata into a human-readable function call, including the function signature, arguments, and contract interaction type. This decoded call becomes the foundation for the explanation shown to the user.

We also use Sourcify data for deeper contract intelligence. Verified source files and metadata help the analyzer identify security-relevant capabilities such as owner/admin controls, upgradeability patterns, pause mechanisms, blacklist logic, minting functions, fund recovery methods, delegate execution, and privileged role management.

A particularly important use case is proxy and upgradeable contract analysis. Users usually interact with the proxy address, but the actual execution logic may live in a separate implementation contract. When Sourcify provides proxy or implementation context, our analyzer follows that relationship and inspects the verified implementation logic as well, not only the visible target address. This helps us explain the real behavior behind the transaction instead of stopping at the proxy surface.

Sourcify also strengthens selector and ABI consistency checks. A four-byte function selector can be ambiguous or decoded incorrectly if the wrong ABI is used. By using verified ABI and source context from Sourcify, our analyzer checks whether the selector resolves to the expected function in the verified contract, whether the decoded arguments are consistent with that ABI, and whether the interaction matches the apparent user intent.

The Sourcify-derived contract context is combined with transaction simulation results. Simulation shows the practical effects of the transaction, such as token transfers, approvals, balance changes, state-changing calls, or execution failures. Sourcify provides the verified explanation layer behind those effects: which function was called, what the contract is designed to do, whether the logic belongs to a proxy implementation, and which security-relevant capabilities exist in the codebase.

For developers, we expose this evidence more directly: decoded function signatures, ABI source, verification status, proxy or implementation context, notable contract capabilities, and limitations when verification is missing. For regular users and beginners, the same evidence is transformed into simpler language: whether the app is asking for token access, whether funds may move now or later, whether the contract identity is verified, and whether the transaction contains behavior that deserves attention.

**Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway**

How We Use Verified Fetch on Swarm

SignGuard uses Swarm to store complete transaction analysis snapshots for developer debugging, comparison, and review. After a transaction is simulated and analyzed, a developer can save the full result to Swarm and later share it with another developer, compare it with a newer simulation, or use it as context for AI-assisted debugging.

For this workflow, verified fetching is important because the saved analysis becomes part of the developer’s debugging evidence. If the data is loaded through a public Swarm gateway without verification, the developer still has to trust that the gateway returned the correct content. That is a problem for our use case because even a small change in the fetched analysis could completely change the interpretation of a transaction.

For example, a tampered response could hide a new internal call, change a decoded selector, remove a suspicious spender, alter a gas estimate, or modify the simulation result shown to the developer. If this data is then used for comparison or passed into the AI assistant, the explanation may be based on incorrect evidence. Because of this, SignGuard should not only store analysis snapshots on Swarm, but also verify that the fetched data is exactly the data that was originally saved.

This is where the Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway concept fits directly into our project. When SignGuard retrieves a saved transaction analysis from Swarm, the extension can fetch it from a normal public gateway, but verify it locally before using it. For immutable analysis snapshots, the client can recompute the content hash and confirm that the returned chunks match the expected Swarm reference. For mutable indexes or saved analysis lists, the client can verify signed feed updates instead of blindly trusting the gateway response.

This makes the whole debugging workflow more reliable. Developers can share a Swarm reference to a transaction analysis snapshot, and another developer can fetch it through any available gateway while still having cryptographic confidence that the data was not modified in transit. This is especially important when comparing simulations, where SignGuard may detect changes such as higher gas usage, a new internal call, a changed selector, a new spender, or different proxy implementation context.

Verified fetching is also useful for AI-assisted debugging. Since the AI assistant can answer questions over one or multiple saved analyses, it is important that the retrieved transaction evidence is authentic before it is used as model context. In practice, this means a developer can save a baseline simulation, compare it with a later transaction, and ask questions like “what changed?” or “why did this UserOperation start calling a different contract?” while knowing that the saved Swarm data was verified locally and not trusted blindly from the gateway.

**A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm**

SignGuard uses Swarm as a decentralized storage layer for transaction analysis snapshots, with a strong focus on developer workflows and debugging. After a transaction is analyzed and simulated, a developer can save the full analysis result to Swarm as a persistent, shareable package.

This package can include the original transaction input, decoded calldata, simulation results, balance and approval changes, internal calls, gas estimates, ENS evidence, Sourcify verification context, detected contract capabilities, and generated explanations. Instead of sharing screenshots, temporary logs, or local browser state, developers can store a complete analysis snapshot and send it to another developer for review.

This is especially useful when debugging complex transaction flows. A developer can run a simulation, save the result to Swarm, make changes in the frontend, backend, smart contract, SDK, or transaction builder, and then run the simulation again. SignGuard can compare the new result with the saved Swarm snapshot and show a structured diff of what changed.

For example, the comparison can show that:

gas estimation increased significantly;
a new internal call appeared;
the order of calls changed;
a different function selector is now used;
approval amount changed;
a new spender or recipient appeared;
proxy or implementation context changed;
simulation output is different from the previous run.

This makes Swarm useful as a persistent debugging baseline. Developers can compare transaction behavior across different versions of their app, smart contracts, SDK, or account abstraction setup. The workflow becomes similar to a GitHub diff, but instead of comparing code lines, SignGuard compares transaction behavior and simulation evidence.

Swarm also makes the AI assistant more useful. Because the full analysis context is stored, the developer is not limited only to the predefined UI diff shown by SignGuard. They can ask the AI assistant follow-up questions about one or multiple saved simulations, such as:

“What changed between these two transactions?”
“Why did the gas estimate increase?”
“Which new internal call appeared?”
“Did the spender, selector, or approval amount change?”
“Is this new UserOperation behavior expected?”
“Which part of the workflow became different after my code change?”

The important part is that the AI assistant answers using the structured transaction evidence saved in Swarm: decoded calls, simulation results, internal traces, contract metadata, ENS data, Sourcify context, gas estimates, and detected effects. This makes the assistant grounded in the actual analysis data instead of relying only on a short prompt or incomplete transaction summary.

A practical example is debugging account abstraction and smart wallet flows, such as Kernel-based ERC-4337 transactions. A UserOperation may involve validation logic, session keys, paymasters, plugins, batched calls, delegate execution, and multiple nested contract interactions. These flows are hard to understand from a single wallet prompt or raw simulation log. By saving one analysis snapshot to Swarm, developers get a stable reference point. When a later UserOperation behaves differently, SignGuard can compare both snapshots and the AI assistant can explain what changed in plain language: a different plugin was used, a paymaster was added, a session key permission changed, an internal call target changed, or the gas profile became abnormal.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

## How We Use ENS

SignGuard fits the “Most Interesting Use of ENS” track because we use ENS not only as a readable name for an Ethereum address, but as an active identity and trust signal inside the transaction signing flow.

Most wallets use ENS mainly as a display layer: instead of showing a raw 0x... address, they may show a human-readable name. This improves readability, but it does not fully solve the signing problem. A user may see an ENS name and still not know whether that identity is legitimate, whether it belongs to the expected protocol, whether it is being used to mislead them, or whether the transaction itself could modify their own ENS identity.

SignGuard extends the role of ENS from “address naming” to transaction understanding. When a user is about to sign a transaction, our system analyzes the transaction, simulates its effects, identifies the important actors involved, and then uses ENS as part of the identity layer behind the explanation. These actors may include the target contract, spender, recipient, protocol address, counterparty, owner, or other addresses discovered during simulation.

Instead of asking only:

> “Does this address have an ENS name?”

SignGuard asks more useful questions:

> “Can this ENS identity be trusted in this context?”
> “Does the ENS name actually resolve to the address being shown?”
> “Is this name trying to imitate a known protocol or entity?”
> “Could this transaction change the user’s ENS identity, records, resolver, ownership, or permissions?”

This is where ENS becomes especially valuable for our project. Signing is not only about checking whether a transaction is technically valid. It is also about helping the user understand who they are interacting with and what identity-related consequences the transaction may have.

A core part of our ENS analysis is reverse and forward validation. If an address has a reverse ENS record, SignGuard does not automatically trust it. We verify whether the ENS name resolves back to the same address. If the forward confirmation fails, we treat the name as potentially misleading and show a warning. This helps protect users from situations where a malicious address configures a fake or confusing reverse record to appear more trustworthy in wallets, explorers, or transaction previews.

We also use ENS as a signal for impersonation and phishing detection. SignGuard can compare ENS names against known or expected protocol identities and detect cases where a name appears visually or semantically similar to a trusted entity but resolves to a different address. This is important because attackers often rely on user trust in recognizable names, not only on technical contract exploits. ENS therefore becomes part of our anti-impersonation layer.

ENS is also integrated into our transaction simulation pipeline. SignGuard can detect when a transaction affects ENS-related state, including actions such as changing a resolver, updating address records, modifying text records, updating a contenthash, setting a reverse record, renewing a name, transferring wrapped ENS names, wrapping or unwrapping names, or granting Name Wrapper approvals and permissions.

This allows SignGuard to explain ENS-specific risks in plain language. For example, instead of only showing that a contract call is being made, we can explain that the transaction may change how the user’s ENS name resolves, update public profile records, modify website/contenthash data, transfer control of a name, or grant another address permissions over ENS-related assets.

This gives ENS two important roles in SignGuard:
First, ENS helps identify the counterparty. It helps answer who the user is interacting with, whether the displayed identity is confirmed, and whether there are signs of impersonation or spoofing.
Second, ENS helps explain the impact on the user’s own identity. It helps detect whether the transaction changes the user’s ENS records, resolver, ownership, permissions, public profile, or how their name is represented across Ethereum applications.

The result is a more meaningful signing experience. For beginners, SignGuard translates ENS analysis into simple explanations such as whether the name appears confirmed, suspicious, or potentially misleading. For regular users, we show additional context about the ENS name, resolved address, reverse record, and identity-related risks. For developers, we expose the underlying evidence directly, including forward confirmation results, resolver information, ENS transaction effects, suspicious similarity checks, and structured warnings.

Overall, SignGuard uses ENS in a creative way by turning it from a passive address label into an active identity, trust, and transaction explanation layer. ENS becomes part of the pre-signing security workflow: it helps users understand who they are interacting with, whether that identity is reliable, and whether the transaction can affect their own on-chain identity.
