### Anxin (安心)
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/anxin-35bf) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/VRP2206/MUBA_Hackathon_2026) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://anxin-protect.com) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/xfWZiAKybs8) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Peace of mind, verified twice.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docker-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

**1. The network would quietly hand us the same model twice.**
DeepSeek-V4-Flash is sustainedly saturated on Gonka, and the router's default failover re-routes overflow to MiniMax. Without noticing, a share of our "DeepSeek" verifications would have been answered by MiniMax — turning two independent opinions into one opinion printed on two lines. Fix: every call sends `X-Gonka-No-Fallback: true`, so saturation returns a real 429 instead of a substitute; we compare requested vs actual model on every response; and a 429 is treated as "this leg produced no opinion" — the report degrades to *insufficient* with a "Not cross-verified" badge and confidence capped at 60, never presented as consensus. (`gonka_client.py`, `test_deepseek_429_and_minimax_ok_degrades_honestly`)

**2. Two models disagree — and averaging is a lie.**
`(90 + 10) / 2 = 50` reports a scam one model confidently caught as "medium risk". We replaced averaging with consensus bands: within 20 points they agree; 21–40 drops confidence and reports a lean; beyond 40 we refuse to average contradictory answers and say *insufficient*. Fraud risk is taken as the **maximum**, never averaged down. And an evidence gate caps confidence when no sources were found — with one deliberate exception: phishing has no web evidence by nature, so `high_risk` is read off the message's own structure. (`consensus.py`, 27 tests)

**3. The models can't browse, and can't see images.**
Gonka serves text-in/text-out models: asked to "inspect this URL" they correctly answer "I cannot access this URL", and image input isn't supported. Retrieval moved entirely to our side — `evidence.py` fetches the URL and runs a keyless web search, SSRF-guarded (private, loopback and cloud-metadata hosts blocked, redirects re-validated) — and the models reason over fenced evidence. For screenshots, local Tesseract extracts text only, the user corrects it, and only then does anything go to Gonka. We confirmed this boundary with Gonka's tech lead before building on it.

**4. Real model output is nothing like the schema.**
Reasoning models wrap JSON in ```` ```json ```` fences and `<think>` blocks, improvise labels ("TRUE", "high risk"), and sometimes score 0–1 instead of 0–100. `json_utils.py` extracts tolerantly and the verifier normalises labels and scales — but genuinely unparseable output is still rejected rather than invented (`test_unparseable_output_raises_rather_than_inventing`). One sloppy label never costs us a whole second opinion.

**5. Screenshot mode "worked" while doing nothing.**
On any machine without Tesseract, `pytesseract` raised, the exception was swallowed, and users saw "no text could be extracted" — a claim about their image when the truth was a missing engine. Two more faults hid behind it: Tesseract 5 silently drops a missing language from `eng+chi_sim` and exits 0, so Chinese failed quietly; and pytesseract doesn't strip quotes from config on Windows, so a quoted `--tessdata-dir` reached the binary with the quotes still in the path. Fix: ask Tesseract which packs exist up front, export `TESSDATA_PREFIX`, raise a distinct engine-missing error, and return an honest "OCR engine is not installed" with an editable box. Render's native Python runtime has no Tesseract at all, so the backend now ships as a Docker image. (`ocr.py`, `test_ocr.py`, `backend/Dockerfile`)

**6. Decentralised inference has a long tail.**
The same model answers in under a second or in 40, depending on which node picks up the request. Both verifications run concurrently, each bounded at 45 s with one retry, the UI shows honest stages instead of a spinner, and the frontend's OCR timeout went from 30 s to 90 s after we found a sleeping free-tier backend takes ~30 s just to wake — aborting uploads before the server had read them.

**7. One sentence that over-claimed.**
We described receipts as proof a verdict "came from the network rather than our server". Gonka's tech lead pointed out the receipt is served from GonkaRouter's database, so it's their attestation, not an independent one. We rewrote the claim everywhere it appears — UI, README, docs — to what's defensible: *independently verifiable against GonkaRouter, not something we could fabricate on our own server*, and it does not prove the claim is true.

**8. Accessibility across two scripts.**
Our risk icons were text glyphs (✓ ⚠ ✕). With a Chinese font active the browser substitutes full-width or emoji variants, so the same warning rendered at a different size in EN and ZH. We replaced them with an original inline-SVG icon set, kept the rule that no state is ever colour alone, and never merged the Truth Score with the scam-risk score — a plausible message can still be a scam.

**The problem it solves**

*A scam text lands on a parent's phone. They read Chinese. The person best placed to warn them: their adult child — reads English.* So the message gets forwarded around the family group, and nobody is sure. The tools that could settle it speak one of those languages, and answer with a confident paragraph you're meant to take on faith.

*Anxin (安心, "peace of mind")* takes a forwarded message, a link, or a screenshot and returns, in English and Simplified Chinese:

- a *Truth Score* (0–100): how strongly evidence supports the claim
- a *separate scam-risk score*:  a plausible message can still be a scam, so the two are never merged
- *three plain-language warning signs* and *what to do next*: never "call the number in the message"
- *the Gonka Request ID and public receipt* behind every model call

*How it earns trust:* two independent models (DeepSeek and MiniMax) on the Gonka network, called concurrently on identical evidence, neither shown the other's answer, pinned with X-Gonka-No-Fallback. Disagreement is shown, not averaged: within 20 points they agree, 21–40 drops confidence, beyond 40 we say insufficient. If no sources were found, confidence is capped. A precise score resting on nothing is the most misleading thing we could display.

*What it holds back:* no account, nothing stored; phone and account numbers masked before any model sees them; screenshots read by local OCR only, with the text shown for correction first; every warning is colour plus an icon plus words, in large type — for readers who are older, colour-blind, or on a bad screen.

*Live:* https://anxin-protect.com. And if what got forwarded is a meme, not a scam, it explains the joke in both languages, and says plainly that explaining isn't verifying.

Anxin is not a truth oracle. It is a transparent pause button for bilingual families.

Check our demo: [youtu.be/xfWZiAKybs8](https://youtu.be/xfWZiAKybs8)

**AI For Society**

# Anxin (安心) 

## Gonka Router track

Anxin's entire reasoning and verification pipeline runs exclusively on Gonka Router. Every model call passes through a single module, `backend/app/gonka_client.py` — nothing else in the app is permitted to call a model, and no other provider exists at runtime.

Two independently pinned models, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiniMax-M2.7, are called concurrently on identical evidence, neither seeing the other's answer. Every call sets `X-Gonka-No-Fallback: true`, so a saturated router returns an honest 429 instead of silently serving the same model twice.

Disagreement is handled, not smoothed over: verdicts within 20 points are treated as agreement; a gap of 21–40 lowers confidence; beyond 40, the consensus layer refuses to average and reports the claim as unresolved rather than dressing up a single-model answer as consensus. Scam/fraud risk escalates on disagreement rather than averaging down, and confidence is capped whenever no supporting evidence was found.

Every response's Request ID, devshard, and requested-vs-actual model are captured and shown in the report, each linking to Gonka Router's public receipt — so a user, or a judge, can independently confirm results came from the live decentralized network, not a mock.

---
## AI For Society track

Anxin (安心, "peace of mind") is a bilingual English/Chinese scam and misinformation checker — the kind of "AI fact checker" the brief names as its preferred example — built for the audience misinformation actually reaches: older adults who read Chinese, and the English-reading children who try to warn them.

Users can paste text, a link, or a screenshot. Claims are extracted (via local OCR when needed, then made editable) and typed as factual, opinion, or unverifiable. Anxin's own server fetches the URL and searches the web (SSRF-guarded) so verification runs against real-time evidence, not a model's memory. Each claim gets a Truth Score (0–100) and a separate scam-risk score, with each model's reasoning shown in both English and Chinese alongside plain-language warning signs — so the explanation is legible to the people who need it most, not just to a technical reader.

User-submitted content is always fenced as untrusted data, and both models' raw verdicts are shown side by side so the reader judges any disagreement themselves, rather than Anxin silently resolving it for them.

**Submission:** live at [anxin-protect.com](https://anxin-protect.com) · documented repo with a dedicated Gonka-integration section and 165 offline tests · live fact-check demo: [youtu.be/xfWZiAKybs8](https://youtu.be/xfWZiAKybs8)

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Express.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Express.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Firestore](https://img.shields.io/badge/Firestore-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tesseract OCR](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tesseract%20OCR-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Firebase Authentication](https://img.shields.io/badge/Firebase%20Authentication-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

- **Multi-model reliability:** Running 3 AI models in parallel (DeepSeek, Kimi-K2.6, MiniMax-M2.7) surfaced real-world messiness — one model wrapped its JSON output in `<think>` reasoning tags that broke our parser, and models occasionally timed out inconsistently. We fixed the parsing bug, added retry logic, and measured real reliability (9/10 test runs achieved full 3-model consensus) before trusting the pipeline.
- **Two disconnected fact-extraction systems:** Our conversation-tracking logic and our AI-prompt signal extraction were built as two separate regex-based systems with different field names. This caused a real bug — the risk breakdown panel would show "insufficient information" even when a message clearly had salary and contact details, and facts could leak between unrelated conversations in the same session. We traced this to the root cause and unified both into a single shared extraction path.
- **OCR text doesn't look like normal sentences:** Job flyers and screenshots produce fragmented, bullet-style text very different from a typed message, which broke our narrative-focused signal extraction. We fixed this by falling back to the AI model's own extracted evidence when regex patterns come up empty, instead of only trusting rigid pattern matching.
- **Making "not enough information" feel human, not robotic:** Early versions surfaced raw debug-style text like "Model disagreement detected" directly in the chat when a message was too vague to score. We're actively refining this so the assistant asks a natural clarifying question instead of exposing internal model-consensus mechanics to the user.

**The problem it solves**

- Job scams and fake recruiter messages are widespread and often hard to spot in the moment — a vague "amazing opportunity" DM, a too-good-to-be-true salary, or a recruiter pushing you to WhatsApp/Telegram and asking for a "registration deposit."
- **JobGuard lets anyone paste a message or upload a screenshot of a job offer/recruiter DM and get an instant, evidence-based risk assessment** — not a single AI's guess, but a consensus from 3 independent models cross-checking the same message.
- If the message doesn't have enough detail to judge confidently, JobGuard asks a natural follow-up question (company name, role, pay) instead of guessing — the same way a savvy friend would probe before giving you an opinion.
- Each result comes with a category-by-category breakdown (company legitimacy, compensation realism, urgency tactics, contact method, payment requests) with real reasoning per category, not just a single opaque number.
- Built for anyone actively job hunting — students, international students unfamiliar with local hiring norms, and early-career applicants who are the most common targets of these scams.

**AI For Society**

JobGuard is built around the Gonka Track's core requirement: **all AI reasoning and verification runs through Gonka Router**, using multi-model cross-verification rather than a single model's opinion.

- **Multi-model cross-verification:** every check is sent to 3 independent models via Gonka Router (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Kimi-K2.6, MiniMax-M2.7) in parallel. Results are combined into a weighted consensus, and disagreement between models is surfaced transparently rather than hidden — if models disagree, the user sees that, and confidence is adjusted accordingly.
- **Genuine public value, not a novelty demo:** job and recruitment scams are a real, common problem — especially for students and early-career job seekers who are frequent targets. JobGuard gives anyone a fast, evidence-based second opinion before they act on a suspicious offer.
- **Reasoning trace, not just a score:** each result breaks down risk by category (company legitimacy, compensation realism, urgency tactics, contact method, payment requests) with model-generated reasoning per category — matching the track's emphasis on transparent, explainable verification over a black-box number.
- **Gonka Request IDs are surfaced** in the result output, so every assessment is traceable back to the actual model calls that produced it — not a hardcoded or simulated result.

**The problem it solves**

NUTSCOPE makes crypto options easier to understand and safer to explore, especially for beginners. Instead of searching through complicated options data, users can discover live Thetanuts opportunities, understand the risks and potential payoff, and practise trades using virtual funds.

It provides a simple journey from discovering an option → analyzing it → practising with paper trading → making a real trade when ready.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our main challenges was working with live Thetanuts data, as RPC/API availability could sometimes cause orders or market data to fail to load. We handled this by improving error handling, adding timeouts and fallbacks, and making sure the app does not replace unavailable live data with fake data.

Another challenge was making sure the options calculations were accurate, especially for break-even, maximum loss, payoff scenarios, and multi-leg strategies. We verified the formulas with test cases and reused the same calculation logic across the application.

We also faced challenges with wallet connection and real trade execution. To make trading safer, we added pre-flight checks for the wallet network, order availability, expiry, amount, and trade preview before allowing execution.

**Challenges we ran into**

# Challenges We Ran Into

## 1. AI Responses Were Not Always Valid JSON

One specific bug occurred when some Gonka-hosted models added a `<think>...</think>` reasoning block before the requested JSON response. Even though the model’s answer was correct, our application could not parse it, which caused the entire review to fail.

We solved this by:

- Removing reasoning blocks before parsing.
- Extracting only the JSON object from the response.
- Validating every response against a strict schema.
- Giving the model one controlled retry when its output is malformed.
- Blocking the protection plan if the response still cannot be verified.

This made the three-reviewer council much more reliable without blindly trusting unpredictable AI output.

## 2. Live Options Data Can Change Quickly

Thetanuts orders can change or expire between the moment a plan is reviewed and the moment its transaction preview is generated. Using an outdated quote could show users incorrect costs or unavailable protection.

To overcome this, GoalGuard re-fetches the selected order before creating the preview. It compares the latest order with the reviewed version, checks liquidity and deadlines again, and creates a fingerprint of the quote. If anything has changed, the plan is marked as stale and the user must review fresh information.

## 3. There Was No Safe Testnet Execution Path

The Thetanuts integration for this track uses Base mainnet, so testing a complete trade could involve real funds. We did not want the demo to expose users or judges to unnecessary financial risk.

We therefore designed the hackathon version to use live market data and the real transaction-building process while stopping at an unsigned preview. The application shows exactly what would be sent on-chain, but it never requests a signature, broadcasts a transaction, or claims that the user is protected.

**The problem it solves**

# What is GoalGuard?

GoalGuard helps everyday ETH holders protect money they have set aside for important real-life goals, such as rent, tuition, travel, or emergencies, without requiring them to understand options trading.

## The Problem

Most crypto holders think about what their money is for, not about strikes, premiums, expiries, or complex trading strategies.

When ETH prices fall, money reserved for an important expense can suddenly lose value. Existing options platforms can help manage this risk, but they are often too technical for everyday users.

## How GoalGuard Helps

Users describe their goal in plain language:

> “I have $1,200 in ETH for rent next month, and I cannot afford to lose more than 5%.”

GoalGuard then:

1. Converts the goal into clear financial limits.
2. Searches live Thetanuts options for suitable downside protection.
3. Shows the cost, coverage, expiry, and possible outcomes in simple language.
4. Uses three independent Gonka reviewers to evaluate strategy, risk, and consumer clarity.
5. Generates the exact unsigned Base transaction preview for inspection.

## Why It Is Safer

GoalGuard is designed to keep the user in control:

- Financial calculations are deterministic rather than invented by AI.
- Three independent AI reviewers assess every plan.
- Any rejection, uncertainty, missing data, or stale market information stops the process.
- Users see the risks and trade-offs before any transaction.
- No private keys are sent to the server.
- The hackathon version never requests a signature, broadcasts a transaction, or moves funds.

## Why It Matters

GoalGuard makes on-chain options more understandable and approachable. Instead of asking users to become derivatives experts, it connects protection directly to the purpose behind their money.

> **In one sentence:** GoalGuard turns “I need this ETH for rent next month” into a transparent, independently reviewed downside-protection plan, making on-chain options easier to understand and safer to explore.

**BEST PRODUCT BUILT ON THE THETANUTS SDK**

**Description**
GoalGuard transforms Thetanuts’ options infrastructure into a goal-first consumer product. It searches live OptionBook orders, calculates suitable downside protection and uses the official transaction-building flow to generate an exact unsigned transaction preview on Base.

**Justification**
- Uses Thetanuts throughout the core journey: market discovery, strategy evaluation and transaction construction.
- Turns SDK primitives into a complete, practical consumer use case.
- Makes options accessible without hiding pricing, risk or transaction details.
- Demonstrates real integration, the product’s protection workflow depends on live Thetanuts data.
- Keeps execution safe and user-controlled by stopping before signature or broadcast.

**AI × OPTIONS**

**Description**
GoalGuard combines AI-assisted guidance with live options to translate a user’s goal, deadline and risk limit into an understandable protection plan. Deterministic code performs the financial calculations, while AI reviews goal fit, risk and clarity before presenting the plan to the user.

**Justification**
- Uses options for a meaningful purpose: protecting real-life financial goals from downside risk.
- Uses AI to simplify decision-making and explain complex options clearly.
- Separates responsibilities: code calculates, AI reviews and humans approve.
- Grounds the AI workflow in live market data rather than invented prices or strategies.
- Blocks progress when information is uncertain, keeping the user informed and in control.

**The problem it solves**

# GASX - Ethereum Gas Futures Exchange on Sui

> **AI-native gas futures exchange on Sui, hedged with Thetanuts**

## The Idea

GASX makes Ethereum congestion tradeable. It tracks one index - the **Ethereum Gas Stress Index (EGSI, 0–1000)**, that measures blockspace stress (base fee, block utilization, mempool pressure, etc). AI forecasts EGSI; users trade futures on it with USDC.

---

### Problem Statement

Every single day, thousands of builders, traders, and protocols get **blindsided by gas**. You size a trade, you queue a mint, you schedule a DAO payout; and then the mempool erupts, base fee 10x's in six blocks, and your "$4 transaction" clears at "$60 and my dignity." Ethereum's blockspace is the most valuable real estate in Web3, and it is priced **live, with zero forward guidance, for everyone who touches it.**

It's a **structural, economy-wide volatility tax** on the entire on-chain economy, and until now, nobody has built the instrument to price it, forecast it, or hedge it.

### Market Gap

Every mature market hedges its core input cost. Airlines hedge jet fuel. Farmers hedge wheat. Exporters hedge FX. **On-chain, there is no equivalent for gas** - despite gas being the single most universal, unavoidable, and violently volatile cost of doing business in crypto.

That gap is enormous, and it is sitting in plain sight:

- **DeFi protocols** eat unhedged gas risk on every keeper job, liquidation bot, and rebalance.
- **NFT projects** watch mint margins evaporate the second a drop goes viral and gas spikes with it.
- **DAOs** budget treasury operations in a currency (gas) with no forward curve.
- **Retail traders** - literally anyone who has ever smashed "confirm" during a gas spike - are exposed, unhedged, every single time.

If you have ever watched a gas fee eat your alpha: **you are the market.** GASX exists because that market has never had a product built for it.

### Target Users

- **DeFi-native power users & bots** - keepers, arbitrageurs, liquidators who eat gas cost as a line item and want to hedge it like any other operating expense.
- **NFT & dApp teams** - need predictable unit economics around mint/interaction windows, not a coin flip on network conditions.
- **DAOs & treasuries** - want to budget and hedge blockspace exposure the same disciplined way they'd hedge FX or interest rate risk.
- **Quant / degen traders** - want a clean, liquid, AI-forecasted volatility product that isn't just "another perp on a coin."
- **Anyone who has ever rage-quit a transaction because gas 5x'd mid-confirm.** (Yes, you. We see you.)

### Business Model

GASX monetizes the exact thing it creates: a liquid market for a previously unpriced risk.

- **Trading fees** - a basis-point take on every winning EGSI-1H contract opened and settled. Classic exchange economics, applied to a brand-new asset class.
- **Protocol-owned hedge spread** - GASX's own book captures the spread between what it collects in premium and what it pays to hedge on Thetanuts, turning risk management into a revenue center instead of a cost center.
- **Premium AI insights** - deeper EGSI forecasting, historical analytics, and Kora-powered "gas advisory" for power users, DAOs, and protocols who want to plan treasury ops around a forward curve, not a guess.
- **B2B/API licensing** - the EGSI feed itself is a product: wallets, dApps, and gas estimators can license the index and forecast to power their own UX, the way market data terminals license price feeds today.
- **Expansion flywheel** - every new blockspace market (BASE-GAS, ARB-GAS, BLOB-GAS) reuses the same engine, the same hedge rail, and the same user base, compounding distribution instead of resetting it.

TL;DR: **first-mover in an entirely uncontested category** - gas derivatives, with a credibly neutral settlement layer, a real hedge rail, and a reliable growth path.

---

**Problem, restated simply.** Gas congestion risk is hard to quantify, and there is no direct price discovery for future blockspace stress. Companies need predictable gas costs.

**Solution, restated simply.** Bet on EGSI. If the bet wins, the payout offsets real gas fees.

**Challenges we ran into**

1. Sui pulled the rug on us mid-build - JSON-RPC just stopped working.
Every chain read started failing with "JSON-RPC on public fullnodes has been deprecated." Not a bug we introduced, Sui switched it off network-wide. We migrated the entire read path to gRPC, which turned out to be the right call anyway since it's the same transport the frontend's wallet SDK already used.

2. We built an on-chain oracle publisher and then realized we didn't need one.
Getting the AI's price feed onto Sui meant wrestling a Python SDK through three separate bugs; a config bootstrap that silently required a file that couldn't exist yet, a protocol mismatch, a missing await that let a transaction silently do nothing. We fixed all three.

3. Our first real options trade on Thetanuts kept dying one step from the finish line.
We got all the way to signing a real RFQ on Base mainnet, and it failed with "option expiry must be after offer deadline" - we were pricing the hedge's expiry off the wrong timestamp. Fixed that, then hit a second, sneakier bug: the transaction builder itself was never awaited, so it silently did nothing instead of erroring. Once both were fixed, the trade actually landed on-chain.

4. The trading UI and the smart contract quietly disagreed about "the price", so every single order failed.
The frontend priced trades off the AI's forecast; the contract validated them against the live oracle. Two different numbers, both "correct" in isolation, meant every order tripped a slippage guard. We traced it down to one line and made both sides read from the same source of truth.

**PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS**

Every trade on GASX is collateralized and settled in USDC, a stablecoin on Sui.

Why that matters: if you're trying to hedge against unpredictable costs, the last thing you want is your hedge itself to be unpredictable. A stablecoin means when you win a bet, you know exactly what you're getting, not "some crypto, worth who-knows-what today."

And doing it on Sui specifically means those payments settle in under a second for a fraction of a cent. There's a nice irony we like pointing out: it would be pretty embarrassing to build a tool for gas-fee volatility and then make people pay volatile gas fees just to use it.

**AI × SUI**

The real problem: nobody can plan for Ethereum gas fees. They spike without warning and eat into real money - a trade, a mint, a DAO payment.

AI's job is to sense and predict that problem. It watches live Ethereum data non-stop and turns raw chaos (base fee, mempool, congestion) into one clean number, EGSI, plus a forecast of where it's heading next.

Sui's job is to host the solution. It's where people actually trade a bet on that forecast - cheaply, in under a second, using a language (Move) that makes it much harder to lose or duplicate funds by accident. And crucially, Sui isn't the chain that's congested, so the market itself never distorts the thing it's measuring.

Put together: AI tells you what's coming, Sui gives you a fast, safe place to do something about it.

**BEST PRODUCT BUILT ON THE THETANUTS SDK**

Most integrations use an SDK for one thing — pull a price, show a number. We use Thetanuts as real infrastructure across the whole loop:

We pull live ETH options data from Thetanuts and feed it into our own AI forecast, it's not just displayed; it makes our predictions better.
Our risk engine uses Thetanuts to actually request real price quotes from market makers when it needs to hedge.
And we don't stop at requesting a quote, we settle a real trade with real funds on Base mainnet.

That's sensing, deciding, and acting, all built on the SDK. And because Thetanuts has no testnet, that last step is real money with no dry run.

**AI × OPTIONS**

When enough people bet the same direction on GASX, our own book ends up exposed, if gas spikes, we could owe more than we collect. The AI watches for that risk continuously. When it crosses a threshold, the AI itself decides to hedge, it requests a real options quote from Thetanuts and, if the quote clears our safety checks, executes the trade, no human clicks "buy."

It's not unlimited, though. The AI can request an action, but it can never break the rules: hard caps on position size, a minimum confidence bar before it's allowed to act, a tiny fixed budget it can't exceed. So you get real autonomy, inside a fence it can't climb over.

### ComputeQuest

> Turn verified attention into useful AI compute

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Drizzle](https://img.shields.io/badge/Drizzle-333333?style=flat-square) ![Remotion](https://img.shields.io/badge/Remotion-333333?style=flat-square) ![Viem](https://img.shields.io/badge/Viem-333333?style=flat-square) ![gemini](https://img.shields.io/badge/gemini-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

AI tools are useful, but subscriptions and usage fees block people who only need occasional compute. At the same time, sponsors pay for impressions without a clear connection to a useful user outcome.

ComputeQuest connects those two needs. A user submits an AI task, such as an eight-slide pitch deck. If the account is short of Compute Energy (CE), the user can voluntarily complete a short Sponsor Quest. The server measures eligible active-view signals, pauses earning when those signals disappear, and authorizes the reward only after the required viewing period. A replay-protected CampaignEscrow contract settles the signed receipt on Monad Testnet. After finalization, ComputeQuest issues non-transferable CE, spends it exactly once, and starts the original Gemini job automatically.

Sponsors fund useful work instead of buying an isolated impression. Users receive a concrete AI result instead of a transferable token. ComputeQuest provides the verification, settlement, ledger, and provider-execution layer. The current public product includes separately funded Monad and PayZoll campaigns, an operator-reviewed sponsor intake path, persisted results, and text, JSON, and PDF exports.

## Architecture

![ComputeQuest architecture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Anand-0038/computequest/main/docs/images/computequest-architecture.jpg)

The user-facing task, sponsor-funded CampaignEscrow, verified reward settlement, CE ledger, and Gemini generation remain independently inspectable stages.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest challenge was defining an attention claim a browser can honestly support. A web app cannot lock a laptop or prove where someone is looking. We therefore measure eligible active-view signals instead: visibility, focus, fullscreen, playback, speed, seeking, buffering, Picture-in-Picture state, media-time progression, bounded heartbeat gaps, and server timestamps. Invalid intervals earn zero, and append-only evidence records explain why.

The second challenge was making the money and credit flow exactly-once. PostgreSQL row locks serialize balance decisions, campaign reward claims prevent one account from repeatedly claiming the same campaign, ledger entries are idempotent, and failed provider attempts have attempt-specific refunds. The contract separately protects campaign capacity, budget, signatures, expiry, and session replay.

The third challenge was recovery across network and process failures. Settlement waits for the configured Monad finality boundary, records every relay attempt, and can recover a broadcast transaction from on-chain events. Funded Gemini jobs use a database lease so refreshes or retries do not duplicate provider calls. We also replaced a memory-heavy migration command so the application could boot reliably on Render's constrained runtime.

The result is a public, fail-closed vertical slice backed by 89 application tests, 20 PostgreSQL integration tests, 5 Foundry tests, browser checks, a verified Testnet contract, and publicly inspectable settlement evidence.

### Nexora
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/nexora-d1e6) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Coding-Maestro18/Nexora_Final) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/6QdqhVT7714) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20to%20Devcon%20--%20NITK%20Surathkal-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-nitk-surathkal.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Smarter Finance. On chain.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![scikit-learn](https://img.shields.io/badge/scikit--learn-333333?style=flat-square) ![NumPy](https://img.shields.io/badge/NumPy-333333?style=flat-square) ![pandas](https://img.shields.io/badge/pandas-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

DeFi lets everyone use the same leverage — a brand new trader and someone with years of experience both get 20x if they want it. Nobody's checking if that's actually a good idea for them. Turns out it isn't; new traders get liquidated way more often because nothing ever holds them back.

The obvious fix — let the platform check your trading history — means putting your entire trade record on a public ledger forever. Most people won't accept that trade-off.

What Nexora does
Looks at how you actually trade and sorts you into Novice, Balanced, or Expert
Turns that into real limits — a smart contract enforces them, not just a UI suggestion
Your raw trading history stays private; only the result goes on-chain
Who it's for
New traders who'd rather be held back a little than blow up their first position
Experienced traders who want their track record to actually count for something
Protocols that want risk-based tiers without forcing users to dox their history

Basically: personalized leverage limits, without giving up your privacy to get them.

**Challenges we ran into**

Picking the right model. Started with a Decision Tree — worked, but accuracy sat around 75%. Switched to Random Forest, first with a capped depth, which got to ~85%. Removed the depth limit and landed at ~92.6%. Wasn't obvious upfront which would work best, so we just tried each one and kept what performed.

Figuring out what "private" actually means here. Building real zero-knowledge cryptography from scratch wasn't realistic in the time we had. So instead of pretending we'd built a full ZK-SNARK circuit, we built a hash-based attestation — the risk result gets hashed, and that hash is what goes on-chain, not the raw trading data. It's a stand-in for where a real proof system would sit, not the real thing, and we're upfront about that.

Foundry silently building nothing. forge build kept saying "Nothing to compile" even from the right folder. No foundry.toml, so Forge was looking for source files in completely the wrong place. One config file fixed it.

forge install failing without telling us. It just didn't install anything, no error shown. Worked around it by pulling the library in directly with git clone instead.

Buttons that looked broken but weren't. Backend logs showed every click working. Turned out a CSS rule was quietly keeping the home screen visible no matter what, so the dashboard was rendering underneath it, invisible. Fixed with one CSS rule.

Two traders sharing one identity. Both demo personas were signing from the same blockchain account early on, so their balances and positions kept colliding. Gave each one its own account.

Actually connecting everything. The model, the attestation, the contract, Anvil, and the frontend were all built as separate working pieces — getting them talking to each other as one flow was its own project. Model output had to match what the policy layer expected, the policy had to match what the contract accepted, and the frontend had to poll all of it live without breaking. Most of the bugs here weren't in any single piece — they showed up only once two pieces were forced to agree with each other.

**Private DeFi & Mempools**

Nexora keeps a trader's private behavior — trade history, win rate, drawdown — off the public chain. Instead of exposing that data so the protocol can set leverage limits, the risk model runs on it privately, and only an attested result goes on-chain. Enforcement (leverage caps, collateral limits, liquidations) still happens fully on-chain, so privacy doesn't come at the cost of trustless enforcement.

**Private AI on Ethereum**

The risk tier comes from a Random Forest model reading private trading behavior and classifying the trader. Inference happens off-chain — Ethereum only ever sees the attested output, never the raw data or features that produced it. AI whose result can be enforced on-chain without exposing what drove the decision

**Overall**

Reuse the DeFi & Mempools reasoning here, or a short combined line: "A working end-to-end system — ML risk assessment, private attestation, and on-chain enforcement — demonstrating that personalized DeFi risk management and user privacy aren't mutually exclusive." "Overall" is typically a blanket category open to any solid submission, so there's no real downside to checking it alongside your specific tracks.

### CertHack
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/certhack-45a8) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/shaharyan1826-svg/CertHack) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/DHluUseDXX4?si=czSgKPmbuHWIQyt0) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20To%20Devcon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-iitr.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> AI Certificate Verification

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![SHA-256 Hashes](https://img.shields.io/badge/SHA--256%20Hashes-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tesseract OCR](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tesseract%20OCR-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

CertHack combines OCR, AI-assisted analysis, SHA-256 fingerprinting, and trusted certificate records to identify verified, tampered/invalid, and unverified certificates.

**Challenges we ran into**

While building CertHack, we faced several challenges during development:

- OCR accuracy: Different certificate layouts, fonts, image quality, and scanned PDFs caused OCR to sometimes misread names, dates, or course details.
- False positives: Some genuine certificates were initially classified as suspicious because they were not present in our trusted registry.
- Certificate verification: We learned that visual similarity alone cannot reliably prove whether a certificate is genuine.
- Hash verification :We implemented SHA-256 fingerprinting so that even a small change to a registered certificate can be detected.
- Frontend–backend integration: Connecting the React frontend with the FastAPI backend and displaying different verification states required debugging API responses and UI logic.
- Limited development time: Since the project was developed under hackathon time constraints, we focused on building a working end-to-end prototype rather than a fully trained machine-learning model.

How we overcame them:

We combined multiple verification signals instead of relying on a single AI prediction. CertHack now uses "OCR + AI-assisted analysis + SHA-256 hashing + a trusted certificate registry", and distinguishes between "Verified, Tampered/Invalid, and Unverified" results. This also prevents an unknown certificate from automatically being labelled as fake.

**Self-Sovereignty**

CertHack supports Self-Sovereignty by allowing users to independently verify their certificates using SHA-256 fingerprints, trusted records, OCR, and AI-assisted analysis. Instead of depending entirely on manual issuer verification, users can check whether their credential is verified, potentially tampered with, or unverified. The system can later be extended to decentralized blockchain-based credential verification.

**The problem it solves**

Student achievements such as  : hackathon wins, course certificates, club roles — are scattered across PDFs, college portals, and screenshots, with no easy way to verify them. 
**Proof of You** lets trusted issuers (professors, clubs) issue tamper-***proof badges*** directly to a ***student's wallet***. Once issued, a badge can't be *deleted, altered, or transferred*; giving students a permanent, self-owned record of their achievements that anyone can instantly verify, without emailing anyone or waiting on a college database.

**Challenges we ran into**

We hit a wagmi/RainbowKit version mismatch that silently broke wallet connection with no clear error — traced it to an invalid dependency version and fixed it by pinning wagmi to the version RainbowKit expected.
 We also had a merge conflict in App.jsx when two of us built different pages independently, which we resolved by splitting the UI into separate component files. Finally, we tested our contract's issuer restriction by deliberately removing a team wallet from the approved list, confirming non-approved wallets are correctly blocked from issuing badges.

**Self-Sovereignty**

Students fully own their achievement badges in their own wallet (not locked inside a college database or account that can be lost, deactivated, or controlled by an institution)

**Censorship Resistance**

Once a badge is issued, there's no delete or admin-override function in the contract - not even the deployer can revoke or alter it, so no institution can later erase or suppress a student's verified record.

### DEAD DROP
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/dead-drop-90bc) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/PhAnToMxSD/DEAD_DROP) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://dead-drop-web-six.vercel.app) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/XYqvZQJ7a7Y) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20To%20Devcon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-iitr.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> No Pipe, No trace

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flask](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flask-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Self-custody wallets still funnel every transaction through an RPC provider — the same request carries your IP and your Ethereum address, letting a provider geoblock, censor, or deanonymize you before your transaction ever reaches a mempool. Dead Drop breaks that coupling: the browser signs a transaction fully offline via viem (no wallet extension, no RPC call), then hands the raw signed bytes off over a transport unrelated to Ethereum infra — a Nostr note tagged `#ethrelay`, a QR code, or a clipboard blob. A swarm of volunteer relayers subscribed to that tag decodes, validates, and broadcasts on the sender's behalf via `eth_sendRawTransaction`. Because broadcasting a given signed tx is idempotent, redundant relayers racing to submit is harmless — the sender's network never has to prove they touched Ethereum, since it never did.

**Challenges we ran into**

Getting the signer and relayer to agree byte-for-byte on the envelope format without ever talking to each other directly — solved by pulling encode/decode, the Nostr event/filter schema, and offline tx validation into a shared `packages/protocol` module both sides import, so a wire-format change can't silently desync them. Also had to make sure signing stayed genuinely offline: the only network call the web app is allowed to make is one optional, read-only nonce check that fails soft and never blocks signing. On the relayer side, validating untrusted envelopes (wrong chain ID, missing tip, malformed rawTx) before ever calling `eth_sendRawTransaction` was necessary to keep a swarm of relayers from broadcasting garbage or replaying transactions across chains.

**Censorship Resistance**

Dead Drop is a direct response to this track's second bullet — verifiable, censorship-resistant transaction routing — approached from the client side rather than the RPC side. Instead of aggregating multiple RPC providers (which still assumes RPC is the only path to the chain), it removes the RPC dependency from the sender entirely: transactions are signed fully offline in the browser via viem, and the raw signed bytes are handed off over transports that have nothing to do with Ethereum infrastructure — a Nostr note tagged `#ethrelay`, a QR code, or a clipboard blob — so a network that blocks known RPC endpoints, geoblocks an address, or logs IP↔address correlation never sees the sender touch Ethereum at all. A swarm of independent volunteer relayers then broadcasts on the sender's behalf via `eth_sendRawTransaction`, and because relaying is idempotent (same signed bytes → same tx hash), no single relayer is a chokepoint — any one being blocked, offline, or malicious just gets bypassed by the others. It's censorship resistance built into the transport layer itself, not into which RPC provider you trust.

**The problem it solves**

Problem Description 

Traditional identity verification often requires users to share complete personal documents even when only one specific fact needs to be verified. This leads to unnecessary data exposure, privacy concerns, and security risks.

For example, a platform may only need to know whether a person is an eligible student, but the user may have to reveal their name, ID number, photo, and other personal details.

PrivatePass addresses this problem by enabling users to prove specific eligibility claims while keeping unnecessary personal information private.

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges We Faced

 Implementing the zero-knowledge verification workflow.

 Debugging proof generation and verification issues. 

Ensuring different eligibility criteria work correctly.

Integrating Web3 identity and wallet functionality. 

Deploying the application and resolving local vs. production environment issues.

Building and testing the project within a limited hackathon timeframe.

**Self-Sovereignty**

How PrivatePass Applies Self-Sovereignty 

User-controlled identity: Users have control over their own identity information rather than relying entirely on a central authority. 

Selective sharing: Users choose which specific claim to prove, instead of sharing their complete identity.

Privacy: Unnecessary personal information remains private during verification. 

User-controlled verification: The user decides when and what information to present to a verifier. 

Reduced dependence on centralized databases: The concept supports identity verification without requiring all personal information to be stored in one central system. 

In short: PrivatePass applies self-sovereignty by giving users greater ownership, control, and choice over how their digital identity is used and verified.

> Trust Layer for AI Agents

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/Go-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Blockchain](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blockchain-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

AI agents are getting real payment access (Prava, card tokens) before they have any way to prove they can be trusted with it.
They have no bureau, no history, no signal to prove whether they are capable enough to carry out this transaction or not.

## How Swava solves it: 
Swava checks an agent's on-chain trust score before every purchase and converts it into a real spending limit auto-approve, human review, or block before Prava is even called.

## Why useful today: 
Companies handing AI agents company cards have no way to tell a proven agent from a brand-new one; this is that missing layer.

## What's next: 
Production Browser Harness completion, real merchant-side onboarding, tying Prava payment identity to on-chain agent identity.

**Challenges we ran into**

* Raw complete_checkout needs merchant-side Shopify JWT auth we couldn't self-serve, found via direct API testing, confirmed with Prava's team on Discord.
* Manual checkout completion routes through regional gateways (Razorpay) and fails 3D Secure, since the token is built for programmatic handoff using AI Agents and not humans.
* Learned from Prava's own docs and Birdie that the correct completion path is Browser Harness, which is production-only with no direct API this is documented, not a bug.

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

Every purchase goes through Prava with permissions and controls in place: a spending limit set by the agent's trust score, human review for unproven agents, and hard blocks for agents with low trust, all before Prava's card token is ever issued. 
Approved purchases create a real Prava sandbox session and one-time card, demonstrating agent-initiated commerce with trust and controls built in, not bolted on.

**Most Startup-Ready Product**

## What this is built on
* **SwarmPay**, a reputation bureau for AI agents, in active full-time development
* ERC-8004 identity and reputation registries live on Base mainnet
* Reputation API live, indexing real agent transaction data: As of July 28, 2026: 1.4M+ transactions indexed, 150K+ wallets, 20K+ agents

## What we built for this hackathon
* A real product use case on top of SwarmPay: agentic shopping with a procurement approval engine
* Live Prava integration with real sandbox sessions, real card issuance, real trust-gated decisions
* Deployed end to end: agent discovery (UCP), trust scoring, policy evaluation, payment

## Where we are with the business

* In active conversations with AI agent insurers and marketplace builders as design partners across the US and UK.
* Active Angel investor interest from Investment banks. Closed one angel round of $20k last month.

## What's next

* Prava production access for full checkout completion
* Deeper procurement policy controls
* Expanding the trust model beyond transaction volume

**Agentic Commerce Hackathon**

Swava lets an AI agent discover products across live Shopify merchants, evaluate whether it should be trusted to complete the purchase, and pay through Prava end to end. 

The core piece is a trust check before payment: the buying agent's on-chain history is scored and converted into a spending limit, so a proven agent auto-approves, a new one goes to human review, and a known-bad one is blocked before Prava is ever called. 

Discovery uses UCP against live merchants, and approved purchases create a real Prava sandbox session and card. We hit real integration limits completing checkout end-to-end (documented on our Findings page) but the discovery → trust decision → payment flow is fully working.

**The problem it solves**

Most AI shopping stops at recommendations. OnPoint completes the purchase—but only within explicit user-approved limits. Shoppers first see how an item looks on their own photo, then approve a final price, merchant, and spending limit via passkey. **Challenges we ran into**

Building OnPoint meant solving real integration problems, not demos: we rebuilt our payment flow to match Prava's actual credential contract, combined the production-only CLI with the sandbox REST API behind a single interface, debugged WebAuthn and credential provisioning until successful issuance, handled final checkout totals (including shipping and tax) instead of list prices, designed the system to never fabricate checkout outcomes when payment status is uncertain, and implemented carrier-compliant messaging from day one with opt-out handling, delivery health checks, and safe send controls.

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

OnPoint uses Visa Intelligent Commerce to make AI purchasing trustworthy. Users approve a specific merchant and maximum spend with a passkey, and the agent completes checkout using a single-use, merchant-locked credential that cannot be reused or exceed the authorized amount.

**Most Startup-Ready Product**

OnPoint extends an existing consumer product with secure agent-driven checkout, demonstrating a production-ready path beyond the hackathon rather than a standalone prototype.

**iMessage Agent**

OnPoint is built natively for iMessage with Linq. Users shop, approve purchases, and receive live order updates through interactive message cards, making messaging the primary interface for agentic commerce.

**Agentic Commerce Hackathon**

OnPoint is an end-to-end agentic commerce experience. Prava powers live merchant discovery, binding quotes, and payment credential issuance that lets the agent complete a real purchase. Visa Intelligent Commerce provides explicit user authorization with passkey verification and merchant- and amount-scoped single-use credentials, making autonomous spending safe. Linq delivers the entire workflow natively in iMessage with interactive status updates, while Localhost extends an existing consumer product with production-ready agent checkout rather than a hackathon demo.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs)](https://img.shields.io/badge/Zero--Knowledge%20Proofs%20(ZKPs)-333333?style=flat-square) ![Nodemailer](https://img.shields.io/badge/Nodemailer-333333?style=flat-square) ![Framer](https://img.shields.io/badge/Framer-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

# Challenges We Ran Into 🚧

* **Client-Side Zero-Knowledge Proof Generation:** 
Implementing Zero-Knowledge cryptography directly in the browser is notoriously resource-intensive. We initially struggled with `snarkjs` freezing the UI thread while compiling circuits and generating zk-SNARK proofs for ticket verification. We overcame this by optimizing our WASM builds and ensuring proof generation is handled asynchronously, allowing users to generate privacy-preserving cryptographic proofs without experiencing browser lag.

* **Synchronizing On-Chain State with Off-Chain AI Systems:** 
Echo automatically triggers Google Gemini to broadcast personalized announcements the moment a campaign is deployed to the blockchain. Achieving this required complex synchronization: we had to reliably wait for the Flow EVM transaction to finalize, intercept the transaction receipt, decode the raw EVM logs to extract the newly minted `eventId`, and dynamically inject that data into the AI prompt—all in a single seamless user flow.

* **EVM Compatibility & Custom Event Parsing:** 
While building on the Flow EVM provided incredible scalability, adapting standard Ethereum tooling (like Wagmi and Viem) to handle our specific smart contract architecture presented hurdles. Specifically, parsing the nested data structures of our custom `EventCreated` logs directly from the transaction hash required writing strict, low-level ABI decoders to ensure the frontend could instantly react to the blockchain state changes.

**The problem it solves**

# Echo: The Magic of Campaign Automation 🪄

**The Problem:** 
Traditional event management platforms rely on centralized, highly hackable databases that expose sensitive attendee data. Furthermore, organizers are forced to spend countless hours manually drafting emails, managing guest lists, and tracking ticketing data across disjointed tools.

**The Solution:**
Echo is a decentralized, privacy-first campaign automation platform that merges the security of Zero-Knowledge cryptography with the creative power of AI.

### What it does:
* **Zero-Knowledge Cloaking (Privacy):** Attendees can purchase tickets and prove their identity securely on-chain without ever exposing their personal information to corporate databases. 
* **AI-Crafted Owls (Automation):** Upload a guest list (Excel/CSV), and Echo automatically summons Google Gemini AI to draft and dispatch personalized, beautifully formatted announcements across Email and Telegram.
* **On-Chain Verifications:** All campaigns and verifications are managed transparently and immutably on the Flow EVM, giving organizers total control and ownership of their events.

### Who is it for?
Event organizers, community managers, and marketers who want to effortlessly deploy campaigns, automatically broadcast personalized announcements, and guarantee state-of-the-art privacy for their attendees.

**Best Use of Gemini API**

# Best Use of Gemini API ⚡️

Echo doesn't just use Gemini as a wrapper; it embeds the model deep into the platform's core infrastructure to bridge the gap between complex blockchain data and intuitive user experiences. 

We deployed Gemini in two high-impact ways:
1. **Autonomous Multi-Platform Broadcasting:** Upon smart contract execution, Gemini instantly generates dual-format marketing campaigns—crafting lush HTML for email and emoji-rich plain text for Telegram—and autonomously dispatches them to attendee lists.
2. **Context-Aware Web3 Assistant (Hedwig):** We built a global floating chatbot that continually reads live on-chain smart contract data, feeding it directly into Gemini's context window. This allows users to chat naturally with the blockchain, asking Hedwig for real-time ticket availability, pricing, and campaign statuses.

**Open Innovation**

# How We Fit the Open Innovation Track 💡

Echo is built for the Open Innovation track because it refuses to be constrained to a single technological silo. Rather than solving a narrow, predefined problem, Echo reimagines the entire event management lifecycle by fusing three distinct frontier technologies:

1. **Decentralization (Web3):** Immutable ticketing and campaign management on the Flow EVM.
2. **Advanced Cryptography (zk-SNARKs):** Zero-Knowledge proofs that guarantee attendee privacy and ownership.
3. **Generative AI (Google Gemini):** Autonomous broadcasting and context-aware chatbot assistance.

By bridging Web3, cryptography, and AI into one seamless, Harry Potter-themed user experience, Echo serves as a blueprint for how diverse, cutting-edge tech can be orchestrated to create entirely new paradigms in user privacy and automation.

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/kshetra-3ff3) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/codingWithRakesh/Kshetra) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://kshetra-ten.vercel.app/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-HexaFalls%202-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hexafalls2.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Decentralized Land Ledger

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-333333?style=flat-square) ![Blockchain](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blockchain-333333?style=flat-square) ![React.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/React.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Solana](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solana-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

🧱 Challenges We Ran Into & How We Overcame Them
Building a decentralized application that bridges real-world spatial data with immutable smart contracts presented several unique technical hurdles. Here are the major challenges we faced and how we engineered our way out of them:

1. The "Ghost Owner" Bug: Event Logs vs. Live State
The Problem: Initially, our React frontend relied entirely on parsing the SaveLandRegistry smart contract events to display the marketplace and user dashboards. However, we quickly realized that event logs only record the historical creation of the deed. When a property was sold, the frontend still displayed the original creator as the owner, creating a "ghost owner" desync.
The Solution: We had to completely refactor our data-fetching architecture. Instead of just reading logs, we updated the frontend to first fetch the historical events to find all registry addresses, and then use Promise.all to dynamically connect to every individual child contract. By querying the live state variables (like the current identity hash and owner wallet) directly from the node, we achieved real-time 100% accuracy and built dynamic UI elements (like the "SOLD" overlay) based on that live data.

2. Securing the Factory Pattern & Reentrancy Vulnerabilities
The Problem: We chose a Factory Pattern (AllLandRegistry deploys individual LandRegistry contracts) to keep property states isolated. However, during the implementation of the buyLand function, we initially placed the Ethereum fund transfer (.call{value: msg.value}) before the state updates. This exposed the contract to a critical Reentrancy Attack, where a malicious buyer contract could potentially drain funds.
The Solution: We strictly implemented the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. We refactored the buyLand function to first verify exact payments and ownership rules (Checks), then update the new owner's identity hash and name (Effects), and only then transfer the funds to the previous owner (Interactions).

3. Bridging On-Chain Spatial Data with React-Leaflet
The Problem: Storing massive arrays of GPS coordinates on an EVM blockchain is incredibly gas-intensive. Furthermore, passing that raw on-chain data into our frontend react-leaflet map components resulted in mismatched data types and UI crashes.
The Solution: We implemented a custom encoding/decoding helper function. We stored the coordinates compactly as integers on-chain. On the frontend, we wrote a decodeCoordinate utility using BigInt math to parse the raw contract arguments back into precise decimal [latitude, longitude] arrays. This allowed us to dynamically draw the Polygon boundaries (P1 to P4) seamlessly on the Leaflet map without bloating our gas fees.

4. Managing Asynchronous RPC Rate Limits
The Problem: When querying the blockchain for property records spanning millions of blocks, our Infura RPC endpoint kept throwing rate-limit errors or timing out, causing the frontend to hang endlessly on the loading screen.
The Solution: We built a custom getLogsInChunks helper function in React. Instead of asking the node for all blocks at once, this function breaks the query into safe chunks (9,900 blocks at a time) and utilizes a sleep(300) promise to intentionally throttle our requests. This ensured perfectly stable data syncing regardless of how many properties are added to the ledger.

**The problem it solves**

🚨 The Problem: The Broken Real Estate Standard
Traditional land registries are plagued by inefficiencies, corruption, and outdated technology. Physical title deeds are easily forged, leading to rampant property fraud and double-selling. Furthermore, land boundaries are often documented ambiguously in dense legal text, causing endless neighbor disputes. Finally, tying property ownership to centralized government databases forces citizens to expose highly sensitive personal identification numbers to clerks and third parties, risking identity theft.

💡 The Solution: Decentralized Land Ledger
This project replaces the archaic, paper-based land registry system with an immutable, transparent, and automated Web3 ecosystem. By leveraging the Ethereum blockchain, IPFS, and interactive spatial mapping, we make buying, selling, and verifying land as simple and secure as sending an email.

🛠️ What People Can Use It For:
Fraud-Proof Property Trading (Trustless Escrow):
Buyers no longer need to trust centralized escrow agents. The smart contract utilizes a strict Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. When a user buys a plot, the system atomically transfers the exact ETH amount to the seller while simultaneously transferring the deed to the buyer. If one fails, the entire transaction reverts. Double-selling is mathematically impossible.

Visual Boundary Verification:
Instead of relying on written descriptions of land, this dApp stores precise GPS coordinates (P1–P4) on-chain. These coordinates are dynamically rendered in the browser using interactive OpenStreetMap boundary polygons. Buyers can visually confirm exactly what they are paying for before executing the transaction.

Privacy-Preserving Ownership:
Users can link their government-issued IDs (like a 12-digit ID) to their property without ever exposing the raw number. The dApp hashes the ID locally using Keccak256 before interacting with the blockchain. This allows citizens to mathematically prove ownership of a deed without sacrificing their personal privacy to a public ledger.

Instant Title Searches & Immutable Provenance:
Title companies usually take weeks and charge hefty fees to verify the history of a property. Our decentralized ledger records every transaction permanently. Anyone can instantly search the blockchain to view the full, unalterable chain of custody (e.g., John Doe sold to Jane Smith on MM/DD/YYYY), completely streamlining the due diligence process.

🛡️ Why It is Safer
By decentralizing the registry via a Factory Contract Architecture, every single plot of land is isolated in its own dedicated smart contract. This prevents systemic registry failures. Combined with decentralized IPFS image hosting for the physical deeds, the system eliminates single points of failure—meaning records cannot be destroyed in a server fire, altered by a corrupt official, or lost in a bureaucratic backlog.

**The problem it solves**

The Problem: Millions of citizens struggle to access government and public service systems due to complex bureaucratic procedures, language barriers, and lack of awareness about documentation requirements. As a result, genuine issues : municipal complaints, banking grievances, RTI requests, civic problems often go unfiled, not because digital platforms don't exist, but because the gap between "having a problem" and "knowing how to formally report it" is too wide.


How "Janhit" Solves It:  **Janhit** is a voice-first, multilingual AI civic assistant that bridges this gap through natural conversation. The user describes their problem aloud in their preferred language, and Janhit identifies the issue and portal and advises on the correct portal or authority to approach, and Show the form highlighting specific fields the user must complete themselves to protect sensitive information. 

By the end, the user's issue is on its way to resolution, and they've also learned how to navigate similar procedures independently in the future.

**Challenges we ran into**

DOM Manipulation Issues: While building the form auto-fill feature, we ran into significant challenges with DOM manipulation getting our assistant to correctly identify, target, and populate the right fields across different government portal layouts was trickier than expected, with elements not updating consistently or fields being mismatched.

Sarvam API Issues at 6 AM: During our final hours of development, we hit an unexpected wall with the Sarvam API around 6 AM right when we were trying to test and finalize our STT/TTS integration. With the deadline approaching and limited time to debug, we had to quickly dig into the API documentation, check our request formatting, and test alternative configurations to get it working again.

**Gemini**

Janhit's core intelligence understanding a citizen's problem from natural conversation, identifying the correct procedure or authority, asking relevant follow-up questions, and generating guidance for the user is powered by Google's Gemini models.
Processing the voice transrcipt to reasoning behind the scences.

**Sarvam.ai**

Sarvam AI's STT (Speech-to-Text) and TTS (Text-to-Speech) models power the multilingual, voice-first core of Janhit, enabling citizens to interact entirely through spoken conversation in their native Indian languages.

STT (Speech-to-Text): When a user describes their problem out loud in Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, or any other supported Indian language - Sarvam's STT converts their speech into accurate text, even handling regional accents, dialects, and code-mixed speech (e.g., Hindi-English mix) common in everyday conversation. This text is then passed to the AI to identify the issue and determine the right procedure.

TTS (Text-to-Speech): Once the assistant generates a response follow-up questions, guidance, or confirmation of next steps Sarvam's TTS converts it back into natural-sounding speech in the same language, so the user receives spoken guidance just as they would from a human helper, without needing to read or type.

Together, these enable Janhit to serve users with low literacy, limited English proficiency, or unfamiliarity with digital interfaces, removing the biggest barrier to civic participation: the need to read, type, or navigate in a language or format that isn't theirs. This makes the entire interaction feel like talking to a knowledgeable local helper rather than filling out a form.

**Open Innovation**

Open Innovation is meant for projects that solve real, unconstrained problems using creative, cross-domain approaches—not ones limited to a predefined theme or industry. Janhit fits this perfectly because it tackles a deeply rooted, widespread civic problem (inaccessibility of government and public services) using a novel combination of technologies: multilingual conversational AI, voice interfaces (Sarvam STT/TTS), natural language understanding, and automated form-filling.
The problem itself spans multiple domains—governance, accessibility, language technology, and digital literacy—and our solution doesn't fit neatly into a single vertical like fintech, healthtech, or edtech. Instead, it's a horizontal tool that can plug into any public service system: municipal complaints, banking grievances, RTI requests, utility services, and more.
This open-ended, cross-cutting nature building a general-purpose civic assistant that adapts to diverse procedures and languages rather than solving one narrow use case is exactly the kind of ambitious, broadly-applicable innovation the Open Innovation track is designed to encourage.
