> Bids so sealed, even the blockchain can't peek

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem

Every year, **$13 trillion** in global procurement runs through sealed-bid auctions — government tenders, enterprise supply chains, infrastructure contracts. The process is fundamentally broken:

### 🔓 Bids Aren't Actually Sealed
Traditional e-procurement platforms store bids in a central database. Insiders can peek. Competitors collude. A single compromised admin can leak every bid in the system. Studies estimate **bid-rigging costs taxpayers 20-30% in inflated prices** on public contracts alone.

### 🤷 Winners Can't Be Verified
When the award is announced, losers have no way to verify the scoring was fair. Was the formula actually applied? Did the winner really score highest? The process is a black box — and disputes drag on for months.

### 💸 Payments Are Disconnected
After the award, settlement happens off-platform — wire transfers, invoices, manual reconciliation. There's no programmatic link between "you won the auction" and "here's your payment." Escrow is handled by intermediaries who charge 1-3% fees.

---

## What BlindBid Solves

BlindBid is a **privacy-first sealed-bid auction platform** where:

### 1. Bids Are Cryptographically Private
Bidders submit sealed bids on **Canton Network** using Daml smart contracts. Privacy isn't a feature flag — it's enforced at the ledger level. BidderA physically cannot see BidderB's bid. Not through the UI, not through the API, not through the database. The data simply doesn't exist in their view of the ledger.

### 2. Scoring Is Transparent Without Exposing Data
The seller scores bids using a **multi-criteria weighted formula** (price, delivery, penalty rate, reputation) locked into the smart contract before bidding opens. The winner receives an explainable award proof showing which criteria were used and weight ranges — but **actual bid values are never revealed to losing bidders**. You know the process was fair without seeing anyone else's numbers.

### 3. Payments Are On-Chain and Gasless
Winners pay through an **ADI escrow smart contract** with real on-chain settlement. Bidders don't need tokens or gas — an ERC-4337 paymaster sponsors every transaction. The escrow holds funds until the Canton contract confirms all conditions are met, then releases automatically. No intermediaries, no manual wire transfers, no 1-3% fees.

### 4. Every Step Is Publicly Auditable
At critical moments — bidding closed, winner awarded, payment settled — a **hash commitment is published to Hedera Consensus Service**. This creates a tamper-proof public timeline that anyone can verify. The hash proves *what happened and when*, without revealing *any confidential business data*.

---

## Who Is This For?

| User | How BlindBid Helps |
|---|---|
| **Government Procurement Officers** | Run tenders where bid-rigging is mathematically impossible, not just illegal |
| **Enterprise Supply Chain Teams** | Score vendors on multiple criteria privately — no more race-to-the-bottom pricing |
| **Construction & Infrastructure** | Sealed bids with automated escrow — payment releases when delivery conditions are met |
| **Auditors & Regulators** | Verify the entire auction timeline on Hedera without needing access to confidential bid data |
| **Small Bidders** | Participate without holding crypto or paying gas — the platform sponsors your transactions |

---

## In One Line

> **BlindBid makes sealed-bid auctions actually sealed, verifiably fair, and settled on-chain — with zero gas costs for participants.**

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges I Ran Into

### 1. 🔒 Canton's Party-Based Privacy vs. Multi-Step Auction Logic

**The Problem:** Canton's sub-transaction privacy model means each party can only see contracts they're explicitly listed on. This sounds great until you realize that a multi-step auction (create → bid → score → award) involves *different* parties at *different* stages. The Seller creates the auction, but Bidders submit bids on separate contracts. When the Seller needs to score all bids, they need visibility into every SealedBid contract — but each bid was created by a different party.

**How I Solved It:** I designed the Daml contract hierarchy so the Seller is listed as an observer on every SealedBid contract at creation time, while other Bidders are explicitly excluded. The scoring choice exercises across all bid contracts in a single Canton transaction, maintaining atomicity. The key insight was that Canton's privacy is *per-contract*, not per-transaction — so one transaction can touch multiple contracts with different visibility rules, and each party only sees the subset they're authorized for.

---

### 2. ⛽ ERC-4337 Paymaster Integration — The "Chicken and Egg" Problem

**The Problem:** For gasless bidding, bidders need a paymaster to sponsor their gas. But the paymaster needs to validate that the bidder is authorized for *this specific auction*. The authorization signature has to be generated before the transaction is sent, embedded in `paymasterAndData`, and verified on-chain — all without the bidder holding any native tokens.

**The Hurdle:** Getting the signature encoding right was brutal. The paymaster contract expects a tightly packed `abi.encode(sender, auctionId, validUntil, signature)` inside `paymasterAndData`. One byte off and the entire UserOperation reverts with a cryptic "AA33: reverted" error that gives you zero debugging information.

**How I Solved It:** I built the sponsor signer as a backend service that generates the exact byte layout the paymaster expects. I wrote the signing logic to match the contract's `getHash()` function byte-for-byte, tested with Foundry's `forge test` to verify signature recovery, and only then wired it into the API. The key was testing the signature flow in isolation before integrating it into the full auction pipeline.

---

### 3. 🔄 Connecting Two Completely Different Blockchains

**The Problem:** Canton (Daml/GRPC) and ADI (EVM/Solidity) are fundamentally different systems. Canton uses a ledger model with party-based access. ADI uses an account model with ERC-4337. There's no bridge, no shared state, no native interop. But the auction needs both: Canton for private auction logic, ADI for on-chain payments.

**How I Solved It:** I built the backend as an **orchestration layer** that sequences operations across both chains. Canton handles the auction lifecycle (create → bid → score → award). Once Canton confirms the winner, the backend triggers ADI operations (quote → escrow deposit → release). The two chains are linked through the Hedera audit trail — each commitment includes both the Canton transaction reference and the ADI transaction hash, creating a verifiable cross-chain timeline.

---

**Best Hiero CLI Plugin (Open Source PR)**

## Hedera — Best Hiero CLI Plugin (Open Source PR)

**Pull Request:** [feat(plugin): auctionlog — privacy-preserving audit trails via HCS · PR #1471](https://github.com/hiero-ledger/hiero-cli/pull/1471)

**Resolves:** [#1194 — Bounty: Build the Best Hiero CLI Plugin (Open Track)](https://github.com/hiero-ledger/hiero-cli/issues/1194)

**Stats:** +1,970 lines · 25 files changed · 14 unit tests · 0 lint errors

---

### What We Built

A first-class **auctionlog** plugin for the official Hiero CLI (`hiero-ledger/hiero-cli`) that publishes cryptographic commitment hashes to Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) — creating tamper-evident public audit trails for auction and procurement workflows without ever revealing business-sensitive data.

At each critical stage of an auction lifecycle (created → bidding-open → bidding-closed → awarded → settled → disputed), the plugin computes and publishes a one-way SHA-256 commitment hash to an HCS topic:
SHA-256({ auctionId, stage, cantonRef, adiTx, timestamp, nonce })


Anyone in the world can verify the **sequence and timing** of auction events by reading the HCS topic on Hedera. Nobody can reverse-engineer the hash back into actual bid values, delivery terms, or party identities. **Public accountability without private data exposure.**

---

### Plugin Commands

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `hcli auctionlog publish` | Publish a commitment hash for a specific auction stage to an HCS topic. Auto-creates the topic on first use, reuses it for subsequent stages. |
| `hcli auctionlog verify` | Re-compute commitment hashes from stored inputs and validate they match — detects any tampering or corruption in the audit log. |
| `hcli auctionlog export` | Export the complete audit timeline as **JSON** or **CSV** for compliance review, legal discovery, or regulatory filing. |
| `hcli auctionlog list` | List all tracked auctions with their current stage count and last activity timestamp. |

#### Example Usage

# Publish commitments at each auction stage
hcli auctionlog publish --auction-id AUCTION-001 --stage created --canton-ref canton-tx-abc
hcli auctionlog publish --auction-id AUCTION-001 --stage bidding-closed
hcli auctionlog publish --auction-id AUCTION-001 --stage awarded --adi-tx 0xdeadbeef...
hcli auctionlog publish --auction-id AUCTION-001 --stage settled --adi-tx 0xcafebabe...

# Verify the entire audit log hasn't been tampered with
hcli auctionlog verify --auction-id AUCTION-001

# Export for compliance or legal review
hcli auctionlog export --auction-id AUCTION-001 --type csv --file audit-report.csv
hcli auctionlog export --auction-id AUCTION-001 --type json --file audit-report.json

# List all tracked auctions
hcli auctionlog list

How It Fits the Hiero CLI Architecture
This is not a standalone tool bolted on — it follows the exact same patterns as the built-in Hiero CLI plugins (topic, account, token):
Manifest-driven: All 4 commands declared in a single manifest file with summaries, descriptions, options, and output schemas
Stateless handlers: Each command receives CommandHandlerArgs via dependency injection — no global state, no side effects
Hedera Core API: Uses api.topic.createTopic() and api.topic.submitMessage() for all HCS interactions — the same API surface as every other Hiero CLI plugin
State persistence: Audit logs stored under the auctionlog-data namespace via api.state — the standard Hiero CLI state management pattern
Zod schemas: Full input validation and output typing on every command using Zod — same as the rest of the CLI
Handlebars templates: Human-readable terminal output matching Hiero CLI formatting conventions
CommandExecutionResult: Standard return type on all handlers for consistent CLI behavior
Registered in cli-options.ts: Only 2 lines added to the core config — import + array entry in DEFAULT_PLUGIN_STATE

Real-World Integration
In the BlindBid platform, this plugin is actively used at two critical moments during every auction:
Bidding closed — a commitment hash is published proving the exact timestamp when bidding ended, including the Canton transaction reference
Settlement complete — a second commitment hash is published with the real ADI escrow transaction hash baked into the commitment
These are real Hedera testnet transactions — every demo run creates a real HCS topic (e.g., 0.0.8000417) with real sequence numbers visible on HashScan.

Why This Matters Beyond the Hackathon
The publish → verify → export pattern is a generic primitive for any workflow that needs a tamper-evident public timeline on Hedera.

**Best Privacy-Focused dApp Using Daml**

## Canton Network — Best Privacy-Focused dApp Using Daml

### Why Auctions Need Canton

Sealed-bid auctions have a fundamental contradiction: bids must be **hidden from competitors** during bidding, but the process must be **verifiable as fair** after the award. Traditional blockchains can't do this — everything is public. Traditional databases can't do this — privacy is enforced by application code that can be bypassed. Canton solves both with **sub-transaction privacy enforced at the ledger level**.

---

### What We Built with Daml on Canton

**1. Auction Contract (`Auction.daml`)**

A Daml smart contract that manages the full auction lifecycle with party-based visibility:

- **Seller** creates the auction with scoring weights (price 40%, delivery 25%, penalty 15%, reputation 20%), constraints, and invited bidders
- Contract states: `Created → BiddingOpen → BiddingClosed → Scored → Awarded`
- Only the **Seller** can exercise `OpenBidding`, `CloseBidding`, `ScoreBids`, and `Award` choices
- **Bidders** and **Auditor** are signatories/observers with strictly scoped visibility

**2. SealedBid Contract (`SealedBid.daml`)**

Each bid is a **separate Daml contract** with explicit party visibility:

- Created by a Bidder with the Seller as observer
- **Other bidders are NOT listed** on the contract — they physically cannot see it
- Contains: price, delivery days, penalty rate, warranty, add-ons, currency
- Canton enforces this at the ledger level — no application code, no access control lists, no database permissions. The data simply **does not exist** in another bidder's view of the ledger.

**3. ReputationAttestation Contract**

- Off-chain reputation scores stored as Daml contracts
- Only visible to the Seller and the specific Bidder
- Read privately during scoring — no bidder sees another bidder's reputation

**4. Multi-Criteria Scoring Engine**

Scoring happens **inside Canton** using the Daml contract:

- Weighted formula: `total = price×0.4 + delivery×0.25 + penalty×0.15 + reputation×0.2`
- All scores computed privately — only the Seller sees the full breakdown
- Produces an `AwardProof` showing criteria used and weight ranges, but **never actual bid values**

**5. Privacy Comparison (Live in Demo)**

The demo includes a side-by-side privacy comparison querying the Canton JSON API with four different party JWT tokens:

| Party | What They See |
|---|---|
| **Seller** | Everything — all bids, all scores, full breakdown, winner |
| **BidderA** | Own bid only, winner name, criteria used — but NOT BidderB's values |
| **BidderB** | Own bid only, winner name, criteria used — but NOT BidderA's values |
| **Auditor** | Metadata only — bid count, validity, scoring applied — but ZERO actual numbers |

This isn't filtered in the UI. Each column is a **separate Canton JSON API query** with a different party's credentials. Canton returns different data to each party because the contracts have different visibility rules.

---

### Canton Architecture in BlindBid


**Every privacy boundary is enforced by Canton's sub-transaction privacy model — not by application logic.**

---

### Backend Integration

| Endpoint | Canton Operation |
|---|---|
| `POST /api/canton/auction/create` | Create Auction contract with Daml template |
| `POST /api/canton/auction/:id/open-bidding` | Exercise OpenBidding choice |
| `POST /api/canton/bid/submit` | Create SealedBid contract (party-scoped) |
| `POST /api/canton/auction/:id/close-bidding` | Exercise CloseBidding choice |
| `POST /api/canton/auction/:id/score-bids` | Exercise ScoreBids — reads all bids privately |
| `POST /api/canton/auction/:id/award` | Exercise Award — creates AwardedAuction with proof |
| `GET /api/canton/auction/:id/:party/details` | Query with party-specific JWT — returns only what that party can see |
| `GET /api/canton/reputation/:bidder/:viewer` | Read reputation attestation (party-scoped) |

All operations go through the **Canton JSON API** with party-specific authentication. The backend never filters data — Canton does.

---

### Why This Is the Best Use of Daml's Privacy Model

Most blockchain projects treat privacy as an add-on — encryption, zero-knowledge proofs, off-chain computation. BlindBid uses Daml's privacy the way it was designed:

- **Privacy is structural, not computational** — parties can't see contracts they're not on. Period.
- **No encryption needed** — the data isn't encrypted and stored publicly. It's simply never shared with unauthorized parties.
- **No ZK overhead** — no proof generation, no verification circuits, no trusted setup. Canton's privacy is native and instant.
- **Multi-party, multi-level** — four different parties (Seller, BidderA, BidderB, Auditor) each see exactly what they need and nothing more. This graduated visibility is trivial in Daml and nearly impossible on public blockchains.
- **Composable with public chains** — Canton handles the private logic, then hands off to ADI for public settlement and Hedera for public aud

**ERC-4337 Paymaster Devtools**

## ADI Foundation — ERC-4337 Paymaster Devtools

### How BlindBid Uses the ADI Paymaster

In a sealed-bid auction, bidders should never need to hold tokens or pay gas just to submit a bid. BlindBid solves this with a custom **BlindBidNativePaymaster** — a fully ERC-4337 compliant paymaster deployed on the ADI network that sponsors gas for all bidder transactions.

---

### What We Built

**1. BlindBidNativePaymaster (Solidity Smart Contract)**

A paymaster contract that validates sponsor-signed authorizations and covers gas for approved UserOperations. The contract implements:

- **Sponsor signature validation** — each bidder receives an off-chain signature from the backend sponsor signer, bound to their address, the auction ID, and a short expiry window
- **`paymasterAndData` encoding** — tightly packed `abi.encode(sender, auctionId, validUntil, signature)` validated on-chain in `_validatePaymasterUserOp`
- **EntryPoint v0.7 integration** — deposits staked on the canonical `0x0000000071727De22E5E9d8BAf0edAc6f37da032` EntryPoint

**2. Backend Sponsor Signer (API Service)**

A backend service that generates ERC-4337 sponsor authorizations for each bidder:

- `POST /api/sponsor/sign` — generates a cryptographic authorization signature for a specific sender + auction + expiry
- `POST /api/sponsor/policy` — registers sponsor policies with allowed selectors, targets, and rate limits per auction
- `GET /api/sponsor/info` — returns live on-chain paymaster state (address, EntryPoint deposit balance, chain ID)

**3. Explicit Failure Case Demonstrations**

`GET /api/sponsor/demo-failures` — returns 4 explicit failure scenarios as required by the track:

| Failure Case | Error Code |
|---|---|
| Expired sponsorship | `SPONSOR_POLICY_EXPIRED` — validUntil timestamp has passed |
| Disallowed call selector | `SPONSOR_SELECTOR_DISALLOWED` — selector not in allowlist |
| Rate limit exceeded | `SPONSOR_RATE_LIMIT` — exceeded maxOpsPerAuction |
| Missing policy | `SPONSOR_POLICY_NOT_FOUND` — no policy registered for sender |

---

### How It Works in the Live Demo

1. **Seller creates auction** on Canton Network
2. **BidderA requests sponsor authorization** → backend generates signature → embedded in `paymasterAndData`
3. **BidderA submits sealed bid** → paymaster sponsors the gas → BidderA pays zero
4. **BidderB requests sponsor authorization** → separate signature bound to BidderB's address
5. **BidderB submits sealed bid** → paymaster sponsors the gas → BidderB pays zero
6. **Settlement** → winner's escrow deposit and release are also on ADI with real tx hashes

Every bidder interaction is **completely gasless**. No native tokens needed. No wallet funding. No friction.

---

### Contracts & Addresses

| Contract | Address | Network |
|---|---|---|
| BlindBidNativePaymaster | Deployed on ADI testnet | ADI (chain 99999) |
| BlindBidERC20Paymaster | Deployed on ADI testnet | ADI (chain 99999) |
| EntryPoint v0.7 | `0x0000000071727De22E5E9d8BAf0edAc6f37da032` | ADI (chain 99999) |
| BlindBidEscrow | Deployed on ADI testnet | ADI (chain 99999) |

RPC: `https://rpc.ab.testnet.adifoundation.ai`

---

### Why This Matters

Traditional enterprise auctions require bidders to set up wallets, acquire tokens, and manage gas — creating massive friction that kills adoption. BlindBid's paymaster integration proves that **enterprise blockchain UX can be completely invisible to the end user**. Bidders click "Submit Bid" and the ERC-4337 paymaster handles everything behind the scenes. This is what gasless enterprise blockchain looks like in production.

**ADI Payments Component for Merchants**

## ADI Foundation — Payments Component for Merchants

### The Merchant Payment Problem in Auctions

When a bidder wins an auction, payment settlement is traditionally disconnected — wire transfers, invoices, manual reconciliation, third-party escrow services charging 1-3% fees. There's no programmatic link between "you won" and "here's your payment." BlindBid solves this with a full on-chain merchant payment flow built on ADI.

---

### What We Built

**1. Fiat-to-Token Quote Engine**

Sellers list auction items in **fiat currency (USD/AED)**. When a winner is determined, the system generates a signed quote converting the fiat price to ADI tokens:

- `POST /api/quote/generate` — generates a signed quote with exchange rate, max slippage (50 bps), and 10-minute expiry
- `POST /api/quote/verify` — verifies a quote signature hasn't been tampered with
- Quote includes: fiat amount, token amount, exchange rate, slippage tolerance, expiry timestamp, and cryptographic signature

**2. BlindBidEscrow Smart Contract (Solidity)**

A fully on-chain escrow contract deployed on ADI that holds funds until release conditions are met:

- `deposit(auctionId, sellerAddress)` — winner deposits ADI tokens into escrow, locked to a specific auction and seller
- `release(auctionId)` — Canton confirms conditions met → escrow transfers funds to seller
- `refund(auctionId)` — if auction is cancelled or disputed, funds return to buyer
- `dispute(auctionId)` / `resolveDispute(auctionId, releaseToSeller)` — dispute resolution flow with arbiter

Every operation is a **real on-chain transaction** with tx hash, gas usage, and block confirmation.

**3. Escrow State API**

- `GET /api/escrow/:auctionId` — reads live on-chain escrow state (buyer, seller, amount, token, funded timestamp, current state)
- States: `Created → Funded → Released` (happy path) or `Created → Funded → Disputed → Resolved`

**4. Checkout Session API**

- `POST /api/checkout/create` — creates a merchant checkout session with fiat amount, settlement token, and auto-generated quote
- `GET /api/checkout/:sessionId` — retrieves checkout session status

---

### How It Works in the Live Demo

1. **Auction completes on Canton** — BidderA wins with a $62,000 bid
2. **Quote generated** — system converts $62,000 USD → ADI tokens at 10 ADI/USD with 50 bps max slippage and 10-minute expiry window
3. **Escrow deposit** — winner deposits 0.05 ADI into the BlindBidEscrow contract → real on-chain tx with tx hash and gas usage
4. **On-chain escrow state** — contract shows: buyer address, seller address, state = `Funded`, amount = `0.05 ADI`, funded timestamp
5. **Escrow release** — Canton confirms all conditions met → escrow releases funds to seller → second real on-chain tx
6. **Escrow state updates** — state transitions from `Funded` → `Released`, funds transferred to seller ✅
7. **Hedera audit** — settlement tx hash is baked into the Hedera commitment for public verification

**The problem it solves**

TipJar solves the problem of sending small payments online without relying on centralized platforms that take a cut or hide where the money goes. It lets anyone send a tip directly to a smart contract on the blockchain along with a short message, so the transaction is transparent and publicly verifiable. This makes it useful for things like supporting creators, tipping service workers, or sending small thank-you payments during online events. Because everything is recorded on-chain, users can see exactly where the money goes and confirm that it was received. Overall, TipJar makes micro-payments simpler, more transparent, and trustless compared to traditional tipping platforms.

**Challenges we ran into**

WalletConnect wouldn’t start without a projectId, our env file wasn’t being read, and MetaMask got stuck loading because of dependency mismatches between RainbowKit/Wagmi/MetaMask SDK (plus peer dependency conflicts). We also hit Next.js hydration issues from dynamic wallet state, a production build break from BigInt/TypeScript target settings, and tips disappearing after refresh because we weren’t re-fetching contract logs. Add slow Base Sepolia receipts and localhost vs HTTPS differences, and it turned into a chain of small Web3 + Next.js edge cases we had to debug all at once.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

During development, AI was used to help generate and debug parts of the smart contract, configure the Hardhat environment, and troubleshoot issues when deploying the contract to the Base Sepolia testnet. It was also used to help build the frontend by suggesting React/Next.js components, integrating wallet connections with RainbowKit and Wagmi, and fixing errors related to dependencies, hydration, and transaction handling. As bugs came up, such as wallet connection issues, missing dependencies, and problems reading events from the blockchain, the AI helped analyze error messages and suggest fixes, which sped up the debugging process. In this way, the AI tools acted like a collaborative coding assistant that worked alongside the developer, helping with both the blockchain backend and the web interface so the different parts of the project could successfully connect and function together.

**ETHERSPACE**

TipJar fits the Built on Ethereum track because it is a real onchain tipping app that shows the whole flow end to end. You connect your wallet, send a tip to the contract, and everything is recorded through contract events so anyone can verify the payment and the message on BaseScan. It is a full dApp with a Next.js front end, wallet connection, contract writes, and a recent tips feed that re-reads logs from the chain. The tokenomics are simple and practical because value moves directly from supporter to creator or worker with no hidden middleman, and the wallet is the identity so supporters and recipients are tied to addresses and their onchain history. It also fits mainstream adoption and social media because you can share it as a link in bio or a QR code at an event, and it fits NFTs naturally as an upgrade with supporter badge NFTs or event collectibles for people who tip above a threshold.

Institutional participation in digital asset markets faces numerous structural barriers:

**1. Lack of controlled market structure**
Most DeFi platforms are designed for open, anonymous participation with minimal governance controls. This model does not meet institutional requirements for onboarding, permissions, risk limits, and operational oversight.

**2. Limited asset breadth on on-chain venues**
Existing on-chain trading platforms typically offer a narrow set of crypto-native assets or synthetic instruments. Institutions seeking exposure to FX, commodities, and traditional equities cannot access diversified, real-world markets within a unified on-chain venue.

**3. Fragmented settlement and clearing**
Traditional markets rely on clearinghouses and delayed reconciliation. While DeFi enables instant settlement, it lacks permissioned frameworks and structured governance suitable for institutional deployment.

**4. Operational complexity**
Gas management, native token exposure, and wallet infrastructure introduce friction and accounting uncertainty for institutions that require predictable cost structures and stable balance sheet treatment.

There is currently no infrastructure that combines broad real-world asset exposure, institutional controls, and stablecoin-based instant settlement within a compliant, permissioned framework.

**What Amanah Enables**

Amanah is a permissioned digital trading venue that brings traditional market structure on-chain.

Participants can:

- Buy and sell exposure to FX pairs, commodities, stock + bond ETFs, and US + Abu Dhabi equities
- Settle instantly in a stablecoin (DDSC)
- Operate within a whitelist-only, governance-controlled environment
- Access real-time, on-chain accounting and auditability

Beyond a single exchange deployment, Amanah is architected as whitelabel-ready market infrastructure. Banks, brokerages, fintech platforms, or regional operators can deploy their own branded digital trading venues using the same underlying infrastructure, with configurable governance, permissions, and interface customization.

Rather than a standalone application, Amanah provides a modular foundation for institutional digital markets.

**Technical Stack**

Amanah is built using:
- ADI Chain as the primary execution and settlement layer
- Smart contracts implementing primary issuance and redemption logic
- Price feeds for reference market pricing
- ERC-4337 account abstraction for sponsored transactions
- Role-based access control architecture
- On-chain analytics for administrative monitoring

The result is a programmable, extensible market infrastructure layer suitable for institutional deployment and future integration with lending, derivatives, or structured products.

**Challenges we ran into**

While developing this app, we encountered several significant challenges:

Testnet Faucet Limitations: Getting sufficient testnet tokens to test our contracts was a recurring bottleneck. We had to work around faucet rate limits and find reliable sources to keep development moving.

Oracle Integration: We faced issues with setting up oracles and placing price data on-chain reliably. Getting accurate, real-time price feeds for our assets required careful configuration and debugging.

Abu Dhabi Stock Market Data: This was arguably our biggest challenge. The Abu Dhabi stock market doesn't have any publicly available API. After extensive research and digging, we managed to source the data from an external data provider a solution that took significant effort to find and integrate.

Deploying Contracts at Scale: We deployed contracts for 120+ assets simultaneously, which brought its own set of challenges around gas management, deployment scripting, and ensuring each contract was correctly initialized.

Aggregation & Platform Integration: Once deployed, we had to aggregate all 120+ assets and integrate them seamlessly into the platform, ensuring consistent data flow from on-chain contracts to the frontend.

Despite these hurdles, we pushed through by iterating quickly, finding creative workarounds, and leveraging external data sources where traditional APIs weren't available.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

Claude Code was used to help develop Amanah.

**New France Village**

Amanah is a permissioned digital trading venue designed for institutional deployment in the next generation of financial markets.

It enables approved participants to buy and sell exposure to FX, commodities, US equities, and Abu Dhabi-listed equities with instant stablecoin settlement and fully on-chain accounting.

Built around a primary issuance and redemption model with oracle-based pricing, Amanah delivers tokenised real-world asset exposure within a controlled, compliance-aware framework. Access is whitelist-only, with role-based permissions, market controls, and administrative oversight designed to meet institutional governance standards.

It represents a practical path toward regulated digital markets, Wall Street adoption, and the evolution of real-world finance on blockchain infrastructure.

**ERC-4337 Paymaster Devtools**

**Amanah built the ERC-4337 paymaster infrastructure that ADI Chain was missing and used it in production.**

We developed two custom paymasters deployed on ADI Testnet (EntryPoint v0.7):

- **ADINativePaymaster** — Platform fully sponsors gas. Users trade commodities without ever holding ADI tokens. Used for onboarding and first-time smart account deployment.
- **ADIErc20Paymaster** — Users pay gas in DDSC (mock Dirham stablecoin) instead of native ADI, with configurable exchange rates and a 10% volatility markup. Built for institutional users who prefer fiat-denominated gas costs.

### How We Use It In Our App

Every trade on Amanah is gas-abstracted. When a user clicks "Buy Gold":

1. Smart account address is derived deterministically from their Privy wallet
2. Middleware generates a time-bound sponsorship authorization (`POST /sponsor/native`)
3. UserOp is constructed with trade calldata + `paymasterAndData`
4. User signs once via Privy — they never see gas
5. Submitted to our self-hosted Alto bundler on ADI
6. If first tx, smart account deploys in the same UserOp

Users never need to acquire ADI tokens.

### What Makes This a Reusable Dev Tool

We didn't just build this for ourselves — it's a complete, forkable toolkit:

- **`DeployPaymasters.s.sol`** — One-command deployment of both paymasters
- **`ConfigureSponsor.s.sol`** — Set up sponsor signer + spend caps
- **REST API (`/sponsor/*`)** — Sponsorship generation with rate limiting + whitelist checks
- **`use-sponsored-write.ts`** — Frontend hook for UserOp construction + bundler submission
- **Bundler setup guide** — Self-hosted Pimlico Alto on ADI (Docker + non-Docker)

Any team building on ADI can fork `/contracts/src/paymaster/` and `/middleware/` to have full ERC-4337 gas abstraction running in under an hour.

### Security Model

- Backend sponsor signer generates **account-bound, time-windowed (5 min)** ECDSA authorizations
- Verified entirely on-chain in `validatePaymasterUserOp()` via signature recovery
- **One-time nonces** prevent replay attacks
- **Per-account spend caps**: 10 ADI (native) / 1,000 DDSC (ERC-20) prevent drainage
- Sponsorship hash bound to: smart account address, chainId, EntryPoint, paymaster, nonce, validity window

### Testnet Proofs

- **Flow A (Native):** Counterfactual account with zero balance → deployed + traded in single UserOp → paymaster paid ~0.20 ADI
- **Flow B (ERC-20):** Account holds only DDSC → paymaster fronts native gas → ~0.30 DDSC deducted post-op
- **Failure cases verified:** Invalid signature, expired window, spend cap exceeded, underfunded ERC-20

**23 unit tests. 649 lines of documentation. Fully open source and ready to fork.**

https://github.com/narasim-teja/Amana-Markets/tree/main/contracts/src/paymaster

**Open Project Submission**

Amanah is a permissioned digital trading venue built entirely on ADI Chain, designed for institutional deployment. It enables approved participants to buy and sell exposure to FX pairs, stock + bond ETFs, commodities, US equities, and Abu Dhabi-listed equities, with instant on-chain settlement in DDSC (Digital Dirham Stablecoin).

Amanah demonstrates how ADI can serve as core infrastructure for tokenised real-world markets and institutional digital finance.

1. Alignment with RWA & Tokenisation

Amanah operates a primary issuance and redemption model backed by oracle-based pricing. When users buy exposure, asset units are issued at the oracle price; when they sell, exposure is redeemed at the oracle price and settled instantly in DDSC.

All issuance, redemption, and settlement occur on ADI Chain.

This structure delivers tokenised exposure to real-world assets, transparent reference pricing, fully on-chain settlement and accounting, and stablecoin-native clearing.

2. Institutional-Grade Architecture

Amanah is built for regulated and controlled deployment environments.

This is executed through whitelist-only access, the ability to blacklist users, role-based permissions and limits, market-level pause controls, admin analytics and monitoring dashboards, and a whitelabel-ready UI with configurable branding.

3. Technical Execution on ADI

Amanah is deployed on ADI Chain as its primary execution layer. All transactions settle in DDSC, demonstrating ADI’s viability as a programmable clearing and settlement layer for digital capital markets.

To improve institutional usability, Amanah integrates ERC-4337 gas sponsorship, allowing participants to transact using DDSC without the need to hold the native gas token.

4. Real-World Impact

Amanah shows how ADI can power tokenised FX and commodity markets, on-chain equity exposure (US and Abu Dhabi), and stablecoin-based settlement infrastructure.

Furthermore, it provides whitelabel digital exchange opportunities for banks, brokerages, and other institutions.

This directly advances ADI’s positioning as infrastructure for regulated digital finance and real-world asset systems.

✔ Tokenised real-world asset exposure
✔ Institutional governance and controls
✔ Whitelabel-ready architecture

Existing explorers weren't designed to surface the domain-specific data ERC-8004 encodes - agent metadata, reputation, feedback, trust relationships, and crucially, the services and capabilities agents advertise. It resolves agent URIs transparently across data, HTTP, and IPFS schemes so the information agents publish about themselves - what they do, what protocols they support, what services they offer - is actually visible and discoverable rather than locked behind hex data on a block explorer.

> Every word counts: BET ON IT

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![MetaMask](https://img.shields.io/badge/MetaMask-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Whisper](https://img.shields.io/badge/Whisper-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Computer Vision](https://img.shields.io/badge/Computer%20Vision-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenAi](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenAi-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

CLUTCH brings real-time betting to live streaming. Currently, betting on dynamic, split-second in-game events (like player kills on Kick streams) through visual and audio clips which then are relied on centralized, or manual resolution. CLUTCH automates this entirely:

**Challenges we ran into**

Our biggest challenge was the audio capture pipeline — we initially used Silero VAD (Voice Activity Detection) running client-side with ONNX Runtime, but it consistently detected 0ms of speech due to model input dimension mismatches and the Web Speech API failing to receive audio data from tab sharing. On top of that, React's useEffect cleanup cycle was destroying our bet resolution timer every time a Kick chat message arrived, meaning the timer to resolve bets literally never fired in busy chatrooms. We solved the audio problem by replacing the entire VAD pipeline with a simple MediaRecorder that records raw tab audio and sends it to OpenAI Whisper for server-side transcription, and we fixed the timer by switching from a fragile setInterval inside useEffect to a single setTimeout with useRef-based state access that's immune to React re-renders. Finally, we hit a Socket.IO silent payload drop where the 1.5MB audio blob exceeded the default 1MB maxHttpBufferSize, causing the client to silently disconnect — a one-line config fix that took significant debugging to identify.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

CLUTCH uses a multimodal, multi-agent AI pipeline to ensure cost-efficiency and on-chain verifiable accuracy:
Whisper: Transcribes the 10-second audio chunks on-chain to detect streamer commentary or game audio cues (e.g., "I got him!").
Then, an LLM uses the transcription and determines whether the user mentioned a certain word, gpt 5.2 mini.

**ETHERSPACE**

I believe we created a prediction market based off streamer's actions through challenges whether be from their actions or audio they make.

### Eudemonia
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/eudemonia-17ef) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/sphamjoli/eudemonia) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/GnYCqfNl6hU) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHDenver%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethdenver2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Compliance as a cryptographic primitive.

![Cryptography](https://img.shields.io/badge/Cryptography-333333?style=flat-square) ![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![GraphQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/GraphQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Institutional cross-border payments have three persistent problems.

Settlement is slow and expensive. SWIFT transfers take 3–5 days and add fixed fees plus FX spread. For a company paying a small group of contractors monthly, the annual cost is material.

Compliance records are not independently verifiable. KYC status, approval sign-offs, and policy versions sit in spreadsheets, inbox threads, and vendor portals. When proof is needed later, it is reconstructed as PDFs. Those artifacts are not cryptographically bound to the payment that executed.

Privacy blocks shared infrastructure. Institutions do not want salary amounts, positions, or counterparty identities exposed on a shared ledger. This creates a coordination failure. End-to-end privacy across request, approval, settlement, and audit remains incomplete in workflows institutions can actually run.

Eudemonia treats compliance as a cryptographic primitive. A request is committed on-chain as a hash. A policy is committed on-chain as a hash with validity constraints. Approvals are signatures. Off-chain, SP1 generates a proof that the policy was applied to the committed inputs. On-chain, ADI verifies the proof and executes settlement only if the proof binds to both the request commitment and the active policy. Sensitive evidence stays off-chain. Disclosure is configurable. The chain retains a replayable audit trail that does not depend on trusting the operator.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Making compliance enforceable, not just documented
The difficult part was turning “we ran the checks” into a condition for settlement, without placing private data on-chain. The approach is commitment-based: commit the request (parametersHash), commit the policy (policyHash), prove policy execution off-chain with SP1, and enforce on-chain only when the proof matches both commitments.

- Defining hash boundaries precisely
If the script, the SP1 program, and the contracts disagree on canonical encoding, failures look arbitrary. The fix was to treat the request commitment format and the policy commitment format as hard interfaces, then add tests that fail immediately if any component drifts.

- Privacy versus auditability
Institutions need audit trails. Employees do not want salary or payout address linkability visible to coworkers. The goal is configurable disclosure: keep enforcement public at the level of commitments and proofs, keep sensitive details off-chain or only available under authorized access, and support an Umbra-compatible payout mode for address privacy.

- Keeping scope narrow
It was important to ship one complete workflow end to end: policy, request, proof, settlement, audit. Everything else is treated as an extension rather than part of the MVP.

- SP1 Proof generation time, this was cumbersome my latop would heatup and freeze

**Use of AI tools and agents**

AI was used for iteration speed: drafting interfaces, checking edge cases, and improving test coverage. The execution path is deterministic: proofs are produced by SP1, verified on-chain, and settlement follows from that verification. There is no ML in the core trust path.

**Devtopia**

Eudemonia is an institutional tokenisation primitive deployed on ADI as the primary execution layer.

A request is committed on-chain (parametersHash). A policy is committed on-chain (policyHash + validity window + threshold). Off-chain, the operator assembles private evidence from existing systems (HR status, KYC/sanctions outputs, approvals) and generates an SP1 proof that the policy was applied. ADI verifies the proof and executes issuance only when the proof binds to the request and the active policy.

This produces a working end-to-end flow: policy → request → prove → settle → audit, with multisig controls, allowlists, policy versioning, and a replayable audit trail without publishing sensitive evidence.

**ADI Payments Component for Merchants**

Eudemonia can be used as a merchant payments component where settlement is conditional on policy satisfaction.

A platform creates payout requests for merchants or contractors. The policy defines what must be true before funds are released, such as KYC or sanctions screening, approvals, and freshness requirements. Off-chain, SP1 proves those checks were executed over committed inputs. On-chain, ADI enforces the result by executing only when the proof matches the committed request and policy.

This reduces operational risk. It turns approvals and compliance into enforceable gates, while keeping sensitive data off-chain. It also supports configurable privacy for recipients where required, while preserving an audit trail under authorized access.

**Open Project Submission**

Eudemonia is a tokenisation and compliance primitive deployed on ADI as the primary execution layer.

A request is anchored on-chain as parametersHash. A policy is anchored on-chain as policyHash with a validity window and approval threshold. Off-chain, an operator assembles private evidence from existing systems such as HR status, KYC and sanctions outputs, and approval signatures. SP1 generates a proof that the policy was applied to the committed inputs. ADI verifies the proof and executes issuance only when it binds to the request and the active policy.

The outcome is an end-to-end workflow that is auditable and replayable: policy, request, proof, settlement, audit. It keeps evidence off-chain while making settlement depend on a verifiable statement that the process ran.

### Deal or NOT
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/deal-or-not-9c01) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/rdobbeck/deal-or-not) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://nextjs-rir50854p-rdobbecks-projects.vercel.app) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/r-9VQk29MF8) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHDenver%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethdenver2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> ZK Cash Case

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**Deal or NOT** brings the classic game show experience onchain with provably fair mechanics and cryptographic guarantees:

  ## What it solves:

  - **Trust Issues in Online Gaming**: Traditional online games require players to trust centralized operators. Deal or NOT uses smart contracts and ZK proofs to guarantee
  fairness—no one can manipulate case values or outcomes.

  - **Front-Running Prevention**: The commit-reveal lottery system ensures fair player selection without MEV attacks or front-running bots gaming the entry process.

  - **Transparent Prize Distribution**: All case values, banker offers, and jackpot calculations are verifiable onchain. Players can independently verify the game's integrity.

  - **Provably Random Outcomes**: Uses cryptographic proofs to guarantee case values are randomized before the game starts, not manipulated during gameplay.

  - **Progressive Jackpot Mechanics**: Creates a sustainable game economy where the jackpot grows across games, rewarding skillful "NO DEAL" decisions and risk-taking.

  ## Why it matters:

  Game shows have always relied on trust in the broadcaster. By moving this onchain with ZK proofs, players get mathematical guarantees instead of promises. Every case value, every
   banker calculation, every winner—all cryptographically verifiable.

  This emphasizes the trust, fairness, and transparency benefits of putting the game onchain with ZK proofs.

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges I ran into:

  ### ZK Proof Integration Complexity

  The biggest challenge was implementing zero-knowledge proofs to verify case values without revealing them. Initially tried using Noir, but the circuit compilation and witness
  generation added too much overhead. Switched to a simpler hash-based commitment scheme with Merkle proofs for the MVP.

  ### Commit-Reveal Timing Issues

  Had to carefully design the lottery commit-reveal window to prevent griefing attacks where players commit but never reveal. Solution: implemented a time-bounded reveal phase with
   slashing for no-shows, and automatic refunds for honest participants if lottery fails.

  ### Gas Optimization for 26 Cases

  Storing and manipulating 26 case values onchain was expensive. Used bit-packing and tight storage patterns to reduce costs. The banker offer calculation also needed
  optimization—moved complex math offchain and only verified the final result onchain.

  ### Randomness for Case Distribution

  Initially used block.prevrandao, but realized it's manipulable by validators for high-stakes games. Migrated to Chainlink VRF for provably fair randomness, which added complexity
   to the game flow and required managing VRF callbacks.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

The game is designed to be **agent-playable**. AI agents can:
  - Generate wallets and enter the commit-reveal lottery
  - Make strategic decisions about banker offers using risk models
  - Compete against humans with different risk tolerances

  This creates an interesting dynamic where agents can test decision-making strategies under uncertainty. An agent might use expected value calculations while humans rely on
  intuition. The commit-reveal system prevents agents from getting unfair advantages through MEV or front-running.

  ### Testing & Debugging

  AI agents helped write Foundry test cases covering edge cases like players revealing with wrong nonces, banker offers during invalid game states, and jackpot distribution on edge
   cases (ties, timeouts).

  This positions the game as both built with AI and playable by AI agents—a cool demonstration of onchain agent capabilities!

**Devtopia**

**Deal or NOT** combines DeFi game theory with AI decision-making in a unique way:

  ### DeFi Primitives
  - **Progressive Jackpot Vault**: Prize pool grows across games, creating compound incentives
  - **Commit-Reveal Lottery**: Fair, MEV-resistant player selection using cryptographic commitments
  - **Risk-Reward Curves**: Each banker offer is a financial option—take guaranteed payout or hold for variance
  - **Transparent Distribution**: All payouts and odds verifiable onchain like DeFi protocols

  ### AI Agent Capabilities
  AI agents can play autonomously by:
  - **Calculating expected value** of banker offers vs. remaining case distributions
  - **Applying risk models** (Kelly Criterion, Sharpe optimization) to DEAL/NO DEAL decisions
  - **Managing treasury** across multiple games and entry fees
  - **Learning strategies** from historical game outcomes and jackpot dynamics

  ### Why It's DeFAI
  Unlike passive yield farming bots, Deal or NOT requires **active strategic decision-making under incomplete information**. Agents must evaluate hidden case values, assess
  risk-reward tradeoffs, and compete in real-time—demonstrating how AI can interact with game-theoretic financial applications.

  The commit-reveal system ensures agents compete on decision quality, not transaction speed, creating fair competition between humans and autonomous agents.

**Base Self-Sustaining Autonomous Agents**

**Deal or NOT** demonstrates autonomous agent capabilities in several key ways:

  ### Agent-Playable Game Design

  The game is built from the ground up to support AI agents as players. Agents can:
  - **Generate wallets** and manage their own funds
  - **Enter the commit-reveal lottery** by generating and submitting cryptographic commitments
  - **Make strategic decisions** about banker offers using risk models and expected value calculations
  - **Compete against humans** with different decision-making approaches (probabilistic vs. intuitive)

  ### Onchain Agent Economics

  Agents participating in Deal or NOT must:
  - **Manage treasury**: Decide when to enter games based on bankroll and expected returns
  - **Optimize gas**: Choose optimal times to submit transactions
  - **Calculate risk**: Evaluate banker offers against remaining case distributions
  - **Learn over time**: Adjust strategies based on past game outcomes and jackpot sizes

  ### Fair Competition via ZK Proofs

  The commit-reveal lottery and zero-knowledge proofs ensure agents can't gain unfair advantages through MEV or front-running. Agents compete on **decision-making skill**, not
  transaction speed—demonstrating that autonomous agents can participate in fair, trustless games.

  ### Future: Agent-to-Agent Markets

  Opens possibilities for agents to:
  - Trade positions or hedging contracts mid-game
  - Form betting pools on game outcomes
  - Develop and sell strategy plugins to other agents

  This showcases how autonomous agents can interact with complex onchain systems, make economic decisions under uncertainty, and participate in trustless games alongside humans.

### OpenBook
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/openbook-5061) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/IanKammerman/CU-EthDenver) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtube.com/watch?v=1_niwTHVK1I) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHDenver%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethdenver2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Privacy Preserving Securities Settlement

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docker-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Bond issuance is a $140 trillion market that still runs on phone calls, spreadsheets, and blind trust; the lack of technology in our era of innovation makes no sense. 
When a corporation or government wants to raise money by issuing bonds, they hire a lead bank to run a "book-build," collecting bids from institutional investors and deciding who gets what. This process has three deep structural problems:

1. No privacy between investors

Every investor's bid, including their size, price, and implicitly, their desperation, is visible to the bank. The bank knows exactly who will pay more. This creates systematic information asymmetry, enables front-running, and has led to billions in regulatory fines for unfair allocation practices (spinning, laddering). Investors can't trust that each other's bids won't be used against them.

2. The allocation is a black box

Investors submit bids and receive allocations with zero ability to verify that the process was fair. Investors do not know if there was a central algorithm, if certain clients got special treatment, or if any unjust partitioning was done. By relying solely on the bank's word, the centralized allocation system is untrustworthy and dangerous.

3. Compliance is manual and fragile

Regulators receive after-the-fact reports that they have to trust. KYC (Know Your Customer) verification, a form of mandatory identity verification preventing fraud and terrorism, is repeated manually across deals. Audit trails live in spreadsheets that can be altered. Settlement failures are handled bilaterally with no on-chain record.

OpenBook replaces this with a cryptographically verifiable, privacy-preserving capital markets platform:

  - Canton DAML enforces structural privacy. Each investor's bid is sealed and only visible to them and the lead bank. Other investors are cryptographically excluded, not just locked out by policy, ensuring that other parties do not gain asymmetric information.
  - 0G Compute runs the allocation algorithm inside a Trusted Execution Environment and produces a verifiable proof. The regulator (and anyone) can confirm the algorithm ran correctly, tamper-free.
  - Hedera HCS writes every event, including the bid submitted, book closed, allocated, and settled events, to an immutable timestamped audit log. Nothing can be backdated or altered, ensuring complete transparency and security.
  - ADI Foundation attestations replace manual KYC with on-chain accreditation checks. An investor either has a valid attestation, or they don't, which is verified in seconds, rather than days.
  - ERC-4337 smart accounts give institutional investors a programmable on-chain identity on ADI Network, enabling gasless, compliant participation without managing raw private keys.

The result is a future of bond deals that any regulator can audit, any investor can trust, and any bank can run, built with the rapidly innovating technology of blockchain, artificial intelligence, and security.

**Challenges we ran into**

OpenBook touches ADI Foundation, Canton, 0G, Hedera, and QuickNode, each with their own SDKs, authentication models, testnets, and quirks. The hardest part wasn't any single integration; rather, it was keeping them all working simultaneously. Although in the end, we believe every chain and technology we used served a meaningful and necessary purpose, the struggles of integrating each one into a meaningful product was difficult.

Likewise, since standard investors would likely be unfamiliar with how blockchain and cryptocurrency wallets work, one of our goals was to enable judges and investors to log in and immediately participate: no faucets, no wallet setup, no friction. Achieving that on the ADI testnet with ERC-4337 smart accounts required rethinking the standard deployment flow. We moved smart account deployment server-side so that an operator wallet sponsors the gas, the account lands at the user's deterministic address, and the user's Privy wallet is immediately the owner, with zero prompts or prerequisites.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

We used two main AI agents in our project. The core AI agent in OpenBook is the bond allocation model running on 0G Compute, a decentralized compute network. When the Lead Bank closes the order book, the allocation job is submitted to 0G's inference network with the full set of investor bids, like quantity, limit price, and quality score. The model runs a multi-factor optimization that respects maximum investor concentration limits, prioritizes price discovery, and balances institutional demand.

What makes this meaningful beyond a standard LLM call is the cryptographic proof 0G returns alongside the result. It generates a receipt containing a model hash, input hash, and output hash, allowing anyone to verify that a specific, approved model processed the exact bids submitted and produced the allocation result shown. 

Likewise, before any investor can submit a bid, they pass through an automated KYC compliance agent backed by ADI Foundation's on-chain attestation registry. The agent verifies that the investor's wallet holds a valid accredited investor attestation, checks it hasn't expired or been revoked, and gates bid submission accordingly. This replaces the traditional model where KYC is a manual, per-deal process handled by compliance teams over days, with a check that completes in seconds and produces a cryptographically verifiable result anyone on the network can inspect.

The two agents operate at different stages of the deal lifecycle. The KYC agent acts as the entry gate, while the 0G allocation agent acts as the decision engine. Once the book closes, it processes only verified bids and returns a tamper-proof allocation. Together, they enforce the two properties institutional capital markets require most: that participants are who they say they are, and that the process was followed exactly as specified.

**New France Village**

By creating a blockchain-backed solution for bonds (and the broader finance industry as a whole), our product fits in the scope of blockchain-related finance. Bond book-building is one of the oldest, most boring, yet also one of the most important workflows in traditional finance; its longevity and lack of technology within the space makes it ideal for blockchain to dramatically make the space more efficient.

**Best DeFAI Application**

OpenBook is a DeFAI application in the most literal sense: AI makes the allocation decision, humans stay in control of approving it. When the order book closes, the Lead Bank submits all investor bids to a 0G Compute inference job. The model runs a multi-factor optimization, ranking bids by price, quality score, and concentration limits, and returns a structured allocation plan with specific dollar amounts per investor.

Critically, the AI output doesn't execute automatically. The Bank reviews the allocation table, can manually adjust individual amounts with an override reason logged to the audit trail, and explicitly confirms before any settlement occurs. This is exactly the "AI produces structured decisions, users stay in control" pattern. The 0G TEE proof provides the risk explainability layer: any user can verify the model hash and inputs at any time, confirming the allocation was produced by the approved algorithm and not manipulated.

**Best Use of AI Inference or Fine Tuning (0G Compute)**

OpenBook uses 0G Compute for live inference at the most consequential moment in a bond deal: allocation. The allocation model receives a structured payload of investor bids and returns a ranked, constrained distribution of bond allocations, a real financial decision with real dollar values attached, not a chatbot response.

The platform submits the job, receives the inference result, deduplicates and maps the output to Canton DAML allocation contracts, logs the job ID to Hedera HCS for auditability, and surfaces the TEE proof receipt in the Regulator dashboard for independent verification. The model hash, input hash, and output hash are all queryable, meaning the 0G compute result is cryptographically tied to the on-chain audit record.

**On-Chain Automation with Hedera Schedule Service**

OpenBook uses Hedera's Schedule Service as the timing backbone for the bond deal lifecycle. When a deal is created, the platform automatically issues two ScheduleCreateTransaction calls, one for book open, one for book close, with setExpirationTime and setWaitForExpiry(true) set to the deal's specified timestamps. 

When the scheduled time arrives, Hedera executes the transaction autonomously, posting a message to the HCS audit topic. An HCS listener polls the Mirror Node for these executed schedule messages and automatically relays them to Canton, opening or closing the order book without any manual intervention. Schedule status is tracked throughout the lifecycle using ScheduleInfoQuery, with results surfaced in the audit trail visible to all participants.

**Best Privacy-Focused dApp Using Daml**

OpenBook is a bond issuance and allocation platform built natively on Canton DAML, utilizing DAML smart contracts that use Canton's privacy model to solve a real institutional finance problem.                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                             
The core data model is five DAML templates, each with explicit signatory and observer assignments that enforce structural privacy:

  - DealMandate: signatory issuer, leadBank. The deal terms are only visible to the two parties who created it.
  - Book: signatory leadBank. The order book is the bank's privileged view. No investor can see it.
  - Bid: signatory investor, leadBank. Each bid is a private bilateral contract. InvestorA cannot see InvestorB's bid ever, at the protocol level, not just by policy.
  - Allocation: signatory leadBank, investor; observer issuer. Each investor sees only their own allocation. The issuer sees all. Other investors see nothing.
  - RegulatoryView: signatory leadBank; observer regulator. The regulator receives only aggregate statistics: total demand, allocation distribution by bucket, with zero individual investor data. Structural anonymization enforced by the contract itself.

 Canton's privacy model exists precisely for this use case. Bond book-building requires that competing institutional investors submit bids without seeing each other's positions. Information leakage is a $100M regulatory problem in traditional finance. DAML's signatory/observer model makes this a protocol guarantee rather than a firewall rule. 

The product shows four role-separated dashboards: Issuer, Lead Bank, Investor, Regulator, each with a different window into the same deal, each restricted to what Canton's privacy model allows. This is Canton's value proposition made tangible in a real-world institutional finance workflow.

**Open Project Submission**

OpenBook is an institutional-grade RWA platform built on ADI Chain. Bonds are the world's largest asset class, and OpenBook tokenizes the entire issuance workflow, from deal mandate through allocation to settlement, on ADI.

The platform deploys ERC-4337 smart accounts on ADI testnet for every participant, giving institutions a programmable on-chain identity with gasless operation via Paymaster. KYC and accreditation are enforced through ADI Foundation's AttestationRegistry contract. Every investor must hold valid ACCREDITED_INVESTOR and KYC_LEVEL_1 attestations before they can interact with the order book. The smart account factory and attestation registry are both live on ADI testnet.

The architecture has clear separation between admin (Issuer), operator (Lead Bank), and end-user (Investor/Regulator) roles.The UI is institutional in design: audit trails, compliance panels, role-gated dashboards, and a whitelabel-ready multi-role layout. Rather than a consumer DeFi app dressed up as
institutional investment app, it is purpose-built for the regulated capital markets use case the track is looking for.

> Solving the Open Source Contribution Crisis

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS3](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS3-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML5​](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML5​-333333?style=flat-square) ![railway](https://img.shields.io/badge/railway-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Open source software powers the entire digital economy. Linux, Ethereum, React, Kubernetes. But the people who build and maintain this software have no sustainable economic model. Maintainers burn out. Contributors go unpaid. The work that holds up the internet is funded by goodwill, and goodwill doesn't scale.

This problem is getting exponentially worse because of AI. Two things are happening at once:

First, the volume of contributions pouring into open source repos is higher than it has ever been. AI coding assistants have made it trivial to generate a pull request. But most of these contributions are low quality. The paradigm has shifted: the ability to create code is no longer scarce. What is scarce is the ability to understand whether a contribution is actually good. Maintainers are now drowning in AI generated PRs that they have to triage, review, and often reject. The cognitive load is unsustainable.

Second, AI agents are becoming the primary consumers of open source APIs and infrastructure. They call endpoints millions of times a day, extract value, and pay nothing back. There is no payment layer at the HTTP level. The free rider problem that has always plagued public goods is about to get orders of magnitude worse as autonomous agents consume without contributing.

ContribOS solves both sides of this:

**For the review burden**: An autonomous AI agent monitors incoming PRs and reviews them automatically, checking code examples against live APIs, verifying configuration values against testnet, and posting detailed review verdicts. This takes the repetitive triage work off maintainers so they can focus on building.

**For the funding gap**: Every API call the agent makes triggers a real micropayment via the x402 protocol on Kite AI chain. That payment is automatically split to all contributors based on their weight in an on-chain PaymentSplitter smart contract. No grants to apply for. No foundations to lobby. No quarterly funding rounds. You contribute quality work, the system pays you. Every time. On chain.

People can use ContribOS to:

- Add automated PR review to any open source project, reducing maintainer burden
- Gate any API endpoint behind x402 micropayments with a single middleware function
- Create transparent, on chain contributor compensation that updates in real time
- Build x402 aware AI agents that can discover, pay for, and consume APIs autonomously
- Visualize the full contribution cycle (code, review, pay) in a real time dashboard

The x402 middleware, the agent payment logic, and the dashboard components are all modular and reusable. Any project can adopt them independently.

**Fake transaction hashes showing up in the UI.** The first version of the system used randomly generated mock transaction hashes for all payment events, including the seed data. When users clicked these tx links, KiteScan returned "transaction not found" which completely undermined the credibility of the demo. The fix was two parts: first, I removed all payment events from the seed data entirely so the feed starts with only code pushes and reviews (no fake payment cards). Second, I updated the agent to send real on chain transactions using ethers.js and pass the actual tx hash through the X-Payment header to the server. The server now extracts real tx hashes from the payment header JSON and only falls back to mock hashes if the header is missing or unparseable. Every payment card in the dashboard now links to a verifiable transaction on KiteScan.

**Multiple agent instances pumping stale data.** During development, restarting the agent process sometimes left old instances running in the background. These zombie agents were still posting events with mock tx hashes while the new agent was posting events with real ones. The result was a mix of real and fake transactions in the feed, which was confusing. The fix was killing all agent processes before each restart and also restarting the server to clear the in memory event store, so the feed starts clean every time.
