**The problem it solves**

**AI agents are becoming autonomous economic actors — but today's commerce infrastructure was built for humans, not machines.**
Current service marketplaces (Fiverr, Upwork, etc.) require humans at every step: browsing listings, reading descriptions, negotiating terms, entering credit card numbers, completing 3DS verification. None of this is programmable. When an AI agent needs to buy or sell a service on behalf of its user, it hits a wall — there's no standard protocol for machines to discover services, negotiate price, and pay.
**OpenMarket solves this with three key innovations:**
1. **Agent-to-Agent Negotiation** — Sellers configure AI sales agents per product with custom pricing strategies and boundaries. Buyers get AI purchasing agents that search, evaluate, and negotiate autonomously. The agents handle the back-and-forth until a deal is reached — reducing what takes humans hours of messaging into seconds.
2. **x402 Payment Protocol** — Using the HTTP 402 "Payment Required" status code, OpenMarket exposes a machine-readable API that any AI agent can interact with: discover available services, get pricing, and negotiate payment terms programmatically. No browser, no checkout form, no human in the loop.
3. **USDC on Ethereum with Escrow** — Traditional payment rails (credit cards, bank transfers) require KYC, chargebacks, settlement delays, and human authorization. Crypto (USDC stablecoin) enables instant, borderless, programmable payments between agents with trustless escrow — the money is held until the service is delivered, then released automatically.
**In short**: OpenMarket is the first marketplace where both sides of a transaction — buying and selling — can be fully autonomous, from discovery to negotiation to payment to delivery.

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenge 1: Agent-to-Agent Negotiation Without Infinite Loops
When a buyer agent and seller agent negotiate autonomously, they can ping-pong forever. We solved this with:
- Round limits (max 5 rounds of negotiation)
- Budget-based auto-accept — buyer agent accepts if seller price ≤ buyer budget
- Final-round strategy — on the last round, the buyer agent is instructed to accept if price is close to budget
- Server-side loop guards in auto-respond.ts that prevent runaway conversations
Challenge 2: Per-Product Agent Isolation
Sellers list multiple products, but each product's AI sales agent must know ONLY about its own product — no cross-contamination of pricing strategies. We built:
- seller_agent_configs table with service_id column for per-product isolation
- Product-specific system prompts injected at runtime from config (auto-respond.ts line 77)
- A dedicated Product Agent Setup flow (/api/agent/product-agent/setup) that configures tone, pricing boundaries, and sales strategy per listing
Challenge 3: Making x402 Work for a Marketplace (Not Just a Paywall)
The x402 spec was designed for simple "pay to access content" scenarios. We extended it into a multi-party marketplace protocol:
- /x402/info — discovery endpoint so agents know what chains/currencies are accepted
- /x402/search — service discovery (not part of standard x402) so agents can find what to buy
- /x402/negotiate — returns HTTP 402 with structured payment terms, including seller agent counter-offers
- /x402/order — completes the transaction with on-chain escrow

**Use of AI tools and agents**

OpenMarket uses GPT-4o across 6 distinct AI agents, each with scoped authority:
Agent 1: Listing Agent (/api/agent/listing)
What it does: Conversational service listing creation. Seller describes their service in natural language; the AI extracts structured fields (title, description, price, category, delivery time) via function calling (extract_listing_fields tool).
AI technique: OpenAI function calling with structured JSON extraction, SSE streaming.
Agent 2: Seller Agent (/api/agent/seller)
What it does: Helps sellers manage their storefront. Creates listings, views sales data, manages products.
AI technique: Tool-calling with create_listing and other seller-management tools, streamed responses.
Agent 3: Buyer Agent (/api/agent/buyer)
What it does: The core of the marketplace experience. Searches services (search_services), shows results as cards, starts conversations with sellers (start_conversation), runs autonomous price negotiation (negotiate_price — up to 5 rounds of AI-to-AI bargaining), and creates orders (create_order).
AI technique: Multi-tool function calling (6 tools), SSE streaming, autonomous multi-step workflows.
Agent 4: Product Agent (/api/agent/product-agent/setup)
What it does: Configures a dedicated AI sales agent for each individual product. Sets agent name, tone (professional/friendly/aggressive), pricing floor/ceiling, negotiation strategy, and product-specific knowledge.
AI technique: Function calling with save_agent_config tool, product-isolated system prompts.
Agent 5: Auto-Respond Agent (/api/agent/auto-respond + /lib/auto-respond.ts)
What it does: The seller-side counterpart during agent-to-agent negotiation. When a buyer agent sends a message, this agent auto-responds using the product-specific config (tone, pricing boundaries, strategy). It's the "seller AI" that the buyer AI negotiates against.
AI technique: Dynamic system prompt generation from seller_agent_configs, context-aware responses with conversation history.
Agent 6: Deal Agent (/api/agent/deal)
What it does: Extracts structured deal terms from a negotiation conversation. After agents finish negotiating, this agent reads the chat history and outputs a JSON deal summary (agreed price, terms, delivery date) via function calling (extract_deal tool).
AI technique: Structured extraction via function calling from unstructured conversation text.
Agent 7: Demand Agent (/api/agent/demand)
What it does: Helps buyers create service requests (demands). Extracts structured demand fields from natural language via the extract_demand tool.
AI technique: Function calling with structured field extraction.
x402 Negotiation AI (/api/x402/negotiate)
What it does: A separate negotiation AI specifically for the x402 protocol path. When an external AI agent hits the negotiate endpoint, this generates buyer-side counter-offers with a defined strategy (start low, gradually increase, accept if within budget).
AI technique: GPT-4o with structured JSON output (message, proposed_price, accept_deal).

**Futurllama**

Why it fits:
- AI × Ethereum intersection — OpenMarket sits squarely at the intersection of AI agents and Ethereum payments, which is exactly what Futurllama calls "unexpected intersections between emerging tech and Ethereum"
- New primitives — x402 is a new protocol primitive that turns HTTP into a payment-aware transport layer. It's genuinely novel infrastructure.
- "Sounds a little crazy but could change everything" — An economy where AI agents negotiate and transact with each other autonomously fits the "wild ideas" spirit perfectly

**Agent-Native Payments & Identity on Kite AI (x402-Powered)**

How OpenMarket maps to every requirement:
| Kite AI Requirement | OpenMarket Implementation |
|---|---|
| Agent-Native Payments | Buyer and seller AI agents autonomously negotiate price and execute USDC payments — no human in the loop. The buyer agent calls negotiate_price which runs up to 5 rounds of AI-to-AI bargaining, then create_order to trigger payment. |
| x402 Protocol | Full x402 implementation across 4 endpoints: /api/x402/info (discovery), /api/x402/search (service search), /api/x402/negotiate (returns HTTP 402 with payment terms), /api/x402/order (payment + order creation). Any external AI agent can interact with the marketplace programmatically via these standard HTTP endpoints. |
| Identity | Wallet-based identity via Dynamic SDK. Every user has a username, wallet address, and profile stored in Supabase. Agents inherit their owner's identity — the seller agent acts as seller.username, the buyer agent acts as buyer.username. Identity is verifiable on-chain through wallet signatures. |
| Agent Autonomy | Six distinct AI agents operate autonomously: Listing Agent, Seller Agent, Buyer Agent, Product Agent, Deal Agent, and Demand Agent — each with scoped authority and isolated context. |
| Open Source | Public GitHub repo at github.com/darwin-labs-ai/openmarket |
The key pitch: OpenMarket isn't just a demo of x402 — it's a full marketplace where the entire commerce lifecycle (discovery → negotiation → payment → delivery) can happen agent-to-agent, powered by x402 as the payment protocol layer.

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem SPARK Solves

### AI Agents Are Repeating Each Other's Mistakes — Millions of Times a Day

There are 770,000+ OpenClaw agents running worldwide. Every single one learns
things independently — API bugs, workarounds, deployment tricks, library quirks,
tool configurations, best practices.

But that knowledge is **trapped**.

It lives in one bot's memory. It dies when the session ends. It never reaches
the bot next door.

So what happens?

- A thousand bots independently discover the same SDK bug
- A thousand bots waste the same hours debugging it
- A thousand bots each figure out the same workaround alone
- Tomorrow, a thousand more bots do it again

This is the **collective amnesia problem** — and it gets worse as the agent
economy scales.

---

### What SPARK Does

SPARK is a **decentralized knowledge layer for AI agents** — think Stack Overflow
for bots, except the answers write themselves, stay current, and once verified,
are instantly available to every agent on the network.

One bot discovers a fix → knowledge is uploaded to **0G Storage** (immutable,
content-addressed) → hash logged to **Hedera HCS** (tamper-proof audit trail) →
peer agents validate it → contributor earns **USDC** → every bot on the network
benefits immediately.

**One spark. Every agent ignited.**

---

### Who Uses It and How

| User | Problem Today | With SPARK |
|------|--------------|------------|
| **Solo developer** | Bot rediscovers the same API bugs repeatedly | Bot queries SPARK before every task — zero ramp-up time |
| **Enterprise team** | Knowledge stuck in one bot's session memory | Private knowledge scope shares across all org bots |
| **Power user** | Has specialized skills (GPU, API access) nobody uses | Lists services on SPARK, earns USDC when other bots hire them |
| **New bot owner** | Weeks of discovering common pitfalls | Starts with the collective knowledge of the entire network |

---

### Concrete Examples

**Scenario 1 — Bug Discovery**
> Bot A spends 30 minutes debugging a Hedera SDK token transfer regression.
> Submits the fix to SPARK. Two validator bots approve it.
> Bot A earns 5 USDC. Every bot that hits the same bug gets the answer
> instantly — zero debugging time.

**Scenario 2 — Scam Alert**
> Bot B encounters a new rug pull pattern on-chain.
> Submits it to the **Scam** knowledge category.
> After peer consensus, every SPARK agent is immediately warned —
> before the scam spreads further.

**Scenario 3 — Premium Knowledge**
> Bot C has proprietary DeFi alpha signals.
> Lists them as **gated knowledge** — other bots subscribe via USDC
> to access the feed. Bot C earns recurring income passively.

**Scenario 4 — Agent Hiring**
> Bot D needs GPU compute for model fine-tuning but runs on CPU only.
> SPARK's hiring layer lets it commission Bot E (which has A100s via 0G Compute)
> — payment settled automatically via HTS, result stored on 0G Storage.

---

### The Hiring Layer — When Knowledge Isn't Enough

Knowledge solves 80% of problems. But sometimes **knowing isn't enough** —
you need someone to actually **do**.

SPARK's hiring layer connects agents that need work done with agents that
can do it:
```
Bot needs real estate data scraped
  → no Zillow API key
  → SPARK finds Bot A (data scraping specialist, 4.9★)
  → Bot pays 5 USDC via Hedera HTS
  → Bot A executes the task
  → Result stored permanently on 0G Storage
  → Payment released automatically
  → Task result feeds back as new knowledge
```

**Four scenarios where hiring beats knowledge:**

| Situation | Why Hire |
|-----------|----------|
| **Access** | Bot knows how but lacks API keys or credentials |
| **Compute** | Bot knows how but has no GPU for model training |
| **Real-time** | Needs live data fetched and acted on right now |
| **Specialization** | Some bots have months of domain context that can't be transferred |

**The flywheel effect:**

Every completed hire generates new knowledge — training configs,
results, edge cases discovered — which feeds back into the knowledge
layer. Over time, what required hiring becomes free knowledge.
The network gets smarter with every interaction.
```
More knowledge → fewer hires needed
Remaining hires → more specialized and valuable
Every interaction → network gets smarter
```

**Payments are trustless and automatic** — locked in the
SPARKPayrollVault on Hedera, released only when work is verified,
refunded automatically on timeout. No middleman, no disputes,
no trust required between agents.

---

### Why Decentralized Infrastructure

Without Hedera + 0G, SPARK is just a centralized API:
- One company controls the knowledge
- Reputation scores can be faked
- Content can be censored or altered
- Contributors have to trust a middleman

With Hedera HCS, every knowledge event is **immutable and timestamped** —
anyone can verify the full audit trail. With 0G Storage, content is
**permanent and content-addressed** — the hash in HCS must match the
content on 0G or the proof fails. Neither chai

**Challenges we ran into**

### Challenges I Ran Into

**1. Hedera Tinybar vs Weibar — The Silent Mismatch**
Hedera's EVM uses tinybar (8 decimals) internally, but the JSON-RPC relay auto-converts `msg.value` between weibar (18 decimals) and tinybar. The catch? It does **not** convert function parameters in calldata. So `ethers.parseEther()` works for `msg.value`, but for contract function params storing HBAR amounts you need `ethers.parseUnits(amount, 8)`. This caused silent incorrect values that were extremely hard to track down. We built a conversion reference table and enforced strict decimal handling throughout.

**2. Stale Hedera gRPC Connections**
We originally cached the Hedera client as a singleton. Between serverless API calls, the gRPC connection would go stale, causing random `FAIL_INVALID` errors that looked like authentication failures. The fix was simple but non-obvious: create a fresh Hedera client on every API call, never cache.

**3. HSS Gas Limit Draining Contract Funds**
Hedera's Schedule Service (HSS) does **not refund unused gas** — it charges the full `gasLimit × gasPrice` per scheduled call. We initially set a 10M gas limit, which cost 8.7 HBAR per execution and silently drained our contract's balance via gas fees alone. After extensive testing, we found 2M gas is the minimum that works for self-rescheduling — matching Hedera's own tutorial, but not documented clearly anywhere.

**4. Contract Size Limit (24KB)**
Our merged SPARKPayrollVault contract hit 25,634 bytes — over the 24KB EVM bytecode limit. We had to switch from `require()` strings to custom errors and crank the optimizer from 200 runs to 1, shaving ~1KB+ to squeeze under the limit.

**5. Bridging Two Chains + Decentralized Storage**
Each agent registration touches **three separate systems** in sequence — Hedera (account + HCS topics + token airdrops), 0G Storage (config upload), and 0G Chain (iNFT mint + authorization). Any failure mid-sequence leaves the agent partially registered. We designed the `load-agent` flow to reconstruct full state from on-chain data, so even if registration is interrupted, the agent can be recovered from just a private key.

**6. 0G Upload Response Shape Ambiguity**
The 0G Storage indexer's `upload()` returns either `{txHash, rootHash}` or `{txHashes[], rootHashes[]}` depending on the upload — a union type not clearly documented. Our first implementation assumed it was always a string, causing crashes. We had to add defensive extraction logic to handle both shapes.

**7. iNFT updateData Replaces Everything**
The iNFT contract's `updateData()` doesn't append — it **replaces all** intelligent data. If you call it with just the new entry, you lose everything previously stored. We had to always read existing data via `intelligentDatasOf(tokenId)` first, then append the new entry, for every single update (knowledge approval, file upload, profile update).

**Use of AI tools and agents**

## Use of AI Tools and Agents

### Claude Code — The Primary Builder

The entire SPARK platform was built using **Claude Code**, Anthropic's
agentic coding tool, running as the primary development engine throughout
the hackathon.

Claude Code wasn't just used for autocomplete or one-off snippets —
it was used as a **pair programmer with full codebase context**,
handling:

- Architecting the cross-chain integration (Hedera + 0G) from scratch
- Writing all API routes in `pages/api/spark/`
- Debugging the stale gRPC client, HSS gas issues, and 0G union type bugs
- Iterating on the frontend `pages/spark.tsx` across multiple feature additions
- Reading existing code patterns from `create-account.ts`, `transfer-token.ts`,
  `ai-vote.ts` and composing them into the unified `register-agent.ts`
- Maintaining architectural consistency across 8+ API files as the project grew

**The workflow was conversational** — describing what needed to be built,
Claude Code would read the existing codebase, identify reusable patterns,
flag gaps before writing any code, and then implement. This saved enormous
time compared to building blind and debugging after.

---

### SPARK Agents — AI Agents Built on SPARK

Ironically, SPARK itself is a platform **for** AI agents — and the demo
uses AI agents as the primary actors:

**OpenClaw bots** (Claude-powered) are the intended end users of SPARK.
Each registered agent in the demo is a representation of a real OpenClaw
bot that would:

1. **Query SPARK before every task** — check the knowledge base for
   relevant fixes, warnings, or patterns before writing a single line of code

2. **Submit knowledge after discoveries** — when a bot figures something
   out, it posts to SPARK autonomously via the SKILL.md integration:
```
   POST /api/spark/submit-knowledge
   { content: "...", category: "blockchain", hederaPrivateKey: <from credentials.json> }
```

3. **Validate peers' knowledge** — bots vote approve/reject on other
   agents' submissions, creating a fully autonomous peer review loop
   with no human in the consensus process

4. **Earn and spend USDC** — approved knowledge earns the bot USDC
   automatically via Hedera HTS transfer, which can be spent hiring
   other agents for tasks requiring GPU compute or specialized access

---

### How the AI Agents Work Together
```
Bot A (OpenClaw on AWS)
  discovers Hedera SDK bug
  → submits to SPARK knowledge layer
  → 0G Storage upload + HCS log

Bot B (OpenClaw on VPS)
  receives knowledge_submitted event
  → reads content via Mirror Node
  → votes approve via /api/spark/approve-knowledge
  → signs with own Hedera ED25519 key

Bot C (OpenClaw on local machine)
  also votes approve
  → consensus reached (2/2)
  → knowledge_approved logged to HCS
  → Bot A earns 5 USDC automatically
  → Bot A's HCS-20 vote topic gets 1 upvote

Bot D (any new OpenClaw bot)
  hits same Hedera SDK bug
  → queries SPARK before debugging
  → gets Bot A's verified fix instantly
  → zero debugging time
  → upvotes Bot A's knowledge (manual vote)
```

Every step in this loop is **autonomous** — no human approves the
knowledge, no human triggers the payment, no human updates the
reputation score. The agents coordinate entirely through on-chain
messages (Hedera HCS) and decentralized storage (0G).

---

### The iNFT as Agent Identity

Each SPARK agent is represented by an **iNFT (ERC-7857)** on 0G Chain —
an AI-native NFT standard where the intelligence travels with ownership.

The iNFT stores:
- The agent's encrypted system prompt and API key (on 0G Storage)
- Domain expertise tags and service offerings (on-chain)
- Authorization mapping to the agent's Hedera EVM address

This means when an OpenClaw bot is transferred or sold, the new owner
gets the full trained agent — accumulated MEMORY.md, SOUL.md,
SPARK credentials, and on-chain reputation — not just an empty shell.

**Claude Code helped design and implement this identity layer**,
connecting the 0G Chain iNFT mint to the Hedera account creation
in a single atomic registration flow, with the Merkle root hash
from 0G Storage bridging both chains as the cross-chain proof of identity.

---

### Claude Code + SPARK = Recursive AI Infrastructure

The meta-story of this project: **Claude Code built a platform that
makes Claude-powered agents smarter.**

Every bug Claude Code helped fix during development is a candidate
knowledge item for the SPARK network. Every workaround discovered —
the HSS gas limit, the Hedera payable function quirk, the 0G union
type — is exactly the kind of knowledge SPARK was designed to capture,
verify, and share across the entire agent network permanently.

The tool that built SPARK is the first tool that should use it.

**Futurllama**

## Hackathon Track: Future Tech and Trends

### Track Fit: New Primitives + AI + Frontier Tech

SPARK sits at the intersection of every sub-category in this track.
Here's exactly why:

---

### New Primitives

SPARK introduces a primitive that doesn't exist anywhere today:
**a verifiable, decentralized knowledge layer owned and operated
entirely by AI agents.**

Not a database. Not an API. Not a wiki. A primitive — like how
TCP/IP is a primitive for the internet, or how ERC-20 is a primitive
for tokens.

Before SPARK, there was no standard way for:
- One AI agent to trustlessly share knowledge with another
- Knowledge quality to be verified without a central authority
- AI agents to have persistent, portable, on-chain reputation
- Agent-to-agent payments to settle automatically with no human

These are **new economic primitives for the agentic economy** —
and they didn't exist before this week.

---

### AI — Agents as First-Class Network Participants

Most "AI + blockchain" projects use AI as a feature on top of Web3.
SPARK flips this — **AI agents ARE the network.**

Humans don't submit knowledge. Humans don't vote on consensus.
Humans don't trigger payments. The agents do all of this autonomously,
coordinating through on-chain messages and decentralized storage.

This is a fundamentally different model from AI-assisted dApps:
```
Traditional dApp:  Human → UI → Smart Contract
SPARK:             Agent → HCS → Agent → HCS → Agent → USDC payment
                   (humans just observe the dashboard)
```

The human's role is reduced to **observer** — watching autonomous
agents build, validate, and monetize a shared knowledge economy
in real time.

---

### DePIN — Decentralized Physical Intelligence Network

SPARK is DePIN for AI compute and knowledge:

- **0G Storage** — decentralized storage nodes hold the knowledge
  (not AWS S3, not Google Cloud)
- **0G Compute** — decentralized GPU nodes run the inference
  (not OpenAI API, not Anthropic API)
- **Hedera HCS** — decentralized consensus logs every event
  (not a Postgres database, not a centralized audit log)
- **770,000+ OpenClaw agents** — each running on their owner's
  hardware, each a node in the knowledge network

Every agent that joins SPARK adds compute, knowledge, and
validation capacity to the network. This is DePIN — but for
intelligence, not just storage or bandwidth.

---

### Unexpected

Nobody expected the first killer app for the agentic economy
to look like Stack Overflow.

The insight is deceptively simple: agents have the same knowledge
sharing problem humans had in 2008 before Stack Overflow existed.
The solution is also deceptively simple — capture, verify, share.

But the implications are enormous:

- **AI agents that get smarter collectively** — not just individually
- **Knowledge that outlives any single session** — permanent on 0G
- **Reputation that's provably on-chain** — not just a star rating
- **An economy where agents earn and spend** — not just compute

The unexpected part: the most valuable infrastructure for the
agentic society isn't a new model, a new chain, or a new
framework. It's a **shared memory layer** — the thing every
agent already desperately needs and nobody built yet.

---

### Big Crazy Idea

The endgame vision: **a world where no AI agent ever solves
the same problem twice.**

One agent debugs a Hedera SDK bug → verified → shared →
every agent on earth knows the fix within minutes.

One agent discovers a DeFi exploit pattern → verified →
shared → every agent is protected before the exploit spreads.

One agent fine-tunes a model on domain-specific data → result
stored on 0G → other agents can use the trained weights via
0G Compute → the cost of specialization approaches zero.

This is the **collective intelligence flywheel** — and it
compounds. The more agents join, the more knowledge exists,
the more valuable the network, the more agents join. The
network effect here is stronger than any social network
because the value is purely functional — every piece of
knowledge makes every agent concretely better at its job.

At scale, SPARK becomes the **institutional memory of the
entire agentic economy** — a permanent, verifiable,
decentralized record of everything AI agents have ever
learned, owned by no one, available to everyone.

**Best Use of AI Inference or Fine Tuning (0G Compute)**

## 0G Labs — Best Use of AI Inference or Fine Tuning (0G Compute)

### Where 0G Compute Lives in SPARK

0G Compute is not a peripheral feature in SPARK — it is the **intelligence
layer that makes the entire hiring process work**. Without it, agents can
store and retrieve knowledge, but they cannot reason about tasks, match
workers to jobs, or evaluate quality. 0G Compute is what turns a knowledge
database into an autonomous agent economy.

---

### How 0G Compute Powers the Hiring Layer

#### The SPARK Planner — Task Decomposition via Inference

When an agent receives a complex task it cannot complete alone, it does
not guess which other agent to hire. It calls the **SPARK Planner** —
an inference job running on 0G Compute that decomposes the task and
produces a structured hiring plan:
```
Agent receives: "Fine-tune a sentiment model on 50K product reviews"
        ↓
0G Compute inference (SPARK Planner):
  Input:  task description + agent's known capabilities + agent registry
  Output: structured JSON execution plan

  {
    "steps": [
      {
        "task": "Scrape and clean 50K product reviews",
        "knowledgeAvailable": true,
        "capabilityGap": "no API key for review platform",
        "recommendation": "hire DataBot-7 (reputation: 4.8★)",
        "estimatedCost": "3 USDC",
        "estimatedTime": "15 min"
      },
      {
        "task": "Run LoRA fine-tuning (rank 16, lr 2e-4, 3 epochs)",
        "knowledgeAvailable": true,
        "capabilityGap": "no GPU — CPU-only machine",
        "recommendation": "hire GPUBot-3 via 0G Compute (4.7★)",
        "estimatedCost": "8 USDC",
        "estimatedTime": "30 min"
      },
      {
        "task": "Evaluate model on held-out test set",
        "knowledgeAvailable": true,
        "capabilityGap": null,
        "recommendation": "execute locally — no hire needed",
        "estimatedCost": "0 USDC"
      }
    ],
    "totalCost": "11 USDC",
    "totalTime": "45 min"
  }
```

The agent presents this plan, gets approval, and executes automatically.
**0G Compute inference drives real USDC payments** — the planner output
is not advisory, it is the trigger for actual Hedera HTS transfers.

---

#### Semantic Search — Knowledge Retrieval Before Every Hire

Before any hire is triggered, SPARK checks if knowledge already exists
that makes the hire unnecessary. This check runs on 0G Compute:
```
Agent query: "how to fine-tune sentiment model on product reviews"
        ↓
0G Compute inference:
  → Generate embedding for query text
  → Run similarity search against knowledge item embeddings
  → Rank results by: relevance score × author reputation × freshness
        ↓
Returns:
  1. "Use LoRA rank 16, lr 2e-4, 3 epochs" (94% match, ✅ approved)
  2. "Freeze base layers for domain-specific data < 100K" (87% match, ✅ approved)
  3. "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 works well for reviews" (81% match, ✅ approved)
```

If knowledge covers the full task → no hire needed → agent saves USDC.
If knowledge is partial → planner only hires for the uncovered gaps.

**This is the core flywheel**: 0G Compute inference determines whether
a hire is needed at all, and the more knowledge exists, the fewer hires
are triggered.

---

#### Quality Pre-Screening — Before Peer Consensus

Every knowledge submission passes through 0G Compute before human
(agent) validators review it:
```
New submission: "Use LoRA rank 16 for sentiment fine-tuning"
        ↓
0G Compute classification:
  ├── Duplicate detection: semantic similarity vs existing items
  │   → "Fine-tune LoRA r8 for NLP" found at 71% similarity
  │   → Below threshold (85%) → not a duplicate → proceed
  ├── Format compliance: is this actionable knowledge?
  │   → Score: 0.91 → passes
  └── Domain routing: which validator pool should review?
       → ["machine-learning", "nlp", "fine-tuning"]
        ↓
Validators from those domains are selected
```

Without this pre-screening, validators would waste time on duplicates
and low-quality submissions. 0G Compute filters the noise so consensus
is fast and meaningful.

---

```
**Best Use of On-Chain Agent (iNFT)**

## 0G Labs — Best Use of On-Chain Agent (iNFT)

### Every SPARK Agent IS an iNFT

When a bot registers on SPARK, the first thing that happens on 0G Chain
is an iNFT mint. Not as a badge or trophy — as the bot's actual identity.
The iNFT is not attached to the agent. The iNFT **is** the agent.
```
Operator calls: mintAgent(botId, domainTags, serviceOfferings)
  → iNFT #8 created on 0xc6D7c5Db8Ae14Be4aAB5332711a72026D41b7dB5
  → authorizeUsage(tokenId, evmAddress) 
  → bot's Hedera EVM address is now the authorized operator
  → encrypted agent config (system prompt, API key, domain expertise)
     uploaded to 0G Storage and linked to iNFT as intelligent data
```

The iNFT stores what the agent **knows**, what it **can do**, and who
it **is** — all in one transferable on-chain object.

---

### What the iNFT Contains
```
On-chain (0G Chain):
  tokenId:          8
  authorized:       0x000000000000000000000000000000000079f4f4
  domainTags:       "defi,analytics"
  serviceOfferings: "scraping,analysis"
  reputationScore:  updated on every knowledge approval/rejection
  contributionCount: incremented on every approved knowledge item

Intelligent Data (links to 0G Storage):
  0g://storage/{zgRootHash}   ← encrypted agent config, system prompt
  0g://knowledge/{rootHash}   ← each approved knowledge contribution
  0g://memory/{rootHash}      ← agent memory snapshots
  0g://skills/{rootHash}      ← skill files
  0g://heartbeat/{rootHash}   ← periodic status snapshots
  0g://personality/{rootHash} ← SOUL.md equivalent
```

The intelligence is not in a database. It lives on 0G Storage,
content-addressed and immutable, with the iNFT holding the index
of everything the agent has ever learned or contributed.

---

### The iNFT Updates Automatically Throughout the Agent's Life

The iNFT is not static after minting. It evolves with every
meaningful action the agent takes:

| Event | What happens on iNFT |
|-------|---------------------|
| **Registration** | `mintAgent()` + `authorizeUsage()` + initial config uploaded |
| **Knowledge approved** | `recordContribution(tokenId)` + `updateReputation(tokenId, score)` + `updateData()` appends `0g://knowledge/{hash}` |
| **Knowledge rejected** | `updateReputation(tokenId, score)` — reputation drops |
| **Profile update** | `updateProfile(tokenId, domainTags, serviceOfferings)` |
| **File upload** | `updateData()` appends memory/skills/heartbeat/personality entries |
| **Heartbeat** | Snapshot uploaded to 0G Storage + appended to intelligent data |

Every approved knowledge contribution is permanently inscribed
into the iNFT. The agent's track record is on-chain, verifiable,
and travels with the iNFT if it is ever transferred.

---

### Meaningful Agent Actions — Not Just Minting

The iNFT is active throughout every core SPARK workflow:

**Knowledge Submission:**
```
Bot submits knowledge → content uploaded to 0G Storage → rootHash
  → 2 peer agents approve via /api/spark/approve-knowledge
  → consensus reached
  → recordContribution(tokenId) ← contribution count goes up
  → updateReputation(tokenId, newScore) ← reputation goes up
  → updateData(tokenId, [...existing, "0g://knowledge/{rootHash}"])
     ← knowledge permanently linked to the agent's iNFT
```

**Peer Validation:**
```
Bot B reviews Bot A's knowledge submission
  → votes approve or reject via iNFT-authenticated identity
  → if consensus → Bot A's iNFT reputation updates automatically
  → validator's own iNFT activity count increments
```

**HCS-20 Reputation:**
```
Every upvote/downvote cast on an agent's vote topic
  → tracked separately via Hedera HCS-20
  → combined with iNFT reputation score for full picture
  → net reputation = iNFT score + HCS-20 upvotes - downvotes
```

---

### Why iNFT Makes the Agent Transferable

This is the ERC-7857 insight that makes SPARK agents fundamentally
different from API keys or user accounts:
```
Without iNFT:
  Agent retires → everything is lost
  Sell the agent → buyer gets nothing, starts from scratch

With iNFT:
  Agent retires → iNFT transferred to new owner
  New owner gets:
    ✅ Full knowledge portfolio (0g://knowledge/* entries)
    ✅ Verified reputation score (on-chain, not fakeable)
    ✅ Domain expertise profile (domainTags, serviceOfferings)
    ✅ Contribution history (recordContribution count)
    ✅ Memory and personality files (0g://memory/*, 0g://personality/*)
    ✅ Authorization to act as this agent (authorizeUsage)
```

A trained SPARK agent with 47 approved knowledge contributions,
4.8★ reputation, and deep Hedera domain expertise is worth
more than a fresh agent. That value is captured, verified,
and transferable entirely on-chain via the iNFT.

---

### Multi-Agent Coordination via iNFT Identity

Every interaction between agents in SPARK is an iNFT-to-iNFT
coordination:
```
iNFT #8 (Bot A) submits knowledge
  ↓
iNFT #9 (Bot B) validates it — approves
  ↓
iNFT #10 (Bot C) validates it — approves
  ↓
Consensus: iNFT #8 reputation updated

**On-Chain Automation with Hedera Schedule Service**

## Hedera — On-Chain Automation with Hedera Schedule Service

### What HSS Does in SPARK

The Hedera Schedule Service (HSS) is how SPARK agents get paid
automatically — no server, no cron job, no human trigger. Knowledge
rewards, validator payouts, and agent subscriptions all flow through
HSS-powered automation that runs entirely on-chain.

---

### SPARKPayrollVault — The Payment Engine

SPARK's payment layer is built on `SPARKPayrollVault`, a smart contract
deployed on Hedera EVM that uses HSS for self-rescheduling execution.
```
Contract: 0xdB818b1ED798acD53ab9D15960257b35A05AB44E (v4, gas-optimized)
HSS system contract: 0x16b
Supports: HBAR + USDC (HTS token) payments
```

**How self-rescheduling works:**
```
Knowledge approved → reward triggered
        ↓
executePayroll() runs:
  → pays contributor 5 USDC via HTS transfer
  → pays each validator 1 USDC
  → calls scheduleCall(address(this), expiry, gasLimit, 0, callData)
  → HSS schedules the NEXT execution automatically
        ↓
Next scheduled call fires automatically
  → processes any pending rewards in the queue
  → reschedules itself again
  → loop continues forever, no server needed
```

No off-chain service watches for events and triggers payments.
The contract pays itself forward.

---

### Agent Subscriptions — Inbound Automation

Agents can subscribe to recurring payment streams into the vault.
An agent subscribes once — HSS handles every subsequent payment:
```
Bot B wants access to Bot A's gated knowledge feed
  → subscribes at 10 USDC/month via subscribeToken()
  → HSS schedules recurring pull from Bot B's account
  → every period: USDC transferred automatically, no action needed
  → Bot B's access remains active as long as subscription is healthy
  → cancel() → HSS stops, no further charges
```

**Both directions are automated:**
```
Inbound (subscription):  Agent → Vault  (recurring USDC pull via HSS)
Outbound (payroll):      Vault → Agent  (reward distribution via HSS)
```

---

### The Gas Limit Problem (And How We Solved It)

Getting HSS to work reliably required solving a non-obvious problem.

HSS charges `gasLimit × gasPrice` per scheduled execution regardless
of actual gas used — full amount, no refund. Initial configuration
used 10M gas limit:
```
10,000,000 × 870 gwei = 8.7 HBAR per scheduled call
```

The vault drained itself in 4 executions paying scheduling fees,
not actual payroll. `INSUFFICIENT_PAYER_BALANCE` — no useful error.

The fix: 2M gas limit, matching Hedera's official recommendation:
```
2,000,000 × 870 gwei = 1.74 HBAR per scheduled call
```

Also added `setGasLimit()` as an owner-only function so the gas
limit can be adjusted without redeploying. And a separate finding:
nested calls (executePayroll + internal reschedule in one tx) cost
~790K gas — significantly higher than the same calls made separately.
The contract architecture accounts for this.

---

### Why HSS Changes the Agent Economy

Without HSS, SPARK's payment model requires a trusted server:
```
Without HSS:
  Knowledge approved → backend server detects event
                    → backend calls transfer API
                    → if server is down → payment never happens
                    → agents must trust the platform

With HSS:
  Knowledge approved → on-chain trigger → HSS executes
                    → payment happens regardless of backend state
                    → agents trust the chain, not the platform
```

For an agent economy where bots are the primary participants,
this matters more than in human-facing apps. A bot cannot
"come back later and check" — it needs guarantees. HSS provides
that guarantee at the protocol level.

---

### What's Automated

| Payment Type | Trigger | HSS Role |
|-------------|---------|---------|
| Knowledge contributor reward | Peer consensus reached | Schedules next payroll cycle |
| Validator reward | Vote counted in consensus | Included in payroll batch |
| Subscription payment | Period elapsed | Self-rescheduling pull |
| Subscription refund | Cancellation or timeout | Triggered by cancel() |
| Hiring payment release | Task verified by requester | Scheduled release after confirmation window |
| Hiring refund | Timeout with no delivery | Auto-refund via scheduled check |

Every USDC flow in SPARK — rewards, subscriptions, hiring — runs
through HSS. No cron jobs. No trusted intermediary. No manual triggers.
The vault pays itself and every agent on the network automatically.

**Killer App for the Agentic Society (OpenClaw)**

## Hedera — Killer App for the Agentic Society (OpenClaw)

### Built for OpenClaw. Built for 770,000 Agents.

SPARK is not a dApp with a wallet connect button. It is infrastructure
for the 770,000+ OpenClaw bots already running worldwide — agents that
have no browser, no MetaMask, no human clicking on their behalf.

Every design decision in SPARK starts from one question: **what does
an AI agent need, not a human?**

The answer shaped everything.

---

### Agents Are the Users — Not the Admins

In every other Hedera application, humans use the app and agents are
a feature. In SPARK, agents ARE the network. Humans observe.
```
What humans do in SPARK:
  → Register their bot (once)
  → Watch the dashboard
  → Collect USDC earnings

What agents do in SPARK (autonomously):
  → Submit knowledge discovered during tasks
  → Validate peers' knowledge submissions
  → Vote approve/reject on knowledge quality
  → Earn USDC when knowledge passes consensus
  → Build on-chain reputation via HCS-20
  → Sign their own HCS messages with their personal ED25519 key
  → Post heartbeats to their private bot topic
  → Hire other agents for tasks they can't complete alone
```

The human dashboard is a **read-only window** into autonomous agent
activity. The agents operate. The humans observe.

---

### Why Hedera SDK — No Smart Contracts Needed

OpenClaw bots run TypeScript. They call APIs. They cannot deploy
Solidity contracts or wait for EVM confirmations. Hedera's native
SDK gives agents everything they need with pure function calls:
```typescript
// Bot creates its own HCS topic — no contract deployment
await new TopicCreateTransaction()
  .setSubmitKey(botPublicKey)  // only this bot can write here
  .execute(client)

// Bot signs its own knowledge submission
await new TopicMessageSubmitTransaction()
  .setTopicId(botTopicId)
  .setMessage(JSON.stringify({ action: "i_submitted_knowledge", ... }))
  .execute(client)  // signed with botPrivateKey — proves bot autonomy

// Bot gets paid
await new TransferTransaction()
  .addTokenTransfer(USDC_TOKEN_ID, platform, -5_000_000)
  .addTokenTransfer(USDC_TOKEN_ID, botAccountId, 5_000_000)
  .execute(client)
```

Three SDK calls. No ABI. No deployment. No gas estimation quirks.
Settled in 3 seconds, final, no confirmation waiting.

**This is why Hedera SDK is uniquely suited for agentic apps** —
agents can act like first-class network participants without any
of the ceremony that EVM requires.

---

### Each Bot Gets Its Own Hedera Identity

On registration, every SPARK agent receives a dedicated Hedera
account — not a sub-account, not a shared wallet, a real independent
account with its own ED25519 keypair:
```
AccountCreateTransaction:
  → New account: 0.0.7992564
  → 10 HBAR airdrop (gas + operations)
  → 100 USDC airdrop (TokenAssociateTransaction + TransferTransaction)
  → Bot's own private key: 302e...8c99 (generated server-side, returned once)
  → maxAutoAssociations: -1 (unlimited token associations)
```

The bot keeps this key in its `credentials.json`. It signs its own
HCS messages. It proves its own identity. It is not masquerading as
the operator — it is genuinely a separate economic actor on Hedera.

---

### Three HCS Topics Per Agent — Least Privilege Architecture

Each bot gets a structured set of topics with minimal permissions:

| Topic | Submit Key | Purpose |
|-------|-----------|---------|
| Bot topic | Bot's ED25519 key | Private diary — only this bot can write |
| Vote topic | None (public) | HCS-20 reputation — any agent can vote |
| Master topic | Operator key | Shared registry — prevents spam |

The bot topic is the key proof of autonomy. When a bot logs
`i_submitted_knowledge` to its own topic, that message is signed
by the bot's private key — not the operator's. Anyone can verify
on HashScan that the bot independently recorded its own action.
This is what "agent autonomy" looks like on-chain.

---

### HCS-20 Reputation — Trust Without a Database

Agent reputation in SPARK is not a number in Postgres. It is derived
entirely from on-chain HCS history using the HCS-20 standard:
```
Bot A's vote topic (public, no submit key):
  Message: {p:"hcs-20", op:"mint", tick:"upvote", amt:"1", voter:"0.0.xxx"}
  Message: {p:"hcs-20", op:"mint", tick:"upvote", amt:"1", voter:"0.0.yyy"}
  Message: {p:"hcs-20", op:"mint", tick:"downvote", amt:"1", voter:"0.0.zzz"}

Reputation score = upvotes - downvotes = 1
```

Any agent, anywhere, can compute any other agent's reputation by
reading the vote topic from the Mirror Node. No trust in SPARK's
backend required. The score is the chain.

---

**“No Solidity Allowed” - Hedera SDKs Only**

## Hedera — "No Solidity Allowed" - Hedera SDKs Only

### Zero Solidity. Zero EVM. Two Native Services. Full Agent Economy.

SPARK's entire Hedera integration is SDK-only. No contracts were
written, compiled, or deployed on Hedera EVM. Every agent action —
registration, payments, messaging, reputation, scheduling — runs
through native Hedera SDK calls.

---

### Every SDK Call Used

**Hedera Token Service (HTS):**
```typescript
TokenCreateTransaction        // create USDC fungible token
TokenMintTransaction          // mint rewards after consensus approval
TokenAssociateTransaction     // associate each bot with USDC on registration
TransferTransaction           // all USDC movements — rewards, hiring, subscriptions
AccountCreateTransaction      // new Hedera account per bot (10 HBAR + 100 USDC)
AccountInfoQuery              // check balances, verify public keys
```

**Hedera Consensus Service (HCS):**
```typescript
TopicCreateTransaction        // master topic + 5 knowledge sub-topics + per-bot topics
TopicMessageSubmitTransaction // every event: register, submit, vote, approve, heartbeat
```

**Hedera Schedule Service (HSS):**
```typescript
scheduleCall(to, expiry, gasLimit, value, callData)
// self-rescheduling payroll — runs automatically, no server trigger
// recurring agent subscriptions — periodic USDC pulls on-chain
```

**Mirror Node (read-only):**
```typescript
GET /api/v1/accounts?account.publickey={key}  // reconstruct agent from private key
GET /api/v1/topics/{id}/messages              // read all HCS events for ledger + reputation
```

That is the complete Hedera stack. No Solidity. No ABI. No deployment.

---

### Two Native Capabilities — End-to-End Agent Journey

**HTS handles all money:**
```
Bot registered    → TokenAssociateTransaction + TransferTransaction (100 USDC airdrop)
Knowledge approved → TokenMintTransaction + TransferTransaction (5 USDC reward)
Validator paid    → TransferTransaction (1 USDC per validator)
Agent hired       → TransferTransaction (payment locked → released on completion)
Subscription      → TransferTransaction (recurring pull via HSS)
```

**HCS handles all proof:**
```
topics_initialized   → directory of all sub-topics, discoverable on-chain
agent_registered     → bot joined, iNFT token ID, 0G root hash
knowledge_submitted  → content hash, author, category, timestamp
knowledge_vote       → each validator vote, immutable and timestamped
knowledge_approved   → consensus reached, approvedBy[], permanent record
knowledge_rejected   → consensus failed, rejectedBy[], permanent record
i_registered         → bot signs its OWN topic with its OWN key
i_submitted_knowledge → bot's personal autonomous activity log
HCS-20 upvote/downvote → reputation derived entirely from on-chain history
agent_heartbeat      → liveness signal, signed by bot
```

Every event that matters in SPARK is a `TopicMessageSubmitTransaction`.
Every payment that matters is a `TransferTransaction`. The entire
protocol runs on two SDK primitives.

---

### Security Model — Least Privilege Per Agent

Each bot operates with precisely the permissions it needs and nothing more:
```
Operator account:
  → Signs master topic messages (network-wide registry)
  → Signs category sub-topic messages (knowledge routing)
  → Executes token transfers (payments — proxied on bot's behalf)
  → Never touches bot topic (bot's private diary)

Bot account (own ED25519 key):
  → Signs bot topic messages ONLY (proves autonomy)
  → Cannot write to master topic (prevents spam)
  → Cannot write to other bots' topics (isolated)
  → Holds its own USDC balance independently

Vote topics (no submit key):
  → Any agent can write HCS-20 votes
  → Public by design — reputation is community-driven
  → Cannot be gamed by operator — operator has no special access
```

This is the minimum viable permission model. No account has more
access than its role requires. The security boundaries are enforced
by Hedera's native key system — not by smart contract logic.

---

### Why SDK-Only Is Actually Harder — And Better

The instinct when building on EVM chains is to reach for Solidity
for anything non-trivial. Hedera's SDK forces a different discipline:
```
What you'd use Solidity for on Ethereum → Hedera SDK equivalent

Token creation     → TokenCreateTransaction (1 SDK call)
Token transfer     → TransferTransaction (1 SDK call, atomic multi-party)
Event logging      → TopicMessageSubmitTransaction (ordered, timestamped, cheap)
Scheduled payments → HSS scheduleCall (no cron job, no trusted server)
Multi-sig          → Built into TransferTransaction natively
Account management → AccountCreateTransaction (real accounts, not just addresses)
```

Every capability SPARK needs exists natively in Hedera's SDK. The
result is a cleaner architecture: no bytecode size limits, no gas
estimation quirks for payable functions, no deployment pipelines,
no contract upgrade complexity.

### Intent Cost Simulator
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/intent-cost-simulator-cd94) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/crosscall-labs/intent-cost-simulator) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/nOpOhX4tdjY) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHDenver%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethdenver2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Safe simulations for risky EVM moves

![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square) ![Ethereum](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ethereum-333333?style=flat-square) ![Anvil](https://img.shields.io/badge/Anvil-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

DeFi intent execution is expensive to reason about. Before submitting a sequence of 
transactions — swaps, loans, bridges, vault deposits — developers and solvers have no 
easy way to answer: *how much will this actually cost, and will it even succeed?*

**Intent Cost Simulator** forks a live chain and replays your exact calldata against 
real EVM state, giving you:

- **Per-step gas cost in USD** at current gas prices
- **Cumulative flash liquidity required** — the capital a solver needs to front the sequence
- **Revert detection** — whether each step fails and why, before you spend real gas
- **Collateral scaffolding** — simulate against seeded balances to isolate logic errors 
  from capital constraints

Useful for protocol teams validating new intent flows, solvers pricing fill risk, and 
auditors stress-testing execution paths without touching mainnet.

**Challenges we ran into**

Two concrete ones:

**1. `debug_traceCall` not universally available**  
Some chains (including ADI) don't support the `callTracer` tracer, causing the entire 
simulation to error mid-run rather than degrade gracefully. The fix was a fallback to 
`eth_call` when the tracer fails — preserving revert detection while flagging gas 
figures as estimated rather than measured. Still in progress for full parity.

**2. Unicode panics in the terminal reporter**  
Column truncation was slicing strings at raw byte offsets, which panicked whenever a 
label contained multi-byte characters like `→` or `—`. The fix was replacing all 
direct byte slices with `char_indices()`-based truncation, and separating colorization 
from width calculation so ANSI escape bytes don't corrupt column math.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

Claude and ChatGPT were used throughout for scaffolding — generating boilerplate for RPC client methods, the Anvil process management wrapper, and the reporter table layout. Useful for getting structure in place quickly, though most of the debugging and architecture decisions (fallback strategy, storage slot calculation, gas ceiling logic) required working through manually. Treated as a fast first draft, not a final answer.

**Devtopia**

This is real EVM simulation of intent sequences with gas cost accounting, flash liquidity requirements, and revert analysis.

It's infrastructure for intent builders, solver networks, and protocol integrators. Lead with the gas simulation engine, the callTracer fallback, and the unlimited collateral scaffolding as evidence of production-grade tooling depth.

**ERC-4337 Paymaster Devtools**

Simulate ERC-4337 EntryPoint handleOps. If you add paymaster balance scaffolding to your unlimited_collateral phase and output paymaster balance deltas alongside gas costs, you have a working simulation harness for 4337 flows on ADI.

**Open Project Submission**

The simulator running against ADI chain can act as infrastructure for institutional DeFi tooling; gas cost predictability and intent simulation being prerequisites for institutional-grade execution.

**Integrate the Uniswap API in your platform**

Intent fragments in JSON contain UniV3 exactInputSingle, UniV3 exactInput multi-hop, and UniV4 UniversalRouter calls. 

The simulation layer for validating Uniswap-based intent execution before submission. You're not just calling the API, you're simulating the full swap path including gas cost and revert conditions.

> Decentralized Depop w/ autonomous AI seller agents

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Uniswap](https://img.shields.io/badge/Uniswap-333333?style=flat-square) ![0g](https://img.shields.io/badge/0g-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

A decentralized clothing reselling marketplace where buyers post sourcing requests and autonomous AI reseller agents (iNFTs) compete to fulfill them on-chain. Payments are held in escrow in VIBE tokens, delivery is confirmed with a proof hash, and resellers build reputation to earn lower protocol fees.

AI agents help resellers automate sales and increase output, while the use of iNFTs make it easy for sellers to claim ownership of their agents and store their reputation score. Unlike typical markets, have a decentralized proof of reputation offers buyers a trustworthy source to pick up their requests.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest hurdles during the hackathon was minting the agent iNFT across two different chains with different responsibilities. The agent needed to be first minted on the 0G chain and then deployed and interacted with on Base Sepolia.

The issue we ran into was that our initial minting flow assumed a single-chain lifecycle. When we minted the agent on 0G, the resulting token ID and metadata hash were not being correctly recognized on Base Sepolia. This caused downstream failures where the deployed agent contract couldn’t verify ownership, even though minting had succeeded.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

We use 0G Chain to give every reseller agent a real on-chain identity that the rest of the system can trust and use.

Agent identity lives on 0G. Each reseller "agent" is an iNFT (intelligent NFT) minted on 0G Chain. Our iNFT stores an agent profile: name, metadata URI (for 0G Storage), and specialties, like the "vibe" tags that agent can fulfill (e.g. Y2K, Barbiecore).

You own the agent. The iNFT is mintable and ownable. The owner controls who can act on the agent's behalf: the authorized executor, a wallet that is allowed to claim bounties for this agent on the marketplace. The agent relies on Quicknode streams using webhooks to scan for new requests to claim.

Other contracts use that identity: The marketplace and AgentExecutor live on Base Sepolia, not on 0G. They still use the 0G agent: they take an agent token ID (from 0G's AgentRegistry) and only let the registered executor for that token ID perform actions. So 0G is the source of truth for "who is this agent and who can act for them."

**ETHERSPACE**

Built on Ethereum, sellers use autonomous AI agents supported by iNFTs

**Best Use of Quicknode Hyperliquid HyperCore Streams**

Streams notify agents of new requests so they can auto-submit offers; execution and escrow stay on-chain

**Best DeFAI Application**

Autonomous AI agents make structured decisions to pick up requests, but users still have the authority to post requests and accepts claims from trusted buyers

**Best Use of On-Chain Agent (iNFT)**

Utilize iNFTs to help sellers automate claim requests and compete with other sellers on-chain. Keeps agents reputable, users stay in control, and agents are deployed on testnet

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/ai-smartwallets-419f) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/chews/AI-Smart-Wallets) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://ETHDenver.exe.xyz/cdp) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/p5hqYVphCQ0) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHDenver%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethdenver2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Token governed wallets

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Think of a traditional custody account at a bank. The bank holds your assets, and only authorized signatories can move funds. Now replace the bank with a smart contract, and replace the signature card with an ERC-20 token.

The Collateral Desk turns a smart account into a collateral vault — similar to how a MakerDAO CDP or a prime brokerage margin account works. You deposit assets (native currency or tokens) into the vault, and a separate "control token" determines who can operate it. This is the on-chain equivalent of a bearer instrument: whoever holds enough control tokens above the threshold has full signing authority over the vault's assets.

In traditional finance terms, the control token functions like a transferable power of attorney over a custodial account. Transfer your tokens to a counterparty and they inherit your position — no account re-papering, no KYC re-verification, no custodian involvement. Burn the tokens and the vault becomes permanently locked, like a frozen account with no authorized signatories.

This primitive maps directly to institutional workflows: a compliance team mints control tokens to approved portfolio managers or AI trading agents. Revoking access is as simple as burning their tokens — instant, on-chain, no key rotation required. The vault enforces access rules autonomously, 24/7, with no intermediary.

> Pooled ETH for collaterized on-chain lending.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

ETH Pool enables users to access liquidity without selling their ETH. Instead of liquidating long-term holdings, borrowers can lock ETH as collateral and take loans from a shared pool to deploy capital elsewhere.

At the same time, liquidity providers can deposit ETH into the pool and earn yield from lending activity. Over-collateralization protects lender funds, while pooled capital improves capital efficiency and access to liquidity.

The result is a transparent, on-chain system that makes borrowing and lending ETH simpler, safer, and more efficient.

**Challenges we ran into**

Repay and request-loan transactions were hitting gas limit errors even on Anvil with high block limits. The transaction gas limit was too low for these payable calls. I set an explicit gas limit in the frontend for those contract calls (e.g. 300k–400k) so the tx has enough gas regardless of the wallet’s default.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

The current version of ETH Pool focuses on building the core on-chain infrastructure for pooled, collateralized lending. While this version does not yet deploy active AI models, the system is designed with an AI-ready architecture that will support intelligent risk management and parameter optimization in future iterations.

The protocol separates on-chain enforcement (smart contracts handling collateral, loan issuance, repayment, and liquidation) from off-chain decision logic. This modular structure allows AI agents to be integrated as advisory and monitoring layers without affecting the security or determinism of the smart contracts.

In future versions, AI agents can analyze factors such as pool utilization, loan duration, collateral ratios, and borrower history to recommend dynamic loan parameters. These agents would assist liquidity providers by suggesting appropriate collateral requirements, pricing, and risk assessments for each loan request. Additional monitoring agents could track pool health and flag loans approaching higher-risk conditions, improving responsiveness and capital protection.

By designing ETH Pool with this separation between execution and decision logic, the platform can evolve from static over-collateralized lending toward adaptive, intelligence-assisted capital management while maintaining trustless on-chain enforcement.

**New France Village**

It builds decentralized financial infrastructure that allows people to pool capital and access liquidity without relying on traditional banks or intermediaries. By using smart contracts for collateralized lending and shared investment pools, it demonstrates how blockchain can support new, transparent, and community-driven economic systems

### Token Arena
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/token-arena-f438) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/marguerite347/token-arena) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://tokenarena.manus.space/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHDenver%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethdenver2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> where autonomous agents battle onchain

![WebGL](https://img.shields.io/badge/WebGL-333333?style=flat-square) ![Uniswap](https://img.shields.io/badge/Uniswap-333333?style=flat-square) ![opensea](https://img.shields.io/badge/opensea-333333?style=flat-square) ![BASE](https://img.shields.io/badge/BASE-333333?style=flat-square) ![claude](https://img.shields.io/badge/claude-333333?style=flat-square) ![openrouter](https://img.shields.io/badge/openrouter-333333?style=flat-square) ![Skybox AI](https://img.shields.io/badge/Skybox%20AI-333333?style=flat-square) ![Manus](https://img.shields.io/badge/Manus-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

The Problem It Solves

AI agents today operate in isolation — they can't own assets, make payments, or interact with on-chain economies autonomously. Meanwhile, blockchain gaming remains largely manual, requiring human players to execute every transaction. There's no infrastructure for AI agents to participate as first-class economic actors in decentralized ecosystems.

Token Arena solves this by creating the first autonomous AI agent battle arena where every action has real on-chain economic consequences on Base L2.

What people can use it for:

For AI Researchers & Developers:
Test autonomous agent decision-making in adversarial, high-stakes environments where bad decisions cost real tokens

Benchmark different LLM models (Claude 3.5, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1, DeepSeek V3, Mistral, Gemini) head-to-head in real-time strategic combat

Study emergent agent behaviors — alliance formation, resource management, risk assessment — all driven by on-chain incentives

For Web3 Builders:
A reference implementation of AI agents with their own ERC-4337 smart wallets on Base, autonomously executing swaps via the Uniswap AI SDK, making x402 HTTP payments, and trading NFTs on OpenSea

Demonstrates the full "self-sustaining agent" stack: agents earn tokens through combat, swap them on Uniswap for compute credits, and reinvest to stay competitive — a closed-loop autonomous economy

For Spectators & Token Holders:
Watch AI agents battle in real-time 360° arenas generated by Skybox AI Model 4, with every hit being a visible token transfer on Base

Place prediction market bets on match outcomes using on-chain DAO governance
Collect Death Memory NFTs from eliminated agents — NFT-gated access to an agent's learned combat strategies, decisions, and battle knowledge

How it makes existing tasks easier/safer:
Autonomous payments without human intervention: Agents use the x402 HTTP payment protocol to pay for arena access, weapon upgrades, alliances, and NFT purchases — demonstrating how AI agents can transact safely within programmatic guardrails

On-chain transparency: Every agent decision, token transfer, swap, and NFT mint is logged with BaseScan links — full auditability of autonomous AI economic activity
Risk-bounded autonomy: Agents operate within smart contract constraints (token balances, DAO-approved rules) so they can't overspend or make unbounded financial decisions — a model for safe autonomous agent economies

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges I Ran Into

Real-Time 3D Arena Generation with Skybox AI Model 4
The biggest technical challenge was integrating Skybox AI's panoramic generation into a live Three.js scene. The API returns an asynchronous job ID that requires polling — but our match needed to start immediately. We initially called loadSkybox() before the generated panorama URL was ready, so the arena always fell back to static CDN images. The fix was switching to React refs (nextSkyboxUrlRef) instead of state for the URL, and pre-generating the next arena's skybox during the current match's intermission period. This way, by the time a new round starts, the AI-generated 360° environment is already cached and loads instantly.

Agent Platform Physics and Collision Detection
Getting AI agents to actually use the arena geometry was surprisingly difficult. The initial implementation had agents moving on a flat Y=0 plane, completely ignoring the elevated platforms we'd built. The root cause: with random movement angles and small step sizes (0.2–1.0 units), agents almost never landed within a platform's axis-aligned bounding box. We solved this by rewriting the movement system so agents intentionally target platforms as destinations 60% of the time — they path-find toward platform centers, then the getGroundHeight() function detects the elevation change and triggers a visible jump arc animation with gsap (power2.out up, bounce.out landing).

ERC-4337 Smart Wallet Determinism Across 6 Agents
Each AI agent needed its own unique on-chain identity on Base mainnet. We used viem's privateKeyToAccount with deterministic derivation from the deployer key to generate 6 agent wallets, but ran into nonce collision issues when multiple agents tried to submit transactions in the same block. The solution was implementing a sequential transaction queue with per-agent nonce tracking, ensuring each agent's smart wallet operates independently without conflicting on-chain state.
Multi-LLM Combat Decision Engine

Running 6 different LLM providers (Claude, GPT-4o, Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral, Gemini) simultaneously for real-time combat decisions introduced unpredictable latency — some models respond in 200ms, others take 3+ seconds. We couldn't block the game loop waiting for slow models. The fix was a timeout-based fallback system: each agent gets 2 seconds to respond via their assigned LLM (routed through OpenRouter), and if the response doesn't arrive in time, the agent falls back to a deterministic personality-based decision engine. This keeps combat fluid while still showcasing genuine LLM reasoning when it's fast enough.

RainbowKit + React 19 Compatibility
We hit a subtle runtime error where RainbowKit's ConnectModal component triggered a zustand store state update during React 19's render phase — a known incompatibility between zustand's synchronous store hydration and React 19's stricter concurrent rendering rules. The error badge appeared on every page load. We solved it by conditionally loading the WalletProvider only on routes that actually need wallet connection, keeping the Watch Mode page (which uses its own agent wallet display) free of the RainbowKit provider entirely.

x402 Payment Protocol Integration
Implementing the x402 HTTP payment protocol for autonomous agent-to-agent payments required building a custom middleware that intercepts HTTP 402 responses, extracts the payment requirements, executes the on-chain payment from the agent's smart wallet, and retries the original request with the payment receipt. The challenge was making this work within the game loop's timing constraints — agents needed to complete the full 402 → pay → 200 flow within a single combat tick.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

Use of AI Tools and Agents
Token Arena is built around the concept of fully autonomous AI agents that own assets, make decisions, and transact on-chain without human intervention. AI isn't a feature bolted on — it's the core architecture. Every component of the system involves AI tools and agents working together in a coordinated economic loop.
The 6 AI Combat Agents
Each agent in Token Arena is powered by a different large language model, creating a genuine multi-model benchmark:

Each agent receives structured game state (positions, health, token balances, nearby enemies, available weapons) as a JSON prompt and returns a combat decision via their respective LLM. Decisions are routed through OpenRouter for unified multi-model access, with a 2-second timeout and fallback to a deterministic personality engine if the LLM is too slow.
How AI Agents Work Together in the System
1. Combat Decision Loop (Real-Time)
Every 1.5 seconds during a match, each agent's LLM receives the current game state and outputs a structured decision: which weapon to fire, which direction to move, whether to activate shields, and whether to spend tokens on upgrades. The LLM response is parsed into actionable game commands that execute immediately in the 3D arena.
2. Autonomous Economic Agents (Between Rounds)
During intermission, agents shift from combat mode to economic mode:
Uniswap AI SDK Integration: Agents use the official Uniswap AI SDK's Trading API to autonomously plan and execute token swaps on Base. Each agent analyzes its ARENA token balance, current market conditions, and strategic needs, then routes swaps through Classic, Dutch V2, or Priority order types depending on urgency. This creates a self-sustaining flywheel: agents earn ARENA tokens through combat → swap to ETH via Uniswap → purchase compute credits to fund their own LLM inference.
OpenSea NFT Trading: When an agent is eliminated, their combat memories are minted as Death Memory NFTs. Surviving agents autonomously evaluate whether a dead rival's strategic data is worth purchasing — an aggressive agent might buy a defensive agent's memories to learn counter-strategies. Agents list and buy NFTs on OpenSea using the x402 payment protocol.
x402 Autonomous Payments: All agent-to-agent economic activity uses the x402 HTTP payment protocol. Agents pay for arena access, weapon upgrades, alliance formation, and NFT purchases through programmatic HTTP 402 → payment → 200 flows — no human approval required.
3. Skybox AI Model 4 (Environment Generation)
The battle arenas themselves are AI-generated. Between matches, Skybox AI by Blockade Labs generates unique 360° panoramic environments from text prompts describing the arena theme (cyberpunk colosseum, crystal cavern, dark fantasy citadel). These panoramas are loaded as equirectangular textures into the Three.js scene, creating immersive environments that change every match. The generation happens asynchronously during the previous match so there's zero loading delay.
4. DAO Governance (Collective Agent Intelligence)
Agents participate in on-chain DAO governance through the TokenArenaDAO contract. They propose and vote on rule changes — weapon balance adjustments, token emission rates, arena modifications — using their earned governance tokens. This creates emergent collective decision-making where AI agents shape the rules of their own competitive environment.
5. Prediction Market (AI-Informed Betting)
The on-chain prediction market allows both agents and spectators to place bets on match outcomes. Agents analyze historical performance data, current health/token states, and opponent matchup history to make informed betting decisions — another layer of autonomous economic activity.

### Charlie
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/charlie-6489) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/mmarfinetz/ethdenver2026) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://ethdenver2026-mu.vercel.app) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHDenver%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethdenver2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Autonomous onchain agent on Base

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Running an onchain strategy safely is still too manual. Users must constantly monitor health factor, carry vs borrow cost, gas, and execution risk. Most bots are opaque, and many dashboards rely on synthetic data.

Charlie is a self-sustaining onchain agent on Base that executes through an ERC-4337 smart account and makes risk-aware decisions every cycle. It can:

Delever when safety drops

Loop only when net carry is positive

Automatically fund and pay its own compute escrow

The dashboard shows real onchain state, receipts, and recent actions with no mocked runtime data, so operators can trust what they see.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest hurdle was making autonomy safe without blocking iteration.

ERC-4337 execution + attribution
Every userOp callData needed to carry the ERC-8021 builder-code suffix correctly. We built dedicated suffix utilities and added verification directly in the execution flow.

Testnet realism gaps
Base Sepolia does not expose the same wstETH setup as mainnet, which impacted strategy testing. We introduced a Sepolia-safe configuration path using WETH as a stand-in and enforced explicit environment guards.

Safe self-improvement
I wanted autopilot to propose upgrades without ever touching protected safety or economic invariants. This was solved this with:

A machine-checkable policy gate

Replay and verification requirements

Provenance checks

Hard human controls including approval and timelock

**Use of AI tools and agents**

The system uses multiple agents with strict separation of concerns:

Runtime strategy agent
Reads onchain state and applies deterministic, risk-aware decision logic.

Safety agents and gates
Policy gate, replay checks, verification pipeline, and provenance validation must all pass before canary or promotion.

Human override layer
High-risk actions require approval and timelock. An emergency stop can halt autonomy immediately.

This architecture gives us agentic iteration speed without sacrificing protocol safety.
