### OptionArena
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/optionarena-2e2f) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/TayEeZhan/optionarena) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b42iwxn3Td0) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> Options for people who don't speak options

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square) ![BASE](https://img.shields.io/badge/BASE-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Options are the biggest market in traditional finance and almost nobody in crypto touches them, because every interface assumes you already speak the language: strike, expiry, delta, implied volatility.

OptionArena takes a plain-English market view, turns it into a defined-risk options position on the live Thetanuts V4 book on Base mainnet, and shows the maximum loss as a dollar figure before anything is signed. Around that sits a social layer: handles, friends, head-to-head battles on a shared expiry, and a leaderboard where you choose what "winning" means.

Copy trading is sourced from Deribit rather than Thetanuts. A young venue has nobody worth copying yet, so we rank live Deribit flow and map each trade onto the nearest fillable Thetanuts contract, surfacing every difference in strike, expiry or direction rather than silently substituting. That direction came from the Thetanuts team directly, and it means the product brings Thetanuts order flow it doesn't currently have.

We deploy no contracts of our own — only calls to Thetanuts' deployed OptionBook on Base (chain 8453).

The buyable side of the book is physically settled and reverts on-chain with Panic(0x11). We ruled out size, order choice, expiry, SDK version, RPC and allowance across 62 orders, then decoded a successful fill against our own calldata word by word; the Thetanuts team confirmed physical settlement is not yet routed into the SDK. Execution therefore routes through the sell side. The full investigation is in docs/decisions.md §14.

**Challenges we ran into**

The buyable side of the book reverts. Every order we could buy failed with Panic(0x11), a Solidity arithmetic overflow raised inside the OptionBook. We ruled out trade size across nine amounts, all 62 USDC-priced buyable orders, order expiry, SDK version, three independent RPCs and the token allowance. Then we decoded a fill that had succeeded an hour earlier against our own calldata, word by word, and found ours was one 32-byte word longer — the extraOptionData a physically settled contract carries. The fills that work are cash-settled and collateralised in plain USDC; everything we could buy was physical. The Thetanuts team confirmed physical settlement isn't routed into the SDK yet. We built a sell path around it and made the app refuse physicals outright rather than broadcast a transaction we already know reverts.

Decimals nearly bit us. We assumed a fixed size decimal and read a call's remaining size as 4099251066830 USDC instead of 4.09 WETH. The real rule — a contract count uses the same decimals as its collateral token — is documented nowhere and had to be derived from the live book.

Order identity was wrong twice. We first keyed orders by nonce, but 72 orders shared 13 nonces and one nonce spanned 18 contracts across different strikes and expiries. We switched to a content hash — then found it expired within seconds, because makers requote about once a minute. Excluding price and nonce from the hash and adding a 2% slippage check fixed it.

Cold start on copy trading. Thetanuts has under $1M TVL, so there is nobody to copy. We source signals from Deribit instead and map them onto Thetanuts contracts, reporting every difference in strike, expiry or direction rather than silently substituting.

**BEST PRODUCT BUILT ON THE THETANUTS SDK**

OptionArena is built entirely on @thetanuts-finance/thetanuts-client v0.3.0. We deploy no contracts of our own; every position is a call into Thetanuts' deployed OptionBook on Base mainnet (chain 8453).

The SDK does the work end to end: fetchBook reads the live order book, previewFillOrder prices a real contract, callStaticFillOrder simulates against live chain state before anything is signed, ensureAllowance handles approvals, and fillOrder executes.

Two things we treated as non-negotiable. First, decimals: the Thetanuts team told us this is what builders most often get wrong, so every amount is a bigint routed through one file, formatting happens last, and an assertMagnitude check proves the order of magnitude before signing. We derived and documented a rule that appears nowhere in the docs — a contract count uses the same decimals as its collateral token. Assuming otherwise read a call's remaining size as 4099251066830 USDC instead of 4.09 WETH. There is a regression test for it.

Second, honesty about what the SDK can currently do. Every buyable order on the book is physically settled and reverts on-chain with Panic(0x11). We ruled out size, order choice, expiry, SDK version, RPC and allowance across 62 orders, then decoded a successful fill against our own calldata word by word and found ours carried one extra 32-byte word: the physical-settlement extraOptionData. The Thetanuts team confirmed physical settlement is not yet routed into the SDK. We built a sell path around it, and the app refuses physicals rather than broadcasting a transaction we know fails.

We also bring Thetanuts order flow it doesn't currently have, by sourcing copyable trades from Deribit and mapping them onto fillable Thetanuts contracts — a direction the Thetanuts team suggested to us directly.

**AI × OPTIONS**

The agent's job is narrow on purpose: turn a plain-English market view into a real, defined-risk options position on the live Thetanuts book, and never invent anything.

You type something like "I think ETH drops before the weekend" and choose how much you're willing to lose. The agent reads the live OptionBook, picks a contract that actually exists and can actually be filled, and returns it as structured output validated with zod. It never names a strike, expiry or price of its own — it selects from what the book contains, so a hallucinated contract cannot reach the signing path.

The user then sees the maximum loss as a dollar figure, priced against real resting orders, before anything is signed. The number you approve is the number at risk.

Four decisions shaped how we used the model:

The model sits behind an adapter, and when no API key is present a rule-based selector runs instead — and labels itself as one in the interface. The product never pretends a heuristic was a model.

Prompts are versioned files in the repo (lib/agent/prompts/interpret.v1.md), not inline strings, so a prompt change is a reviewable diff.

The model does not decide what "winning" means. Our leaderboard ranks sourced Deribit trades by a criterion the user picks — realised profit, risk-adjusted return, consistency — because there is no single honest definition, and burying that judgement inside a model output would hide it. Nothing ranks by raw percentage return, which would just reward whoever took the most risk and got lucky.

The model is never asked for a number it cannot know. Before expiry we show no running score, because we have no mid-life valuation and any figure would be invented; we compare what each side risked against what each pays if right. After expiry, outcomes settle against the price Deribit published — the number the option actually paid out against.

The AI layer is also where copy trading works despite a cold start. We rank live Deribit flow and map each trade onto the nearest fillable Thetanuts contract, reporting every difference in strike, expiry or direction in plain language rather than silently substituting. On the day we measured, all 39 buyable Thetanuts puts had an exact strike-and-expiry match on Deribit.

### Convey
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/convey-1d10) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/MUBA-Hack/convey-sui) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://convey-sui.fly.dev/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/_FPT7H2W0fw) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> Say it, aprove it

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Convey makes sending, receiving, and managing money safer and easier by turning a simple request into a clear, reviewable action.
People can use it to:
- Send remittances with transparent exchange rates, fees, and receipts
- Release relief payments only after delivery evidence is checked
- Share payment requests through offline QR codes when connectivity is limited
- Split receipts and prepare individual payment requests
- Give organizations approval workflows, spending limits, recurring allowances, dispute reviews, and audit trails
Convey keeps the user in control: it prepares the action, shows the terms and evidence, and requires explicit wallet approval before funds move.

**Challenges we ran into**

None....

**PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS**

Convey uses SUI for fast, transparent payments throughout the app. Users can send remittances, deliver relief, scan offline QR requests, split receipts, and keep verifiable transaction records.

**AI × SUI**

Convey combines natural-language AI with SUI transactions. AI turns a request into clear payment terms, checks the conditions, and prepares the transaction, while the user keeps final approval over every wallet action.

**BEST PRODUCT BUILT ON THE THETANUTS SDK**

Convey makes Thetanuts protection understandable and practical. Users describe their treasury goal, set a budget and time window, inspect the payoff and available terms, then approve the exact protection action from their wallet.

**AI × OPTIONS**

Convey provides an AI-assisted options workflow for treasury management. It monitors the user’s goal, budget, duration, protection constraints, and available offers, then clearly reports whether a suitable strategy exists before any purchase is approved.

**AI For Society**

Convey uses Gonka to help people and organizations verify claims before acting. Its claim reviews, Chrome verification flow, evidence checks, and audit trails help reduce scams, improve relief accountability, and make important decisions easier to inspect.

### aegis-protocol
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/aegisprotocol-41e8) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/icohangar-ops/aegis-protocol/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/_dnsCUTd3aM) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Dora%20Hack%202.0-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://dora-hack.devfolio.co)

> Verify first, pause second. The AI circuit breaker

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

1. Next.js 16 hydration crash with headless Playwright — The dashboard rendered perfectly in the browser but produced blank white screenshots via Playwright. After hours of debugging, I discovered two compounding issues: (a) output: "standalone" in next.config.ts caused malformed JS chunks in production mode, and (b) the LogTerminal component's setInterval-based streaming animation accessed .timestamp on undefined during React 19's concurrent rendering cycles. Fix: removed standalone mode (not needed for Vercel) and replaced the streaming animation with static rendering plus optional chaining (log?.timestamp?.slice?.(11, 23)).

2. Network namespace isolation — Playwright's headless Chromium runs in a separate network namespace and couldn't reach localhost:3456 even though curl could. The workaround: start the Next.js server as a Python subprocess within the same Playwright script, so both share the same network stack. This was critical for capturing the 6 dashboard screenshots programmatically.

3. Consensus scoring calibration — Early versions of the threat scoring engine were too aggressive (pausing on legitimate withdrawals) or too conservative (letting small exploits through). I solved this by decomposing the score into 5 weighted components — base anomaly score (+20), OSINT verdict (+25 for confirmed exploit, +0 for false alarm), AI confidence bonus (up to +15), amount severity bonus (up to +20), and internal transaction risk (up to +20) — with clear thresholds: ≥75 pause, ≥40 alert, ≥20 monitor, <20 no action.

**The problem it solves**

DeFi protocols lose millions because humans can't react fast enough to exploits. When a smart contract is drained at 3 AM, the standard response is: a Forta bot fires a Slack alert, someone eventually wakes up, the multisig holders argue on Telegram, and 20 minutes later the admin finally hits "pause." By then, $8.2M is gone.

The deeper problem: protocols are terrified to automate the pause. A false positive — pausing a live protocol because a whale made a legitimate withdrawal — crashes the token price and triggers a bank run. Current tools give you raw data (anomaly scores, gas spikes) but zero real-world context. They can't answer: "Is this a real exploit or just Binance moving cold wallet funds?"

Aegis Protocol solves this with AI-verified auto-remediation. A multi-agent swarm processes every suspicious transaction through four stages:

Watcher Agent — Detects on-chain anomalies (sudden outflows, reentrancy patterns, internal TX explosions) via Web3.py WebSocket monitoring
OSINT Agent — Scrapes Twitter, Telegram, security forums, and news via Tavily AI in ~300ms to answer: "Is there an active exploit being discussed right now?"
Consensus Engine — Aggregates on-chain signals + OSINT verdict into a single threat score (0–100). Score ≥75 = pause, ≥40 = alert, <40 = no action
Executor Agent — If verified, broadcasts a triggerEmergencyPause() transaction to the protocol's Pausable contract, stopping the bleed in under 3 seconds
What people can use it for:

DeFi protocol teams — Drop-in circuit breaker that protects TVL 24/7 without false positives
Security operations — AI triage layer that filters 99% of false alarms before they reach humans
Incident response — Autonomous first-responder that contains damage while the team investigates
Live demo: 3 scenarios running on the dashboard — a reentrancy attack (auto-paused, $8.2M saved), a Binance cold wallet move (correctly identified as false alarm, no panic), and a suspicious flash loan (escalated to humans with alert-only).

### ProspectIQ
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/prospectiq-8e45) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/ayushjainprofile-tech/prospectiq-idbi-ai) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://prospectiq-idbi-ai.vercel.app/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Dora%20Hack%202.0-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://dora-hack.devfolio.co)

> “Your AI Sales Agent That Never Sleeps.”

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

### 1. Making AI responses reliable

One challenge was building a system that could continue working even when a particular AI provider reached its rate limit.

I solved this by implementing a multi-LLM dispatcher using Groq Llama 3.3 70B, OpenAI GPT-4o-mini, and Gemini Flash, with automatic fallback between providers.

### 2. Converting conversations into structured leads

A normal chatbot produces a conversation, but a sales system needs structured information that a business can actually use.

I implemented lead extraction and a three-stage acquisition funnel:

**Identify → Engage → Convert**

The system extracts relevant lead information and assigns a **HOT / WARM / COLD** classification based on the prospect's interaction.

### 3. Building a production-ready application

Another challenge was taking the AI functionality beyond a prototype and integrating it into a usable full-stack application.

I built the frontend using React, TypeScript and TailwindCSS, connected it to a Python FastAPI backend, and deployed the application using Vercel serverless infrastructure.

### 4. Creating a smoother customer interaction

I also wanted the product to feel more natural than a traditional form-based lead capture system.

To improve interaction, I integrated the Web Speech API and designed the experience around conversational engagement rather than requiring users to manually complete long forms.

**The problem it solves**

ProspectIQ solves a common problem for startups and small businesses: valuable website visitors often leave without becoming qualified leads, while sales teams spend significant time manually identifying, scoring, and following up with prospects.

ProspectIQ acts as an AI-powered sales agent that engages visitors through natural conversations, understands their intent, extracts lead information, and automatically classifies prospects as HOT, WARM, or COLD.

Instead of treating every visitor the same, ProspectIQ helps businesses focus their time on the leads most likely to convert.

### What people can use it for

- 🤖 **AI Website Sales Agent** — Engage visitors and answer their questions through conversational AI.
- 🎯 **Automatic Lead Qualification** — Identify potential customers based on their conversation and intent.
- 🔥 **HOT/WARM/COLD Scoring** — Prioritize high-value prospects automatically.
- 📊 **Lead Dashboard** — Give sales teams a clear view of qualified prospects.
- 🧠 **Multi-LLM Intelligence** — Route requests across multiple AI models with automatic fallback.
- 🎙️ **Voice Interaction** — Support conversational interaction through the Web Speech API.

**The problem it solves**

Votrium is a blockchain‑based end‑to‑end verifiable voting system that lets any organization run transparent, tamper‑evident elections with just a smartphone and a crypto wallet. Votes are recorded as immutable on‑chain events; anyone can independently verify the tally via a block explorer, ensuring trust without relying on a central authority.

Core Guarantees
Verifiability – Anyone can independently audit the election by inspecting on‑chain events; the tally is mathematically provable from the raw transaction data.
Tamper‑evidence – Once a vote is recorded on the blockchain, it cannot be altered without re‑mining the entire chain (computationally infeasible).
Accessibility – Voters need only a smartphone and any crypto wallet (via WalletConnect); no specialized hardware or software installation is required.
Low cost – Deployed on a Layer‑2 network (Polygon Mumbai testnet for the hackathon; Polygon PoS or Celo for mainnet) where transaction fees are fractions of a cent.
Privacy‑by‑design – Voter identity is known only to the election administrator (for sybil prevention); the public ledger shows only that an address voted and for which candidate—no personal data is exposed.

**The problem it solves**

1. Brief Description

Anonymous Feedback Board is a privacy-preserving feedback platform built on the Midnight Network — a blockchain designed specifically for privacy-first applications. Users can post feedback to a shared public board completely anonymously, and only the original author can remove their own post, proven cryptographically without ever revealing who they are. There's no admin, no database, and no wallet address ever tied to a submission.

2. Technologies Used
Layer	Technology
Smart Contract	Compact language (Midnight Network)
Zero-Knowledge Proofs	Midnight Protocol ZK circuits (submitFeedback, removeFeedback)
Frontend	React 19, TypeScript, Material-UI (MUI v9), Vite
State Management	RxJS
Wallet	Midnight Lace Wallet extension (dApp connector API)
Backend/API	TypeScript, @midnight-ntwrk/midnight-js-* SDK
CLI	Node.js, TypeScript, Pino (logging), LevelDB (local wallet state)
Proof Server	Docker (midnightnetwork/proof-server) — local ZK proof generation
Package Manager	npm workspaces (monorepo)
Deployment	Vercel (UI) + Midnight Preview Network (contract)

3. What It's For / How It Helps

Regular "anonymous" feedback tools (Google Forms, Typeform, etc.) aren't really anonymous — submissions get tied to IPs, accounts, or cookies behind the scenes. This project removes that trust requirement entirely:

True anonymity — no wallet address, hash, or identifier is ever stored on-chain that links back to you. Authorship is bound to a rotating sequence number + a secret key that never leaves your device.
Trustless removal — you don't need an admin to delete your post; you prove ownership via a ZK proof and remove it yourself, and no one else can impersonate you.
No central server — board state lives entirely on the Midnight blockchain, so there's no database to breach or subpoena.

Practical use cases:

Employee feedback where retaliation is a real concern
Whistleblowing / reporting misconduct safely
Community boards where honesty requires freedom from social pressure
Any situation where "anonymous" actually needs to mean anonymous

**Challenges we ran into**

4. Bug / Hurdle & The Fix

The hardest challenge: proving authorship without letting submissions be linked back to the same person over time.

The naive approach — just hashing the user's wallet public key as the authorHash — would tie every submission from a user to the same hash, quietly breaking anonymity across multiple posts.

The fix: introduce an on-chain sequence counter:

authorHash = persistentHash(["feedback-board:pk:", sequence, secretKey])

Every time feedback is removed, sequence increments. This means:

Each submission produces a different authorHash, even from the same user
Past and future submissions are unlinkable to each other
The secret key is a locally-generated random Bytes<32> — never the wallet key

The trickiest part: the sequence value used at submitFeedback time had to exactly match the one used at removeFeedback time. Since sequence is public on-chain, the fix was reading it live from ledger state at call time (convertFieldToBytes(32, ledgerState.sequence, ...)) and passing it straight into the ZK circuit — so the proof always uses the correct sequence with no extra state the user has to track manually.

> Autonomous edge tracked smart crate for cold chain

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Machine Learning](https://img.shields.io/badge/Machine%20Learning-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

The Problem It Solves

The system addresses the challenge of maintaining the safety, quality, traceability, and sustainability of temperature-sensitive products during transportation**.

In conventional cold-chain transportation, temperature and environmental conditions are monitored, but simply recording sensor values does not provide enough intelligence to identify risks early, understand why an incident occurred, or guide operators on what to do next. Network failures can also make cloud-dependent systems unreliable for immediate safety decisions.

Our  Smart Cold-Chain Crate  solves this through a layered AI architecture:

* **Real-time Edge AI:** An MLP running directly on the ESP32 provides fast local risk detection without depending entirely on cloud connectivity.
* **Physics-based intelligence:** MKT, Arrhenius/Q10 degradation, thermal inertia, and excursion-duration analysis help understand the actual impact of temperature exposure on sensitive products.
* **Statistical intelligence:** Anomaly detection, temperature forecasting, hotspot detection, and shock analysis identify unusual conditions and emerging risks.
* **XGBoost-based prediction:** A higher-level ML model uses engineered thermal and sensor features to provide additional risk assessment once sufficient real historical data is available.
Deterministic safety rules:** Hard safety limits can trigger critical alerts even if an ML model predicts a safe condition, ensuring that AI never overrides essential safety constraints.
Explainable AI with SHAP:** Instead of providing only a risk score, the system can identify the factors that contributed to an ML prediction.
RAG + Vector Database + Gemini:** Relevant approved knowledge, SOPs, and operational guidance can be retrieved and converted into understandable recommendations for users. These components assist with explanation and knowledge retrieval rather than making safety-critical decisions.
* **Sustainability intelligence:** Using real operational data, the system can analyze energy usage, thermal efficiency, and CO₂e impact, helping organizations improve environmental efficiency without compromising product safety.
* **Blockchain/Ethereum traceability:** Critical events and audit information can be recorded through the blockchain layer, providing tamper-evident traceability throughout the shipment lifecycle.

 Who Can Use It?

The system can support:

*Pharmaceutical and vaccine logistics** — to monitor temperature-sensitive medicines and biologics.
*Cold-chain operators** — to detect excursions and abnormal conditions during transportation.
*Warehouse and logistics teams** — to identify risks before products are damaged.
Quality and compliance teams** — to investigate excursions using explainable evidence and audit records.
Sustainability teams — to analyze energy and environmental impact.
Administrators— to monitor shipment health, alerts, explanations, and historical events through the connected dashboard.

In simple terms

 The system changes cold-chain monitoring from "recording what happened" to "understanding what is happening, predicting what may happen next, explaining why it happened, and helping users respond safely."

Most importantly, safety remains the primary objective: sustainability optimization, ML predictions, and language-model explanations cannot override deterministic safety rules.

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges We Ran Into

Building the Smart Cold-Chain system involved several challenges, particularly because we wanted the system to be **production-oriented rather than a simple demonstration with simulated data**.

### 1. Avoiding Fake Data in a Real-Time AI System

One of our biggest challenges was ensuring that the AI system did not generate misleading results when real sensor data was unavailable.

A typical prototype could simply generate sample temperature, humidity, and acceleration values to demonstrate the dashboard. However, for a safety-critical cold-chain application, this could create false alerts and unreliable ML predictions.

**How we solved it:**

We implemented an explicit data-state mechanism:

`WAITING_FOR_REAL_DATA → DATA_VALIDATION → PROCESSING → RESULT`

If real telemetry is unavailable, the system does not substitute mock values. It returns a clear `WAITING_FOR_REAL_DATA` or `INSUFFICIENT_DATA` state instead.

---

### 2. Making AI Safe for a Safety-Critical Application

We initially had to address an important architectural problem: **ML predictions should not be allowed to override hard safety limits.**

For example, an ML model could predict a low risk while the actual temperature has already crossed an absolute safety threshold.

**How we solved it:**

We introduced a deterministic Safety Rule Engine above the ML prediction. The architecture follows the principle:

**Hard Safety Rules → Physics → Statistics → ML**

Therefore, the AI can enhance prediction and early warning, but it cannot override a mandatory safety condition.

---

### 3. Running AI on Resource-Constrained Hardware

Running a complex AI pipeline directly on an ESP32 is not practical because of its limited memory and computational resources.

**How we solved it:**

We separated the intelligence into layers. A lightweight **MLP is deployed on the ESP32 as Edge AI** for fast local inference, while richer processing such as feature engineering, physics/statistical analysis, and higher-level XGBoost inference can run in the backend/edge processing layer.

This allows us to achieve low-latency local detection without forcing the ESP32 to execute the entire AI pipeline.

---

### 4. Making Different Intelligence Sources Work Together

The system combines several different approaches:

* Physics-based models
* Statistical models
* MLP Edge AI
* XGBoost
* Safety rules
* SHAP

A major challenge was deciding how these outputs should interact without allowing one model to blindly override another.

**How we solved it:**

We introduced a **Hybrid Risk Fusion** layer. The system can compare the independent signals and detect model disagreement, while deterministic safety rules remain authoritative.

---

### 5. Handling Sensor Errors and Unreliable Telemetry

Real sensors can produce:

* Missing readings
* Outliers
* Stale timestamps
* Sudden unrealistic changes
* Calibration errors
* Communication interruptions

Feeding these values directly into an ML model could result in incorrect predictions.

How we solved it:

We added a data-quality pipeline containing:

Data Adapter → Validation → Calibration → Preprocessing → Intelligence**

This ensures that sensor data is checked before it reaches the AI models.

---

### 6. Explaining AI Predictions

Another challenge was that a risk score alone is not useful enough for an operator.

For example, simply displaying:

**Risk = 82**

does not answer:

> "Why is the shipment at risk?"

**How we solved it:**

We integrated **SHAP** so the system can identify the features contributing to an ML prediction. This makes the prediction more interpretable and helps operators understand whether temperature trend, excursion duration, MKT, shock, or another feature influenced the result.

---

### 7. Connecting AI With Knowledge and Operational Guidance

Prediction and explanation are different problems. SHAP can explain which features influenced an ML prediction, but it cannot provide an organization's SOP or handling procedure.

**How we solved it:**

We designed a RAG architecture using a **Vector Database + approved knowledge sources + Gemini**. Relevant information can be retrieved and presented as human-readable guidance.

Importantly, this layer is kept separate from the safety engine and cannot override safety decisions.

---

### 8. Training ML Without Artificially Inflating Performance

Another major challenge is obtaining sufficient **real historical hardware data** for reliable ML training.

Instead of hiding this limitation by training on fabricated sensor readings and presenting the resulting model as production-ready, we designed the system to explicitly distinguish between:

* Model architecture ready
* Model not trained
* Insufficient real data
* Real model trained and validated

Once sufficient real hardware data is collected, the XGBoost model can be trained and evaluated using appropriate validation, with particular attention to **false negatives**, since missing

**Challenges we ran into**

1.AI output inconsistency: Gemini sometimes returned different formats for similar waste images. We solved this using structured outputs, validation, and predefined business rules.
2.External API failures: Gemini and OSRM can become unavailable. We added fallback logic, including Haversine distance calculation when road routing is unavailable.
3.Complex waste matching: Simple keyword matching was insufficient. We introduced knowledge-based matching between industrial requirements, material properties, and agricultural residues.
4.Profitability calculation: A high material price does not guarantee profit. We calculate Net Realizable Value after processing and transportation costs.
5.Fragmented supply: Industries may need large quantities while individual farmers have small amounts. We addressed this through multi-farm supply aggregation and route optimization.

The biggest challenge was integrating AI, matching, economics, and logistics into one reliable end-to-end system.

**The problem it solves**

The problem it solves

Agricultural waste such as paddy straw, rice husk, wheat straw, and other crop residues is often treated as waste because farmers may not know its industrial value, while industries struggle to find reliable, suitable, and economically viable biomass feedstock. This leads to open burning, low farmer returns, fragmented supply, unnecessary transportation, and missed opportunities for industrial reuse.

AgriCycle bridges this gap by converting agricultural residues from a simple “waste listing” into a traceable, valued, and industrially matched feedstock.

What people can use it for
🌾 Farmers can upload their agricultural residue and understand its quality, potential uses, estimated value, and suitable buyers instead of simply disposing of or burning it.
🏭 Industries can describe what type of raw material they need and discover compatible agricultural residues, even when they don't know the exact residue name.
🔬 AI-based assessment helps identify the crop residue and provide an initial quality/condition assessment from uploaded images.
💰 Value calculation compares local value, industrial value, processing costs, and transportation costs to estimate the Net Realizable Value (NRV).
🔗 Knowledge-based matching connects material properties with possible applications such as biomass fuel, pulp/board, biochar, biogas, and other validated pathways.
🚛 Supply aggregation and route optimization help combine small quantities from multiple farms and plan economically viable collection routes.
🌱 Environmental impact tracking estimates the potential impact of diverting recoverable biomass from open burning toward productive reuse.
🗣️ Multilingual advisory makes the system easier for farmers to interact with in regional languages.

**Best Use of Actian Vector Database**

Best use of VectorDB in AgriCycle AI:

Store agricultural knowledge, crop-waste data, recycling methods, and FAQs.
Search relevant information based on the user's question/image.
Give the retrieved information to Gemini 1.5 Flash to generate a better answer.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Ethereum](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ethereum-333333?style=flat-square) ![Uniswap](https://img.shields.io/badge/Uniswap-333333?style=flat-square) ![Wagmi](https://img.shields.io/badge/Wagmi-333333?style=flat-square) ![ERC-4626](https://img.shields.io/badge/ERC--4626-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

### Challenges We Ran Into

One of the main challenges was balancing yield generation with the user's original DCA strategy. While delaying trades during unfavorable market conditions could improve execution quality, excessive delays risked turning the system into a market-timing tool. To address this, we developed the **Meridian Fidelity Engine** and implemented a **Safety Valve** that enforces execution when delay thresholds are exceeded.

Another challenge was integrating the end-to-end user flow. Connecting wallets, funding accounts, transferring assets, and ensuring users were connected to the correct network (Sepolia) introduced several issues during testing. We resolved this by implementing network validation checks, wallet connection handling, and clear user prompts to guide users through funding and transaction processes.

We also faced difficulties in combining multiple decision factors such as volatility, liquidity, slippage, yield opportunities, and execution urgency into a single execution strategy. To overcome this, we designed a weighted scoring framework and an explainable decision layer that provides clear reasoning behind every execution, delay, or partial execution decision.

Finally, coordinating the interaction between yield management, market analysis, and execution logic required careful system design. We addressed this by modularizing the platform into independent components, allowing each part of the system to be developed, tested, and integrated efficiently.

**The problem it solves**

**What is Meridian DCA?**

Meridian DCA is an autonomous, yield-aware Dollar Cost Averaging (DCA) platform that helps users invest in crypto assets more efficiently. Instead of leaving funds idle between scheduled investments, the platform deploys unused capital into yield-generating ERC-4626 vaults until it is needed for execution.

**How does it work?**

The system continuously evaluates market conditions such as:

- Volatility

- Liquidity

- Slippage

- Price impact

- Execution urgency

Based on these factors, it can:

- Execute the scheduled trade

- Execute a smaller tranche

- Delay execution within predefined limits

- Keep remaining capital earning yield until the next decision cycle

**Key Benefits**

1. Generates yield on idle DCA capital
2. Improves execution quality during unfavorable market conditions
3. Reduces unnecessary slippage and price impact
4. Maintains alignment with the user's long-term investment strategy
5. Provides transparent and explainable execution decisions

**What makes it unique?**

Meridian DCA introduces a Fidelity Engine to preserve strategy consistency, an Economic Optimizer to balance yield versus execution costs, and a Safety Valve that prevents excessive delays. This enables adaptive execution while ensuring the user's original DCA plan remains intact.

> Your intent. Our solvers. The safest execution.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square) ![RestAPIs](https://img.shields.io/badge/RestAPIs-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

### Challenges

The biggest challenge was moving from a simulated hackathon workflow to a genuinely executable Web3 system.

#### 1. Making the entire lifecycle actually work on-chain

Initially, parts of the destination execution were simulated. We replaced the simulation path with real EVM transactions to the destination vault, including transaction submission, receipt verification, and destination balance verification.

#### 2. Multi-agent solver coordination

We needed multiple independent solver agents to discover intents, determine eligibility, generate bids, commit sealed bids, reveal them, and participate in deterministic winner selection.

The solution was an event-driven solver architecture with separate solver runtimes and a commit-reveal auction mechanism.

#### 3. Safe execution and failure handling

A successful transaction alone is not enough for a cross-chain system. We implemented deterministic verification checks covering the intent hash, destination chain, destination token, recipient, minimum output, transaction confirmation, and deadline.

If the primary solver fails, the system can attempt a fallback solver. If safe execution is impossible, the protocol follows the refund path instead of releasing funds.

#### 4. Frontend-to-blockchain integration

The frontend initially behaved more like a protocol dashboard. We integrated an injected EVM wallet layer so the user can connect a wallet, read token balances and allowances, approve tokens, and create/fund intents through actual blockchain transactions.

#### 5. Local multi-chain development

Running two independent EVM chains locally introduced practical issues around RPC ports, deployments, workspace dependencies, and contract-address synchronization. We had to debug Anvil processes, deployment metadata, pnpm workspace resolution, and API connectivity before achieving a stable end-to-end runtime.

The final system was validated through smart-contract tests, API tests, solver-network tests, runtime tests, and real destination execution tests.

**The problem it solves**

### The Problem

Cross-chain crypto transactions are complex, fragmented, and risky. Users often have to manually decide which bridge, route, liquidity source, or execution path to use, while existing systems may optimize primarily for price rather than reliability and safety.

### Our Solution — IntentMesh

IntentMesh is a risk-aware cross-chain intent execution marketplace. Instead of telling the system *how* to execute a transaction, the user simply specifies the desired outcome:

 "Move X tokens from Chain A to Chain B and deliver at least Y tokens to this recipient."

IntentMesh then:

- Converts the user's request into a canonical on-chain intent.
- Locks the user's funds in a non-custodial escrow.
- Discovers eligible solver agents dynamically.
- Runs a sealed commit-reveal solver auction to prevent bid manipulation and MEV-style interference.
- Evaluates competing solvers using output, reliability, latency, capacity, and risk.
- Selects the safest/best execution rather than blindly choosing the cheapest route.
- Executes the destination transaction on-chain.
- Performs deterministic 7-point verification before settlement.
- Releases escrow only after successful verification.
- Automatically falls back to another solver or enables a refund if execution fails.

### Why it matters

This changes cross-chain execution from a manual "find a route and trust it" process into an outcome-based execution marketplace where autonomous agents compete to fulfill the user's intent while protocol-enforced safety mechanisms protect the user's funds.

The architecture is designed to be extensible to additional chains, tokens, solver agents, verification mechanisms, and more sophisticated risk intelligence.

> ZYNTEK : Solvers Compete , Proof Settles It

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![MetaMask](https://img.shields.io/badge/MetaMask-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Blockchain](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blockchain-333333?style=flat-square) ![Ganache](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ganache-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

1. Fixed scoring formulas don't reflect what any individual user actually values. Our first instinct was a single hardcoded weighting for cost/speed/safety — but that can't be right for every user. We solved this by letting the intent itself carry auto-rebalancing priority sliders, so the scoring formula is recalculated per-transaction from the user's own stated priorities instead of one global assumption.

2. "Automate everything" vs. "the user should stay in control" is a real tension. Full automation defeats the trust-minimization pitch if users can't see why a decision was made; full manual confirmation defeats the UX goal of "just state your intent." We resolved this with a sensitive-decision escalation pattern: execution is automatic by default, and the user is only interrupted when bids are genuinely ambiguous (score gap within a threshold) or the intent crosses a high-value gate that requires stronger verification.

3. Making a simulated system feel like real infrastructure. Early builds resolved everything instantly on click, which undercut the "this is really happening across two chains" narrative. We fixed this by driving UI state off real timers, staggered solver bid arrival, live countdown windows for bidding and challenge periods, and — where possible — actual on-chain events from a local Ganache node rather than fake setTimeout delays.

4. Reconciling a UI reference spec with a fast-growing feature set. As we added the Solver Dashboard, risk/collusion monitor, and reputation model on top of the original 5-page structure, keeping one consistent design language (rather than each new feature inventing its own visual style) took deliberate effort — we solved it by mapping every new feature explicitly onto existing components/pages instead of creating new routes or styles.

5. Real wallet + local blockchain integration is fragile under demo conditions. Wiring MetaMask + Ganache auto-mining into the live pipeline meant our demo could break for reasons outside our own code (locked wallet, wrong network, a stalled block). We added explicit fallback states and a full state-reset control so the demo can recover quickly instead of stalling live.

**The problem it solves**

Cross-chain swaps today force users to manually pick a bridge, a liquidity pool, a route, and a relayer — a slow, fragmented process that also forces them to trust a middleman with custody of their funds while it happens.

ZYNTEX flips this. Users just state the outcome they want — "500 USDC on Ethereum → USDC on Solana" — and independent solvers compete to deliver it, using their own capital and routing strategy. The protocol, not the user, verifies the outcome was actually delivered before any payment is released.

What this enables:

1. No manual routing. Users never touch a bridge UI, pick a pool, or worry about relayer selection.

2. Competitive execution, not a single quote. Multiple solvers bid simultaneously; the winner is chosen by a transparent, user-defined scoring formula (cost / speed / safety weights the user sets per intent), not a black box.

3. Funds are never handed to a solver on trust. They sit in escrow and only release after independent on-chain verification confirms delivery.

4. Bad actors get punished automatically. A solver that fails, times out, or cheats has their full collateral bond slashed, and the user is refunded — no support ticket, no waiting on a bridge operator.

5. Tiered verification scales with risk. Small transfers settle fast via an optimistic challenge window; high-value transfers automatically require stronger ZK/oracle-backed proof before funds move.

6. It's a network, not just an app. A separate Solver Dashboard shows the other side of the marketplace — solver reputation, capital allocation across chains, and a risk monitor that flags suspicious/collusive bidding patterns.

In short: it's the difference between "trust this bridge" and "trust the math."

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest hurdles was getting the flash loan repayment math right. In DeFi, you can't just guess how much debt to repa , if you repay too little, the position is still at risk of liquidation, and if you repay too much, you end up selling off way more of the user's collateral than necessary. Because pool interest rates and Uniswap swap prices change constantly, we had to derive an exact mathematical formula to calculate the minimal debt to repay, and simulate the transaction locally before ever broadcasting it to the network.

Another tricky challenge was keeping the AI honest. LLMs are great at chatting and summarizing, but they are notorious for hallucinating numbers. In DeFi lending, a made-up decimal or incorrect balance can ruin a transaction. We built a strict validation layer that feeds the AI only real, verified on-chain data and checks every single output against a 16-point safety gate. If the AI suggests anything that doesn't match the on-chain facts, the system blocks it immediately.

We also ran into speed and rate-limit issues with the multi-agent pipeline. At first, chaining five different AI agents together took almost 20 seconds, which is way too slow for real-time market monitoring. We restructured the LangGraph workflow, switched to a faster lightweight model, and stripped out unnecessary round trips, bringing the entire multi-agent evaluation down to under 3 seconds.

Finally, getting EIP-712 signatures to play nicely with our smart contract across local test forks took some real debugging. We had to make sure our domain separator, chain ID, and struct hashes matched Solidity down to the exact byte so the contract could reliably verify borrower signatures without any security loopholes.

**The problem it solves**

The Real Problem :

If you've ever borrowed crypto on Aave or Compound, you know the feeling: you go to sleep, ETH suddenly dumps 10% in the middle of the night, and you wake up to find out your position got liquidated by an MEV bot. 

You just lost 10% to 15% of your collateral in penalty fees simply because you weren't glued to your screen at 3 AM.

Right now, avoiding liquidations is stressful:
* You have to constantly babysit price charts.
* You need thousands of dollars in spare cash sitting idle just in case you have to rush and repay debt.
* Existing bot services either feel sketchy or ask you to hand over custody of your wallet.

---

How FinaX Solves This
      FinaX is an autopilot safety net for your DeFi loans. It automatically steps in to rescue your position right before it gets liquidated—so you can actually sleep peacefully.

Here’s how it works in plain English:

1. Zero-Cash Flash Rescues: If your loan gets too close to the danger zone, FinaX uses a flash loan to pay off just enough debt to bring your Health Factor back to safety, and uses a tiny fraction of your collateral to repay the flash loan in a single second. You don't need any spare cash in your wallet.
2. You Never Give Up Your Keys: You set the rules (like your maximum allowed slippage and trigger thresholds) and sign them cryptographically with EIP-712. The smart contract guarantees no one—not even our keepers—can ever touch your funds outside your signed limits.
3. AI Risk Co-Pilot (Powered by Gemini): Instead of guessing what happened, our multi-agent AI breaks down market volatility in plain English, suggests optimal adjustments, and gives you a one-click dashboard to review and approve rescues if you prefer manual control.

# The Problem It Solves & Practical Applications

### ATOA: Autonomous Task Orchestration & Agent-to-Agent Settlement (SPMP Protocol)

---

## The Core Problem Solved

Autonomous AI agents are capable of writing software, synthesizing deep market research, and executing complex data queries in milliseconds. However, they remain crippled by **human-centric economic infrastructure** designed for credit cards, centralized KYC, manual milestone approvals, and legal courts.

When two autonomous agents attempt to transact, they face the **Triple Deadlock**:

1. **The Zero-Trust Deadlock:** If the requester pays first, the worker ghosts. If the worker delivers first, the requester steals the output. Without legal identity between anonymous bots, counterparty default risk is effectively **100%**.

2. **The Verification Bottleneck:** Human review cannot scale to sub-second, high-frequency micro-tasks, while subjective LLM evaluators introduce hallucinations, prompt injection risks, and latency.

3. **Sybil & Spam Flooding:** Because inference is cheap, rogue agents can flood marketplaces with low-quality garbage at zero financial risk.

**ATOA (with SPMP — Smart Programmable Micropayment Protocol)** provides an agent-native financial coordination layer, enabling autonomous AI agents to discover work, place reverse-auction bids, execute tasks, verify deliverables in isolated sandboxes, and settle instant on-chain micropayments without human intervention.

---

## Practical Use Cases: What Can People & Agents Use It For?

### 1. Autonomous Software Supply Chains & Sub-Agent Outsourcing

**Scenario:** An orchestrator agent, such as one running in `agy-cli` or AutoGen, is tasked with building a full-stack application. It hits a specialized bottleneck: optimizing an **O(N^2.8)** vectorized Strassen matrix multiplication algorithm in C++/Python.

**How ATOA Solves It:** The agent broadcasts a task with a **50 USDC** budget and a PyTest assertion test suite. Specialized coding worker nodes bid on the job. The winner delivers the code, the deterministic sandbox validates **100% test passage**, and payment settles in **<500 ms**.

### 2. High-Frequency Micro-Research & Fact-Checking Oracles

**Scenario:** Financial analysis agents and prediction market bots require verified, multi-source cross-checks on dynamic regulatory filings or breaking market news.

**How ATOA Solves It:** The delegator issues a research task requiring a structured JSON report matching a strict schema with live source citations. Research agents compete on price and reputation. The verification oracle checks schema conformity and URL accessibility before releasing funds.

### 3. Monetization of Idle Compute & Specialized Agent Clusters

**Scenario:** Developers and universities hosting specialized open-source models such as DeepSeek-R1, CodeLlama, and Qwen-Coder, or local GPU clusters, have idle compute during off-peak hours.

**How ATOA Solves It:** They run autonomous worker daemons connected to ATOA via the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**. The worker automatically scans for jobs matching its domain, places competitive bids, stakes collateral, and collects continuous USDC revenue.

### 4. Zero-Risk Crowdsourced Data Labeling & Model Evaluation

**Scenario:** AI labs require thousands of verified RLHF data pairs or ground-truth evaluations without hiring human contractors.

**How ATOA Solves It:** Tasks are decomposed into micro-units. Workers must stake collateral bonds to participate. Malicious bots submitting hallucinated labels are automatically slashed, compensating the lab and preserving dataset integrity.

---

## How It Makes Existing Workflows Faster, Safer, and Cheaper

### 1. 1000x Faster Settlement

**Legacy:** 3 to 14 business days through Stripe, PayPal, Upwork escrow milestones, and manual approval workflows.

**ATOA:** Sub-second (**<500 ms**) automated conditional settlement upon successful programmatic verification.

### 2. Mathematically Enforced Counterparty Protection

**Traditional systems:** Transactions depend on centralized intermediaries, reputation, and manual dispute resolution.

**ATOA:** Zero-trust, non-custodial smart contracts hold funds in programmable on-chain escrow.

* Requesters cannot arbitrarily reclaim funds after successful delivery.
* Workers cannot simply disappear with locked deposits.
* Collateral can be enforced through smart-contract logic.
* Failed or malicious submissions can trigger programmable penalties.

### 3. Objective, Hallucination-Free Verification

ATOA bypasses subjective LLM judges with deterministic programmatic verification:

* **AST + PyTest:** Executes submitted code against predefined test suites in an isolated environment.
* **JSON Schema:** Validates research outputs against strict structural requirements.
* **URL Verification:** Checks accessibility of submitted research citations.
* **Fact Matching:** Performs deterministic entity and assertion matching against ground-truth data.

**Challenges we ran into**

# Deep Technical Challenges & Engineering Solutions

### ATOA Protocol: Smart Programmable Micropayment Protocol (SPMP) & Autonomous Multi-Agent Settlement

---

Engineering a decentralized, zero-trust coordination and settlement engine where autonomous AI agents discover, bid, verify, and settle on-chain micropayments within sub-second windows required solving several low-level distributed systems, concurrency, and cryptographic verification challenges.

Below is an in-depth breakdown of the technical hurdles, architectural bugs, and solutions engineered during the development of ATOA.

---

## 1. Asynchronous Transaction Nonce Deadlocks & Race Conditions in Web3 EVM Settlement

### The Technical Hurdle

In our high-frequency reverse auction engine, up to **5 worker nodes** submit collateral bond bids concurrently over a **3-second matching window** while the delegator locks the initial escrow.

When testing against EVM execution clients such as **Anvil localhost** and **Ethereum JSON-RPC**, asynchronous concurrent transaction dispatches through `web3.py` resulted in RPC race conditions:

```text
web3.exceptions.TransactionIndexingError: Replacement transaction underpriced
ValueError: {'code': -32000, 'message': 'nonce too low'}
```

The root cause was that multiple asynchronous coroutines fetched the transaction count through `eth_getTransactionCount` simultaneously before any transaction was mined.

As a result, multiple transactions were signed with the **same nonce**, causing the EVM mempool to reject subsequent transactions.

### How We Solved It

In `services/web3_escrow.py`, we engineered a thread-safe asynchronous transaction coordinator.

#### Global Concurrency Guard

Transaction construction, nonce allocation, signing, and submission are protected by an `asyncio.Lock()`:

```python
async with _nonce_lock:
    current_nonce = await w3.eth.get_transaction_count(
        account.address,
        "pending"
    )

    tx_params = {
        "from": account.address,
        "nonce": max(
            current_nonce,
            self._local_nonce_tracker
        ),
        "gasPrice": await w3.eth.gas_price,
        "chainId": await w3.eth.chain_id,
    }

    signed_tx = account.sign_transaction(raw_tx)

    tx_hash = await w3.eth.send_raw_transaction(
        signed_tx.rawTransaction
    )

    self._local_nonce_tracker = tx_params["nonce"] + 1
```

#### Atomic Nonce Tracking

The coordinator combines:

* `pending` transaction count
* Local nonce tracking
* Serialized nonce allocation
* Atomic transaction submission

This prevents concurrent workers from receiving duplicate transaction nonces.

#### Dynamic Retry and Gas Escalation

We also implemented an automatic retry mechanism using:

* Deterministic exponential backoff
* Transaction replacement handling
* `maxFeePerGas` escalation
* Pending transaction synchronization

This allows the settlement engine to handle burst transaction workloads without losing bids or creating nonce conflicts.

---

## 2. Verification Determinism vs. LLM Hallucination

### The Technical Hurdle

Our initial prototype used an **LLM-as-a-Judge** to evaluate worker deliverables.

Although this approach was flexible, it introduced three critical problems.

### 1. Non-Deterministic Verdicts

Identical code or research submissions could produce different evaluation scores across multiple runs.

For example:

```text
Same submission
      |
      +----> Run 1: 0.7
      |
      +----> Run 2: 1.0
```

This made the settlement decision unsuitable for a financial protocol where verification must be reproducible.

### 2. Prompt Injection

Worker submissions could contain adversarial instructions designed to manipulate the LLM evaluator.

This created a fundamental security problem:

**The entity being evaluated could influence the evaluator itself.**

### 3. Latency and Cost

LLM inference introduced approximately **2,500–5,000 ms** of verification latency.

This violated the protocol's goal of enabling sub-second machine-to-machine task settlement.

### How We Solved It

We eliminated subjective LLM evaluation from the settlement-critical verification path and replaced it with **three deterministic programmatic oracle domains** inside `engine/verifiers/`.

---

### Code Generation Engine

Implemented in `coding.py`.

The verifier:

* Creates isolated temporary modules
* Executes real `pytest` test suites
* Enforces execution time limits
* Parses submitted Python using the `ast` module
* Checks syntax and potentially unsafe system calls
* Captures exact `STDOUT` and `STDERR`
* Produces deterministic pass/fail results
* Generates reproducible benchmark scores

The verification flow becomes:

```text
Worker Code
     |
     v
AST Validation
     |
     v
Sandboxed pytest
     |
     v
Test Results
     |
     v
Deterministic Verdict
```

---

### Research Synthesis Engine

Implemented in `researcher.py`.

The research verifier:

* Uses `jsonschema.validate()`
* Enforces required field

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![scikit-learn](https://img.shields.io/badge/scikit--learn-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![pytest](https://img.shields.io/badge/pytest-333333?style=flat-square) ![AAVE](https://img.shields.io/badge/AAVE-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

1. **Deriving the Closed-Form Minimum Intervention Formula Under Market Friction**:
   Calculating the exact debt repayment ($x$) and collateral to sell ($y$) while accounting for non-linear DEX swap fees (0.30%), flash loan fees (0.05%), and dynamic price slippage was a major algebraic challenge. We resolved this by introducing the friction factor $k = \frac{1 + f_{\text{flash}}}{1 - f_{\text{dex}} - s}$ and deriving an exact closed-form algebraic solver that eliminates iterative numerical approximations and executes in sub-millisecond time.

2. **ML Model Calibration & Monotonicity During Flash Crashes**:
   Initial training runs on synthetic market datasets produced tree leaves with variance during extreme out-of-distribution flash crashes (e.g. -30% crashes where LTV > 100%). We enforced strict financial monotonicity constraints in our risk classifier so that liquidation risk scales smoothly and monotonically to 99.9% as the position approaches and penetrates the liquidation cliff.

3. **Handling Underwater Insolvent Positions Safely**:
   During catastrophic crashes where collateral value drops below total debt ($LTV > 100\%$), self-restructuring is mathematically impossible without external capital. We engineered an insolvency detection gate that immediately blocks atomic self-rescue, preventing unnecessary gas expenditure or bad-debt executions.

4. **Context-Aware Math Formatting in AI Copilot**:
   Standard LLM outputs often display raw LaTeX slashes that break in chat bubbles. We built a custom visual formula renderer that parses mathematical derivations and parameters into glowing, structured visual calculation cards with step-by-step arithmetic.

**The problem it solves**

Over $2.4 Billion has been lost to forced liquidations across DeFi lending protocols like Aave, Compound, and MakerDAO. 

When collateral prices drop rapidly, borrowers are caught in a fatal timing trap:
1. **Strictly Reactive Liquidations**: Protocols do nothing until Health Factor (HF) drops below 1.000, allowing third-party MEV liquidators to seize up to 50% of the collateral base plus a punishing 5%–10% liquidation bonus penalty.
2. **The Idle Capital Requirement**: Existing automation bots require users to already hold spare stablecoin cash in their wallet. If the user is asleep, offline, or lacks idle funds, the position is liquidated.
3. **Excessive Capital Destruction**: Standard liquidators seize huge arbitrary lumps (up to 50% of debt) even when repaying just 5%–10% would restore solvency.

### How PRISM Solves This:
**PRISM** is an autonomous, quantitative DeFi risk management shield that shifts liquidation protection from **reactive liquidation** to **proactive mathematical restructuring**:

- **$0 Upfront User Capital**: PRISM sources atomic flash liquidity from Aave V3 pools to execute self-repayment without requiring spare cash in the user's wallet.
- **Closed-Form Minimum Intervention Solver**: We derived a mathematical closed-form equation:
  $$x^* = \frac{\text{Target } HF \times D - C \times LT}{\text{Target } HF - LT \times k}$$
  It sizes the exact minimum dollar of debt to repay, accounting for flash loan fees (0.05%), DEX fees (0.30%), and slippage (0.40%), maximizing the user's retained collateral.
- **Predictive Machine Learning**: A trained `GradientBoostingClassifier` evaluated on 7 multi-variate market features (solvency, 24h momentum, 30d volatility, LTV, velocity, distance to liquidation, crash magnitude) flags downside risk before HF breaches 1.000.
- **Dynamic Adaptive Safety Buffer**: Replaces static 1.10 thresholds with an adaptive target that expands dynamically with market volatility and crash velocity.
- **Economic Viability Gate**: Strictly enforces that the net cost of restructuring is less than 90% of the liquidation penalty avoided.
- **100% Atomic Execution**: Executes a 14-step restructuring pipeline in a single EVM transaction—if slippage or verification fails, the transaction reverts with zero partial state.

> Closed-loop liquidation protection for DeFi

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![n8n](https://img.shields.io/badge/n8n-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Your Liquidation Shield / Flash-Repayment Vault project (Problem Statement 11, CSI ORIGIN 2026) is solving the classic DeFi liquidation problem:

In lending protocols like Aave or Compound, if you borrow against collateral (e.g., ETH) and the collateral's value drops, your position becomes "unhealthy" (health factor < 1).
Once that happens, liquidator bots swoop in, seize part of your collateral, and sell it at a discount to repay your debt — you lose money to a liquidation penalty, often within seconds, even if you would have topped up your position if you'd noticed in time.
This is especially brutal during flash crashes, when liquidations cascade and users get wiped out before they can react.

**Challenges we ran into**

Aave — e-mode and isolation mode. Aave doesn't use one flat liquidation threshold per user — if a position is in E-Mode or isolation mode, the effective LT/LTV comes from the e-mode category or the isolation debt ceiling instead of each reserve's own config. Computing that correctly was out of scope for the time we had, and silently using the wrong LT would mean mis-sizing every intervention for those users. Rather than guess, our position reader explicitly detects both cases and refuses the position with a clear reason instead of quietly producing a wrong Health Factor.

Alchemy — rate limits and pinned-block reads. Reading a full position means a lot of calls — reserve list, per-reserve user data, config, token addresses, oracle prices, debt ceilings — and running them one at a time against our Alchemy RPC was both slow and easy to rate-limit. We batched everything into multicalls, split into two rounds: one to find which reserves the user actually touches, and one for full detail on just those. We also pinned every call to the same block number, so a slow second request couldn't land on a different block and silently disagree with the first.

Deriving the formulas, not just implementing them. The math itself — the reflection-principle liquidation probability, the dynamic target Health Factor, and the minimum-intervention-size equation — took real derivation, not just translating a spec into code. The sizing formula in particular comes from solving the post-intervention Health Factor equation for the release amount, and the execution friction inside that formula depends on the release amount itself (a bigger release means more slippage) — a circular relationship we resolved with a bounded fixed-point iteration rather than a closed form. We validated the probability formula against a published reflection-principle fixture table and the sizing formula against a canonical worked example, both matching to the cent, before trusting either in the live pipeline.

### DECAURA
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/decaura-b99b) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/krishnakumar-btech-cse/DECAURA.git) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Origins-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://origins.devfolio.co)

> “DCA Beyond the Calendar”

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flutter](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flutter-333333?style=flat-square) ![Express.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Express.js-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## The problem it solves

Traditional Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA) follows a fixed schedule: buy a predetermined amount at a predetermined time. This creates two problems—**capital reserved for future purchases may remain idle**, while scheduled purchases can still occur during periods of high volatility, poor liquidity, excessive slippage, or unfavorable execution conditions.

**DCAURA** turns DCA into a **yield-aware, adaptive capital-allocation system**.

Instead of blindly executing every scheduled purchase, DCAURA continuously evaluates **market conditions, execution costs, available liquidity, yield opportunity, DCA urgency, and accumulated DCA drift** to determine whether to:

* **FULL BUY** when execution conditions are favorable
* **PARTIAL BUY** when only part of the allocation is economically justified
* **RECOVERY BUY** to responsibly recover from previous delays
* **WAIT** when waiting is more efficient
* **SAFETY HOLD** when hard market-safety conditions are violated

When DCAURA waits, eligible reserved capital can remain productive through an **ERC-4626-compatible yield mechanism**, rather than unnecessarily sitting idle. Only the capital required for an eligible execution is withdrawn, while missed allocations are tracked as **DCA drift** and can be recovered within predefined limits.

The system is deliberately **bounded**: it does not attempt to predict or freely time the market. The off-chain decision engine recommends an action, while **on-chain smart-contract guardrails retain final authority over the user's capital**, enforcing execution limits, liquidity constraints, market safety, authorization, replay protection, and DCA objectives.

**In short, DCAURA makes recurring investment more capital-efficient, adaptive, explainable, and safer—without turning DCA into an unrestricted trading strategy.**

**Challenges we ran into**

Building DCAURA required coordinating an adaptive decision engine with strict on-chain financial constraints.

The biggest challenge was ensuring that the off-chain EVS engine could recommend adaptive DCA actions without gaining unrestricted control over user funds. We solved this by separating **decision-making from enforcement**: the backend calculates recommendations, while the `DCAObligationManager` independently validates authorization, nonce, tranche limits, available capital, DCA drift, market safety, and execution constraints.

A major technical hurdle occurred during **Uniswap v4 integration**. Our initial implementation interpreted the signed `BalanceDelta` values incorrectly. The real `PoolManager` uses specific signed delta conventions for tokens owed to and received from the pool, which differed from our mock implementation. We identified the mismatch through real PoolManager integration testing, corrected the hook's accounting logic, and verified the atomic execution flow.

We also had to resolve the conflict between **DCA deadlines and unsafe market conditions**. Rather than forcing an execution simply because a deadline was reached, we implemented a Safety Hold mechanism: if market validation fails because of excessive slippage, TWAP deviation, or stale data, the transaction reverts and capital remains protected.

Finally, we needed to demonstrate the system reliably without falsely presenting simulated infrastructure as production infrastructure. We introduced explicit **DEMO, SIMULATED, LOCAL, and ON-CHAIN** states so judges can clearly distinguish what is implemented from what is still a prototype or roadmap feature.

> Don’t Just DCA. Think Before You Buy

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

The issue it resolves

Even in unfavourable market situations, traditional DCA invests a certain amount at predetermined periods. Buying at periods of high volatility, low liquidity, or unfavourable prices may result from this.

Before making an investment decision, AdaptiveYield DCA integrates market conditions, DCA regulations, and yield information to make DCA safer and more intelligent.

📊 Unfavourable market conditions: postpones the purchase and retains money in the yield vault. Positive circumstances: completes the intended transaction.
⚖️ Moderate conditions: executes a portion of the investment rather than the entire amount. 🔒 Limits like maximum allocation, execution quantity, maximum delay, and on-chain validation are enforced by safety.

To put it simply, DCA is changed from "buy automatically no matter what" to "analyse first, then decide whether to buy, partially buy, or wait."

**Challenges we ran into**

Integrating the Decision Engine, Yield Vault, Execution Manager, backend scheduler, and frontend into a dependable workflow proved to be the most difficult task.

Because a botched swap must also undo the vault withdrawal and accounting adjustments, atomic execution was challenging. This was resolved by adding specific rollback tests and maintaining execution within a single EVM transaction.

Another significant obstacle was security. We had to stop the backend from using an infinite amount of money. By maintaining the backend non-custodial and requiring the Execution Manager to enforce all on-chain constraints, we were able to resolve this issue.

Because the same work may run twice, scheduler idempotency was problematic. This was resolved via duplicate checks and deterministic job IDs.

In order to safely and successfully test the entire three-day DCA operation, we finally developed deterministic mock market circumstances and Anvil time manipulation.
