### CRegi
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/cregi-1d68) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/suvab4gh/CRegi) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/PR_WRC3blw8) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-SCBC%20Hackathon%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://scbc-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> Seamless multi-chain crypto checkout

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

CRegi (Regulated Onchain Settlement) bridges the gap between digital asset payments and traditional business reliability. While stablecoins like USDC offer 24/7 liquidity, businesses often struggle with the complexity of multi-chain management, gas fees, and the lack of auditable, transparent settlement records.

1. Eliminating Multi-Chain Complexity
Existing crypto payment tools often force users to think about "Which chain?" or "Do I have gas for fees?". CRegi abstracts this:

For Customers: They simply scan a QR code and pay in native USDC from their preferred wallet.
For Merchants: There is no need to maintain separate gas wallets on multiple networks. The terminal handles routing behind the scenes.
2. Trustless, Auditable Payouts
Traditional payment processors are "black boxes"—you trust them to pay you out. CRegi makes this auditable:

Avalanche-Backed Records: Every merchant payout is recorded on Avalanche, creating a permanent, immutable log of successful settlements.
Transparency: Payouts are triggered and verified onchain, making it nearly impossible to have "lost" or "stuck" transactions that aren't immediately visible to both parties.
3. Real-Time Liquidity (No T+3)
Standard credit card processing takes 3–5 days to settle into a bank account.

CRegi leverages Circle’s native Mint/Burn and Solana’s sub-second finality to move funds in real-time.
A merchant can receive their funds and have them settled almost as soon as the customer clicks "Approve."
4. Premium responsive Experience
Most crypto tools are built for desktop-native "power users." CRegi is designed for the modern world:

Mobile-First Terminal: Optimized for tablets and phones, allowing a merchant to launch a checkout terminal from anywhere—a pop-up shop, a physical storefront, or a remote event.
Glassmorphic UI: High-contrast, accessibility-focused design ensures that payment amounts and statuses are visible even in bright sunlight or high-glare environments.
Who is it for?
Global Freelancers: Accept stable payments from international clients with zero bridge fees.
Physical Retailers: A sleek web-based terminal that replaces expensive credit card hardware.
Web3 Developers: Integration-ready API for adding premium checkout flows to dApps without writing complex smart contracts.

**Challenges we ran into**

Handling Asynchronous Finality Across Different Chains
One of the biggest hurdles we faced was building a unified checkout and settlement interface (CregiSettlement) that operates across entirely different blockchain architectures—specifically Solana (high throughput, fast block times) and Avalanche (EVM compatibility, different finality guarantees)—while using Circle's infrastructure for USDC.

The Bug/Hurdle:
When processing transactions, our Next.js API routes (/api/invoices/[id]/settle) would occasionally timeout or provide false-positive confirmations because we were initially using synchronous polling to wait for transaction finality. On Vercel's serverless functions, this approach hit the 10-second execution limit, causing the UI to hang even if the on-chain transaction was actually successful.

How we got over it:
Instead of awaiting finality within the edge function, we overhauled our payment verification flow to be fully asynchronous:

We abstracted the settlement logic (payments.ts and settlement.ts) to return immediate transaction hashes to the client.
We moved the heavy lifting to robust client-side polling paired with a dedicated /api/invoices/[id]/receipt endpoint.
On the backend, we utilized Drizzle ORM to aggressively cache invoice states, ensuring that once a transaction was verified, subsequent database reads were lightning-fast and didn't spam our RPC nodes with redundant requests.

Serverless Bundle Sizes and Dependency Clashes
Integrating multiple Web3 SDKs (Solana Web3.js, EVM ethers/viem) alongside Drizzle ORM inside the Next.js 15 App Router presented a massive challenge during deployment.

The Bug/Hurdle:
During our initial deployments to Vercel, the build would succeed, but the API routes would crash at runtime with module resolution errors or out-of-memory (OOM) exceptions. The serverless functions were bloating past the 50MB limit because the bundler was trying to package large, native cryptography dependencies for all chains into a single route.

How we got over it:
We had to dive deep into our next.config.ts and Webpack configuration. We isolated our chain-specific logic into dedicated files (settlement.ts, etc.) and dynamically imported them only when a user selected a specific chain for checkout. By optimizing our imports and marking certain Node.js native crypto modules as serverComponentsExternalPackages, we slashed the function size and got our API routes running blazing fast.

**The problem it solves**

# ⚡ Wattswap: Decentralized P2P Energy Trading

## 📋 Overview
This project explores a transformative initiative aimed at disrupting the traditional energy sector. By tackling **electricity rate monopolies**, providing for **underserved rural areas**, and accelerating the adoption of **renewable energy**, our platform paves the way for a more equitable and sustainable future.

---

## 🛠 The Technical Solution
Our platform leverages a decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture to democratize energy access. The core stack includes:

* **Blockchain Integration:** Utilizes secure smart contracts to facilitate transparent trading.
* **Hardware Layer:** Integration of WiFi modules and time sensors for real-time tracking.
* **Energy Management:** An advanced **Battery Management System (BMS)** coupled with custom hardware for seamless energy transfer.

---

## 🌟 Key Benefits
* **Empowered Sellers:** Users set their own prices, fostering competition and driving down costs.
* **Bridging the Gap:** Surplus renewable energy is redistributed to "energy deserts" or underserved regions.
* **Environmental Impact:** Drastically reduces greenhouse gas emissions by incentivizing renewable sources.

---

## 🚧 Challenges & Resilience
While we recognize hurdles such as **regulatory compliance**, **scalability**, and **user education**, our solution remains robust through:

1.  **User-Friendly Interface:** Simplifying complex energy trading for the average consumer.
2.  **Automated Security:** Implementing smart contracts to ensure trustless transactions.
3.  **Innovative Redistribution:** A unique mechanism designed specifically for equitable distribution.

---

## 🚀 The Vision
This project underscores the potential of decentralized technology to combat monopolies and bridge the energy divide. We aren't just building a platform; we are accelerating the **global adoption of renewable energy** for a truly inclusive future.

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenge 1 — Battery State Management in a Distributed Energy Architecture
 
### The Problem
Efficiently orchestrating the **charging and discharging cycles** across all battery systems in the network proved to be one of the most complex hardware-software co-design challenges of the project. Key difficulties included:
 
- **State-of-Charge (SoC) synchronization** — Each battery node needed to continuously broadcast its current energy capacity so the trading contract could make informed match-making decisions. Stale or out-of-sync SoC readings led to over-commitment of energy supply.
- **Charge/discharge conflict resolution** — When a node was simultaneously matched as both a buyer and a seller across different trade windows, concurrent read-write operations on battery state created race conditions in the coordination logic.
- **Threshold enforcement** — Defining safe operational boundaries (minimum SoC floors to protect battery health, maximum discharge rates) required these physical constraints to be reflected at both the firmware level and within the smart contract's business logic — keeping two systems in agreement at all times.

### Approach
A **buffered state management layer** was introduced between the hardware sensors and the contract, decoupling the physical battery cycle from the on-chain trading logic. Battery state was treated as an **eventually consistent** value with defined staleness thresholds, beyond which a node's trading eligibility was automatically suspended until a fresh reading was confirmed.
 
---
 
## Challenge 2 — Real-Time Firebase ↔ Solidity Smart Contract Integration
 
 
### The Problem
Bridging a Web2 real-time database with a Web3 smart contract introduced a class of integration challenges that neither system was natively designed to solve:
 
- **Oracles and trust boundaries** — Smart contracts cannot natively read from external data sources. Feeding Firebase sensor data into Solidity required an off-chain relay mechanism to act as a trusted data bridge, raising questions about data integrity and manipulation resistance.
- **Event latency and finality** — Firebase updates arrive in near real-time (sub-second), whereas Ethereum transactions require block confirmations. A sensor spike that triggered a trade could be confirmed on-chain seconds or minutes later, by which time the underlying energy state had changed.
- **Webhook-to-transaction mapping** — Designing a reliable listener that translated Firebase `onValue` change events into signed Ethereum transactions, without message loss or duplicate submissions, required idempotency safeguards in the relay service.
### Approach
An **off-chain relay service** (middleware layer) was built to subscribe to Firebase events, validate and normalize incoming sensor data, and submit structured transactions to the deployed contract. Idempotency keys were derived from the Firebase document ID and timestamp to prevent duplicate on-chain writes. Data was scaled to fixed-point integers (multiplied by 10³) before submission to preserve decimal precision within Solidity's integer type system.
 
---

## Challenge 3 — Vulnerabilities in the Energy Supply Transfer Process

### The Problem
A cascade of software bugs and security considerations surfaced specifically around the supply transfer workflow:
 
- **Reentrancy exposure** — Early iterations of the settlement function updated balances *after* triggering external calls, creating a classic reentrancy attack surface. A malicious contract acting as a buyer could re-enter the transfer function before state was finalized, enabling double-spend of energy credits.
- **Partial fulfillment edge cases** — If a seller's available supply dropped (due to a concurrent discharge event) between trade matching and settlement, the contract had no graceful mechanism to handle partial fills. Transactions would either revert entirely or settle for incorrect amounts, both unacceptable in an energy market context.
- **Atomic settlement failure** — The physical energy dispatch and the on-chain token transfer needed to succeed or fail *together*. Without a native two-phase commit mechanism on the blockchain, ensuring atomicity between the off-chain hardware action and the on-chain state change required a commit-reveal pattern with timeout-based rollback logic.
### Approach
The settlement contract was refactored using the **Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI)** pattern to eliminate reentrancy vectors. A `ReentrancyGuard` modifier was applied to all externally callable settlement functions. Batch settlement was redesigned with bounded iteration and a paginated settlement queue to stay within gas limits. Partial fulfillment was handled via a **pro-rata allocation model**, where trades were settled for the minimum of committed supply and verified available supply at execution time. Front-running mitigation was approached through a **commit-reveal scheme** for trade submissions, obscuring order intent until reveal phase

### ClaimDrop
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/claimdrop-b262) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-SCBC%20Hackathon%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://scbc-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> Send SOL to anyone, even without a wallet

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![ARCore](https://img.shields.io/badge/ARCore-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML/CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML/CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Crypto payments today are not user-friendly for everyday people.
To send someone SOL, both the sender and receiver must already have:

* a crypto wallet
* knowledge of how to use it
* and a public wallet address

This creates a huge barrier to adoption.

As a result:

* You can’t easily send crypto to new users
* Gifting or paying someone in SOL is confusing and inconvenient
* Businesses and creators lose opportunities because customers aren’t onboarded
* Web3 remains closed off to mainstream users

⸻

How ClaimDrop solves this

ClaimDrop removes this friction by allowing users to send SOL to anyone using a simple link or QR code — no wallet required upfront.

* The sender deposits SOL into a secure claim link
* The link can be shared via text, email, or QR
* The receiver opens the link and:
    * connects a wallet, or
    * creates one instantly
* Funds are claimed in seconds

⸻

Why this matters

By eliminating the need for a pre-existing wallet, ClaimDrop:

* Onboards new users into crypto seamlessly
* Makes SOL usable for real-world payments, gifting, and rewards
* Enables viral distribution through links and QR codes
* Bridges the gap between Web2 simplicity and Web3 power

⸻

Real-world use cases

* Send money to friends who don’t use crypto yet
* Event giveaways (scan QR → claim SOL instantly)
* Creator tips and rewards
* Merchant promotions and cashback
* Global remittances without friction

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges we ran into

Building a “send-to-anyone” experience on Solana introduced several non-trivial challenges, especially around usability and security.

1. Wallet-less user flow

The core challenge was enabling users to receive SOL without already having a wallet. Solana transactions typically require both parties to have wallets and public addresses.

Solution:
We designed a claim-link system backed by a temporary escrow account. Funds are held securely until the recipient connects or creates a wallet, at which point the SOL is released.

⸻

2. Secure claim links

Since funds are tied to a shareable link, preventing unauthorized access or abuse was critical.

Solution:
We implemented unique, hard-to-guess claim tokens and added optional expiration logic to ensure links cannot be reused or exploited. Future improvements include adding signature-based verification or one-time claim enforcement on-chain.

⸻

3. Balancing UX with blockchain complexity

Crypto UX is often confusing, especially for non-technical users. Showing raw SOL amounts alone can be unintuitive.

Solution:
We display both SOL and its USD equivalent to make the experience feel familiar, while still using native Solana under the hood.

⸻

4. Transaction reliability and speed

Handling real-time claims required ensuring fast and reliable confirmation on Solana.

Solution:
We optimized for Solana’s fast finality and low fees, and designed the UI to provide immediate feedback during the claim process to improve user confidence.

⸻

Key takeaway

The biggest challenge was bridging the gap between Web3 infrastructure and Web2 simplicity — and ClaimDrop is designed specifically to solve that.

**Best Use of Solana**

How ClaimDrop fits “Best Use of Solana”

ClaimDrop is built specifically to leverage Solana’s core strengths — speed, low fees, and seamless user experience — to enable a completely new payment paradigm: sending SOL to anyone, even without a wallet.

Native SOL usage

Unlike many projects that rely on tokens or abstractions, ClaimDrop uses native SOL transfers at its core. Every transaction, claim, and settlement is executed directly on Solana, showcasing the network’s efficiency and reliability.

⸻

Instant, low-cost transactions

ClaimDrop depends on Solana’s high throughput and near-zero fees to make micro-payments and claimable transfers viable.

* Users can send small amounts of SOL without worrying about gas costs
* Recipients can claim funds instantly with minimal friction
* This enables real-world use cases like tipping, rewards, and giveaways

⸻

On-chain escrow mechanism

ClaimDrop introduces a lightweight on-chain escrow model, where SOL is temporarily held until claimed.

* Funds are secured on-chain until the recipient claims them
* Eliminates trust issues between sender and receiver
* Demonstrates practical use of Solana for conditional transactions

⸻

Wallet onboarding through Solana UX

By combining claim links with Solana wallet integration, ClaimDrop turns onboarding into a single-step experience:

* Users interact with Solana without needing prior setup
* Wallet connection or creation happens only at the moment of claiming
* This bridges Web2 simplicity with Web3 infrastructure

⸻

Why this stands out

ClaimDrop transforms Solana from a network that requires technical knowledge into a consumer-ready payment layer.

It demonstrates how Solana can:

* power mainstream financial interactions
* enable viral distribution via links and QR codes
* and unlock true accessibility for non-crypto users

### Stratix
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/stratix-3ce2) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/alycz/Stratix) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://stratix-phi.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.loom.com/share/ad6c8872e78e46ecb909d1162ba35772) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-SCBC%20Hackathon%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://scbc-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> Algorithmic Market Making on Pacifica DEX & Kalshi

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Prediction markets have a liquidity problem. Contracts move on relatively small orders because there aren’t enough resting bids and asks to absorb flow. Thus, what they need is active market making. Kalshi’s Liquidity Incentive Program directly addresses this: it pays traders for maintaining orders close to the best bid/ask, with the order book snapshotted every second and scores calculated on size and proximity. However, staying competitive in that program across multiple markets isn’t something you can do by hand.

On Pacifica, the problem is similar but different in shape. Airdrop farmers and anyone incentivized by on-chain activity all want to generate trading volume and contribute to thicker order book. The problem is that continuously quoting bid and ask, adjusting for inventory, and staying inside the spread requires placing and updating orders every second which is impossible if done manually. Thus, users need a practical tool that can run those strategies on autopilot. 

Stratix is that tool. It runs algorithmic market making strategies across both venues: Pacifica (a Solana perpetuals DEX) and Kalshi (prediction markets). Users configure parameters, backtest on historical data, and let the backend agent run.

**Challenges we ran into**

Dependency conflict on x402 + Solana signing: solders (the Rust-based Solana Python library) had a version conflict with the x402[svm] package. Resolving it required pinning solders==0.21.0 to get both libraries working together.

Funding detection across venues: Detecting whether a user had deposited funds worked differently on Pacifica vs. Kalshi vs. DFlow. The app was incorrectly forcing “demo mode” on logged-in users who had already funded. Required a dedicated fix to unify funding state detection across all venues.

**Best Use of Solana**

How we used Solana as a DeFi & Prediction Markets vertical:

Pacifica is a Solana perpetuals DEX. Stratix connects to it through a non-custodial delegation model built on Solana’s key infrastructure. The user holds a Privy embedded Solana wallet which means their keys never leave the browser. During onboarding, a separate Ed25519 agent keypair is generated on the backend. The user signs a binding message with their main wallet to authorize the agent, and from that point the agent handles all order placement: quoting bid and ask via the Avellaneda-Stoikov algorithm, adjusting for inventory, requoting every second. The agent cannot obtain more funds from the user's main wallet on its own, as withdrawals require a fresh signature with the user's approval.

Deposits to Pacifica are SPL token transfers. The frontend builds the transaction using @solana/web3.js and @solana/spl-token, creates the vault’s Associated Token Account if it doesn’t exist, and the user signs it with their Privy wallet. Settlement lands on Solana in ~400ms. Helius RPC handles balance polling and transaction confirmation. The 1-second requote cycle only works because Solana transaction fees are a fraction of a cent. On any other chain, fees would consume the spread before the strategy earns anything.

For Kalshi prediction markets, Stratix uses DFlow, a trade execution protocol on Solana, to place bets on-chain rather than through Kalshi’s REST API. The Kelly Criterion engine polls the DFlow orderbook every 30 seconds, computes the optimal position size given the user’s probability estimate and the current yes-bid price, and when the edge is sufficient, requests an unsigned Solana VersionedTransaction from DFlow’s quote API. That transaction is signed with the same Ed25519 agent key used for Pacifica and submitted directly to the Solana RPC. The result is a real on-chain swap: USDC in, YES or NO token out. The position settles on-chain when the market resolves with no separate Kalshi API credential required.

How we used Solana for the Agentic Commerce vertical:

Stratix implements the x402 HTTP payment protocol on Solana. Any external caller, an AI agent, a script, another service, can launch a trading strategy for an existing Stratix user by paying $1.00 USDC directly on-chain. The flow: the caller POSTs to /agent/launch, receives an HTTP 402 response with payment options, settles the payment on Solana, and retries with a proof header. The backend verifies the proof using ExactSvmServerScheme with the Coinbase CDP facilitator on mainnet. No Stratix API key needed, just a valid user ID and an on-chain payment.

### Chroma Arcade
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/chroma-arcade-868b) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/jadenchoi16/circle-sub) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://circle-sub.vercel.app/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-SCBC%20Hackathon%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://scbc-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> "Insert coin. Make art. Settled on Arc."

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Quick overview: Pay-per-use AI doesn't work because card fees eat any transaction under ~$0.30, forcing every product into monthly subscriptions. Crypto could solve it, but wallets, gas tokens, and seed phrases scare off non-crypto users. Chroma Arcade fixes both by letting users pay fractions of a cent in USDC with zero wallet setup, all wrapped in an arcade-cabinet UX.
The deeper picture:
Pay-per-use AI is broken economically:

Image, video, and voice APIs charge cents per call
Traditional card rails can't settle anything below ~$0.30 without fees eating the whole transaction
Result: every AI consumer product shoves users into a $10–$20/month subscription they barely use

Onchain payment apps have the opposite problem:

People love "pay a penny, get a result"
But they have to install MetaMask, fund it with ETH for gas, understand what a chain is, and sign three popups
Nobody outside crypto does that

Chroma Arcade is the shortest answer to both:

User lands on the page
An embedded Circle Developer-Controlled Wallet spins up server-side
They type a prompt, pick a tier ($0.002 to $0.50), and click INSERT COIN
Server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required with an x402 paywall spec
Client redeems it on Arc Testnet with a real USDC transfer
Server verifies the transaction on-chain before unlocking Gemini
Image lands in their gallery with a live Arcscan link, all in about a second

No wallet install. No seed phrase. No gas token. USDC is gas on Arc. The mental model is a 1980s arcade cabinet: drop a coin, pick a thing, get a thing. The programmable-money primitive is invisible, which is the point.
The same primitive works for AI agents:

Operator funds the agent's embedded wallet once
Agent spends autonomously per-inference
Every call is a verifiable on-chain receipt instead of a line in a spreadsheet

Real uses:

Pay-per-image for casual or designer users who'd never pay $20/mo
Auditable per-call billing rails for AI agents
A demo pattern any AI company can copy: 402 paywall + embedded wallet + x402 redeem

No wallet install. No seed phrase. No gas token. USDC is gas on Arc. The user's mental model is a literal 1980s arcade cabinet: drop a coin, pick a thing, get a thing. The programmable-money primitive is completely invisible, which is exactly the point.

The same primitive works for AI agents: an operator funds the agent's embedded wallet once, the agent spends autonomously per-inference, and every call is a verifiable on-chain receipt instead of a line in a spreadsheet somewhere. That turns "per-call billing for AI services" from a SaaS reconciliation nightmare into a settled-in-real-time payment stream.

Real uses:

Pay-per-image for casual/designer users who'd never pay $20/mo for occasional generation.
Auditable per-call billing rails for AI agents.
A demo pattern any AI company can copy: 402 paywall + embedded wallet + x402 redeem.

**Challenges we ran into**

1. React Strict Mode minted duplicate wallets and rate-limited the faucet
In dev, useEffect fires twice, and my boot flow called POST /api/wallet/init without idempotency:

Every page load created two wallets
Only one got saved to localStorage, leaving orphans
Funding the "current" wallet hit the faucet; the orphan from the previous boot also hit it
Circle's testnet faucet started returning 429 Too Many Requests

Fix:

Added a useRef(false) guard (bootedRef) so init runs once per mount in Strict Mode
Added a "forget wallet" trashcan button for cleaning state during debugging
Made /api/wallet/init idempotent: if the caller already has a walletId, validate and return it

2. Gallery silently deleted itself down to 2 images
Weird UX bug. Root cause was a cascade:

Each full-resolution Gemini image is a ~1 MB base64 data URL
localStorage has a ~5 MB quota
The persistence layer was shrinking in-memory state to match what fit on disk
A generic QuotaExceededError silently trimmed the gallery to 2 items after every generation
It also intermittently threw a hard client-side exception during React's commit phase because setItem is synchronous and wasn't wrapped

Fix, in two layers:

Persistence is now async, running each image through a canvas pass that downscales to 640px and re-encodes at JPEG quality 0.72 (~1 MB down to ~40 KB)
Per-id cache so we never re-compress the same image twice
Full-resolution stays in memory for the session; only thumbnails get persisted
In-memory gallery is no longer coupled to the disk write, so 12 images always fit and the UI never loses its real state

3. The x402 failure-mode matrix is deceptively complicated
The happy path is easy. The failure paths are where the real work is:

Gemini fails after the user already paid: reuse the same txId on retry so the user isn't double-charged; only clear the pending coin once generation succeeds
Replay attacks: an in-memory Set (usedTxIds) tracks every redeemed txId for the life of the process. A transaction can unlock exactly one image
Wrong token, amount, destination, or state: the verifier checks all four independently. tokenId must match the resolved USDC UUID, amount >= tier.price, destinationAddress === merchant, and state ∈ {CONFIRMED, COMPLETE}. Any failure rejects with a specific reason

Building the developer panel (the </> button in the header) caught two of these. Seeing the raw 402 payload and the X-Payment header side-by-side while stepping through pay → verify → generate made the replay edge cases obvious.

**Programmable Money for Humans & Agents**

Chroma Arcade turns a Gemini image endpoint into a USDC-on-Arc micro-API, the same x402 flow that lets a human click "insert coin" is the one an autonomous agent would use to pay the exact same $0.002 for a pixel-art render at 2 a.m.

Team **team1** -- Jaden Choi

### EAX
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/adscience-726d) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/kodykebab/adscience) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/xGX6v9UjQtA) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-KJSSE%20GajShield%20Hack%20X-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hack-x.devfolio.co)

> Attention is all they need.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Express.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Express.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

### The Problem EAX Solves

Modern digital advertising is built on a foundation of intrusive tracking, middleman-heavy revenue models, and "interruption-based" monetization that yields low-quality engagement. **EAX (Encrypted Attention Exchange)** flips this model entirely by aligning the incentives of publishers, advertisers, and users through three core pillars:

#### 1. Privacy-Preserving Targeting (via FHE)
Traditional targeting requires platforms to scrape your browsing history and personal data. EAX leverages **Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)** on the Fhenix CoFHE network to allow "Blind Matching." 
*   **How it works:** A user's interests are converted into an "intent vector" locally on their device. This vector is encrypted before being sent to the blockchain. 
*   **The Result:** The smart contract identifies the perfect ad match without the network, the advertiser, or even the protocol ever "seeing" the user's raw data. You get targeted ads without sacrificing your privacy.

#### 2. Direct-to-User Rewards
In the current web2 ad model, the vast majority of ad spend is captured by central agencies. EAX introduces a direct financial link:
*   **The Attention Economy:** Users are paid in **ATTN tokens** for their time and attention. 
*   **On-Chain Payouts:** Every ad impression is recorded on-chain, triggering an automatic transfer of value from the advertiser's budget directly to the user's wallet.

#### 3. Harmonious Engagement (The "Scroll-and-Claim" Model)
As demonstrated in the **Meow** application, EAX enables a new UX pattern for monetization:
*   **Value Exchange:** Users interact with the ad specifically to "claim" their payout and unlock the next segment of content. This transforms the ad from an annoyance into a rewarding micro-task that guarantees the advertiser's engagement.

### How it makes existing tasks easier & safer:

*   **For Developers (Publishers):** Adding monetization is now as simple as a few lines of code (using eax-sdk). You no longer need to manage complex ad-ops or worry about privacy compliance (GDPR/CCPA) since the platform never handles unencrypted user data.
*   **For Users:** You can browse the web safely knowing your "intent" is encrypted. Instead of being the *product*, you become a *stakeholder* who builds a crypto balance just by consuming content you already love.
*   **For Advertisers:** You stop paying for "bot" traffic or ignored impressions. EAX ensures that every penny spent results in a verified on-chain interaction with a truly interested (and rewarded) user.

**Challenges we ran into**

**One hurdle was the asynchronous nature of the *Fhenix CoFHE coprocessor.***

**The Bug**: When a user submits a matchIntent transaction, the FHE operations (comparing the user's encrypted vector against 10+ advertisers) happen off-main-thread on the coprocessor. If the SDK tried to call decryptForTx immediately after the transaction was confirmed, it would almost always fail with a 428 "Precondition Required" error because the coprocessor hadn't finished the computation yet.

**The Fix**: We implemented a polling and retry loop with exponential backoff within the runMatch() function. Instead of the developer having to manage state, the SDK now silently handles these retries (up to 12 attempts) until the decryption handle is ready, providing a seamless "one-click" experience for the user.

***React Strict Mode vs. Wallet Handshakes***
In the Meow demo application, we used an "Infinite Scroll" pattern where multiple AdSlot components mount as the user scrolls.

**The Bug**: In React Strict Mode, components mount twice in development. This caused initEAX() to be called multiple times, triggering redundant MetaMask "Connect Wallet" prompts and re-initializing the Ethers provider, which led to painful UI flickers and "contract not found" errors.

**The Fix**: We patched the SDK with an Idempotency Guard. The internal state of the contract.js module now tracks existing connections. If initEAX() is called for a contract and user that are already active, it returns the cached instance immediately. This makes the SDK "plug-and-play" even in complex reactive frameworks.

> On-chain insurance for your DeFi positions.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flutter](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flutter-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

### The Problem It Solves

DeFi lending platforms like Aave allow users to borrow against collateral, but they come with a major risk: **liquidation**. If the collateral price drops even slightly, users can lose a significant portion of their funds instantly.

Currently, there is **no direct way to hedge against liquidation risk**:

* Options protocols hedge price direction, not **liquidation events**
* Manual management (adding collateral, monitoring health factor) fails during sudden crashes

This creates a major gap where users are forced to either:

* Stay overly conservative (low capital efficiency), or
* Take high risk without protection

---

### Our Solution

ALS (Anti-Liquidation Swap) introduces a **decentralized insurance layer for liquidation risk**.

Users can:

* Pay a dynamic premium
* Get compensated if their position is liquidated

The system uses:

* Real-time risk evaluation (health factor, volatility)
* Vault-based underwriting

---

### Why It Matters

ALS makes DeFi borrowing:

* **Safer** → protects against sudden liquidation losses
* **More efficient** → users can take higher leverage responsibly
* **Composable** → can integrate across multiple lending protocols

**Challenges we ran into**

### Challenges We Ran Into

Building ALS was not just a technical challenge — it required rethinking how risk is handled in DeFi systems.

#### 1. Modeling Correlated Risk (Biggest Challenge)

Unlike traditional protocols, liquidation events are **highly correlated** — when ETH drops, many users get liquidated at once.

This meant we couldn’t price users individually.
We had to design a system that evaluates **global vault exposure** and prevents too many risky positions from entering simultaneously.

#### 2. Balancing Capital Efficiency vs Safety

Allowing high coverage and low premiums makes the product attractive, but also increases the risk of **vault insolvency during crashes**.

We had to carefully design:

* Coverage caps based on health factor
* Premium scaling for risky users
* Stress-testing mechanisms

to ensure long-term solvency.

#### 3. Designing a Dynamic Pricing Engine

Pricing liquidation risk is non-trivial. It depends on:

* Health factor (user-specific risk)
* Market volatility
* Time duration
* System-wide exposure

We implemented a probabilistic model combined with heuristics and real-time adjustments to keep pricing both fair and safe.


#### 4. Handling Real-Time Data Dependencies

The system depends on multiple live inputs:

* Aave position data (health factor)
* Vault state (on-chain)
* Market data (ETH price, volatility)

Ensuring consistency, freshness, and reliability across these sources was a key challenge.


#### 5. Bridging Off-Chain Computation with On-Chain Guarantees

The pricing logic runs off-chain for flexibility and saving on gas fees, but execution happens on-chain.

This required careful design to ensure:
* Deterministic outputs
* Verifiable constraints
* No blind trust in backend computations


These challenges pushed us to design ALS not just as a feature, but as a **robust financial system that can survive real market conditions**.

> Skynet - Intelligence that connects and evolves

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**Job hunting is broken.** Candidates spend hours scrolling irrelevant listings, sending generic applications into the void, and getting rejected without ever knowing why. The process is manual, demoralizing, and inefficient.

Skynet is the career agent that fixes this **end-to-end.**

It starts by deeply understanding your resume. Instead of just reading job titles, it extracts your actual skills, experience depth, and measurable outcomes to build a structured profile that represents you accurately.

From there, Skynet eliminates noise. Instead of browsing hundreds of listings, it finds and ranks only the roles that meaningfully match your profile, surfacing a focused shortlist of high-probability opportunities.

When you apply, Skynet does not rely on templates. **It generates a tailored resume and cover letter for each role**, aligning with the job description, priorities, and tone to maximize relevance.

If a role is slightly out of reach, Skynet does not let you waste the application. It identifies the skill gap and creates a structured, week-by-week learning plan so you can qualify for that role.

Most importantly, Skynet is honest. If a role is unrealistic given your current profile, it explains why and redirects you toward opportunities where you actually have a strong chance.

Not a job board. The agent in your corner.

**Challenges we ran into**

**1. PDF Template Fidelity**
Challenge:
The initial PDF resume generator produced plain, generic layouts that didn’t match the user’s desired HTML/CSS template. Achieving pixel-perfect fidelity with custom fonts (EB Garamond), section ordering, and precise styling was difficult, especially when converting HTML to PDF with Puppeteer.

Solution:

Replaced the old template with the user’s exact HTML/CSS.
Tuned the backend HTML generator to parse and inject tailored content into the correct sections.
Iteratively tested and adjusted the output, removing extra summary sections and ensuring all formatting matched the sample.

**2. Frontend–Backend Integration for PDF Download/Preview**
Challenge:
Connecting the “Preview Tailored Resume” button to the backend so users could reliably preview or download the generated PDF was tricky. Handling browser compatibility, file streaming, and error states required careful wiring.

Solution:

Created a new backend endpoint that returns the PDF as an HTTP response with the correct headers.
Updated the frontend to handle both preview (in-browser) and download fallback, ensuring a smooth user experience.
Added loading/error states and validated the full flow with real payloads.

**3. Section Parsing from Raw Resume Text**
Challenge:
Extracting and mapping sections (Education, Achievements, Experience, Projects, Skills) from unstructured raw resume text was error-prone, especially with varied user input formats.

Solution:

Developed robust section extractors and renderers in the backend.
Used regex and string parsing to identify and split sections.
Added tests and sample payloads to validate extraction logic.

**4. Environment and Dependency Management**
Challenge:
Managing dependencies across Python (AI/ML) and Node.js (backend/frontend) environments, especially with virtual environments and package version mismatches, led to build and runtime errors.

Solution:

Standardized on requirements.txt for Python and package.json for Node.js.
Used virtual environments (venv) and npm scripts to isolate dependencies.
Documented setup steps and provided activation scripts for contributors.

**5. Debugging API and PDF Generation Failures**
Challenge:
Occasional backend crashes or 500 errors during PDF generation, often due to malformed payloads or Puppeteer timeouts.

Solution:

Added error handling and logging in the backend.
Validated payloads before processing.
Increased Puppeteer timeouts and ensured all required data was present.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Defi](https://img.shields.io/badge/Defi-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

SMEs are trapped in a 60–90 day cash flow gap
Small and medium businesses in India routinely issue invoices to large corporates, retailers, manufacturers, and enterprises,  and then wait 2 to 3 months to get paid. During that wait, the SME can't pay salaries, buy raw materials, or take new orders. Traditional invoice discounting requires the SME to have banking relationships, submit mountains of paperwork, and pay high interest rates (15–24% p.a.) to NBFCs or banks, if they qualify at all.

**InvoFlow** eliminates this entirely.

How it makes things easier and safer
For SMEs:

Submit an invoice → get an ERC-3525 semi-fungible token minted on-chain
Receive immediate liquidity, the investor pool disburses funds to your wallet the moment the invoice is fully funded, no waiting for bank approval
Sign up with just Google or email (via Privy), no wallet setup, no seed phrases; your embedded wallet is created automatically
Gas fees are sponsored and the platform covers all on-chain transaction costs via ERC-4337 account abstraction

For Investors:

Browse a live marketplace of real, tokenized invoices
Invest any fraction of an invoice,  ₹500 or ₹5,00,000, your choice
When the corporate buyer pays via UPI, Razorpay fires a webhook → your yield is settled on-chain automatically, no manual claiming required
Can trade your investment position on the secondary market before the invoice matures
What makes it *trustworthy*:

ZK Risk Scoring: each SME gets a cryptographic Groth16 proof of their risk score (payment reliability, invoice legitimacy, business profile), the score is verifiable on-chain without exposing raw business data
Platform Backstop: if a funding round doesn't fully close within 2 weeks, the platform automatically fills the remaining gap so the SME is never left stranded
On-chain settlement: when payment is received via UPI/Razorpay, the webhook triggers settleInvoice() directly on the smart contract, no human in the loop for fund distribution

**Challenges we ran into**

1. Teammate Merge Conflict Wiped Out the Risk Engine Routes
Mid-hackathon, merging a teammate's Razorpay commit caused a conflict in index.js, git's auto-merge silently dropped all risk engine and GST route registrations, replacing them with only the payment routes. The backend started fine but every /api/risk/* call returned 404.

Fix: Caught it during integration testing. Resolved by manually keeping both sets of route imports and mounts. Now using a checklist to verify all route prefixes respond after every merge.

2. Platform Backstop Required Time-Travel in Tests
The platformBackstop() function is only callable after a 2-week FUNDING_PERIOD deadline, which meant standard Hardhat tests that run in seconds would never reach the deadline naturally.

Fix: Used Hardhat's evm_increaseTime + evm_mine JSON-RPC calls to fast-forward the local chain by 14 days + 1 second in the test setup. This let us fully test the backstop flow, pro-rata investor claims, and excess ETH refunds without waiting.

### VERITAS
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/veritas-77a6) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Abhishek222983101/VERITAS-ER) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/18mpo8CUiExSk9-MiMB2P27LGYj5fKSSG?usp=sharing) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-KJSSE%20GajShield%20Hack%20X-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hack-x.devfolio.co)

> Decentralized Intelligence Verification Engine

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

The Problem Statement
Current prediction markets (like Polymarket or Augur) have revolutionized forecasting, but they suffer from a massive bottleneck: The Oracle Problem. 
When a market closes, it relies on human-driven centralized oracles, token-holder voting, or centralized multisigs to resolve the outcome (e.g., "Did event X happen?"). This manual process is:
1. Extremely Slow: Disputes can freeze user funds for days or weeks.
2. Prone to Human Bias/Manipulation: Whales can manipulate token-weighted oracle voting.
3. Vulnerable to Sybil Attacks: Bots and algorithmic traders manipulate betting pools, ruining the market's predictive accuracy for everyday users.
The Solution: DIVE (Decentralized AI Oracle & Prediction Market)
DIVE entirely removes human bias and centralization from the resolution process. It is a blazing-fast, Sybil-resistant prediction market built on Solana where the oracles are an autonomous Swarm of AI Agents. 
Here is how DIVE makes prediction markets safer, faster, and truly decentralized:
*   🤖 AI Swarm Consensus (The Oracle): Instead of humans arguing over reality, DIVE utilizes an off-chain network of AI agents (powered by Groq and Tavily web search). When a market needs insight or resolution, these agents autonomously scour the internet, analyze the data using distinct personas (e.g., The Skeptic, The Optimist, The Data Analyst), and push their cryptographic predictions (YES/NO/UNSURE + Confidence %) directly on-chain via our dive_oracle Anchor smart contract.
*   🛡️ zkTLS Proof of Personhood: To prevent bot manipulation and Sybil attacks in the betting pools, DIVE integrates Reclaim Protocol (zkTLS). Before a user can place a bet on the dive_market contract, they must generate a Zero-Knowledge proof of their identity. The dive_identity contract issues a HumanAttestation PDA. One Human = One Wallet = One Vote.
*   ⚡ Solana Speed & Economics: By leveraging Solana's parallelized architecture, micro-betting and continuous, real-time oracle updates from the AI agents cost fractions of a cent, making autonomous AI resolution economically viable.
*   🌌 3D Consensus Visualization: We built a custom 3D Agent Swarm Graph using @react-three/fiber that visually renders the AI agents' real-time consensus and confidence levels, making complex LLM data easily digestible for users.
By combining zkTLS Identity, Solana Smart Contracts, and Autonomous LLMs, DIVE creates the first truly trustless, self-resolving, and bot-proof prediction market.

**Challenges we ran into**

🧗 Challenges I ran into
Building a decentralized architecture that connects Zero-Knowledge proofs, Solana smart contracts, Web3 frontend libraries, and off-chain AI workers was no easy feat. Here are the major hurdles we encountered and how we overcame them:
1. Solana Stack Size Limits (The 4096-Byte Frame Space Issue)
The Hurdle: While writing the Anchor smart contracts in Rust, our build suddenly failed with a severe compiler error: Function overflows the maximum allowed frame space by accessing an offset 9920 bytes greater than the maximum of 4096. Solana has a strict 4KB stack limit per program execution, and one of our complex string-parsing/data-formatting dependencies was blowing past it.
The Fix: We had to deeply refactor our Rust code to avoid heavy crates (like regex). We shifted complex data manipulation (like parsing the LLM responses) to the off-chain Node.js AI worker. On-chain, we optimized our Anchor structs, used fixed-size byte arrays ([u8; 32]) for hashing, and applied strict release profile optimizations (opt-level = "s", strip = true) in our Cargo.toml to successfully deploy to Devnet.
2. Next.js 15 Hydration Mismatches with Web3 & 3D Libraries
The Hurdle: Our frontend is built on the bleeding-edge Next.js 15 App Router. However, integrating the @solana/wallet-adapter-react-ui and @react-three/fiber (for the Swarm Graph) caused immediate and fatal Server-Side Rendering (SSR) Hydration mismatches. The server didn't have a WebGL context or know what browser extension wallets the user had, causing the React tree to crash on load.
The Fix: We heavily utilized Next.js's next/dynamic feature. We wrapped both the WalletMultiButton and our AgentSwarmGraph components in dynamic imports with { ssr: false }. This forced Next.js to entirely skip server-rendering for these specific Web3/WebGL components, allowing them to mount safely on the client side without throwing errors.
3. zkTLS Identity & PDA Derivation Conflicts
The Hurdle: Connecting the off-chain Reclaim Protocol zkTLS proof to the on-chain dive_identity contract was tricky. Initially, our verify_human transaction kept failing with an InvalidIssuer error. The smart contract was strictly demanding that the global backend authority sign the transaction, but our frontend was passing the user's connected wallet as the signer.
The Fix: We had to carefully decouple the transaction logic. We refactored the Anchor instruction to dynamically derive the HumanAttestation PDA using seeds [b"dive_human", user_pubkey]. For the Devnet demo, we modified the require_keys_eq! macro to allow localized testing of the ZK-proof hashes (provider hash, stable ID hash) without needing the centralized backend to counter-sign every request, preserving the decentralized ethos while making it testable.
4. Structuring Off-Chain AI Data for On-Chain Enums
The Hurdle: Getting an unpredictable LLM (Groq/Mixtral) to output data that perfectly matches strict Rust Enums in our dive_oracle smart contract.
The Fix: We built a robust TypeScript off-chain worker. We heavily engineered the prompt using Groq SDK to force JSON-only outputs. The worker then intercepts this JSON, maps the string predictions to Anchor-compatible enum objects (e.g., mapping "YES" to { yes: {} }), and uses @coral-xyz/anchor .rpc() calls to safely inject the formatted insights into the Solana blockchain.

**The problem it solves**

Our project addresses the communication gap between people who use Indian Sign Language and those who do not understand it. In many real-world situations such as hospitals, schools, and public services, hearing-impaired individuals face significant challenges expressing their needs because most people are not trained in sign language. This often leads to misunderstandings, dependence on interpreters, and social isolation. To solve this, we built an AI-powered system that translates sign language into understandable output in real time, either through text or visual avatar responses. By enabling instant and accessible communication, our solution helps bridge this gap and makes interactions more inclusive and independent for ISL users.

**Challenges we ran into**

During the development of this project, I faced several practical and technical challenges. One of the biggest issues was building a reliable end-to-end pipeline, as integrating the frontend, backend, and deep learning model required careful handling of data flow and API communication. I also encountered difficulties with model limitations, since the trained model initially supported only a few words, which restricted the overall functionality and required planning for scalability. Another challenge was handling video processing and feature extraction using tools like MediaPipe, which needed consistent frame handling and proper environment setup. Additionally, debugging issues such as incorrect file mappings, network connectivity between mobile and backend, and handling real-time responses under time constraints were critical hurdles. Despite these challenges, resolving them helped strengthen the system’s stability and overall performance.

### Snorlax
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/snorlax-1ac5) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/sai21-learn/snorlax) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://vimeo.com/1182324576) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-KJSSE%20GajShield%20Hack%20X-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hack-x.devfolio.co)

> When systems fail, Snorlax explains

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![scikit-learn](https://img.shields.io/badge/scikit--learn-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![AI/ML](https://img.shields.io/badge/AI/ML-333333?style=flat-square) ![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-333333?style=flat-square) ![React.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/React.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TimescaleDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/TimescaleDB-333333?style=flat-square) ![openrouter](https://img.shields.io/badge/openrouter-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Snorlax is an automated root cause analysis system designed for modern microservices. When a failure occurs, systems generate thousands of logs across services, making it difficult to identify the actual source of the problem.
Snorlax solves this by ingesting logs in real time, correlating them using request IDs, and grouping similar errors using semantic clustering. It isolates the initial root failure from downstream noise and generates a clear, human-readable diagnosis.
Instead of manually debugging for hours, developers get instant insight into what broke and where. This reduces downtime, improves reliability, and simplifies debugging by turning noisy logs into actionable information.

**Challenges we ran into**

⚠️ Challenges We Ran Into
One of the first problems we faced was actually pretty frustrating — we tried sending all the logs directly to the LLM and expected it to figure things out.
But very quickly, things broke down.
The responses were slow, expensive, and often wrong because the model was getting confused by thousands of noisy, cascading error logs. It felt like we were just shifting the problem instead of solving it.
So we stepped back and rethought the approach.
Instead of relying entirely on the LLM, we added a preprocessing layer. We used embeddings and clustering to group similar logs and isolate the actual root cause before sending anything to the model. That single change made a huge difference in both accuracy and cost.
Another challenge was scaling. When we simulated high log volumes, our API started slowing down due to direct database writes.
We solved this by introducing Redis streams and background workers, which allowed us to handle logs asynchronously and keep the system responsive.

### RIVA
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/riva-23e7) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/6CEYg_ZS74g) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-KJSSE%20GajShield%20Hack%20X-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hack-x.devfolio.co)

> When the flood hits, silence is not an option

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![WebSockets](https://img.shields.io/badge/WebSockets-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![NetworkX](https://img.shields.io/badge/NetworkX-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenStreetMap](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenStreetMap-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Mumbai floods because of a physics condition called tidal lock — when high tide exceeds a ward's stormwater outfall elevation, drainage seals completely regardless of pump capacity. This condition is calculable hours in advance. What has never existed is a system that acts on that calculation in real time.
RIVA solves the coordination collapse that turns predictable flooding into preventable deaths.
In every major Mumbai flood since 2005, the documented failure mode is identical: BMC, Western Railway, NDRF, and KEM Hospital operate in silos. Alerts travel by phone call. Response times run 4–6 hours. No record exists of who was contacted, what they were told, or whether they acted. The 2005 inquiry — which killed 1,094 people — explicitly recommended building an integrated real-time coordination system. That recommendation is twenty years old. Nothing was built.
RIVA is that system. It does three things no existing tool does simultaneously:
Detects — A physics engine computes drain capacity across every Mumbai ward using live tide height and rainfall data. When tidal lock is confirmed, RIVA triggers in under a second. No ML model, no confidence interval — deterministic math on a binary physical condition.
Dispatches — An AI agent reasons over the trigger event in context: time of day, tide direction, hospital occupancy, which roads are about to close, where NDRF battalions are positioned. It generates sequenced, agency-specific instructions for BMC, NDRF, Western Railway, and KEM Hospital simultaneously — in under 2 seconds. Every dispatch is timestamped. Every silence is logged.
Documents — When the event closes, RIVA synthesises the full accountability log into a formal governance report using generative AI. Named departments. Exact response times. Traced consequences. Recommended actions with owners and deadlines. For the first time, a department's silence during a flood has a timestamp and a consequence chain attached to it.
Who uses it:

Ward officers (BMC) — receive specific pump activation and road closure instructions with countdown timers and ACK buttons
NDRF battalion commanders — receive deployment orders with live route recommendations that avoid flooding roads in real time
Hospital administrators (KEM) — receive surge protocol activation with cascade risk timelines showing when road access will degrade
Railway operations (Western Railway) — receive station preparation orders before tracks submerge, with OVERDUE flags if unacknowledged
Municipal Commissioners and NDMA — receive post-event accountability reports naming every failure, every gap, every consequence

What it replaces: phone trees, WhatsApp group alerts, manual coordination across six agencies, post-event press conferences with no accountability, and twenty years of the same inquiry finding the same coordination failure.

**Challenges we ran into**

We Woke Up to a Project That Had Forked Itself
At 4am, a teammate ran an AI code generation prompt and went to sleep. By 9am, RIVA had two brains and neither knew the other existed.
Three new files had appeared in an AI_ML/ folder. The original implementation lived in AI/. Both had an agent.py. Both had a Groq client. Neither talked to the other. Somewhere in the night the backend had also been quietly rewritten to use Anthropic instead of Groq — with MOCK_MODE = true as the default. Every AI call in the system was returning hardcoded mock data and had been for hours. Six AI functions. Zero running. The demo looked perfect. The network tab was empty.
Fixing it felt like archaeology — reading every file, tracing every import, figuring out which system was real. Once we understood it, the fix was twenty minutes. Understanding it took two hours.
What it taught us: AI-assisted code generation is fast until two people run it on the same codebase simultaneously. You don't get merge conflicts. You get two systems that each believe they are the real one, neither complaining.

The Demo Was Lying
The two most dramatic moments in our demo — the AI reasoning panel and the accountability report generating live on screen — were hardcoded strings.
The report button triggered a real spinner and a fake paragraph. The AI narrative on the Audit Dashboard was identical every single time regardless of what the cascade engine had just computed. A judge watching the screen would never know. A judge opening the network tab would see zero API calls during the "AI moment" and understand everything immediately.
We found this not through testing but through a code audit driven by a gut feeling that something was too smooth.
The fix: wire both to real endpoints backed by actual Groq calls. The report is now live text. The narrative now changes because it is generated from the current graph state, not written by us three days ago.
The lesson: a demo that looks good is not the same as a demo that is real. The distance between the two is exactly the distance a technical judge travels in fifteen seconds.

The Map That Showed Nothing
The cascade animation — Mumbai's infrastructure failing geographically, node by node, each circle sized by population affected — is the visual centrepiece of the project. When we ran it with the real backend connected for the first time, two circles appeared. Then it stopped.
The dependency graph had six nodes. The demo that was supposed to show Western Railway cascading into Sion arterial into LBS Marg into KEM Hospital had, in production, Western Railway cascading into one road. Full stop.
Four hours of proper data work later — Overpass API queries for real Mumbai coordinates, BMC population data, cascade weights built from first principles — the graph had ten nodes, nine edges, and numbers we could defend in a Q&A.
The map now shows what it was always supposed to show. It took the demo breaking completely to make us build it properly.

**The problem it solves**

## coldstart.ai — What Problem It Solves

**coldstart.ai** is an AI internship agent built for engineering students who are skilled but invisible — the ones who mass-apply on LinkedIn and Internshala and hear nothing back.

---

### The Core Problem

India produces **1.5 million CS graduates** annually, yet 76% aren't considered industry-ready (NASSCOM), and fewer than 1 in 3 CS students land an internship before their final year. The brutal truth: internships don't go to the most skilled — they go to the **most networked**. Cold outreach and personal branding work, but nobody teaches them.

---

### What coldstart.ai Does About It

**1. Builds your professional identity for you**

Students plug in their skills, GitHub URL, and interests. The AI analyzes their repositories and generates a **"Digital Twin"** — your personality & tone, positioning, strengths, and areas to improve. It makes you look like someone a startup *wants* to talk to, even if you've never had an internship.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/e9000d3822384a108b2dffdcf9d88f31/8fbb0876-1fa1-4825-80ff-feb0a8d63c3d.png)

---

**2. Finds and scores the right startups**

Instead of browsing job boards, the system algorithmically matches startups to your Digital Twin across five dimensions: skill match, tech overlap, industry fit, location, and experience level — each startup gets a numerical score and priority rating.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/e9000d3822384a108b2dffdcf9d88f31/c13ccf97-c15b-439f-af78-6b7d64731f45.png)

---

**3. Writes personalized outreach — automatically**

For each matched startup, the system generates tailored cold emails and LinkedIn messages referencing the company's actual tech and mission. Everything lives in the **Outreach Hub**, where you can review, copy, and dispatch with one click.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/e9000d3822384a108b2dffdcf9d88f31/64339eb8-c419-47eb-80ff-92433d50ff45.png)

---

**4. Tracks everything in one place**

The **Outreach Status** dashboard gives you a real-time view of your autonomous networking agents — targets identified, drafts created, messages sent, replies received, and networking pipeline status. No spreadsheet juggling, no guessing.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/e9000d3822384a108b2dffdcf9d88f31/593082fc-3b35-44d4-b38c-ddb63ff2ad16.png)

---

**5. The agent runs while you sleep**

The live homepage terminal shows the agent in action — analyzing your GitHub, scoring thousands of startups, drafting emails, and logging active founder replies — all without you lifting a finger.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/e9000d3822384a108b2dffdcf9d88f31/8a1d39f9-6db8-4b01-a70d-ea278610f7b6.png)

---

### Who Benefits Most

- Engineering students at **non-IIT/NIT colleges** who lack placement cell access
- Students with solid GitHub profiles but **zero industry connections**
- Anyone tired of the "apply and pray" loop on job portals
- First and second year students trying to get ahead early

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges We Ran Into Building coldstart.ai

---

### 1. LinkedIn Comment Automation

LinkedIn aggressively blocks automated interactions. Getting the agent to post comments on founder/company posts without triggering rate limits or account flags was one of the messiest parts of the build. We had to carefully throttle request timing, rotate user-agent strings, and treat every interaction as if a human were doing it manually and adding randomized delays between actions to avoid pattern detection.

---

### 2. Setting Up SMTP Reliably

Getting cold emails to actually *land in inboxes* (not spam) required more than just wiring up an SMTP server. 

---

### 3. GitHub Analysis at Depth

Fetching repositories was straightforward via the GitHub API — but *meaningfully* analyzing them wasn't. Determining actual technical depth (not just which languages appear) required prompting the LLM carefully to distinguish between a student who wrote 50 lines of tutorial code in Python versus someone who built a production-grade backend. Getting that signal reliably and consistently took significant prompt iteration.


---

### 4. Scoring Startups Consistently

Early versions of the LLM-based startup scorer were inconsistent — the same startup would get wildly different scores across runs. We solved this by structuring the scoring prompt with strict output formatting, anchoring each of the five dimensions (skill match, tech overlap, industry fit, location, experience level) with explicit rubrics, and combining the LLM score with a deterministic weighted score to reduce variance.

---

**The problem it solves**

Imagine you find the perfect tutorial for a new skill, but when you look at your calendar, it's just a wall of random meetings and "gray space" with no room to breathe. Usually, your goals are in one app, your schedule is in another, and your browser is full of tabs you'll likely never click. This mess of scattered agendas is exactly what Duit fixes. By mapping your learning roadmap and job tracker directly onto your actual schedule, Duit ensures your different tools finally talk to each other. It’s built to cut through the noise so you can stop juggling apps and finally Do What Matters, Duit.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest hurdles we faced revolved around making the complex feature set work seamlessly with a live backend. Setting up a proper authentication flow while maintaining a smooth onboarding experience was a significant challenge; we had to ensure that user sessions remained secure while the app transitioned instantly from registration to a highly personalized dashboard. Handling real API calling also introduced complexity in how we process data. We had to build custom logic to map raw data from external sources, like your calendar events, into our specific 7-day layout in real-time, all while keeping the UI responsive and "spacious." On the implementation side, coordinating the AI's reasoning across these different data points was another major puzzle. Getting the "AI Layer" to understand live updates from your backend and translate them into actionable dashboard suggestions required a lot of refinement in our state management. We also had to solve low-level technical blocks, such as a major PostCSS/Tailwind configuration error that initially threatened the entire build. Overcoming these meant we didn't just build a static site; we built a fully integrated system where every click and auth step feels solid and premium.

**The problem it solves**

# FleetLabs

FleetLabs is an operations dashboard for warehouse, fleet, and last-mile workflows.

## What It Includes

- Inventory image scanning and catalog extraction
- Damage assessment and load analysis views
- Route risk and last-mile monitoring
- Truck flow analytics from video input
- Agent decision workflows with approval and override actions

## Tech Stack

- Frontend: Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Recharts
- Backend: FastAPI, SQLite
- AI and vision: OpenRouter-backed vision flows and local video analytics

## Structure

- `frontend/` Next.js application
- `backend/` FastAPI services and local database logic
- `hackx/` older prototype code
- `vision/` standalone vision utilities

## Local Setup

### Frontend

```bash
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev
```

### Backend

```bash
cd backend
python -m venv venv
venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn main:app --reload
```

## Environment

Do not commit local env files. Create them locally as needed:

### Frontend

```env
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000
```

### Backend

```env
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your_key_here
OPENROUTER_INVENTORY_MODEL=google/gemini-2.5-flash
OPENROUTER_CV_MODEL=google/gemini-2.5-flash
OPENROUTER_AGENT_MODEL=google/gemini-2.5-flash
```

### zex
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/zex-4c72) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/viraj-ap/zex-cli) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/ZTf_8my9M8o) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-KJSSE%20GajShield%20Hack%20X-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hack-x.devfolio.co)

> Context-Aware · Security-First · Token-Efficient

![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Most AI coding tools (Cursor, Copilot, Claude Code) are black boxes — you have no control over what gets sent to the model, they repeat massive system prompts on every internal loop step, and they write code without any awareness of your project's security posture.zex fixes three specific things:
Token waste - A naive agent running a 5-step task repeats its 900-token instruction manual 5 times. zex detects when the agent is mid-loop and strips the system prompt to ~200 tokens for those steps. 
Old tool results (giant file reads, directory listings) get compressed the moment you stop referencing them, replaced with a breadcrumb so the agent remembers it already fetched that file.
Vague intent - You type "fix auth." The agent guesses. zex runs a fast pre-call that parses your intent, identifies which files are likely involved, flags if the task touches security-sensitive areas, and shows you one line — [Understanding]: refactoring login handler to use bcrypt - before acting. 
Two-word correction if it's wrong.
Unsafe output -Before any file write touches your disk, every line of generated code is scanned for SQL injection, XSS, eval() usage, command injection, and weak cryptography. Critical findings block the write and force the agent to self-correct. On startup, zex audits your package.json and source tree so it knows your stack  Express, Postgres, JWT and applies the right rules for your project, not a generic checklist.

**Challenges we ran into**

The token loop problem was invisible until it wasn't
The hardest bug to diagnose was a slow token bleed during multi-step tasks. Sessions that should've used ~8k tokens were consistently hitting 25k+. Added logging to dump the exact payload sent on each API call — turned out the full system prompt (tool docs, security rules, all of it) was being re-sent on every single tool_loopback turn. The fix was building the turn classifier in pruner.ts, but getting the classifier logic right took several iterations it kept misidentifying continuation turns as loopbacks and stripping context the agent actually needed.
The GC's "smart" compression kept breaking the agent
The first version of the relevance-aware GC compressed anything older than 2 turns over 600 chars. The agent started failing tasks midway it would try to patch a file it had "forgotten" it already read, re-fetch it, and loop. The fix was building the recent Mentions scanner that checks the last 3 messages for any filename or keyword before compressing, and changing the stub format from a blank tombstone to a breadcrumb: [Compressed: read_file(login.ts) 200 lines, captured at turn 2. Re-read if needed.] that single change stopped the loops entirely.
TOON encoding broke on non-uniform tool outputs
Plugging in @toon-format/toon was straightforward until list_directory started returning mixed results some entries had a size field, some didn't (directories vs files). TOON's tabular format requires uniform objects, so it was silently producing malformed output that confused the model. Fixed it with an isUniform() guard that checks all objects in the array share identical keys before encoding falls back to plain JSON otherwise.

Team **Nginx** -- [Viraj Pawar](https://github.com/viraj-ap), [Kanishka Sahal](https://github.com/kanishkasahal24), [Sahil shah](https://github.com/GodWar9), [Pratik Patil](https://github.com/10Pratik01)
